abstract: We describe a class of connectionist networks that have learned to play back(cid:173) gammon at an intermediate-to-advanced level. TIle networks were trained by a supervised learning procedure on a large set of sample positions evaluated by a human expert. In actual match play against humans and conventional computer programs, the networks demonstrate substantial ability to generalize on the basis of expert knowledge. Our study touches on some of the most important issues in net(cid:173) work learning theory, including the development of efficient coding schemes and training procedures, scaling, generalization, the use of real-valued inputs and out(cid:173) puts, and techniques for escaping from local minima. Practical applications in games and other domains are also discussed.

paragraphs: This paper describes neural networks that learn backgammon from positions evaluated by a human expert. Training is supervised: the expert’s judgments provide the examples the networks learn to reproduce. The task therefore tests whether a network can absorb useful knowledge about a game from a collection of evaluated situations.

The networks reach an intermediate-to-advanced level of play. Matches against humans and conventional computer programs provide evidence that the learned knowledge transfers to actual play. The authors interpret this as substantial generalization from expert examples: the training supports useful decisions in the broader setting of a match.

The study also uses backgammon to examine practical learning questions. These include how to encode positions efficiently, organize training, handle real-valued inputs and outputs, scale the approach, and escape local minima during learning. Together, these issues connect representation and optimization to playing ability. The stated result shows that supervised expert knowledge can support meaningful game performance, with potential applications discussed for games and other domains.
summary.tldr: Networks trained on expert-evaluated positions generalize well enough to play backgammon at an intermediate-to-advanced level.

title: A 'Neural' Network that Learns to Play Backgammon

abstract: The invariance of an objects' identity as it transformed over time provides a powerful cue for perceptual learning. We present an un(cid:173) supervised learning procedure which maximizes the mutual infor(cid:173) mation between the representations adopted by a feed-forward net(cid:173) work at consecutive time steps. We demonstrate that the network can learn, entirely unsupervised, to classify an ensemble of several patterns by observing pattern trajectories, even though there are abrupt transitions from one object to another between trajecto(cid:173) ries. The same learning procedure should be widely applicable to a variety of perceptual learning tasks.

We demonstrate that the network can learn, entirely unsupervised, to classify an ensemble of several patterns by observing pattern trajectories, even though there are abrupt transitions from one object to another between trajecto(cid:173) ries. paragraphs: An object's appearance can change over time while its identity remains the same. This paper uses that persistence as a learning signal for categorization. Rather than supplying category labels, it lets a feed-forward network observe trajectories of changing patterns and learn from the relationship between neighboring observations.

The learning procedure maximizes mutual information between the network's representations at consecutive time steps. Mutual information measures how informative one representation is about the next. The objective therefore encourages the network to discover structure that carries across successive appearances, using temporal relationships to help organize its representation of the observed patterns.

The authors demonstrate entirely unsupervised classification of an ensemble of several patterns. The observed sequences include abrupt changes from one object to another between trajectories, so the demonstration does not require every neighboring observation to belong to the same object. The result supports temporal coherence as a useful cue for learning categories. The authors also suggest that the procedure could apply to other perceptual learning tasks.
summary.tldr: A network learns categories without labels by maximizing information shared between representations of consecutive observations.

title: Learning to categorize objects using temporal coherence

abstract: We introduce a new algorithm designed to learn sparse percep(cid:173) trons over input representations which include high-order features. Our algorithm, which is based on a hypothesis-boosting method, is able to PAC-learn a relatively natural class of target concepts. Moreover, the algorithm appears to work well in practice: on a set of three problem domains, the algorithm produces classifiers that utilize small numbers of features yet exhibit good generalization performance. Perhaps most importantly, our algorithm generates concept descriptions that are easy for humans to understand. 1

paragraphs: The paper introduces an algorithm for learning sparse perceptrons from representations containing high-order features. Such features allow a classifier to use combinations of input properties. Sparsity means that the final classifier relies on relatively few features, so a rich input representation need not lead to an equally complicated learned description.

The algorithm is based on hypothesis boosting. The authors establish that it can learn a particular class of target concepts in the probably approximately correct, or PAC, framework. This provides a formal learning guarantee for that class. The theoretical contribution concerns obtaining reliable learning while retaining a sparse perceptron representation.

Across three problem domains, the algorithm produces classifiers that use small numbers of features and generalize well. The authors also emphasize that the resulting concept descriptions are easy for people to understand. Together, these findings connect feature economy with prediction and interpretability: the selected features form both a working classifier and a compact description of what it has learned.
summary.tldr: A boosting-based algorithm learns sparse perceptrons with theoretical guarantees and compact, understandable classifiers in three tested domains.

title: Learning Sparse Perceptrons

abstract: We examine a psychophysical law that describes the influence of stimulus and context on perception. According to this law choice probability ratios factorize into components independently con(cid:173) trolled by stimulus and context. It has been argued that this pat(cid:173) tern of results is incompatible with feedback models of perception. In this paper we examine this claim using neural network models defined via stochastic differential equations. We show that the law is related to a condition named channel separability and has little to do with the existence of feedback connections. In essence, chan(cid:173) nels are separable if they converge into the response units without direct lateral connections to other channels and if their sensors are not directly contaminated by external inputs to the other chan(cid:173) nels. Implications of the analysis for cognitive and computational neurosicence are discussed.

paragraphs: This paper examines a perceptual law in which ratios of choice probabilities separate into two components: one controlled by the stimulus and another controlled by context. Such a pattern has been interpreted as evidence against feedback models of perception. The authors investigate whether that conclusion follows from the observed separation of influences.

They analyze neural-network models described by stochastic differential equations and relate the law to a condition called channel separability. In this condition, processing channels converge on response units without direct lateral connections between channels. Their sensors also avoid direct contamination from external inputs supplied to the other channels.

The analysis finds that the factorization law has little to do with whether feedback connections exist. Instead, the relevant issue is how information channels interact and receive inputs. This changes what the behavioral pattern can establish about an underlying model: a separation of stimulus and context effects points toward channel organization, rather than serving as a general argument against feedback in perception.
summary.tldr: Factorized stimulus and context effects are tied to channel separability and do not generally rule out feedback models of perception.

title: Information Factorization in Connectionist Models of Perception

abstract: Bayesian networks are graphical representations of probability distributions. In virtually all of the work on learning these networks, the assumption is that we are presented with a data set consisting of randomly generated instances from the underlying distribution. In many situations, however, we also have the option of active learning, where we have the possibility of guiding the sampling process by querying for certain types of samples. This paper addresses the problem of estimating the parameters of Bayesian networks in an active learning setting. We provide a theoretical framework for this problem, and an algorithm that chooses which active learning queries to generate based on the model learned so far. We present experimental results showing that our active learning algorithm can significantly reduce the need for training data in many situations.

This paper addresses the problem of estimating the parameters of Bayesian networks in an active learning setting. We provide a theoretical framework for this problem, and an algorithm that chooses which active learning queries to generate based on the model learned so far. We present experimental results showing that our active learning algorithm can significantly reduce the need for training data in many situations.

paragraphs: Learning a Bayesian network’s probabilities usually assumes a passively collected random sample. In some applications, however, the learner can request particular kinds of observations. This paper studies how to use that control to estimate network parameters with fewer examples.

The authors develop a theoretical framework for active parameter learning and an algorithm that chooses queries according to the model learned so far. Sampling decisions therefore change as uncertainty and estimated structure evolve. The approach makes data acquisition part of the estimation procedure rather than a separate fixed input.

Experiments show that active selection can substantially reduce training-data needs in many settings. The contribution demonstrates the value of targeting observations that improve the current probabilistic model. It concerns choosing informative samples for parameter estimation, so its benefit depends on having access to the query mechanism assumed by the active-learning setting.
summary.tldr: An active-learning strategy selects observations using the current Bayesian network to reduce parameter-estimation data requirements.

title: Active Learning for Parameter Estimation in Bayesian Networks

abstract: We study properties of popular near–uniform (Dirichlet) priors for learning undersampled probability distributions on discrete nonmetric spaces and show that they lead to disastrous results. However, an Occam–style phase space argument expands the priors into their infinite mixture and resolves most of the observed problems. This leads to a surprisingly good estimator of entropies of discrete distributions.
originalAbstract: We study properties of popular near–uniform (Dirichlet) priors for learning undersampled probability distributions on discrete nonmetric spaces and show that they lead to disastrous results. However, an Occam–style phase space argument expands the priors into their infinite mixture and resolves most of the observed problems. This leads to a surprisingly good estimator of entropies of discrete distributions.

paragraphs: Estimating a discrete probability distribution becomes difficult when the observations undersample its possible outcomes. This paper examines popular near-uniform Dirichlet priors in that setting, specifically for discrete spaces without a metric. The issue is how assumptions about probabilities affect inference when the observations leave much of the distribution unresolved.

The authors show that these priors can produce disastrous results in the setting they study. They then use an Occam-style argument about phase space to expand the priors into an infinite mixture. The proposed remedy changes the prior construction itself, addressing problems associated with relying on the original near-uniform family in undersampled inference.

This mixture resolves most of the observed problems and produces an entropy estimator that the authors report as surprisingly good. Entropy is a summary of a distribution's uncertainty, so the contribution concerns both distribution learning and estimation of that summary. The stated result is a substantial improvement in the examined setting, with 'most' remaining an important qualification on how completely the prior-related problems are resolved.
summary.tldr: An infinite mixture of priors addresses most observed failures of near-uniform Dirichlet priors and yields a strong entropy estimator.

title: Entropy and Inference, Revisited

abstract: We consider loopy belief propagation for approximate inference in prob- abilistic graphical models. A limitation of the standard algorithm is that clique marginals are computed as if there were no loops in the graph. To overcome this limitation, we introduce fractional belief propagation. Fractional belief propagation is formulated in terms of a family of ap- proximate free energies, which includes the Bethe free energy and the naive mean-ﬁeld free as special cases. Using the linear response correc- tion of the clique marginals, the scale parameters can be tuned. Simula- tion results illustrate the potential merits of the approach.
originalAbstract: We consider loopy belief propagation for approximate inference in prob- abilistic graphical models. A limitation of the standard algorithm is that clique marginals are computed as if there were no loops in the graph. To overcome this limitation, we introduce fractional belief propagation. Fractional belief propagation is formulated in terms of a family of ap- proximate free energies, which includes the Bethe free energy and the naive mean-ﬁeld free as special cases. Using the linear response correc- tion of the clique marginals, the scale parameters can be tuned. Simula- tion results illustrate the potential merits of the approach.

paragraphs: The paper addresses approximate inference in probabilistic graphical models containing loops. Standard loopy belief propagation computes clique marginals, the probabilities for groups of related variables, using a treatment that acts as though the graph had no loops. The authors identify this as a limitation and introduce fractional belief propagation to address it.

The method is expressed through a family of approximate free energies, mathematical objectives used to formulate the inference problem. This family contains both the Bethe and naive mean-field free energies as special cases. Fractional belief propagation therefore places these existing approximations within a broader parameterized framework.

The scale parameters can be tuned using a linear-response correction to the clique marginals. This supplies a way to adjust the approximation rather than committing to one fixed member of the family. Simulations illustrate possible benefits of the approach. Their role is to show promise for the adjustable formulation; the abstract does not claim that it universally resolves inference errors caused by loops.
summary.tldr: Fractional belief propagation introduces tunable free-energy approximations that include Bethe and naive mean-field inference as special cases.

title: Fractional Belief Propagation

abstract: We interpret non-negative matrix factorization geometrically, as the problem of ﬁnding a simplicial cone which contains a cloud of data points and which is contained in the positive orthant. We show that under certain conditions, basically requiring that some of the data are spread across the faces of the positive orthant, there is a unique such simpli- cial cone. We give examples of synthetic image articulation databases which obey these conditions; these require separated support and facto- rial sampling. For such databases there is a generative model in terms of ‘parts’ and NMF correctly identiﬁes the ‘parts’. We show that our theoretical results are predictive of the performance of published NMF code, by running the published algorithms on one of our synthetic image articulation databases.

paragraphs: The paper asks when non-negative matrix factorization can recover the actual parts that generated data. It gives the problem a geometric interpretation: find a simplicial cone that encloses the observed points while remaining inside the region where every coordinate is non-negative.

The authors show that this cone is unique under certain conditions, broadly requiring data to spread across faces of that non-negative region. They construct synthetic image-articulation databases satisfying the conditions through separated support and factorial sampling. For these databases, a generative description in terms of parts exists, and NMF correctly identifies those parts.

The conditions matter because the recovery claim is tied to how the data occupy the space and how the examples are generated. The authors test published NMF algorithms on one of their synthetic databases and find that their theoretical results predict the algorithms' performance. The contribution connects geometric uniqueness, a specific parts-based generative setting, and observed behavior of existing implementations.
summary.tldr: Geometric conditions establish when NMF uniquely recovers generating parts, with supporting results on synthetic image data.

title: When Does Non-Negative Matrix Factorization Give a Correct Decomposition into Parts?

abstract: We present an extension to the Jojic and Frey (2001) layered sprite model which allows for layers to undergo affine transformations. This extension allows for affine object pose to be inferred whilst simultaneously learn- ing the object shape and appearance. Learning is carried out by applying an augmented variational inference algorithm which includes a global search over a discretised transform space followed by a local optimisa- tion. To aid correct convergence, we use bottom-up cues to restrict the space of possible affine transformations. We present results on a number of video sequences and show how the model can be extended to track an object whose appearance changes throughout the sequence.

This extension allows for affine object pose to be inferred whilst simultaneously learn- ing the object shape and appearance. To aid correct convergence, we use bottom-up cues to restrict the space of possible affine transformations. paragraphs: This paper extends a layered sprite model so that its layers can undergo affine transformations. The extension allows the system to infer an object's affine pose while learning its shape and appearance at the same time. The object representation and its placement in the image are therefore estimated together.

Learning uses an augmented variational inference procedure with two stages of search. It first searches globally over a discretized space of transformations, then refines the result through local optimization. Bottom-up image cues restrict the transformations considered, helping the procedure converge correctly. These cues guide the search within a model that jointly explains object appearance and pose.

The authors present results on several video sequences and describe an extension for tracking an object whose appearance changes over time. That extension matters because the representation being tracked need not remain visually fixed throughout a sequence. The contribution is a generative framework that brings affine localization, appearance learning, and tracking into a shared inference process.
summary.tldr: An extended layered sprite model jointly learns object appearance and shape while estimating affine pose and supporting video tracking.

title: Generative Affine Localisation and Tracking

abstract: A generative probabilistic model for objects in images is presented. An object consists of a constellation of features. Feature appearance and pose are modeled probabilistically. Scene images are generated by drawing a set of objects from a given database, with random clutter sprinkled on the remaining image surface. Occlusion is allowed. We study the case where features from the same object share a common reference frame. Moreover, parameters for shape and appearance densities are shared across features. This is to be contrasted with previous work on probabilistic ‘constellation’ models where features depend on each other, and each feature and model have different pose and appearance statistics [1, 2]. These two differences allow us to build models containing hundreds of features, as well as to train each model from a single example. Our model may also be thought of as a probabilistic revisitation of Lowe’s model [3, 4]. We propose an efficient entropy-minimization inference algorithm that constructs the best interpretation of a scene as a collection of objects and clutter. We test our ideas with experiments on two image databases. We compare with Lowe’s algorithm and demonstrate better performance, in particular in presence of large amounts of background clutter.

paragraphs: This paper describes objects as collections of features whose appearances and poses are modeled probabilistically. A scene can contain several objects drawn from a database, together with background clutter, and objects may be partly occluded. Recognition therefore involves finding a plausible explanation of the entire scene in terms of objects and clutter.

The model gives features belonging to an object a shared reference frame and shares parameters for shape and appearance distributions across features. These choices reduce the need for separate statistics for every feature and model. According to the authors, they make it possible to use hundreds of features while training each object model from a single example.

An efficient inference algorithm minimizes entropy to construct the best scene interpretation under the approach. Experiments on two image databases compare the method with Lowe's algorithm and report better performance, especially with substantial background clutter. The findings support the usefulness of the shared representation for combining detailed object descriptions with probabilistic treatment of confusing scene content.
summary.tldr: A shared-frame probabilistic object model supports hundreds of features, single-example training, and improved recognition in the reported cluttered-image comparisons.

title: Common-Frame Model for Object Recognition

abstract: We present Epoch-Greedy, an algorithm for multi-armed bandits with observable side information. Epoch-Greedy has the following properties: No knowledge of a time horizon $T$ is necessary. The regret incurred by Epoch-Greedy is controlled by a sample complexity bound for a hypothesis class. The regret scales as $O(T^{2/3} S^{1/3})$ or better (sometimes, much better). Here $S$ is the complexity term in a sample complexity bound for standard supervised learning.
originalAbstract: We present Epoch-Greedy, an algorithm for multi-armed bandits with observable side information. Epoch-Greedy has the following properties: No knowledge of a time horizon $T$ is necessary. The regret incurred by Epoch-Greedy is controlled by a sample complexity bound for a hypothesis class. The regret scales as $O(T^{2/3} S^{1/3})$ or better (sometimes, much better). Here $S$ is the complexity term in a sample complexity bound for standard supervised learning.

paragraphs: A multi-armed bandit learner repeatedly chooses actions while learning from their rewards. Observable side information adds context that can help guide those choices. This paper introduces Epoch-Greedy for that setting and relates its performance to the difficulty of supervised learning over a chosen hypothesis class.

The algorithm does not require advance knowledge of the time horizon T, meaning the number of rounds need not be specified beforehand. Its regret is controlled by a sample-complexity bound for the hypothesis class. Regret measures accumulated loss relative to a comparison strategy, while sample complexity describes how much data supervised learning needs.

The stated regret scaling is O(T^(2/3) S^(1/3)) or better, where S is the complexity term in a standard supervised-learning sample-complexity bound. Some cases can be much better. The result connects sequential decision-making performance to a familiar learning-theoretic quantity: the complexity of learning within the selected class. It also provides a guarantee for an algorithm that can operate without a preselected stopping horizon.
summary.tldr: Epoch-Greedy needs no known time horizon and links contextual-bandit regret to supervised-learning sample complexity.

title: The Epoch-Greedy Algorithm for Multi-armed Bandits with Side Information

abstract: Clustering stability is an increasingly popular family of methods for performing model selection in data clustering. The basic idea is that the chosen model should be stable under perturbation or resampling of the data. Despite being reasonably effective in practice, these methods are not well understood theoretically, and present some difficulties. In particular, when the data is assumed to be sampled from an underlying distribution, the solutions returned by the clustering algorithm will usually become more and more stable as the sample size increases. This raises a potentially serious practical difficulty with these methods, because it means there might be some hard-to-compute sample size, beyond which clustering stability estimators 'break down' and become unreliable in detecting the most stable model. Namely, all models will be relatively stable, with differences in their stability measures depending mostly on random and meaningless sampling artifacts. In this paper, we provide a set of general sufficient conditions, which ensure the reliability of clustering stability estimators in the large sample regime. In contrast to previous work, which concentrated on specific toy distributions or specific idealized clustering frameworks, here we make no such assumptions. We then exemplify how these conditions apply to several important families of clustering algorithms, such as maximum likelihood clustering, certain types of kernel clustering, and centroid-based clustering with any Bregman divergence. In addition, we explicitly derive the non-trivial asymptotic behavior of these estimators, for any framework satisfying our conditions. This can help us understand what is considered a 'stable' model by these estimators, at least for large enough samples.

paragraphs: Clustering stability selects models by asking whether their groupings persist when data are perturbed or resampled. A potential problem appears as datasets grow: many clustering solutions become increasingly stable. If all candidate models look stable, their remaining differences might reflect sampling artifacts rather than meaningful distinctions.

This paper provides general sufficient conditions under which stability estimators remain reliable in the large-sample regime. These conditions give a way to establish reliability without restricting the analysis to particular toy distributions or specific idealized clustering setups. Their sufficiency matters: satisfying them ensures the stated result, while the abstract does not claim that every reliable estimator must satisfy them.

The authors demonstrate applicability to maximum-likelihood clustering, certain kernel-clustering methods, and centroid-based clustering using any Bregman divergence. They also derive nontrivial asymptotic behavior for frameworks meeting their conditions. This helps explain how stability comparisons behave even when overall stability increases, and clarifies what these estimators favor as a stable model once the sample is sufficiently large.
summary.tldr: General sufficient conditions establish when clustering-stability comparisons remain reliable as sample sizes grow.

title: On the Reliability of Clustering Stability in the Large Sample Regime

abstract: We consider the question of computing Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) assignment in an arbitrary pair-wise Markov Random Field (MRF). We present a randomized iterative algorithm based on simple local updates. The algorithm, starting with an arbitrary initial assignment, updates it in each iteration by first, picking a random node, then selecting an (appropriately chosen) random local neighborhood and optimizing over this local neighborhood. Somewhat surprisingly, we show that this algorithm finds a near optimal assignment within $2n\ln n$ iterations on average and with high probability for {\em any} $n$ node pair-wise MRF with {\em geometry} (i.e. MRF graph with polynomial growth) with the approximation error depending on (in a reasonable manner) the geometric growth rate of the graph and the average radius of the local neighborhood -- this allows for a graceful tradeoff between the complexity of the algorithm and the approximation error. Through extensive simulations, we show that our algorithm finds extremely good approximate solutions for various kinds of MRFs with geometry.

Somewhat surprisingly, we show that this algorithm finds a near optimal assignment within $2n\ln n$ iterations on average and with high probability for {\em any} $n$ node pair-wise MRF with {\em geometry} (i.e. MRF graph with polynomial growth) with the approximation error depending on (in a reasonable manner) the geometric growth rate of the graph and the average radius of the local neighborhood -- this allows for a graceful tradeoff between the complexity of the algorithm and the approximation error. paragraphs: The paper asks when local updates can efficiently find a nearly optimal maximum a posteriori assignment in a pairwise Markov random field. The proposed randomized algorithm starts from any assignment. Each iteration chooses a random node, selects an appropriately randomized neighborhood around it, and optimizes the assignment within that neighborhood.

The main guarantee applies to graphs with polynomial growth, described as having geometry. For any such n-node pairwise model, the algorithm finds a near-optimal assignment within 2n ln n iterations on average and with high probability. The approximation error depends on the graph’s geometric growth rate and the average radius of the selected neighborhoods.

This dependence creates a trade-off between local computational effort and approximation quality. Neighborhood size affects both the work required by an update and the resulting error guarantee, so the iteration count does not by itself describe all computation. Extensive simulations find very good approximate solutions across several kinds of models with the required geometry.
summary.tldr: Randomized neighborhood optimization has near-optimal MAP guarantees for pairwise graphical models whose graphs have polynomial growth.

title: Local Rules for Global MAP: When Do They Work ?

abstract: A Bayesian approach to partitioning distance matrices is presented. It is inspired by the 'Translation-Invariant Wishart-Dirichlet' process (TIWD) in (Vogt et al., 2010) and shares a number of advantageous properties like the fully probabilistic nature of the inference model, automatic selection of the number of clusters and applicability in semi-supervised settings. In addition, our method (which we call 'fastTIWD') overcomes the main shortcoming of the original TIWD, namely its high computational costs. The fastTIWD reduces the workload in each iteration of a Gibbs sampler from O(n^3) in the TIWD to O(n^2). Our experiments show that this cost reduction does not compromise the quality of the inferred partitions. With this new method it is now possible to 'mine' large relational datasets with a probabilistic model, thereby automatically detecting new and potentially interesting clusters.

Our experiments show that this cost reduction does not compromise the quality of the inferred partitions. With this new method it is now possible to 'mine' large relational datasets with a probabilistic model, thereby automatically detecting new and potentially interesting clusters.

paragraphs: Some datasets describe relationships through distances between pairs of items. Partitioning such data means using those distances to infer groups. This paper introduces fastTIWD, a Bayesian method inspired by the Translation-Invariant Wishart-Dirichlet process. It retains a probabilistic treatment of clustering, automatic selection of the number of groups, and support for settings with some supervision.

The main change targets computation. In the original method, each Gibbs-sampling iteration requires work proportional to the cube of the number of items. The proposed method reduces this to quadratic work per iteration. This matters because a large collection can make repeated cubic-cost updates particularly expensive, even when the underlying statistical model is attractive.

The experiments show that the reduction in computational cost does not compromise partition quality in the evaluated cases. That is an empirical finding about the resulting groups, alongside the stated reduction in iteration cost. The method makes probabilistic exploration of larger relational datasets more practical while retaining the ability to discover a number of clusters determined through inference.
summary.tldr: fastTIWD reduces Bayesian distance-based clustering from cubic to quadratic work per sampling iteration without sacrificing partition quality in experiments.

title: Bayesian Partitioning of Large-Scale Distance Data

abstract: We prove a new oracle inequality for support vector machines with Gaussian RBF kernels solving the regularized least squares regression problem. To this end, we apply the modulus of smoothness. With the help of the new oracle inequality we then derive learning rates that can also be achieved by a simple data-dependent parameter selection method. Finally, it turns out that our learning rates are asymptotically optimal for regression functions satisfying certain standard smoothness conditions.

To this end, we apply the modulus of smoothness. With the help of the new oracle inequality we then derive learning rates that can also be achieved by a simple data-dependent parameter selection method. Finally, it turns out that our learning rates are asymptotically optimal for regression functions satisfying certain standard smoothness conditions.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes support vector machines used for regularized least-squares regression with Gaussian radial-basis-function kernels. The central question is how quickly prediction quality improves as more data becomes available. The authors establish a new oracle inequality, giving a theoretical tool for assessing the performance of this regression procedure.

The proof uses the modulus of smoothness, which expresses the smoothness properties relevant to the analysis. From the oracle inequality, the authors derive learning rates. They also show that a simple parameter-selection method based on the data can achieve those rates. This connects the theoretical performance result to a way of choosing the method’s parameters from observed data.

The resulting rates are asymptotically optimal for regression functions satisfying certain standard smoothness conditions. Both parts of that qualification matter: optimality describes the large-sample behavior and applies to the specified smoothness setting. The contribution is a linked set of guarantees, moving from an oracle inequality to achievable rates and then to conditional asymptotic optimality.
summary.tldr: Gaussian-kernel least-squares SVMs achieve asymptotically optimal rates under stated smoothness conditions, including with simple data-dependent parameter selection.

title: Optimal learning rates for least squares SVMs using Gaussian kernels

abstract: State-of-the-art statistical methods in neuroscience have enabled us to fit mathematical models to experimental data and subsequently to infer the dynamics of hidden parameters underlying the observable phenomena. Here, we develop a Bayesian method for inferring the time-varying mean and variance of the synaptic input, along with the dynamics of each ion channel from a single voltage trace of a neuron. An estimation problem may be formulated on the basis of the state-space model with prior distributions that penalize large fluctuations in these parameters. After optimizing the hyperparameters by maximizing the marginal likelihood, the state-space model provides the time-varying parameters of the input signals and the ion channel states. The proposed method is tested not only on the simulated data from the Hodgkin-Huxley type models but also on experimental data obtained from a cortical slice in vitro.

paragraphs: A neuron’s voltage trace is observable, but the input signals and ion channel states underlying it are partly hidden. This paper develops a Bayesian method for estimating those changing quantities from a single trace. The targets include both the mean and variance of synaptic input and the dynamics of each ion channel.

The method formulates the task as inference in a state-space model, linking observed voltage to hidden quantities that evolve over time. Prior distributions penalize large fluctuations in the parameters. This assumption favors smoother changes while allowing the estimates to vary, providing structure for interpreting a single measured signal.

The authors choose hyperparameters by maximizing marginal likelihood, then use the fitted model to estimate input parameters and channel states over time. They test the method on simulated data from Hodgkin–Huxley type models and on experimental recordings from a cortical slice in vitro. The work thus brings several hidden aspects of neuronal dynamics into one inference procedure and examines it with both simulated and experimental voltage data.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian state-space method estimates changing synaptic input statistics and ion channel states from a single neuronal voltage trace.

title: Estimating time-varying input signals and ion channel states from a single voltage trace of a neuron

abstract: Stochastic gradient descent is popular for large scale optimization but has slow convergence asymptotically due to the inherent variance. To remedy this problem, we introduce an explicit variance reduction method for stochastic gradient descent which we call stochastic variance reduced gradient (SVRG). For smooth and strongly convex functions, we prove that this method enjoys the same fast convergence rate as those of stochastic dual coordinate ascent (SDCA) and Stochastic Average Gradient (SAG). However, our analysis is significantly simpler and more intuitive. Moreover, unlike SDCA or SAG, our method does not require the storage of gradients, and thus is more easily applicable to complex problems such as some structured prediction problems and neural network learning.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent is useful for large optimization problems, but randomness in its gradient estimates can slow its progress as training continues. This paper introduces stochastic variance reduced gradient, or SVRG, to address that obstacle directly. Its central idea is to reduce the variability in stochastic updates so that randomness interferes less with convergence.

For objectives that are smooth and strongly convex, the authors prove that SVRG achieves the same fast convergence rate as stochastic dual coordinate ascent and Stochastic Average Gradient. These conditions define the scope of the stated guarantee. The paper also presents its analysis as simpler and more intuitive, making the reason for the acceleration easier to understand.

A practical distinction is that SVRG does not require storing gradients as the compared methods do. That reduces a storage burden that can complicate more elaborate learning problems. The authors identify some structured prediction problems and neural network learning as settings where this makes the method easier to apply. The broader contribution is a variance-reduction approach combining a conditional convergence guarantee with practical flexibility.
summary.tldr: SVRG reduces stochastic-gradient variance, achieving fast convergence for smooth, strongly convex objectives without requiring stored gradients.

title: Accelerating Stochastic Gradient Descent using Predictive Variance Reduction

abstract: We propose a technique for decomposing the parameter learning problem in Bayesian networks into independent learning problems. Our technique applies to incomplete datasets and exploits variables that are either hidden or observed in the given dataset. We show empirically that the proposed technique can lead to orders-of-magnitude savings in learning time. We explain, analytically and empirically, the reasons behind our reported savings, and compare the proposed technique to related ones that are sometimes used by inference algorithms.
originalAbstract: We propose a technique for decomposing the parameter learning problem in Bayesian networks into independent learning problems. Our technique applies to incomplete datasets and exploits variables that are either hidden or observed in the given dataset. We show empirically that the proposed technique can lead to orders-of-magnitude savings in learning time. We explain, analytically and empirically, the reasons behind our reported savings, and compare the proposed technique to related ones that are sometimes used by inference algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper addresses parameter learning in Bayesian networks by breaking one estimation problem into independent learning problems. The target is the learning calculation itself: how to estimate the network’s parameters from data. Independence between the resulting problems matters because it allows the relevant pieces to be learned separately instead of keeping the entire estimation task coupled.

The technique applies to incomplete datasets and can exploit variables that are hidden as well as variables that are observed. This makes the contribution relevant to learning settings where the dataset does not reveal every variable. The decomposition therefore does not depend simply on having complete observations throughout the network.

Empirical results show that the technique can reduce learning time by orders of magnitude. The authors examine the reasons for these savings through both analysis and experiments, and compare their approach with related decompositions sometimes used for inference. The reported benefit is a potentially substantial reduction in estimation effort. Its strength is qualified: the abstract says such savings can occur, rather than guaranteeing the same improvement for every Bayesian network or dataset.
summary.tldr: Decomposing Bayesian-network parameter learning into independent problems can yield orders-of-magnitude time savings, including with incomplete data.

title: Decomposing Parameter Estimation Problems

abstract: The process of dynamic state estimation (filtering) based on point process observations is in general intractable. Numerical sampling techniques are often practically useful, but lead to limited conceptual insight about optimal encoding/decoding strategies, which are of significant relevance to Computational Neuroscience. We develop an analytically tractable Bayesian approximation to optimal filtering based on point process observations, which allows us to introduce distributional assumptions about sensory cell properties, that greatly facilitates the analysis of optimal encoding in situations deviating from common assumptions of uniform coding. The analytic framework leads to insights which are difficult to obtain from numerical algorithms, and is consistent with experiments about the distribution of tuning curve centers. Interestingly, we find that the information gained from the absence of spikes may be crucial to performance.

The analytic framework leads to insights which are difficult to obtain from numerical algorithms, and is consistent with experiments about the distribution of tuning curve centers. paragraphs: Estimating a changing hidden state from discrete events, such as neural spikes, is generally computationally intractable when done optimally. Numerical sampling can produce useful estimates, but it can be harder to see from those computations why a particular encoding or decoding strategy works. This paper develops a Bayesian approximation designed to make that reasoning analytically manageable.

The framework allows the researchers to describe sensory cell properties through distributions. This makes it easier to investigate neural populations that depart from uniform coding assumptions. Instead of treating numerical performance as the only outcome, the approach supports analysis of how the distribution of cell properties relates to the information available for estimating a state.

The resulting analysis produces insights that are difficult to obtain from numerical algorithms and is consistent with experiments concerning the locations of tuning curve centers. One finding is that silence can matter: the absence of spikes may provide information crucial to performance. This is a qualified finding about the value of non-events, supported by an approximate filtering framework.
summary.tldr: An analytically tractable Bayesian filtering approximation helps explain neural encoding and shows that the absence of spikes may be crucial information.

title: A Tractable Approximation to Optimal Point Process Filtering: Application to Neural Encoding

abstract: We consider the problem of estimating the latent state of a spatiotemporally evolving continuous function using very few sensor measurements. We show that layering a dynamical systems prior over temporal evolution of weights of a kernel model is a valid approach to spatiotemporal modeling that does not necessarily require the design of complex nonstationary kernels. Furthermore, we show that such a predictive model can be utilized to determine sensing locations that guarantee that the hidden state of the phenomena can be recovered with very few measurements. We provide sufficient conditions on the number and spatial location of samples required to guarantee state recovery, and provide a lower bound on the minimum number of samples required to robustly infer the hidden states. Our approach outperforms existing methods in numerical experiments.

We show that layering a dynamical systems prior over temporal evolution of weights of a kernel model is a valid approach to spatiotemporal modeling that does not necessarily require the design of complex nonstationary kernels. Furthermore, we show that such a predictive model can be utilized to determine sensing locations that guarantee that the hidden state of the phenomena can be recovered with very few measurements. Our approach outperforms existing methods in numerical experiments.

paragraphs: This paper considers a continuous phenomenon that changes across space and time, while only a few sensor measurements are available. The goal is to infer its hidden state. The authors combine a kernel representation of the spatial function with a dynamical systems prior governing how the model's weights evolve over time.

This construction provides a valid approach to spatiotemporal modeling without necessarily requiring the design of complicated nonstationary kernels. Temporal structure enters through the evolving weights. The predictive model also informs where measurements should be taken, connecting the representation of the phenomenon with the design of the sensing process.

The authors give sufficient conditions on both the number and spatial placement of samples that guarantee recovery of the hidden state. They also establish a lower bound on the measurements needed for robust inference. These results distinguish arrangements that suffice for recovery from a fundamental requirement on sample count. Numerical experiments show the approach outperforming existing methods, supporting the combined use of dynamical modeling and carefully chosen sensing locations.
summary.tldr: Kernel observers combine evolving model weights with sensor placement theory to recover spatiotemporal hidden states from few measurements.

title: Kernel Observers: Systems-Theoretic Modeling and Inference of Spatiotemporally Evolving Processes

abstract: The combinatorial stochastic semi-bandit problem is an extension of the classical multi-armed bandit problem in which an algorithm pulls more than one arm at each stage and the rewards of all pulled arms are revealed. One difference with the single arm variant is that the dependency structure of the arms is crucial. Previous works on this setting either used a worst-case approach or imposed independence of the arms. We introduce a way to quantify the dependency structure of the problem and design an algorithm that adapts to it. The algorithm is based on linear regression and the analysis uses techniques from the linear bandit literature. By comparing its performance to a new lower bound, we prove that it is optimal, up to a poly-logarithmic factor in the number of arms pulled.

paragraphs: In a combinatorial semi-bandit problem, an algorithm chooses several arms at each step and observes the reward from each selected arm. Selecting multiple arms makes their statistical dependencies important. Information from a collection of rewards depends on how those rewards vary together, so treating all dependency patterns alike can miss useful structure.

The paper considers known covariance and introduces a way to quantify the dependency structure. It then designs an algorithm that adapts to that structure, using linear regression and analytical tools from linear bandits. This replaces the earlier alternatives of assuming independent arms or relying on a worst-case treatment of their dependencies.

The authors also establish a new lower bound, providing a benchmark for what an algorithm can achieve. Against that benchmark, their algorithm is optimal up to a factor that is polylogarithmic in the number of arms selected. This is a qualified near-optimality result: the remaining gap is controlled, and the guarantee belongs to the setting in which the covariance structure is known.
summary.tldr: A regression-based semi-bandit algorithm uses known reward dependencies to achieve optimal performance up to a polylogarithmic factor.

title: Combinatorial semi-bandit with known covariance

abstract: In this paper, we prove a conjecture published in 1989 and also partially address an open problem announced at the Conference on Learning Theory (COLT) 2015. For an expected loss function of a deep nonlinear neural network, we prove the following statements under the independence assumption adopted from recent work: 1) the function is non-convex and non-concave, 2) every local minimum is a global minimum, 3) every critical point that is not a global minimum is a saddle point, and 4) the property of saddle points differs for shallow networks (with three layers) and deeper networks (with more than three layers). Moreover, we prove that the same four statements hold for deep linear neural networks with any depth, any widths and no unrealistic assumptions. As a result, we present an instance, for which we can answer to the following question: how difficult to directly train a deep model in theory? It is more difficult than the classical machine learning models (because of the non-convexity), but not too difficult (because of the nonexistence of poor local minima and the property of the saddle points). We note that even though we have advanced the theoretical foundations of deep learning, there is still a gap between theory and practice.

For an expected loss function of a deep nonlinear neural network, we prove the following statements under the independence assumption adopted from recent work: 1) the function is non-convex and non-concave, 2) every local minimum is a global minimum, 3) every critical point that is not a global minimum is a saddle point, and 4) the property of saddle points differs for shallow networks (with three layers) and deeper networks (with more than three layers). paragraphs: Training a neural network involves searching a loss surface for good parameter settings. Nonconvex surfaces can make this difficult because a locally best point need not be best overall. This paper investigates whether that particular obstacle occurs in theoretical models of deep networks, distinguishing local minima from saddle points.

For the expected loss of a deep nonlinear network, the authors establish four properties under an independence assumption adopted from earlier work. The loss is neither convex nor concave, every local minimum is globally optimal, and every other critical point is a saddle. They also show that saddle-point properties differ between networks with three layers and those with more layers.

The same four conclusions hold for deep linear networks of arbitrary depth and widths, without the unrealistic assumptions needed for the nonlinear analysis. These results identify settings where nonconvexity does not produce inferior local minima. They advance the theoretical understanding of training difficulty, but do not establish that practical deep-network training is universally easy. The authors explicitly acknowledge a remaining gap between their theory and practice.
summary.tldr: The paper proves the absence of inferior local minima for deep linear networks and, under an independence assumption, a nonlinear-network expected loss.

title: Deep Learning without Poor Local Minima

abstract: We introduce an efficient algorithmic framework for model selection in online learning, also known as parameter-free online learning. Departing from previous work, which has focused on highly structured function classes such as nested balls in Hilbert space, we propose a generic meta-algorithm framework that achieves online model selection oracle inequalities under minimal structural assumptions. We give the first computationally efficient parameter-free algorithms that work in arbitrary Banach spaces under mild smoothness assumptions; previous results applied only to Hilbert spaces. We further derive new oracle inequalities for matrix classes, non-nested convex sets, and $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with generic regularizers. Finally, we generalize these results by providing oracle inequalities for arbitrary non-linear classes in the online supervised learning model. These results are all derived through a unified meta-algorithm scheme using a novel "multi-scale" algorithm for prediction with expert advice based on random playout, which may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: The paper develops a framework for online model selection, also described as parameter-free online learning. It aims to give performance guarantees that compare the learner with suitable choices among candidate models. Earlier approaches emphasized highly structured collections, such as nested balls in Hilbert spaces; this work seeks a more general scheme.

The proposed meta-algorithm obtains online model-selection oracle inequalities under minimal structural assumptions. Under mild smoothness assumptions, it yields the first computationally efficient parameter-free algorithms for arbitrary Banach spaces, extending previous Hilbert-space results. The authors also derive new guarantees for matrix classes, non-nested convex sets, and finite-dimensional spaces equipped with generic regularizers.

The framework further provides oracle inequalities for arbitrary nonlinear classes in online supervised learning. These results share a multiscale prediction-with-expert-advice algorithm based on random playout. The significance is the common mechanism behind guarantees for substantially different model families: online model selection can be analyzed beyond the restrictive geometric arrangements emphasized in earlier work, while retaining the stated assumptions where required.
summary.tldr: A unified multiscale meta-algorithm extends parameter-free online learning and model-selection guarantees to much broader function classes.

title: Parameter-Free Online Learning via Model Selection

abstract: The past decade has seen a revolution in genomic technologies that enabled a flood of genome-wide profiling of chromatin marks. Recent literature tried to understand gene regulation by predicting gene expression from large-scale chromatin measurements. Two fundamental challenges exist for such learning tasks: (1) genome-wide chromatin signals are spatially structured, high-dimensional and highly modular; and (2) the core aim is to understand what are the relevant factors and how they work together. Previous studies either failed to model complex dependencies among input signals or relied on separate feature analysis to explain the decisions. This paper presents an attention-based deep learning approach; AttentiveChrome, that uses a unified architecture to model and to interpret dependencies among chromatin factors for controlling gene regulation. AttentiveChrome uses a hierarchy of multiple Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) modules to encode the input signals and to model how various chromatin marks cooperate automatically. AttentiveChrome trains two levels of attention jointly with the target prediction, enabling it to attend differentially to relevant marks and to locate important positions per mark. We evaluate the model across 56 different cell types (tasks) in human. Not only is the proposed architecture more accurate, but its attention scores also provide a better interpretation than state-of-the-art feature visualization methods such as saliency map.

paragraphs: Predicting gene expression from chromatin measurements requires handling many signals whose positions and interactions matter. The paper also treats interpretation as a central goal: a useful model should help identify relevant chromatin marks and how they work together. AttentiveChrome addresses prediction and interpretation within one architecture.

The model uses a hierarchy of Long Short-Term Memory modules to encode the spatially structured inputs and represent relationships among chromatin marks. Two jointly trained attention levels emphasize relevant marks and important positions within each mark. This gives the prediction system a way to weight both which signal matters and where its useful information occurs.

Evaluation across 56 human cell types finds improved predictive accuracy and better interpretation through attention scores than the compared feature visualization methods, including saliency maps. The finding supports integrating an explanatory weighting mechanism into the predictive model itself. The attention scores provide an interpretation of the model's decisions and the dependencies it learns, connecting its predictions to particular marks and locations.
summary.tldr: AttentiveChrome jointly learns gene-expression predictions and attention over chromatin marks and positions, improving accuracy and interpretation across 56 cell types.

title: Attend and Predict: Understanding Gene Regulation by Selective Attention on Chromatin

abstract: Linear Dynamical Systems (LDSs) are fundamental tools for modeling spatio-temporal data in various disciplines. Though rich in modeling, analyzing LDSs is not free of difficulty, mainly because LDSs do not comply with Euclidean geometry and hence conventional learning techniques can not be applied directly. In this paper, we propose an efficient projected gradient descent method to minimize a general form of a loss function and demonstrate how clustering and sparse coding with LDSs can be solved by the proposed method efficiently. To this end, we first derive a novel canonical form for representing the parameters of an LDS, and then show how gradient-descent updates through the projection on the space of LDSs can be achieved dexterously. In contrast to previous studies, our solution avoids any approximation in LDS modeling or during the optimization process. Extensive experiments reveal the superior performance of the proposed method in terms of the convergence and classification accuracy over state-of-the-art techniques.

paragraphs: Linear dynamical systems provide models for data that vary across space and time. Although their modeling capabilities are useful, the space of these systems does not follow ordinary Euclidean geometry. As a result, conventional learning operations cannot simply be applied to their parameters without accounting for that structure.

The paper develops a projected gradient descent method for a general class of loss functions on linear dynamical systems. It first derives a canonical parameter representation, then shows how to compute gradient updates and project them onto the space of valid systems. This representation and projection machinery make optimization compatible with the objects being learned.

The authors apply the method to clustering and sparse coding with linear dynamical systems. They state that their solution avoids approximations both in the system modeling and during optimization, distinguishing it from prior approaches. Experiments report stronger convergence performance and classification accuracy than the compared leading techniques. The contribution is a common optimization procedure that supports multiple learning tasks while respecting the geometry of the models.
summary.tldr: A canonical representation and projected gradient method enable efficient clustering and sparse coding with linear dynamical systems.

title: Efficient Optimization for Linear Dynamical Systems with Applications to Clustering and Sparse Coding

abstract: High dimensional sparse learning has imposed a great computational challenge to large scale data analysis. In this paper, we investiage a broad class of sparse learning approaches formulated as linear programs parametrized by a {\em regularization factor}, and solve them by the parametric simplex method (PSM). PSM offers significant advantages over other competing methods: (1) PSM naturally obtains the complete solution path for all values of the regularization parameter; (2) PSM provides a high precision dual certificate stopping criterion; (3) PSM yields sparse solutions through very few iterations, and the solution sparsity significantly reduces the computational cost per iteration. Particularly, we demonstrate the superiority of PSM over various sparse learning approaches, including Dantzig selector for sparse linear regression, sparse support vector machine for sparse linear classification, and sparse differential network estimation. We then provide sufficient conditions under which PSM always outputs sparse solutions such that its computational performance can be significantly boosted. Thorough numerical experiments are provided to demonstrate the outstanding performance of the PSM method.

paragraphs: Many sparse-learning problems can be written as linear programs controlled by a regularization parameter. This paper studies solving a broad class of these problems with the parametric simplex method. A central benefit is obtaining the complete solution path as regularization varies, giving access to more than a solution at one selected setting.

The method also provides a high-precision stopping criterion through a dual certificate. The authors emphasize that it can produce sparse solutions in very few iterations and that sparsity reduces the work required within each iteration. Thus, sparsity matters both as a property sought in the learned model and as a source of computational savings.

The paper considers the Dantzig selector for regression, sparse support vector machines for classification, and sparse differential network estimation. It provides sufficient conditions under which the method always produces sparse solutions, supporting the associated computational benefit under those conditions. Numerical experiments report strong performance across the studied approaches, connecting the theoretical sparsity argument with practical optimization results.
summary.tldr: The parametric simplex method efficiently traces regularization paths for sparse linear programs, with sparsity guarantees under sufficient conditions.

title: Parametric Simplex Method for Sparse Learning

abstract: We introduce a new framework for learning in severely resource-constrained settings. Our technique delicately amalgamates the representational richness of multiple linear predictors with the sparsity of Boolean relaxations, and thereby yields classifiers that are compact, interpretable, and accurate. We provide a rigorous formalism of the learning problem, and establish fast convergence of the ensuing algorithm via relaxation to a minimax saddle point objective. We supplement the theoretical foundations of our work with an extensive empirical evaluation.
originalAbstract: We introduce a new framework for learning in severely resource-constrained settings. We supplement the theoretical foundations of our work with an extensive empirical evaluation.

paragraphs: The paper addresses classification in settings with severe resource constraints. The goal is to learn predictors that remain compact while retaining useful predictive capacity and interpretability. These requirements motivate a framework that brings together multiple linear predictors and sparsity, treating model size and representational richness as joint design concerns.

The proposed technique combines the expressive capacity of several linear predictors with sparsity obtained through Boolean relaxations. Multiple predictors supply a richer representation, while the sparse structure contributes to compactness. The authors state that this combination yields classifiers that are compact, interpretable, and accurate, making the structure of the learned predictor central to the contribution.

The work also formalizes the learning problem and establishes fast convergence for the resulting algorithm through a relaxation to a minimax saddle point objective. An extensive empirical evaluation supplements these theoretical foundations. The paper thus contributes both a framework for constructing small predictors and an optimization treatment, addressing how to learn the proposed compact models as well as how to represent them.
summary.tldr: The framework combines multiple linear predictors with sparse Boolean relaxations to learn compact, interpretable classifiers with fast convergence guarantees.

title: Learning SMaLL Predictors

abstract: Natural images may lie on a union of disjoint manifolds rather than one globally connected manifold, and this can cause several difficulties for the training of common Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). In this work, we first show that single generator GANs are unable to correctly model a distribution supported on a disconnected manifold, and investigate how sample quality, mode dropping and local convergence are affected by this. Next, we show how using a collection of generators can address this problem, providing new insights into the success of such multi-generator GANs. Finally, we explain the serious issues caused by considering a fixed prior over the collection of generators and propose a novel approach for learning the prior and inferring the necessary number of generators without any supervision. Our proposed modifications can be applied on top of any other GAN model to enable learning of distributions supported on disconnected manifolds. We conduct several experiments to illustrate the aforementioned shortcoming of GANs, its consequences in practice, and the effectiveness of our proposed modifications in alleviating these issues.

title: Disconnected Manifold Learning for Generative Adversarial Networks

abstract: Social goods, such as healthcare, smart city, and information networks, often produce ordered event data in continuous time. The generative processes of these event data can be very complex, requiring flexible models to capture their dynamics. Temporal point processes offer an elegant framework for modeling event data without discretizing the time. However, the existing maximum-likelihood-estimation (MLE) learning paradigm requires hand-crafting the intensity function beforehand and cannot directly monitor the goodness-of-fit of the estimated model in the process of training. To alleviate the risk of model-misspecification in MLE, we propose to generate samples from the generative model and monitor the quality of the samples in the process of training until the samples and the real data are indistinguishable. We take inspiration from reinforcement learning (RL) and treat the generation of each event as the action taken by a stochastic policy. We parameterize the policy as a flexible recurrent neural network and gradually improve the policy to mimic the observed event distribution. Since the reward function is unknown in this setting, we uncover an analytic and nonparametric form of the reward function using an inverse reinforcement learning formulation. This new RL framework allows us to derive an efficient policy gradient algorithm for learning flexible point process models, and we show that it performs well in both synthetic and real data.

It addresses the described maximum-likelihood approach's reliance on a predetermined intensity function and its lack of direct monitoring of sample quality during training.

This leads to an efficient policy-gradient algorithm for fitting the point-process model. Experiments on synthetic and real data report good performance. The contribution connects flexible event generation with a training signal derived from observed behavior, reducing reliance on a hand-crafted intensity specification.
summary.tldr: A recurrent event-generation policy learns temporal point processes using a reward derived through inverse reinforcement learning.

title: Learning Temporal Point Processes via Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Multi-Task Learning (MTL) is appealing for deep learning regularization. In this paper, we tackle a specific MTL context denoted as primary MTL, where the ultimate goal is to improve the performance of a given primary task by leveraging several other auxiliary tasks. Our main methodological contribution is to introduce ROCK, a new generic multi-modal fusion block for deep learning tailored to the primary MTL context. ROCK architecture is based on a residual connection, which makes forward prediction explicitly impacted by the intermediate auxiliary representations. The auxiliary predictor's architecture is also specifically designed to our primary MTL context, by incorporating intensive pooling operators for maximizing complementarity of intermediate representations. Extensive experiments on NYUv2 dataset (object detection with scene classification, depth prediction, and surface normal estimation as auxiliary tasks) validate the relevance of the approach and its superiority to flat MTL approaches. Our method outperforms state-of-the-art object detection models on NYUv2 dataset by a large margin, and is also able to handle large-scale heterogeneous inputs (real and synthetic images) with missing annotation modalities.

ROCK uses a residual connection so that intermediate auxiliary representations explicitly affect the forward prediction. The auxiliary predictor also uses intensive pooling operations intended to make its intermediate representations more complementary. This gives the supporting tasks a concrete architectural route into the primary task, alongside their role in training the network.

Experiments on NYUv2 use object detection as the primary task, supported by scene classification, depth prediction, and surface normal estimation. The authors report improvements over flat multi-task approaches and a large margin over state-of-the-art object detectors on that dataset. The method also handles large-scale mixtures of real and synthetic images when some annotation modalities are missing, supporting its use with heterogeneous training inputs.
summary.tldr: ROCK feeds auxiliary-task representations into primary predictions through a residual fusion block, improving object detection on NYUv2.

title: Revisiting Multi-Task Learning with ROCK: a Deep Residual Auxiliary Block for Visual Detection

abstract: Causal discovery from a set of observations is one of the fundamental problems across several disciplines. For continuous variables, recently a number of causal discovery methods have demonstrated their effectiveness in distinguishing the cause from effect by exploring certain properties of the conditional distribution, but causal discovery on categorical data still remains to be a challenging problem, because it is generally not easy to find a compact description of the causal mechanism for the true causal direction. In this paper we make an attempt to find a way to solve this problem by assuming a two-stage causal process: the first stage maps the cause to a hidden variable of a lower cardinality, and the second stage generates the effect from the hidden representation. In this way, the causal mechanism admits a simple yet compact representation. We show that under this model, the causal direction is identifiable under some weak conditions on the true causal mechanism. We also provide an effective solution to recover the above hidden compact representation within the likelihood framework. Empirical studies verify the effectiveness of the proposed approach on both synthetic and real-world data.

paragraphs: Determining which categorical variable causes another is difficult because the mechanism connecting them may lack an obvious compact description. The paper addresses this by imposing a particular two-stage causal model. A cause first maps to an unobserved variable with fewer possible values, and that hidden representation then generates the effect.

The hidden variable provides a compact intermediate description of how the cause influences the effect. Instead of representing the entire relationship directly, the method seeks a smaller representation through which it can operate. Under this model and some weak conditions on the true mechanism, the authors show that the causal direction is identifiable: the model can distinguish the generating direction.

The paper also provides a likelihood-based method for recovering the hidden representation from observations. Synthetic and real-world studies support the effectiveness of the approach. Its central contribution is therefore both structural and computational: it identifies a model under which categorical causal direction can be recovered and supplies a way to fit that model. The identifiability claim depends on the stated causal structure and conditions.
summary.tldr: A compact hidden intermediate variable enables causal-direction identification for categorical data under the proposed model and stated conditions.

title: Causal Discovery from Discrete Data using Hidden Compact Representation

abstract: Asynchronous momentum stochastic gradient descent algorithms (Async-MSGD) have been widely used in distributed machine learning, e.g., training large collaborative filtering systems and deep neural networks. Due to current technical limit, however, establishing convergence properties of Async-MSGD for these highly complicated nonoconvex problems is generally infeasible. Therefore, we propose to analyze the algorithm through a simpler but nontrivial nonconvex problems --- streaming PCA. This allows us to make progress toward understanding Aync-MSGD and gaining new insights for more general problems. Specifically, by exploiting the diffusion approximation of stochastic optimization, we establish the asymptotic rate of convergence of Async-MSGD for streaming PCA. Our results indicate a fundamental tradeoff between asynchrony and momentum: To ensure convergence and acceleration through asynchrony, we have to reduce the momentum (compared with Sync-MSGD). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first theoretical attempt on understanding Async-MSGD for distributed nonconvex stochastic optimization. Numerical experiments on both streaming PCA and training deep neural networks are provided to support our findings for Async-MSGD.
