paragraphs: Asynchronous momentum stochastic gradient descent combines two techniques used in distributed learning: momentum and updates that proceed asynchronously. Establishing convergence for complicated nonconvex applications is difficult. This paper studies streaming principal component analysis as a simpler but still nonconvex problem, using it to investigate how these two acceleration mechanisms interact.

The authors apply a diffusion approximation of stochastic optimization to derive the algorithm's asymptotic convergence rate for streaming PCA. Their analysis indicates a tradeoff: to obtain convergence and acceleration through asynchrony, momentum must be reduced relative to the synchronous momentum method. The two mechanisms therefore cannot simply be combined without accounting for their interaction in the analyzed setting.

Numerical experiments on streaming PCA and deep neural-network training support the findings. The formal convergence analysis concerns streaming PCA, while the neural-network experiments supply evidence relevant to a more complex application. The work provides a theoretical starting point for understanding asynchronous momentum in nonconvex optimization and a concrete reason to consider momentum and asynchrony jointly when assessing acceleration.
summary.tldr: Streaming-PCA analysis reveals a momentum–asynchrony tradeoff, supported by experiments on PCA and neural-network training.

title: Towards Understanding Acceleration Tradeoff between Momentum and Asynchrony in Nonconvex Stochastic Optimization

abstract: Deep generative models (DGMs) have achieved remarkable advances. Semi-supervised variational auto-encoders (SVAE) as a classical DGM offers a principled framework to effective generalize from small labelled data to large unlabelled ones, but it is difficult to incorporate rich unstructured relationships within the multiple heterogeneous entities. In this paper, to deal with the problem, we present a semi-supervised co-embedding model for attributed networks (SCAN) based on the generalized SVAE for the heterogeneous data, which collaboratively learns low- dimensional vector representations of both nodes and attributes for partially labelled attributed networks semi-supervisedly. The node and attribute embeddings obtained in a unified manner by our SCAN can benefit not only for capturing the proximities between nodes but also the affinities between nodes and attributes. Moreover, our model also trains a discriminative network to learn the label predictive distribution of nodes. Experimental results on real-world networks demonstrate that our model yields excellent performance in a number of applications such as attribute inference, user profiling and node classification compared to the state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Attributed networks contain connections between nodes alongside information describing those nodes. When only some nodes have labels, learning must combine labeled and unlabeled information with these heterogeneous relationships. The paper addresses the difficulty of incorporating such relationships into a semi-supervised variational auto-encoder, a generative framework for learning from partially labeled data.

The proposed model, SCAN, generalizes that framework to jointly learn low-dimensional representations of nodes and attributes. Learning both together is intended to capture proximity between nodes as well as affinity between nodes and attributes. A discriminative network additionally learns a predictive distribution over node labels, connecting the shared representations to the available supervision.

Experiments on real-world networks report strong performance relative to state-of-the-art baselines in attribute inference, user profiling, and node classification. These tasks assess different uses of the jointly learned representations. The contribution is a unified way to combine network relationships, descriptive attributes, and partial labels, so the resulting embeddings can support both relationships among nodes and associations between nodes and their attributes.
summary.tldr: SCAN jointly embeds nodes and attributes using partial labels, supporting attribute inference, user profiling, and node classification.

title: Semi-supervisedly Co-embedding Attributed Networks

abstract: We study a deep learning inspired formulation for the blind demodulation problem, which is the task of recovering two unknown vectors from their entrywise multiplication. We consider the case where the unknown vectors are in the range of known deep generative models, $\mathcal{G}^{(1)}:\mathbb{R}^n\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^\ell$ and $\mathcal{G}^{(2)}:\mathbb{R}^p\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^\ell$. In the case when the networks corresponding to the generative models are expansive, the weight matrices are random and the dimension of the unknown vectors satisfy $\ell = \Omega(n^2+p^2)$, up to log factors, we show that the empirical risk objective has a favorable landscape for optimization. That is, the objective function has a descent direction at every point outside of a small neighborhood around four hyperbolic curves. We also characterize the local maximizers of the empirical risk objective and, hence, show that there does not exist any other stationary points outside of these neighborhood around four hyperbolic curves and the set of local maximizers. We also implement a gradient descent scheme inspired by the geometry of the landscape of the objective function. In order to converge to a global minimizer, this gradient descent scheme exploits the fact that exactly one of the hyperbolic curve corresponds to the global minimizer, and thus points near this hyperbolic curve have a lower objective value than points close to the other spurious hyperbolic curves. We show that this gradient descent scheme can effectively remove distortions synthetically introduced to the MNIST dataset.

paragraphs: Blind demodulation seeks two unknown vectors when only their elementwise product is observed. This paper constrains each vector to be an output of a known deep generative model. Those generative priors give structure to a recovery problem in which the two unknown quantities otherwise interact multiplicatively.

The landscape analysis assumes expansive networks with random weight matrices and an output dimension at least on the order of the sum of the squared latent dimensions, up to logarithmic factors. summary.tldr: Under explicit generative-network assumptions, the paper characterizes blind demodulation’s optimization landscape and develops a geometry-informed recovery algorithm.

title: Global Guarantees for Blind Demodulation with Generative Priors

abstract: Current approaches for predicting sets from feature vectors ignore the unordered nature of sets and suffer from discontinuity issues as a result. We propose a general model for predicting sets that properly respects the structure of sets and avoids this problem. With a single feature vector as input, we show that our model is able to auto-encode point sets, predict the set of bounding boxes of objects in an image, and predict the set of attributes of these objects.
originalAbstract: Current approaches for predicting sets from feature vectors ignore the unordered nature of sets and suffer from discontinuity issues as a result. We propose a general model for predicting sets that properly respects the structure of sets and avoids this problem. With a single feature vector as input, we show that our model is able to auto-encode point sets, predict the set of bounding boxes of objects in an image, and predict the set of attributes of these objects.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to predict an unordered set from a single feature vector. A set's elements have no meaningful first or last position. The authors identify a problem with existing approaches: treating set outputs in a way that ignores this unordered structure introduces discontinuity issues.

They propose a general prediction model that respects the structure of sets and avoids that problem. The central design objective is to make the output representation compatible with what is being predicted. For tasks whose answer is a collection, an ordering imposed on its elements should not become an additional property the model needs to represent.

The demonstrations span three types of output. The model can auto-encode point sets, predict a set of object bounding boxes from an image, and predict a set of object attributes. All use a single feature vector as input. Together, these examples show the model's applicability to both geometric collections and collections describing objects, making unordered output structure the common modeling concern across the tasks.
summary.tldr: A general set-prediction model respects unordered outputs and demonstrates point-set reconstruction, object-box prediction, and object-attribute prediction.

title: Deep Set Prediction Networks

abstract: When training complex neural networks, memory usage can be an important bottleneck. The question of when to rematerialize, i.e., to recompute intermediate values rather than retaining them in memory, becomes critical to achieving the best time and space efficiency. In this work we consider the rematerialization problem and devise efficient algorithms that use structural characterizations of computation graphs---treewidth and pathwidth---to obtain provably efficient rematerialization schedules. Our experiments demonstrate the performance of these algorithms on many common deep learning models.
originalAbstract: When training complex neural networks, memory usage can be an important bottleneck. paragraphs: Training a complex neural network can require retaining many intermediate values, making memory a bottleneck. Rematerialization addresses this by recomputing some values when they are needed instead of keeping them in memory throughout training. The central scheduling question is which values to retain and when to recompute the others.

The paper develops algorithms that use the structure of a network’s computation graph to answer that question. Specifically, it draws on structural characterizations called treewidth and pathwidth to construct rematerialization schedules with provable efficiency. These graph properties give the algorithms a way to organize the dependencies among intermediate computations when planning memory use and recomputation.

The authors also evaluate their algorithms on many common deep learning models. The contribution connects a practical training bottleneck with a graph-based approach to scheduling: the dependency structure of the computation becomes a resource for managing time and memory. Its theoretical guarantees and experimental evaluation address the same underlying task of deciding how to make effective use of limited storage during training.
summary.tldr: Graph-structural algorithms produce provably efficient schedules for recomputing neural network intermediates instead of storing them.

title: Efficient Rematerialization for Deep Networks

abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants have established themselves as the go-to algorithms for large-scale machine learning problems with independent samples due to their generalization performance and intrinsic computational advantage. However, the fact that the stochastic gradient is a biased estimator of the full gradient with correlated samples has led to the lack of theoretical understanding of how SGD behaves under correlated settings and hindered its use in such cases. In this paper, we focus on the Gaussian process (GP) and take a step forward towards breaking the barrier by proving minibatch SGD converges to a critical point of the full loss function, and recovers model hyperparameters with rate $O(\frac{1}{K})$ up to a statistical error term depending on the minibatch size. Numerical studies on both simulated and real datasets demonstrate that minibatch SGD has better generalization over state-of-the-art GP methods while reducing the computational burden and opening a new, previously unexplored, data size regime for GPs.

However, the fact that the stochastic gradient is a biased estimator of the full gradient with correlated samples has led to the lack of theoretical understanding of how SGD behaves under correlated settings and hindered its use in such cases. In this paper, we focus on the Gaussian process (GP) and take a step forward towards breaking the barrier by proving minibatch SGD converges to a critical point of the full loss function, and recovers model hyperparameters with rate $O(\frac{1}{K})$ up to a statistical error term depending on the minibatch size. paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent is widely used with independent samples, but correlated observations complicate its analysis. In the setting studied here, a stochastic gradient can be biased relative to the full gradient. This makes familiar intuition about minibatch updates insufficient and has limited theoretical understanding of their use for Gaussian processes.

The paper establishes that minibatch SGD converges to a critical point of the full Gaussian-process loss. It also proves recovery of model hyperparameters at an O(1/K) rate up to a statistical error term that depends on minibatch size. The result separates progress in optimization from the remaining statistical error associated with the minibatch setting.

Numerical studies use both simulated and real datasets. They report better generalization than the state-of-the-art Gaussian-process methods compared, together with lower computational demands and access to a larger data-size regime. The findings provide theoretical and empirical support for minibatch training in this correlated setting, with the convergence claim specifically concerning a critical point rather than a guaranteed global optimum.
summary.tldr: For Gaussian processes with correlated samples, minibatch SGD has convergence guarantees up to a batch-dependent statistical error and favorable empirical results.

title: Stochastic Gradient Descent in Correlated Settings: A Study on Gaussian Processes

abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained deep networks on a small dataset is an important component in the deep learning pipeline. A critical problem in fine-tuning is how to avoid over-fitting when data are limited. Existing efforts work from two aspects: (1) impose regularization on parameters or features; (2) transfer prior knowledge to fine-tuning by reusing pre-trained parameters. In this paper, we take an alternative approach by refactoring the widely used Batch Normalization (BN) module to mitigate over-fitting. We propose a two-branch design with one branch normalized by mini-batch statistics and the other branch normalized by moving statistics. During training, two branches are stochastically selected to avoid over-depending on some sample statistics, resulting in a strong regularization effect, which we interpret as ``architecture regularization.'' The resulting method is dubbed stochastic normalization (\textbf{StochNorm}). With the two-branch architecture, it naturally incorporates pre-trained moving statistics in BN layers during fine-tuning, exploiting more prior knowledge of pre-trained networks. Extensive empirical experiments show that StochNorm is a powerful tool to avoid over-fitting in fine-tuning with small datasets. Besides, StochNorm is readily pluggable in modern CNN backbones. It is complementary to other fine-tuning methods and can work together to achieve stronger regularization effect.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a pretrained network on a small dataset risks overfitting to limited examples. This paper addresses the problem by changing batch normalization, a component that adjusts features using summary statistics. The proposed StochNorm makes the choice of normalization statistics itself part of the regularization process.

StochNorm has two branches: one normalizes using the current mini-batch statistics, and the other uses moving statistics. Training selects between these branches stochastically, discouraging dependence on a particular set of sample statistics. The authors describe this as architecture regularization. The moving-statistics branch also naturally incorporates statistics retained from pretraining, bringing additional prior information into fine-tuning.

Extensive experiments show that the method helps avoid overfitting when fine-tuning with small datasets. It can be inserted into modern convolutional network backbones and combined with other fine-tuning methods for stronger regularization. Its contribution is therefore both a new source of randomness during adaptation and a way to reuse more of what normalization layers learned before fine-tuning.
summary.tldr: StochNorm reduces fine-tuning overfitting by randomly switching between mini-batch and moving-statistics normalization.

title: Stochastic Normalization

abstract: Attention modules, as simple and effective tools, have not only enabled deep neural networks to achieve state-of-the-art results in many domains, but also enhanced their interpretability. Most current models use deterministic attention modules due to their simplicity and ease of optimization. Stochastic counterparts, on the other hand, are less popular despite their potential benefits. The main reason is that stochastic attention often introduces optimization issues or requires significant model changes. In this paper, we propose a scalable stochastic version of attention that is easy to implement and optimize. We construct simplex-constrained attention distributions by normalizing reparameterizable distributions, making the training process differentiable. We learn their parameters in a Bayesian framework where a data-dependent prior is introduced for regularization. We apply the proposed stochastic attention modules to various attention-based models, with applications to graph node classification, visual question answering, image captioning, machine translation, and language understanding. Our experiments show the proposed method brings consistent improvements over the corresponding baselines.

paragraphs: Attention modules determine how a model distributes emphasis across available information. Most use deterministic weights because they are straightforward to train. This paper develops stochastic attention modules that preserve practical optimization while allowing attention weights to come from learned probability distributions.

The construction starts with distributions that support reparameterization, allowing their sampling process to participate in differentiable training. Normalization turns the resulting values into attention weights constrained to sum to one. The authors learn the distribution parameters within a Bayesian framework and introduce a data-dependent prior to regularize them. This addresses a central obstacle to stochastic attention: incorporating randomness without making optimization unwieldy.

The modules are applied to graph node classification, visual question answering, image captioning, machine translation, and language understanding. Across the reported experiments, they consistently improve on the corresponding baseline models. The contribution is thus both a distributional formulation of attention and a practical way to incorporate it into several existing attention-based architectures. The empirical findings support its usefulness across the tested applications.
summary.tldr: Bayesian attention modules make stochastic attention differentiable and practical, with consistent improvements across the tested applications.

title: Bayesian Attention Modules

abstract: Off-Policy Actor-Critic (OffP-AC) methods have proven successful in a variety of continuous control tasks. Normally, the critic's action-value function is updated using temporal-difference, and the critic in turn provides a loss for the actor that trains it to take actions with higher expected return. In this paper, we introduce a flexible and augmented meta-critic that observes the learning process and meta-learns an additional loss for the actor that accelerates and improves actor-critic learning. Compared to existing meta-learning algorithms, meta-critic is rapidly learned online for a single task, rather than slowly over a family of tasks. Crucially, our meta-critic is designed for off-policy based learners, which currently provide state-of-the-art reinforcement learning sample efficiency. We demonstrate that online meta-critic learning benefits to a variety of continuous control tasks when combined with contemporary OffP-AC methods DDPG, TD3 and SAC.

paragraphs: In off-policy actor-critic learning, the critic estimates action values through temporal-difference updates. It then supplies a loss that encourages the actor to choose actions with higher expected return. This paper adds a meta-critic that learns another source of training guidance for the actor.

The meta-critic observes the learning process and learns an additional actor loss intended to accelerate learning and improve its outcome. It is trained online within a single task, so the method does not depend on first learning across a family of tasks. The design specifically accommodates off-policy learners, connecting the extra learned objective to that style of actor-critic training.

The authors demonstrate benefits across a variety of continuous-control tasks when combining the meta-critic with DDPG, TD3, and SAC. These results support augmenting the usual critic-provided objective with guidance learned during the same task. The contribution is a flexible way to adapt the actor's training signal as learning unfolds, with empirical evidence of usefulness across several contemporary off-policy methods.
summary.tldr: An online meta-critic learns an additional actor loss within a single task, improving evaluated off-policy continuous-control learners.

title: Online Meta-Critic Learning for Off-Policy Actor-Critic Methods

abstract: Normalizing flows, autoregressive models, variational autoencoders (VAEs), and deep energy-based models are among competing likelihood-based frameworks for deep generative learning. Among them, VAEs have the advantage of fast and tractable sampling and easy-to-access encoding networks. However, they are currently outperformed by other models such as normalizing flows and autoregressive models. While the majority of the research in VAEs is focused on the statistical challenges, we explore the orthogonal direction of carefully designing neural architectures for hierarchical VAEs. We propose Nouveau VAE (NVAE), a deep hierarchical VAE built for image generation using depth-wise separable convolutions and batch normalization. NVAE is equipped with a residual parameterization of Normal distributions and its training is stabilized by spectral regularization. We show that NVAE achieves state-of-the-art results among non-autoregressive likelihood-based models on the MNIST, CIFAR-10, CelebA 64, and CelebA HQ datasets and it provides a strong baseline on FFHQ. For example, on CIFAR-10, NVAE pushes the state-of-the-art from 2.98 to 2.91 bits per dimension, and it produces high-quality images on CelebA HQ. To the best of our knowledge, NVAE is the first successful VAE applied to natural images as large as 256x256 pixels. The source code is publicly available.

NVAE investigates whether careful neural architecture design can improve hierarchical VAEs. Its focus complements work on statistical formulations by examining the networks used to implement image generation.

The model combines depth-wise separable convolutions and batch normalization in a deep hierarchy. It also uses a residual parameterization of Normal distributions and spectral regularization to stabilize training. These architectural and training choices form a coordinated design for building a capable hierarchical image VAE.

On CIFAR-10, the reported result improves from 2.98 to 2.91 bits per dimension. NVAE also produces high-quality CelebA HQ images. summary.tldr: NVAE advances hierarchical VAE image generation through architecture and training design, achieving leading results among non-autoregressive likelihood-based models on several datasets.

title: NVAE: A Deep Hierarchical Variational Autoencoder

abstract: We develop a method to generate prediction intervals that have a user-specified coverage level across all regions of feature-space, a property called conditional coverage. A typical approach to this task is to estimate the conditional quantiles with quantile regression---it is well-known that this leads to correct coverage in the large-sample limit, although it may not be accurate in finite samples. We find in experiments that traditional quantile regression can have poor conditional coverage. To remedy this, we modify the loss function to promote independence between the size of the intervals and the indicator of a miscoverage event. For the true conditional quantiles, these two quantities are independent (orthogonal), so the modified loss function continues to be valid. Moreover, we empirically show that the modified loss function leads to improved conditional coverage, as evaluated by several metrics. We also introduce two new metrics that check conditional coverage by looking at the strength of the dependence between the interval size and the indicator of miscoverage.

paragraphs: Prediction intervals aim to contain the true outcome at a chosen rate. Conditional coverage asks for that rate across different regions of the input space, so overall coverage alone is insufficient. Quantile regression approaches the desired coverage in the large-sample limit, but the authors find that its finite-sample conditional coverage can be poor.

The proposed method modifies the quantile-regression loss to encourage independence between interval width and whether an interval misses its outcome. For the true conditional quantiles, these quantities are independent. Encouraging this relationship therefore adds a criterion that remains compatible with the target quantiles while addressing an observable pattern associated with uneven coverage.

Experiments show improved conditional coverage according to several metrics. The paper also introduces two measures that examine dependence between interval size and missed outcomes. These measures connect evaluation to the same relationship used during training. The stated improvement is empirical: the large-sample property of quantile regression and the validity of the modified loss do not themselves establish exact finite-sample coverage everywhere.
summary.tldr: A quantile-regression loss that discourages dependence between interval width and prediction misses empirically improves conditional coverage.

title: Improving Conditional Coverage via Orthogonal Quantile Regression

abstract: We develop a new approach to tackle communication constraints in a distributed learning problem with a central server. We propose and analyze a new algorithm that performs bidirectional compression and achieves the same convergence rate as algorithms using only uplink (from the local workers to the central server) compression. To obtain this improvement, we design MCM, an algorithm such that the downlink compression only impacts local models, while the global model is preserved. As a result, and contrary to previous works, the gradients on local servers are computed on perturbed models. Consequently, convergence proofs are more challenging and require a precise control of this perturbation. To ensure it, MCM additionally combines model compression with a memory mechanism. This analysis opens new doors, e.g. incorporating worker dependent randomized-models and partial participation.

paragraphs: Distributed learning with a central server requires communication both from workers to the server and back again. Compressing these messages reduces communication demands, but compression also affects the learning process. This paper proposes MCM, an algorithm that compresses both directions while achieving the same convergence rate as algorithms that compress only worker-to-server messages.

Its key design choice is to preserve the central model while allowing downlink compression to perturb the models held by individual workers. Workers therefore compute gradients using these perturbed local models. The distinction matters because errors introduced during distribution remain in local copies instead of directly altering the global model being maintained by the server.

Proving convergence requires careful control of the local perturbations. MCM combines model compression with a memory mechanism to support that control. The analysis establishes the claimed convergence-rate improvement and opens possibilities for incorporating worker-dependent randomized models and partial participation. The contribution connects a specific model-preservation design with guarantees for communication-efficient distributed optimization.
summary.tldr: MCM preserves the central model while compressing both communication directions, matching the convergence rate of uplink-only compression.

title: Preserved central model for faster bidirectional compression in distributed settings

abstract: Normalizing flows are a promising tool for modeling probability distributions in physical systems. While state-of-the-art flows accurately approximate distributions and energies, applications in physics additionally require smooth energies to compute forces and higher-order derivatives. Furthermore, such densities are often defined on non-trivial topologies. A recent example are Boltzmann Generators for generating 3D-structures of peptides and small proteins. These generative models leverage the space of internal coordinates (dihedrals, angles, and bonds), which is a product of hypertori and compact intervals. In this work, we introduce a class of smooth mixture transformations working on both compact intervals and hypertori.Mixture transformations employ root-finding methods to invert them in practice, which has so far prevented bi-directional flow training. To this end, we show that parameter gradients and forces of such inverses can be computed from forward evaluations via the inverse function theorem.We demonstrate two advantages of such smooth flows: they allow training by force matching to simulation data and can be used as potentials in molecular dynamics simulations.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows can model probability distributions and energies, but physical applications also need smooth derivatives to compute forces. Molecular coordinates introduce another complication: angles and bond-related coordinates occupy spaces with periodic and bounded structure. This paper develops smooth flow transformations suited to compact intervals and hypertori, addressing both differentiability and the geometry of those spaces.

The transformations use mixtures whose inverses are computed numerically through root finding. That inversion procedure had prevented bidirectional flow training. The authors apply the inverse function theorem to show that parameter gradients and forces associated with an inverse can be calculated from forward evaluations, making the necessary derivative information accessible.

The paper demonstrates two uses of the resulting smooth flows: training through force matching against simulation data and serving as potentials in molecular dynamics simulations. These applications require more than approximating distribution values accurately; they also depend on usable energy derivatives. The contribution joins smooth transformations on the relevant coordinate spaces with a way to differentiate their numerically obtained inverses.
summary.tldr: Smooth mixture flows support force-based training and molecular dynamics by enabling derivatives through numerically computed inverse transformations.

title: Smooth Normalizing Flows

abstract: We categorize meta-learning evaluation into two settings: $\textit{in-distribution}$ [ID], in which the train and test tasks are sampled $\textit{iid}$ from the same underlying task distribution, and $\textit{out-of-distribution}$ [OOD], in which they are not. While most meta-learning theory and some FSL applications follow the ID setting, we identify that most existing few-shot classification benchmarks instead reflect OOD evaluation, as they use disjoint sets of train (base) and test (novel) classes for task generation. This discrepancy is problematic because -- as we show on numerous benchmarks -- meta-learning methods that perform better on existing OOD datasets may perform significantly worse in the ID setting. In addition, in the OOD setting, even though current FSL benchmarks seem befitting, our study highlights concerns in 1) reliably performing model selection for a given meta-learning method, and 2) consistently comparing the performance of different methods. To address these concerns, we provide suggestions on how to construct FSL benchmarks to allow for ID evaluation as well as more reliable OOD evaluation. Our work aims to inform the meta-learning community about the importance and distinction of ID vs. OOD evaluation, as well as the subtleties of OOD evaluation with current benchmarks.

paragraphs: Meta-learning evaluation can ask two different questions. In-distribution evaluation samples training and test tasks independently from the same task distribution. Out-of-distribution evaluation changes that relationship. This paper argues that distinguishing the two is essential because success under one evaluation setting need not imply success under the other.

The authors identify a mismatch between much meta-learning theory and common few-shot classification benchmarks. Theory often assumes the in-distribution setting, while benchmarks commonly generate training and test tasks from disjoint classes, making their evaluation out of distribution. Across numerous benchmarks, methods that perform better under the latter setting can perform significantly worse under the former.

The study also identifies difficulties within existing out-of-distribution evaluation: reliably selecting a model for a given method and consistently comparing different methods. It offers suggestions for constructing benchmarks that support in-distribution tests and more reliable out-of-distribution tests. The practical message is that benchmark construction determines which kind of generalization a result measures, and that rankings can change when the task-distribution relationship changes.
summary.tldr: Meta-learning method rankings can change between in-distribution and out-of-distribution evaluation, motivating clearer and more reliable benchmark design.

title: Two Sides of Meta-Learning Evaluation: In vs. Out of Distribution

abstract: Machine Learning (ML) can help solve combinatorial optimization (CO) problems better. A popular approach is to use a neural net to compute on the parameters of a given CO problem and extract useful information that guides the search for good solutions. Many CO problems of practical importance can be specified in a matrix form of parameters quantifying the relationship between two groups of items. There is currently no neural net model, however, that takes in such matrix-style relationship data as an input. Consequently, these types of CO problems have been out of reach for ML engineers. In this paper, we introduce Matrix Encoding Network (MatNet) and show how conveniently it takes in and processes parameters of such complex CO problems. Using an end-to-end model based on MatNet, we solve asymmetric traveling salesman (ATSP) and flexible flow shop (FFSP) problems as the earliest neural approach. In particular, for a class of FFSP we have tested MatNet on, we demonstrate a far superior empirical performance to any methods (neural or not) known to date.

paragraphs: Neural methods can support combinatorial optimization by extracting information from a problem's parameters to guide the search for good solutions. Many practical problems describe relationships between two groups of items using a matrix. This paper focuses on providing a neural architecture that can directly accept and process that form of relationship data.

The proposed Matrix Encoding Network, or MatNet, makes those matrix-valued parameters available to an end-to-end optimization model. The authors demonstrate it on the asymmetric traveling salesman problem and the flexible flow shop problem, presenting these applications as the earliest neural approaches to the two problems.

For a particular class of flexible flow shop problems tested in the paper, MatNet achieves substantially better empirical performance than the previously known methods considered, including non-neural ones. The scope of that result is the tested class, rather than every scheduling or combinatorial optimization problem. The broader contribution is an input-processing architecture that lets neural optimization methods work with problems naturally specified by relationships in a matrix.
summary.tldr: MatNet processes matrix-defined optimization problems and reports strong results on routing and a tested class of scheduling problems.

title: Matrix encoding networks for neural combinatorial optimization

abstract: Self-supervised disentangled representation learning is a critical task in sequence modeling. The learnt representations contribute to better model interpretability as well as the data generation, and improve the sample efficiency for downstream tasks. We propose a novel sequence representation learning method, named Contrastively Disentangled Sequential Variational Autoencoder (C-DSVAE), to extract and separate the static (time-invariant) and dynamic (time-variant) factors in the latent space. Different from previous sequential variational autoencoder methods, we use a novel evidence lower bound which maximizes the mutual information between the input and the latent factors, while penalizes the mutual information between the static and dynamic factors. We leverage contrastive estimations of the mutual information terms in training, together with simple yet effective augmentation techniques, to introduce additional inductive biases. Our experiments show that C-DSVAE significantly outperforms the previous state-of-the-art methods on multiple metrics.

paragraphs: A sequence contains information that stays constant and information that changes over time. This paper proposes C-DSVAE, a self-supervised representation learning method designed to separate those two kinds of information in its latent variables. The motivation is to obtain representations that support interpretation, data generation, and more sample-efficient learning for downstream tasks.

The central change is a new evidence lower bound for training the sequential variational autoencoder. It encourages the latent factors to retain information about the input while penalizing mutual information between the static and dynamic factors. These objectives address two different needs: the representation should remain informative, and its two components should avoid duplicating one another's information.

The method estimates the mutual information terms contrastively and uses data augmentations to introduce additional learning biases. Together, these choices guide the model toward the intended separation of constant and changing factors. The authors report significant improvements over previous state-of-the-art methods on multiple metrics, providing empirical support for this training approach to disentangled sequence representations.
summary.tldr: C-DSVAE uses contrastive information objectives to learn informative but separated static and dynamic representations of sequences.

title: Contrastively Disentangled Sequential Variational Autoencoder

abstract: Recent advances in the design of neural network architectures, in particular those specialized in modeling sequences, have provided significant improvements in speech separation performance. In this work, we propose to use a bio-inspired architecture called Fully Recurrent Convolutional Neural Network (FRCNN) to solve the separation task. This model contains bottom-up, top-down and lateral connections to fuse information processed at various time-scales represented by stages. In contrast to the traditional approach updating stages in parallel, we propose to first update the stages one by one in the bottom-up direction, then fuse information from adjacent stages simultaneously and finally fuse information from all stages to the bottom stage together. Experiments showed that this asynchronous updating scheme achieved significantly better results with much fewer parameters than the traditional synchronous updating scheme on speech separation. In addition, the proposed model achieved competitive or better results with high efficiency as compared to other state-of-the-art approaches on two benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Speech separation requires a network to process temporal information effectively. This paper uses a biologically inspired Fully Recurrent Convolutional Neural Network, or FRCNN, whose stages represent different time scales. Bottom-up, top-down, and lateral connections allow information from those stages to be combined, making the update schedule an important part of the architecture.

The proposed schedule has three steps. First, stages update one at a time in the bottom-up direction. Next, information from adjacent stages is fused simultaneously. Finally, information from every stage is combined at the bottom stage. This asynchronous sequence changes how information is brought together compared with the traditional approach of updating stages in parallel.

Experiments show that the asynchronous scheme achieves significantly better speech-separation results with many fewer parameters than the synchronous scheme. On two benchmark datasets, the proposed model also achieves competitive or better performance than other state-of-the-art approaches while maintaining high efficiency. The findings highlight the update order across time-scale representations as a useful design choice, alongside the network’s recurrent connections.
summary.tldr: An asynchronous update schedule improves speech separation in a fully recurrent convolutional network while using fewer parameters than synchronous updating.

title: Speech Separation Using an Asynchronous Fully Recurrent Convolutional Neural Network

abstract: We investigate the classical active pure exploration problem in Markov Decision Processes, where the agent sequentially selects actions and, from the resulting system trajectory, aims at identifying the best policy as fast as possible. We propose a problem-dependent lower bound on the average number of steps required before a correct answer can be given with probability at least $1-\delta$. We further provide the first algorithm with an instance-specific sample complexity in this setting. This algorithm addresses the general case of communicating MDPs; we also propose a variant with a reduced exploration rate (and hence faster convergence) under an additional ergodicity assumption. This work extends previous results relative to the \emph{generative setting}~\cite{pmlr-v139-marjani21a}, where the agent could at each step query the random outcome of any (state, action) pair. In contrast, we show here how to deal with the \emph{navigation constraints}, induced by the \emph{online setting}. Our analysis relies on an ergodic theorem for non-homogeneous Markov chains which we consider of wide interest in the analysis of Markov Decision Processes.

paragraphs: This paper studies how an agent can identify the best policy in a Markov decision process as quickly as possible. The agent gathers evidence by choosing actions and following the resulting trajectory. Its objective is pure exploration: learning which policy is best, with a specified probability of giving the correct answer.

The authors derive a problem-dependent lower bound on the average number of steps needed to answer correctly with probability at least 1−δ. They also provide an algorithm with instance-specific sample complexity for communicating MDPs. With the additional assumption of ergodicity, a variant can use a lower exploration rate and converge faster.

A central issue is navigation. Unlike a generative setting where any state-action pair can be queried directly, an online agent must reach states through its own actions. The paper accounts for these constraints in its analysis and algorithm. Its reasoning uses an ergodic theorem for non-homogeneous Markov chains, connecting the changing exploration process to guarantees about learning from actual trajectories.
summary.tldr: The paper gives problem-dependent limits and an instance-specific algorithm for identifying the best policy while respecting online navigation constraints.

title: Navigating to the Best Policy in Markov Decision Processes

abstract: The Expectation Maximization (EM) algorithm is the default algorithm for inference in latent variable models. As in any other field of machine learning, applications of latent variable models to very large datasets make the use of advanced parallel and distributed architecture mandatory. This paper introduces FedEM, which is the first extension of the EM algorithm to the federated learning context. FedEM is a new communication efficient method, which handles partial participation of local devices, and is robust to heterogeneous distribution of the datasets. To alleviate the communication bottleneck, FedEM compresses appropriately defined complete data sufficient statistics. We also develop and analyze an extension of FedEM to further incorporate a variance reduction scheme. In all cases, we derive finite-time complexity bounds for smooth non-convex problems. Numerical results are presented to support our theoretical findings, as well as an application to federated missing values imputation for biodiversity monitoring.

paragraphs: Expectation Maximization is a standard method for fitting models that contain unobserved variables. Applying it across distributed datasets introduces practical problems: communication can be expensive, devices may participate only intermittently, and their data distributions may differ. This paper introduces FedEM as an extension of EM to the federated learning setting that addresses these issues.

FedEM reduces communication by compressing appropriately defined complete-data sufficient statistics. These statistics are the quantities the method uses to summarize information relevant to estimation. The algorithm accommodates partial device participation and heterogeneous datasets. The authors also develop a version with variance reduction, adding a mechanism for reducing variability in the estimation procedure.

For both versions, the paper derives finite-time complexity bounds for smooth, non-convex problems. These results characterize computational progress without restricting the objective to a convex setting. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings, and an application fills in missing values in federated biodiversity-monitoring data. The contribution brings communication-aware distributed computation to latent-variable inference while explicitly accounting for uneven data and device availability.
summary.tldr: FedEM adapts Expectation Maximization to federated data through compressed statistics, partial participation support, and an optional variance-reduction scheme.

title: Federated-EM with heterogeneity mitigation and variance reduction

abstract: There has been a recent surge in methods that aim to decompose and segment scenes into multiple objects in an unsupervised manner, i.e., unsupervised multi-object segmentation. Performing such a task is a long-standing goal of computer vision, offering to unlock object-level reasoning without requiring dense annotations to train segmentation models. Despite significant progress, current models are developed and trained on visually simple scenes depicting mono-colored objects on plain backgrounds. The natural world, however, is visually complex with confounding aspects such as diverse textures and complicated lighting effects. In this study, we present a new benchmark called ClevrTex, designed as the next challenge to compare, evaluate and analyze algorithms. ClevrTex features synthetic scenes with diverse shapes, textures and photo-mapped materials, created using physically based rendering techniques. ClevrTex has 50k examples depicting 3-10 objects arranged on a background, created using a catalog of 60 materials, and a further test set featuring 10k images created using 25 different materials. We benchmark a large set of recent unsupervised multi-object segmentation models on ClevrTex and find all state-of-the-art approaches fail to learn good representations in the textured setting, despite impressive performance on simpler data. We also create variants of the ClevrTex dataset, controlling for different aspects of scene complexity, and probe current approaches for individual shortcomings. Dataset and code are available at https://www.robots.ox.ac.uk/~vgg/research/clevrtex.

paragraphs: Unsupervised multi-object segmentation aims to separate a scene into individual objects without dense training annotations. Many methods had shown strong results on simple images with uniformly colored objects and plain backgrounds. ClevrTex tests whether that progress carries over to scenes with varied textures, materials, shapes, and more complicated lighting effects.

The dataset uses physically based rendering to create synthetic scenes containing three to ten objects. Its main collection has 50,000 examples built from 60 materials, with another 10,000 test images using 25 different materials. The authors also construct variants that control different aspects of scene complexity, allowing them to examine particular difficulties rather than treating complexity as one undifferentiated property.

In the reported benchmark, all evaluated state-of-the-art approaches fail to learn good representations in the textured setting despite impressive results on simpler data. This finding identifies a substantial gap between success on visually simple scenes and handling richer appearance. ClevrTex provides both a harder comparison task and controlled variants for probing the weaknesses behind that gap.
summary.tldr: ClevrTex shows that strong unsupervised object segmentation results on simple scenes do not carry over to its textured scenes.

title: ClevrTex: A Texture-Rich Benchmark for Unsupervised Multi-Object Segmentation

abstract: We introduce an offline multi-agent reinforcement learning ( offline MARL) framework that utilizes previously collected data without additional online data collection. Our method reformulates offline MARL as a sequence modeling problem and thus builds on top of the simplicity and scalability of the Transformer architecture. In the fashion of centralized training and decentralized execution, we propose to first train a teacher policy as if the MARL dataset is generated by a single agent. After the teacher policy has identified and recombined the "good" behavior in the dataset, we create separate student policies and distill not only the teacher policy's features but also its structural relations among different agents' features to student policies. Despite its simplicity, the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art model-free offline MARL baselines while being more robust to demonstration's quality on several environments.

paragraphs: This paper learns policies for multiple agents from an existing dataset, without collecting additional online experience. It casts the learning problem as sequence modeling, allowing the framework to build on the Transformer architecture. The design combines centralized learning from the dataset with separate policies that agents can execute independently.

Training begins with a teacher policy that treats the multi-agent dataset as though it came from one agent. The teacher identifies and recombines useful behavior within that data. Separate student policies are then created for the individual agents and trained through knowledge distillation from the teacher.

The transfer includes both the teacher's features and the structural relationships among features belonging to different agents. This makes relationships across agents part of the knowledge passed to the decentralized policies. On several environments, the method outperforms the state-of-the-art model-free offline multi-agent baselines evaluated and is more robust to demonstration quality. The results support sequence modeling and relational distillation as a practical combination for learning coordinated behavior from fixed data.
summary.tldr: A centralized Transformer teacher distills behavior and relationships into separate agent policies, improving offline multi-agent learning in the evaluated environments.

title: Offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Knowledge Distillation

abstract: Utilizing messages from teammates can improve coordination in cooperative Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL). To obtain meaningful information for decision-making, previous works typically combine raw messages generated by teammates with local information as inputs for policy. However, neglecting the aggregation of multiple messages poses great inefficiency for policy learning. Motivated by recent advances in representation learning, we argue that efficient message aggregation is essential for good coordination in MARL. In this paper, we propose Multi-Agent communication via Self-supervised Information Aggregation (MASIA), with which agents can aggregate the received messages into compact representations with high relevance to augment the local policy. Specifically, we design a permutation invariant message encoder to generate common information aggregated representation from raw messages and optimize it via reconstructing and shooting future information in a self-supervised manner. Each agent would utilize the most relevant parts of the aggregated representation for decision-making by a novel message extraction mechanism. Empirical results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms strong baselines on multiple cooperative MARL tasks for various task settings.

paragraphs: Cooperating reinforcement-learning agents can use messages from teammates to coordinate their actions. Simply passing raw messages alongside local observations to a policy, however, leaves that policy to work out how the messages fit together. This paper proposes MASIA to organize incoming communication into compact information useful for decisions.

A message encoder aggregates the received messages into a shared representation. It is permutation invariant, so changing the order of the messages does not change the aggregation. The encoder learns through self-supervised objectives involving reconstruction and future information. A separate extraction mechanism then lets each agent select the portions of the aggregated representation most relevant to its own decision.

This separates the task of combining team information from the task of using that information locally. The authors report significant performance improvements over strong baselines across multiple cooperative tasks and task settings. The findings support the value of learning how to summarize and select communicated information, alongside learning the policies that ultimately choose actions.
summary.tldr: MASIA learns compact summaries of teammate messages and lets each agent extract the information most relevant to its decisions.

title: Efficient Multi-agent Communication via Self-supervised Information Aggregation

abstract: Providing densely shaped reward functions for RL algorithms is often exceedingly challenging, motivating the development of RL algorithms that can learn from easier-to-specify sparse reward functions. This sparsity poses new exploration challenges. One common way to address this problem is using demonstrations to provide initial signal about regions of the state space with high rewards. However, prior RL from demonstrations algorithms introduce significant complexity and many hyperparameters, making them hard to implement and tune. We introduce Monte Carlo Actor-Critic (MCAC), a parameter free modification to standard actor-critic algorithms which initializes the replay buffer with demonstrations and computes a modified $Q$-value by taking the maximum of the standard temporal distance (TD) target and a Monte Carlo estimate of the reward-to-go. This encourages exploration in the neighborhood of high-performing trajectories by encouraging high $Q$-values in corresponding regions of the state space. Experiments across $5$ continuous control domains suggest that MCAC can be used to significantly increase learning efficiency across $6$ commonly used RL and RL-from-demonstrations algorithms. See https://sites.google.com/view/mcac-rl for code and supplementary material.

paragraphs: Sparse rewards are easier to specify than detailed reward functions, but they leave reinforcement learning agents with little guidance about where to explore. Demonstrations can provide an initial signal about promising behavior. This paper seeks a simple way to use that signal without the complexity and numerous hyperparameters of earlier demonstration-based methods.

Monte Carlo Actor-Critic initializes the replay buffer with demonstrations and changes the value-learning target. It takes the larger of the standard TD target and a Monte Carlo estimate of remaining reward. This encourages high estimated values around successful trajectories, giving the agent an incentive to explore their neighborhoods. The modification adds no tuning parameters.

Experiments across five continuous-control domains suggest that MCAC can substantially improve learning efficiency when applied to six existing reinforcement learning and demonstration-based algorithms. The contribution is a small change to standard actor-critic learning that makes demonstration returns influential during exploration, including in the setting of suboptimal demonstrations addressed by the paper.
summary.tldr: MCAC uses demonstration returns to raise value targets near successful trajectories, improving sparse-reward learning efficiency in the reported experiments.

title: Monte Carlo Augmented Actor-Critic for Sparse Reward Deep Reinforcement Learning from Suboptimal Demonstrations

abstract: Modern deep neural networks (DNNs) are extremely powerful; however, this comes at the price of increased depth and having more parameters per layer, making their training and inference more computationally challenging. In an attempt to address this key limitation, efforts have been devoted to the compression (e.g., sparsification and/or quantization) of these large-scale machine learning models, so that they can be deployed on low-power IoT devices.In this paper, building upon recent research advances in the neural tangent kernel (NTK) and random matrix theory, we provide a novel compression approach to wide and fully-connected \emph{deep} neural nets. Specifically, we demonstrate that in the high-dimensional regime where the number of data points $n$ and their dimension $p$ are both large, and under a Gaussian mixture model for the data, there exists \emph{asymptotic spectral equivalence} between the NTK matrices for a large family of DNN models. This theoretical result enables ''lossless'' compression of a given DNN to be performed, in the sense that the compressed network yields asymptotically the same NTK as the original (dense and unquantized) network, with its weights and activations taking values \emph{only} in $\{ 0, \pm 1 \}$ up to scaling. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world data are conducted to support the advantages of the proposed compression scheme, with code available at https://github.com/Model-Compression/Lossless_Compression.

Experiments on both synthetic and real-world data are conducted to support the advantages of the proposed compression scheme, with code available at https://github.com/Model-Compression/Lossless_Compression.

paragraphs: Large neural networks impose substantial training and inference costs, motivating compression for devices with limited resources. This paper proposes a compression approach for wide, fully connected deep networks using neural tangent kernel analysis and random matrix theory. The theoretical comparison centers on NTK matrices associated with different network models.

The result applies in a high-dimensional regime where both the number of data points and their dimensionality are large, under a Gaussian mixture model for the data. In that setting, the authors establish asymptotic spectral equivalence among NTK matrices for a broad family of networks. This equivalence provides the basis for the compression scheme.

The compressed network's weights and activations take only zero or signed unit values, up to scaling. The term lossless has a specific asymptotic meaning here: the compressed model yields the same limiting NTK as the dense, unquantized model. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data support the scheme's advantages. The theoretical claim therefore concerns kernel preservation under the stated assumptions, rather than exact identity of every finite network output.
summary.tldr: Under high-dimensional Gaussian-mixture assumptions, networks with ternary weights and activations can asymptotically preserve the neural tangent kernel of dense networks.

title: "Lossless" Compression of Deep Neural Networks: A High-dimensional Neural Tangent Kernel Approach

abstract: We study the design of computationally efficient online learning algorithms under smoothed analysis. In this setting, at every step, an adversary generates a sample from an adaptively chosen distribution whose density is upper bounded by $1/\sigma$ times the uniform density. Given access to an offline optimization (ERM) oracle, we give the first computationally efficient online algorithms whose sublinear regret depends only on the pseudo/VC dimension $d$ of the class and the smoothness parameter $\sigma$. In particular, we achieve \emph{oracle-efficient} regret bounds of $ O ( \sqrt{T d\sigma^{-1}} ) $ for learning real-valued functions and $ O ( \sqrt{T d\sigma^{-\frac{1}{2}} } )$ for learning binary-valued functions. Our results establish that online learning is computationally as easy as offline learning, under the smoothed analysis framework. This contrasts the computational separation between online learning with worst-case adversaries and offline learning established by [HK16].Our algorithms also achieve improved bounds for some settings with binary-valued functions and worst-case adversaries. These include an oracle-efficient algorithm with $O ( \sqrt{T(d |\mathcal{X}|)^{1/2} })$ regret that refines the earlier $O ( \sqrt{T|\mathcal{X}|})$ bound of [DS16] for finite domains, and an oracle-efficient algorithm with $O(T^{3/4} d^{1/2})$ regret for the transductive setting.

paragraphs: Online learning requires decisions to be updated as examples arrive. This paper studies an adversary that can adapt its sampling distribution over time but cannot concentrate it arbitrarily: its density is bounded by 1/σ times the uniform density. This smoothing assumption creates a setting between unrestricted adversarial inputs and a fixed data distribution.

Given access to an offline empirical-risk-minimization oracle, the authors construct computationally efficient online algorithms with sublinear regret controlled by class complexity and smoothness. For T rounds and dimension d, the bounds scale as the square root of T d/σ for real-valued functions and the square root of T d/√σ for binary-valued functions. Thus, stronger concentration allowances worsen the stated guarantees.

Under this framework, the results establish that efficient offline optimization can support efficient online learning, contrasting with the computational separation under worst-case adversaries. The paper additionally improves oracle-efficient regret bounds for binary-valued functions in finite-domain and transductive worst-case settings. The main equivalence remains tied to the specified smoothing assumption and access to the offline oracle.
summary.tldr: With bounded-density adversarial sampling and an offline optimization oracle, online learning admits efficient algorithms with dimension-dependent sublinear regret.

title: Oracle-Efficient Online Learning for Smoothed Adversaries

abstract: Decoders built on Gaussian processes (GPs) are enticing due to the marginalisation over the non-linear function space. Such models (also known as GP-LVMs) are often expensive and notoriously difficult to train in practice, but can be scaled using variational inference and inducing points. In this paper, we revisit active set approximations. We develop a new stochastic estimate of the log-marginal likelihood based on recently discovered links to cross-validation, and we propose a computationally efficient approximation thereof. We demonstrate that the resulting stochastic active sets (SAS) approximation significantly improves the robustness of GP decoder training, while reducing computational cost. The SAS-GP obtains more structure in the latent space, scales to many datapoints, and learns better representations than variational autoencoders, which is rarely the case for GP decoders.

paragraphs: Gaussian-process decoders are appealing because they marginalize over nonlinear functions instead of committing to a single decoder function. In practice, these models can be expensive and difficult to train. This paper revisits active-set approximations as a way to make their training more robust and computationally manageable.

The authors develop a stochastic estimate of the log-marginal likelihood using connections to cross-validation. They then introduce a computationally efficient approximation to that estimate, producing the stochastic active sets method, or SAS. The approach changes how the training objective is estimated, offering another route to scaling Gaussian-process decoders alongside existing inducing-point and variational techniques.

The reported results show substantially more robust training with lower computational cost. SAS-GP scales to many datapoints, produces a more structured latent space, and learns better representations than variational autoencoders in the demonstrated comparisons. These findings matter because they address both the practical difficulty of fitting GP decoders and the quality of the representations obtained, two obstacles to their wider use.
summary.tldr: Stochastic active sets make Gaussian-process decoder training cheaper and more robust while improving the demonstrated latent representations.

title: Revisiting Active Sets for Gaussian Process Decoders

abstract: Unrestricted color attacks, which manipulate semantically meaningful color of an image, have shown their stealthiness and success in fooling both human eyes and deep neural networks. However, current works usually sacrifice the flexibility of the uncontrolled setting to ensure the naturalness of adversarial examples. As a result, the black-box attack performance of these methods is limited. To boost transferability of adversarial examples without damaging image quality, we propose a novel Natural Color Fool (NCF) which is guided by realistic color distributions sampled from a publicly available dataset and optimized by our neighborhood search and initialization reset. By conducting extensive experiments and visualizations, we convincingly demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method. Notably, on average, results show that our NCF can outperform state-of-the-art approaches by 15.0%$\sim$32.9% for fooling normally trained models and 10.0%$\sim$25.3% for evading defense methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/VL-Group/Natural-Color-Fool.

paragraphs: Color-based adversarial attacks alter meaningful image colors to make neural networks produce incorrect outputs. Their challenge is to preserve a natural-looking image while allowing enough freedom to create effective attacks. This paper argues that existing approaches restrict that freedom too much, limiting their performance against black-box models.

Natural Color Fool, or NCF, guides image changes using realistic color distributions sampled from a publicly available dataset. It combines that guidance with neighborhood search and initialization resets to optimize the attack. The intended benefit is stronger transferability of adversarial examples while preserving image quality, using realistic color distributions to guide the search.

Experiments and visualizations support the method's effectiveness. The authors report average improvements over state-of-the-art approaches ranging from 15.0% to 32.9% when fooling normally trained models and from 10.0% to 25.3% when evading defenses. These results show that realistic color guidance can coexist with stronger attacks in the evaluated settings. The contribution is an attack design that treats natural appearance and effective black-box transfer as compatible goals.
summary.tldr: Natural Color Fool uses realistic color distributions and search refinements to improve black-box adversarial attacks while preserving image quality.

title: Natural Color Fool: Towards Boosting Black-box Unrestricted Attacks

abstract: Data-free Knowledge Distillation (DFKD) has attracted attention recently thanks to its appealing capability of transferring knowledge from a teacher network to a student network without using training data. The main idea is to use a generator to synthesize data for training the student. As the generator gets updated, the distribution of synthetic data will change. Such distribution shift could be large if the generator and the student are trained adversarially, causing the student to forget the knowledge it acquired at the previous steps. To alleviate this problem, we propose a simple yet effective method called Momentum Adversarial Distillation (MAD) which maintains an exponential moving average (EMA) copy of the generator and uses synthetic samples from both the generator and the EMA generator to train the student. Since the EMA generator can be considered as an ensemble of the generator's old versions and often undergoes a smaller change in updates compared to the generator, training on its synthetic samples can help the student recall the past knowledge and prevent the student from adapting too quickly to the new updates of the generator. Our experiments on six benchmark datasets including big datasets like ImageNet and Places365 demonstrate the superior performance of MAD over competing methods for handling the large distribution shift problem. Our method also compares favorably to existing DFKD methods and even achieves state-of-the-art results in some cases.

Such distribution shift could be large if the generator and the student are trained adversarially, causing the student to forget the knowledge it acquired at the previous steps. To alleviate this problem, we propose a simple yet effective method called Momentum Adversarial Distillation (MAD) which maintains an exponential moving average (EMA) copy of the generator and uses synthetic samples from both the generator and the EMA generator to train the student. Since the EMA generator can be considered as an ensemble of the generator's old versions and often undergoes a smaller change in updates compared to the generator, training on its synthetic samples can help the student recall the past knowledge and prevent the student from adapting too quickly to the new updates of the generator. Our experiments on six benchmark datasets including big datasets like ImageNet and Places365 demonstrate the superior performance of MAD over competing methods for handling the large distribution shift problem. Our method also compares favorably to existing DFKD methods and even achieves state-of-the-art results in some cases.

paragraphs: Data-free knowledge distillation trains a student to learn from a teacher without using the original training data. A generator supplies synthetic examples instead. As that generator changes, its examples come from a changing distribution; adversarial training can make the changes large enough that the student forgets knowledge acquired earlier.

Momentum Adversarial Distillation maintains an exponential moving average copy of the generator. The student trains on examples from both the current generator and this averaged copy. Because the averaged generator incorporates earlier versions and often changes more gradually, its samples can help preserve earlier knowledge while moderating the student's adaptation to the newest examples.

Experiments on six benchmark datasets, including ImageNet and Places365, show better performance than competing methods for handling large distribution shifts. The method also compares favorably with existing data-free distillation approaches and reaches state-of-the-art results in some cases. Its central contribution is a way to stabilize the synthetic training distribution while retaining samples from the actively updated generator.
summary.tldr: Training on samples from both current and averaged generators helps data-free distillation reduce forgetting during large synthetic-data shifts.

title: Momentum Adversarial Distillation: Handling Large Distribution Shifts in Data-Free Knowledge Distillation

abstract: One of the most important AI research questions is to trade off computation versus performance since ``perfect rationality" exists in theory but is impossible to achieve in practice. Recently, Monte-Carlo tree search (MCTS) has attracted considerable attention due to the significant performance improvement in various challenging domains. However, the expensive time cost during search severely restricts its scope for applications. This paper proposes the Virtual MCTS (V-MCTS), a variant of MCTS that spends more search time on harder states and less search time on simpler states adaptively. We give theoretical bounds of the proposed method and evaluate the performance and computations on $9 \times 9$ Go board games and Atari games. Experiments show that our method can achieve comparable performances to the original search algorithm while requiring less than $50\%$ search time on average. We believe that this approach is a viable alternative for tasks under limited time and resources. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/YeWR/V-MCTS.git}.
originalAbstract: One of the most important AI research questions is to trade off computation versus performance since ``perfect rationality" exists in theory but is impossible to achieve in practice. However, the expensive time cost during search severely restricts its scope for applications. This paper proposes the Virtual MCTS (V-MCTS), a variant of MCTS that spends more search time on harder states and less search time on simpler states adaptively. We give theoretical bounds of the proposed method and evaluate the performance and computations on $9 \times 9$ Go board games and Atari games. Experiments show that our method can achieve comparable performances to the original search algorithm while requiring less than $50\%$ search time on average. We believe that this approach is a viable alternative for tasks under limited time and resources. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/YeWR/V-MCTS.git}.

paragraphs: Monte-Carlo tree search can improve decisions by exploring possible future actions, but that exploration can consume substantial time. This paper asks how to spend search computation more selectively. Its proposed variant, Virtual MCTS, adapts the amount of search to the difficulty of the state being considered.

The guiding idea is to devote more time to harder states and less to simpler ones. This makes the allocation of computation part of the search method itself. The authors provide theoretical bounds for their approach and evaluate both decision performance and computational cost, keeping the quality of the resulting actions alongside the time required to choose them.

Experiments use 9-by-9 Go and Atari games. In these evaluations, Virtual MCTS achieves performance comparable to the original search algorithm while using less than half its search time on average. The average-time qualification matters: the method deliberately varies effort across states. These results support adaptive search allocation as a viable approach for tasks with limited computation or decision time.
summary.tldr: Virtual MCTS allocates search time by state difficulty, retaining comparable game performance with less than half the average search time in reported experiments.

title: Spending Thinking Time Wisely: Accelerating MCTS with Virtual Expansions

abstract: We investigate the problem of learning an undirected, weighted bipartite graph under the Gaussian Markov random field model, for which we present an optimization formulation along with an efficient algorithm based on the projected gradient descent. Motivated by practical applications, where outliers or heavy-tailed events are present, we extend the proposed learning scheme to the case in which the data follow a multivariate Student-$t$ distribution. As a result, the optimization program is no longer convex, but a verifiably convergent iterative algorithm is proposed based on the majorization-minimization framework. Finally, we propose an efficient and provably convergent algorithm for learning $k$-component bipartite graphs that leverages rank constraints of the underlying graph Laplacian matrix. The proposed estimators outperform state-of-the-art methods for bipartite graph learning, as evidenced by real-world experiments using financial time series data.
