It uses rank constraints on the graph Laplacian and comes with an efficient, provably convergent algorithm. Experiments on real financial time series show the proposed estimators outperforming state-of-the-art bipartite graph learning methods. The paper thus connects distributional modeling and structural graph constraints, with empirical advantages demonstrated in that application.
summary.tldr: The paper develops convergent bipartite graph learning methods for Gaussian data, heavy tails, and specified numbers of connected components.

title: Learning Bipartite Graphs: Heavy Tails and Multiple Components

abstract: Monte Carlo integration is a key technique for designing randomized approximation schemes for counting problems, with applications, e.g., in machine learning and statistical physics. The technique typically enables massively parallel computation, however, with the risk that some of the delegated computations contain spontaneous or adversarial errors. We present an orchestration of the computations such that the outcome is accompanied with a proof of correctness that can be verified with substantially less computational resources than it takes to run the computations from scratch with state-of-the-art algorithms. Specifically, we adopt an algebraic proof system developed in computational complexity theory, in which the proof is represented by a polynomial; evaluating the polynomial at a random point amounts to a verification of the proof with probabilistic guarantees. We give examples of known Monte Carlo estimators that admit verifiable extensions with moderate computational overhead: for the permanent of zero--one matrices, for the model count of disjunctive normal form formulas, and for the gradient of logistic regression models. We also discuss the prospects and challenges of engineering efficient verifiable approximation schemes more generally.

Delegation introduces a verification problem when some computations contain accidental or adversarial errors. This paper asks how to accompany the result with evidence of correctness that is cheaper to check than recomputing the answer.

The paper also discusses challenges in engineering broader verifiable approximation schemes. Its contribution is probabilistic verification of delegated approximation computations, with concrete examples demonstrating the approach.
summary.tldr: Algebraic proof systems let selected Monte Carlo computations carry correctness evidence that is cheaper to verify than to recompute.

title: Trustworthy Monte Carlo

abstract: Due to the rapid growth in the scale of circuits and the desire for knowledge transfer from old designs to new ones, deep learning technologies have been widely exploited in Electronic Design Automation (EDA) to assist circuit design. In chip design cycles, we might encounter heterogeneous and diverse information sources, including the two most informative ones: the netlist and the design layout. However, handling each information source independently is sub-optimal. In this paper, we propose a novel way to integrate the multiple information sources under a unified heterogeneous graph named Circuit Graph, where topological and geometrical information is well integrated. Then, we propose Circuit GNN to fully utilize the features of vertices, edges as well as heterogeneous information during the message passing process. It is the first attempt to design a versatile circuit representation that is compatible across multiple EDA tasks and stages. Experiments on the two most representative prediction tasks in EDA show that our solution reaches state-of-the-art performance in both logic synthesis and global placement chip design stages. Besides, it achieves a 10x speed-up on congestion prediction compared to the state-of-the-art model.

paragraphs: Circuit design produces several kinds of information, including the netlist describing connectivity and the layout describing geometry. Treating these sources independently can miss useful connections between them. This paper proposes a shared representation that integrates both kinds of information for learning across electronic-design-automation tasks and stages.

The representation, called Circuit Graph, is a heterogeneous graph that combines topological and geometric information. Circuit GNN processes it through message passing that uses vertex features, edge features, and the differences among information types. The aim is a versatile circuit representation that can serve multiple tasks rather than requiring each information source to be handled separately.

Experiments on two representative prediction tasks report state-of-the-art performance in both logic synthesis and global placement stages. For congestion prediction, the method also achieves a tenfold speedup over the state-of-the-art comparison model. These findings support the practical value of combining circuit connectivity and geometry in one graph, with benefits spanning prediction quality and computation time in the evaluated design settings.
summary.tldr: Circuit Graph and Circuit GNN combine connectivity and layout information, achieving strong cross-stage prediction results and a reported tenfold congestion-prediction speedup.

title: Versatile Multi-stage Graph Neural Network for Circuit Representation

abstract: We introduce the notion of performative power, which measures the ability of a firm operating an algorithmic system, such as a digital content recommendation platform, to cause change in a population of participants. We relate performative power to the economic study of competition in digital economies. Traditional economic concepts struggle with identifying anti-competitive patterns in digital platforms not least due to the complexity of market definition. In contrast, performative power is a causal notion that is identifiable with minimal knowledge of the market, its internals, participants, products, or prices.Low performative power implies that a firm can do no better than to optimize their objective on current data. In contrast, firms of high performative power stand to benefit from steering the population towards more profitable behavior. We confirm in a simple theoretical model that monopolies maximize performative power. A firm's ability to personalize increases performative power, while competition and outside options decrease performative power. On the empirical side, we propose an observational causal design to identify performative power from discontinuities in how digital platforms display content. This allows to repurpose causal effects from various studies about digital platforms as lower bounds on performative power. Finally, we speculate about the role that performative power might play in competition policy and antitrust enforcement in digital marketplaces.

paragraphs: Performative power measures how much a firm operating an algorithmic system can causally change the behavior of a participating population. The paper proposes this concept as a way to study competition in digital markets, where traditional analysis can struggle to define the relevant market. Its identification requires little knowledge of market internals.

The theory links this power to a firm's incentives. With low performative power, optimizing its objective on current data is the best it can do. High power creates opportunities to benefit by steering behavior. In a simple theoretical model, monopolies maximize this power, personalization increases it, and competition and outside options reduce it.

The authors propose an observational causal design based on discontinuities in how platforms display content. This lets causal effects from existing platform studies serve as lower bounds on performative power. The paper thereby connects a theoretical measure to observable behavior. Its discussion of competition policy and antitrust remains speculative, proposing a possible role for the concept rather than establishing a policy prescription.
summary.tldr: Performative power measures a platform's causal influence on participants and connects that influence to competition, personalization, and possible policy analysis.

title: Performative Power

abstract: In this paper, we derive upper bounds on generalization errors for deep neural networks with Markov datasets. These bounds are developed based on Koltchinskii and Panchenko's approach for bounding the generalization error of combined classifiers with i.i.d. datasets. The development of new symmetrization inequalities in high-dimensional probability for Markov chains is a key element in our extension, where the spectral gap of the infinitesimal generator of the Markov chain plays a key parameter in these inequalities. We also propose a simple method to convert these bounds and other similar ones in traditional deep learning and machine learning to Bayesian counterparts for both i.i.d. and Markov datasets. Extensions to $m$-order homogeneous Markov chains such as AR and ARMA models and mixtures of several Markov data services are given.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we derive upper bounds on generalization errors for deep neural networks with Markov datasets. These bounds are developed based on Koltchinskii and Panchenko's approach for bounding the generalization error of combined classifiers with i.i.d. datasets. The development of new symmetrization inequalities in high-dimensional probability for Markov chains is a key element in our extension, where the spectral gap of the infinitesimal generator of the Markov chain plays a key parameter in these inequalities. We also propose a simple method to convert these bounds and other similar ones in traditional deep learning and machine learning to Bayesian counterparts for both i.i.d. and Markov datasets. Extensions to $m$-order homogeneous Markov chains such as AR and ARMA models and mixtures of several Markov data services are given.

paragraphs: This paper develops upper bounds on the generalisation error of deep neural networks trained on Markov datasets. Such data has dependence between observations, so an analysis built for independent samples does not directly describe the same setting. The authors extend an existing approach for bounding the errors of combined classifiers with independent, identically distributed data.

The central technical contribution is a set of new symmetrisation inequalities for Markov chains. These provide the probabilistic machinery needed for the extension. A key parameter is the spectral gap of the chain's infinitesimal generator, making a property of the data-generating process part of the generalisation analysis rather than treating dependence as irrelevant.

The authors also propose a simple conversion from these bounds, and other similar learning bounds, to Bayesian counterparts for both independent and Markov datasets. Further extensions cover higher-order homogeneous Markov chains, including AR and ARMA models, and mixtures of Markov data sources. The result is a broader theoretical framework for generalisation under dependent data, rather than an empirical claim about a particular trained network.
summary.tldr: New probability inequalities extend neural network generalisation bounds to Markov data and support Bayesian and higher-order extensions.

title: Generalization Error Bounds on Deep Learning with Markov Datasets

abstract: We develop a simple and unified framework for nonlinear variable importance estimation that incorporates uncertainty in the prediction function and is compatible with a wide range of machine learning models (e.g., tree ensembles, kernel methods, neural networks, etc). In particular, for a learned nonlinear model $f(\mathbf{x})$, we consider quantifying the importance of an input variable $\mathbf{x}^j$ using the integrated partial derivative $\Psi_j = \Vert \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{x}^j} f(\mathbf{x})\Vert^2_{P_\mathcal{X}}$. We then (1) provide a principled approach for quantifying uncertainty in variable importance by deriving its posterior distribution, and (2) show that the approach is generalizable even to non-differentiable models such as tree ensembles. Rigorous Bayesian nonparametric theorems are derived to guarantee the posterior consistency and asymptotic uncertainty of the proposed approach. Extensive simulations and experiments on healthcare benchmark datasets confirm that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing classical and recent variable selection methods.

In particular, for a learned nonlinear model $f(\mathbf{x})$, we consider quantifying the importance of an input variable $\mathbf{x}^j$ using the integrated partial derivative $\Psi_j = \Vert \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{x}^j} f(\mathbf{x})\Vert^2_{P_\mathcal{X}}$. We then (1) provide a principled approach for quantifying uncertainty in variable importance by deriving its posterior distribution, and (2) show that the approach is generalizable even to non-differentiable models such as tree ensembles. Rigorous Bayesian nonparametric theorems are derived to guarantee the posterior consistency and asymptotic uncertainty of the proposed approach. Extensive simulations and experiments on healthcare benchmark datasets confirm that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing classical and recent variable selection methods.

paragraphs: Knowing which inputs matter to a nonlinear prediction model requires more than a single importance score when the learned function itself is uncertain. This paper develops a common framework for estimating variable importance while carrying that uncertainty into the result. It is designed to work across model families, including neural networks, kernel methods, and tree ensembles.

The importance measure is the squared partial derivative of the prediction function, integrated over the input distribution. In plain language, it summarizes how sensitive predictions are to changes in a particular input. The authors derive a posterior distribution for this importance quantity, so the output expresses uncertainty about importance rather than treating the learned prediction function as fixed.

The approach extends to models that are not differentiable, including tree ensembles. Bayesian nonparametric theory provides guarantees concerning posterior consistency and asymptotic uncertainty. Simulations and healthcare benchmark experiments report better variable selection than classical and recent alternatives. The contribution brings a shared sensitivity-based definition and uncertainty analysis to otherwise different nonlinear modelling approaches.
summary.tldr: The paper estimates nonlinear variable importance with posterior uncertainty and theoretical guarantees across several model families.

title: Towards a Unified Framework for Uncertainty-aware Nonlinear Variable Selection with Theoretical Guarantees

abstract: Bipartite graphs can be used to model a wide variety of dyadic information such as user-rating, document-term, and gene-disorder pairs. Biclustering is an extension of clustering to the underlying bipartite graph induced from this kind of data. In this paper, we leverage optimal transport (OT) which has gained momentum in the machine learning community to propose a novel and scalable biclustering model that generalizes several classical biclustering approaches. We perform extensive experimentation to show the validity of our approach compared to other OT biclustering algorithms along both dimensions of the dyadic datasets.

paragraphs: Many datasets describe relationships between two kinds of entities, such as documents and terms or genes and disorders. A bipartite graph represents these two sides and the connections between them. Biclustering seeks groups across both sides, allowing the structure of their relationships to guide how the data are organized.

This paper proposes a scalable biclustering model built on optimal transport. The model generalizes several classical biclustering approaches, placing them within a broader formulation. That connection matters because the contribution is both a new approach to grouping paired data and a framework that encompasses established ways of expressing the problem.

The authors evaluate the method extensively against other optimal-transport biclustering algorithms, examining results along both dimensions of the datasets. Their experiments support the validity of the approach for the paired-data setting. Assessing both sides is central to the task: a useful biclustering method must account for the organization of each entity type as well as the relationships linking the two.
summary.tldr: A scalable optimal-transport model generalizes classical biclustering approaches and is evaluated on both sides of paired datasets.

title: Efficient and Effective Optimal Transport-Based Biclustering

abstract: We develop and analyze algorithms for distributionally robust optimization (DRO) of convex losses. In particular, we consider group-structured and bounded $f$-divergence uncertainty sets. Our approach relies on an accelerated method that queries a ball optimization oracle, i.e., a subroutine that minimizes the objective within a small ball around the query point. Our main contribution is efficient implementations of this oracle for DRO objectives. For DRO with $N$ non-smooth loss functions, the resulting algorithms find an $\epsilon$-accurate solution with $\widetilde{O}\left(N\epsilon^{-2/3} + \epsilon^{-2}\right)$ first-order oracle queries to individual loss functions. Compared to existing algorithms for this problem, we improve complexity by a factor of up to $\epsilon^{-4/3}$.

paragraphs: Distributionally robust optimization seeks solutions that account for uncertainty about the data distribution. This paper studies the problem for convex losses and two specified forms of uncertainty: group-structured sets and sets bounded by an f-divergence. Its goal is to reduce the computational work needed to obtain an accurate solution.

The approach uses an accelerated optimization method built around a ball optimization oracle. This oracle is a subroutine that minimizes the objective within a small ball surrounding a supplied point. The main contribution is an efficient implementation of that local optimization subroutine for the distributionally robust objectives under consideration.

For N nonsmooth loss functions, the resulting algorithms reach epsilon accuracy using approximately N times epsilon to the power negative two-thirds, plus epsilon to the power negative two, first-order queries, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Relative to existing algorithms, the complexity improvement can be as large as a factor of epsilon to the power negative four-thirds. These are guarantees about query requirements for the specified convex problems, showing how efficient local optimization can support faster overall optimization.
summary.tldr: Efficient local ball optimization enables accelerated algorithms with improved query complexity for specified convex distributionally robust problems.

title: Distributionally Robust Optimization via Ball Oracle Acceleration

abstract: In this work, we study the simple yet universally applicable case of reward shaping in value-based Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL). We show that reward shifting in the form of a linear transformation is equivalent to changing the initialization of the $Q$-function in function approximation. Based on such an equivalence, we bring the key insight that a positive reward shifting leads to conservative exploitation, while a negative reward shifting leads to curiosity-driven exploration. Accordingly, conservative exploitation improves offline RL value estimation, and optimistic value estimation improves exploration for online RL. We validate our insight on a range of RL tasks and show its improvement over baselines: (1) In offline RL, the conservative exploitation leads to improved performance based on off-the-shelf algorithms; (2) In online continuous control, multiple value functions with different shifting constants can be used to tackle the exploration-exploitation dilemma for better sample efficiency; (3) In discrete control tasks, a negative reward shifting yields an improvement over the curiosity-based exploration method.

paragraphs: This paper studies how shifting rewards changes learning in value-based deep reinforcement learning. Its central result connects a linear reward transformation with changing the initialization of the approximated Q-function. That equivalence gives a way to understand reward shifting through the value estimates that guide an agent's decisions.

The authors identify different effects for the direction of the shift. Positive reward shifting encourages conservative exploitation, while negative shifting encourages curiosity-driven exploration. They use the former to improve value estimation in offline learning and the latter to support exploration during online interaction. The same simple intervention therefore serves different purposes depending on how it is applied.

Experiments support these insights across several settings. Conservative exploitation improves offline performance with existing algorithms. In online continuous control, multiple value functions with different shift constants improve sample efficiency by addressing exploration and exploitation together. For discrete control, negative reward shifting improves a curiosity-based exploration method. These are reported task-level improvements, grounded in the proposed initialization equivalence.
summary.tldr: Reward shifts act like changes to Q-function initialization, supporting conservative offline learning or exploratory online learning depending on their sign.

title: Exploit Reward Shifting in Value-Based Deep-RL: Optimistic Curiosity-Based Exploration and Conservative Exploitation via Linear Reward Shaping

abstract: Automatically determining whether a text and a corresponding image are semantically aligned is a significant challenge for vision-language models, with applications in generative text-to-image and image-to-text tasks. In this work, we study methods for automatic text-image alignment evaluation. We first introduce SeeTRUE: a comprehensive evaluation set, spanning multiple datasets from both text-to-image and image-to-text generation tasks, with human judgements for whether a given text-image pair is semantically aligned. We then describe two automatic methods to determine alignment: the first involving a pipeline based on question generation and visual question answering models, and the second employing an end-to-end classification approach by finetuning multimodal pretrained models. Both methods surpass prior approaches in various text-image alignment tasks, with significant improvements in challenging cases that involve complex composition or unnatural images. Finally, we demonstrate how our approaches can localize specific misalignments between an image and a given text, and how they can be used to automatically re-rank candidates in text-to-image generation.

paragraphs: A generated image and its text can appear broadly related while disagreeing on specific meaning. This paper studies automatic evaluation of that semantic alignment for both text-to-image and image-to-text generation. The authors introduce SeeTRUE, an evaluation collection spanning several datasets with human judgments about whether individual text-image pairs agree. It provides a common basis for assessing automatic alignment methods.

The paper develops two approaches. One generates questions and uses visual question-answering models to check the image against the text. The other fine-tunes pretrained multimodal models to classify alignment directly. These approaches offer different routes to the same judgment: checking through questions or learning an end-to-end decision from the paired inputs.

Both methods outperform previous approaches across various alignment tasks, with substantial gains on difficult compositions and unnatural images. The authors also demonstrate localization of specific disagreements and automatic reranking of text-to-image candidates. This connects evaluation to practical generation workflows: an alignment method can help identify what is wrong and choose among alternative outputs, as well as assign an overall judgment.
summary.tldr: SeeTRUE and two automatic evaluation methods improve text-image alignment judgments, identify specific mismatches, and support reranking generated images.

title: What You See is What You Read? Improving Text-Image Alignment Evaluation

abstract: There is growing interest in improving our algorithmic understanding of fundamental statistical problems such as mean estimation, driven by the goal of understanding the fundamental limits of what we can extract from limited and valuable data.The state of the art results for mean estimation in $\mathbb{R}$ are 1) the optimal sub-Gaussian mean estimator by [Lee and Valiant, 2022], attaining the optimal sub-Gaussian error constant for all distributions with finite but unknown variance, and 2) the analysis of the median-of-means algorithm by [Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi and Lugosi, 2013] and a matching lower bound by [Devroye, Lerasle, Lugosi, and Oliveira, 2016], characterizing the big-O optimal errors for distributions that have tails heavy enough that only a $1+\alpha$ moment exists for some $\alpha \in (0,1)$.Both of these results, however, are optimal only in the worst case.Motivated by the recent effort in the community to go "beyond the worst-case analysis" of algorithms, we initiate the fine-grained study of the mean estimation problem:Is it possible for algorithms to leverage *beneficial* features/quirks of their input distribution to *beat* the sub-Gaussian rate, without explicit knowledge of these features?We resolve this question, finding an unexpectedly nuanced answer: "Yes in limited regimes, but in general no".Given a distribution $p$, assuming *only* that it has a finite mean and absent any additional assumptions,we show how to construct a distribution $q_{n,\delta}$ such that the means of $p$ and $q$ are well-separated, yet $p$ and $q$ are impossible to distinguish with $n$ samples with probability $1-\delta$, and $q$ further preserves the finiteness of moments of $p$.Moreover, the variance of $q$ is at most twice the variance of $p$ if it exists.The main consequence of our result is that, no reasonable estimator can asymptotically achieve better than the sub-Gaussian error rate for any distribution, up to constant factors, which matches the worst-case result of [Lee and Valiant, 2022].More generally, we introduce a new definitional framework to analyze the fine-grained optimality of algorithms, which we call "neighborhood optimality", interpolating between the unattainably strong "instance optimality" and the trivially weak admissibility/Pareto optimality definitions.As an application of the new framework, we show that the median-of-means algorithm is neighborhood optimal, up to constant factors.It is an open question to find a neighborhood-optimal estimator *without* constant factor slackness.
originalAbstract: There is growing interest in improving our algorithmic understanding of fundamental statistical problems such as mean estimation, driven by the goal of understanding the fundamental limits of what we can extract from limited and valuable data.The state of the art results for mean estimation in $\mathbb{R}$ are 1) the optimal sub-Gaussian mean estimator by [Lee and Valiant, 2022], attaining the optimal sub-Gaussian error constant for all distributions with finite but unknown variance, and 2) the analysis of the median-of-means algorithm by [Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi and Lugosi, 2013] and a matching lower bound by [Devroye, Lerasle, Lugosi, and Oliveira, 2016], characterizing the big-O optimal errors for distributions that have tails heavy enough that only a $1+\alpha$ moment exists for some $\alpha \in (0,1)$.Both of these results, however, are optimal only in the worst case.Motivated by the recent effort in the community to go "beyond the worst-case analysis" of algorithms, we initiate the fine-grained study of the mean estimation problem:Is it possible for algorithms to leverage *beneficial* features/quirks of their input distribution to *beat* the sub-Gaussian rate, without explicit knowledge of these features?We resolve this question, finding an unexpectedly nuanced answer: "Yes in limited regimes, but in general no".Given a distribution $p$, assuming *only* that it has a finite mean and absent any additional assumptions,we show how to construct a distribution $q_{n,\delta}$ such that the means of $p$ and $q$ are well-separated, yet $p$ and $q$ are impossible to distinguish with $n$ samples with probability $1-\delta$, and $q$ further preserves the finiteness of moments of $p$.Moreover, the variance of $q$ is at most twice the variance of $p$ if it exists.The main consequence of our result is that, no reasonable estimator can asymptotically achieve better than the sub-Gaussian error rate for any distribution, up to constant factors, which matches the worst-case result of [Lee and Valiant, 2022].More generally, we introduce a new definitional framework to analyze the fine-grained optimality of algorithms, which we call "neighborhood optimality", interpolating between the unattainably strong "instance optimality" and the trivially weak admissibility/Pareto optimality definitions.As an application of the new framework, we show that the median-of-means algorithm is neighborhood optimal, up to constant factors.It is an open question to find a neighborhood-optimal estimator *without* constant factor slackness.

paragraphs: Can a mean estimator automatically exploit favorable properties of a distribution to outperform guarantees designed for the worst case? This paper gives a qualified answer: improvement is possible in limited regimes, but not generally. It studies this question assuming only that the distribution has a finite mean, without supplying additional structural information.

The core construction creates another distribution whose mean is well separated from the original, yet which cannot be reliably distinguished from it with the specified sample size and confidence. This alternative preserves whichever moments are finite; when variance exists, its variance is at most twice the original's. The ambiguity limits how accurately an estimator can adapt to apparently favorable data.

The authors conclude that no reasonable estimator can asymptotically beat the sub-Gaussian error rate by more than constant factors for any distribution. They introduce neighborhood optimality to formalize a useful middle ground between overly demanding instance optimality and weak admissibility. Median-of-means is neighborhood optimal up to constants; removing that constant-factor slack remains open.
summary.tldr: Indistinguishable nearby distributions limit adaptive mean estimation, motivating a neighborhood-optimality framework in which median-of-means is optimal up to constants.

title: Optimality in Mean Estimation: Beyond Worst-Case, Beyond Sub-Gaussian, and Beyond $1+\alpha$ Moments

abstract: The combination of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) with ensemble methods has been proved to be highly effective in addressing complex sequential decision-making problems. This success can be primarily attributed to the utilization of multiple models, which enhances both the robustness of the policy and the accuracy of value function estimation. However, there has been limited analysis of the empirical success of current ensemble RL methods thus far. Our new analysis reveals that the sample efficiency of previous ensemble DRL algorithms may be limited by sub-policies that are not as diverse as they could be. Motivated by these findings, our study introduces a new ensemble RL algorithm, termed \textbf{T}rajectories-awar\textbf{E} \textbf{E}nsemble exploratio\textbf{N} (TEEN). The primary goal of TEEN is to maximize the expected return while promoting more diverse trajectories. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that TEEN not only enhances the sample diversity of the ensemble policy compared to using sub-policies alone but also improves the performance over ensemble RL algorithms. On average, TEEN outperforms the baseline ensemble DRL algorithms by 41\% in performance on the tested representative environments.

paragraphs: Ensemble reinforcement learning combines multiple models to improve decision making and value estimation. Yet having several sub-policies does not necessarily produce sufficiently varied experience. The paper analyzes existing ensemble methods and finds that limited diversity among their sub-policies may restrict sample efficiency, reducing the benefit obtained from each interaction with the environment.

The proposed algorithm, TEEN, pursues high expected return while encouraging diverse trajectories. A trajectory is the sequence of experience generated as decisions unfold, so the diversity objective concerns how policies move through the task over time. This connects exploration to the variety of complete experiences produced by the ensemble.

Experiments show that TEEN increases the ensemble policy's sample diversity compared with using sub-policies alone and improves performance over the evaluated ensemble algorithms. The reported average performance gain is 41% across the tested representative environments. These results support the paper's diagnosis that trajectory diversity is a useful design target, with the numerical improvement applying to its evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: TEEN promotes diverse trajectories alongside reward maximization, improving exploration and average performance in the tested ensemble reinforcement learning environments.

title: Keep Various Trajectories: Promoting Exploration of Ensemble Policies in Continuous Control

abstract: Given a set of calibrated images of a scene, we present an approach that produces a simple, compact, and actionable 3D world representation by means of 3D primitives. While many approaches focus on recovering high-fidelity 3D scenes, we focus on parsing a scene into mid-level 3D representations made of a small set of textured primitives. Such representations are interpretable, easy to manipulate and suited for physics-based simulations. Moreover, unlike existing primitive decomposition methods that rely on 3D input data, our approach operates directly on images through differentiable rendering. Specifically, we model primitives as textured superquadric meshes and optimize their parameters from scratch with an image rendering loss. We highlight the importance of modeling transparency for each primitive, which is critical for optimization and also enables handling varying numbers of primitives. We show that the resulting textured primitives faithfully reconstruct the input images and accurately model the visible 3D points, while providing amodal shape completions of unseen object regions. We compare our approach to the state of the art on diverse scenes from DTU, and demonstrate its robustness on real-life captures from BlendedMVS and Nerfstudio. We also showcase how our results can be used to effortlessly edit a scene or perform physical simulations. Code and video results are available at https://www.tmonnier.com/DBW.

paragraphs: Differentiable Blocks World builds a compact three-dimensional scene description from calibrated images. Its target is a small collection of textured geometric primitives that people can interpret and manipulate. Such a representation also supports physical simulation, giving the reconstruction a practical role beyond reproducing how a scene looks.

The method represents primitives as textured superquadric meshes and optimizes their parameters from scratch. Differentiable rendering connects the current three-dimensional description to rendered images, allowing image mismatch to guide fitting. Each primitive also has transparency, which the authors identify as crucial for optimization and for accommodating varying numbers of primitives.

The reported results show faithful reconstruction of input images and accurate modeling of visible three-dimensional points, alongside completion of unseen object regions. Comparisons use diverse DTU scenes, while additional real captures from BlendedMVS and Nerfstudio demonstrate robustness. Scene editing and physical simulation examples show why a compact primitive decomposition is useful: the recovered scene consists of manipulable components rather than only a visual reconstruction.
summary.tldr: Differentiable Blocks World reconstructs calibrated images as compact collections of textured 3D primitives suitable for editing and simulation.

title: Differentiable Blocks World: Qualitative 3D Decomposition by Rendering Primitives

abstract: The objective of pedestrian trajectory prediction is to estimate the future paths of pedestrians by leveraging historical observations, which plays a vital role in ensuring the safety of self-driving vehicles and navigation robots. Previous works usually rely on a sufficient amount of observation time to accurately predict future trajectories. However, there are many real-world situations where the model lacks sufficient time to observe, such as when pedestrians abruptly emerge from blind spots, resulting in inaccurate predictions and even safety risks. Therefore, it is necessary to perform trajectory prediction based on instantaneous observations, which has rarely been studied before. In this paper, we propose a Bi-directional Consistent Diffusion framework tailored for instantaneous trajectory prediction, named BCDiff. At its heart, we develop two coupled diffusion models by designing a mutual guidance mechanism which can bidirectionally and consistently generate unobserved historical trajectories and future trajectories step-by-step, to utilize the complementary information between them. Specifically, at each step, the predicted unobserved historical trajectories and limited observed trajectories guide one diffusion model to generate future trajectories, while the predicted future trajectories and observed trajectories guide the other diffusion model to predict unobserved historical trajectories. Given the presence of relatively high noise in the generated trajectories during the initial steps, we introduce a gating mechanism to learn the weights between the predicted trajectories and the limited observed trajectories for automatically balancing their contributions. By means of this iterative and mutually guided generation process, both the future and unobserved historical trajectories undergo continuous refinement, ultimately leading to accurate predictions. Essentially, BCDiff is an encoder-free framework that can be compatible with existing trajectory prediction models in principle. Experiments show that our proposed BCDiff significantly improves the accuracy of instantaneous trajectory prediction on the ETH/UCY and Stanford Drone datasets, compared to related approaches.

paragraphs: Pedestrian prediction becomes difficult when a person appears suddenly and there is little motion history to observe. BCDiff addresses this instantaneous prediction setting by generating both a possible unobserved past and a future trajectory. The idea is that these two estimates contain complementary information that can help improve each other despite the limited observations.

The framework couples two diffusion models through repeated mutual guidance. One generates future paths using the observed motion and the current estimate of the missing history. The other reconstructs that history using the observations and the predicted future. Because generated paths are particularly noisy early in this process, a learned gate balances their influence against the available observations.

This iterative exchange progressively refines both trajectory estimates. Experiments on ETH/UCY and Stanford Drone report significantly improved instantaneous prediction accuracy relative to related approaches. BCDiff also avoids an encoder, and the authors describe compatibility with existing trajectory predictors in principle. That compatibility is an architectural possibility, distinct from the demonstrated accuracy gains on the evaluated datasets.
summary.tldr: BCDiff improves prediction from limited pedestrian observations by letting diffusion models jointly refine missing history and future paths.

title: BCDiff: Bidirectional Consistent Diffusion for Instantaneous Trajectory Prediction

abstract: Bayesian bandit algorithms with approximate Bayesian inference have been widely used in real-world applications. However, there is a large discrepancy between the superior practical performance of these approaches and their theoretical justification. Previous research only indicates a negative theoretical result: Thompson sampling could have a worst-case linear regret $\Omega(T)$ with a constant threshold on the inference error measured by one $\alpha$-divergence. To bridge this gap, we propose an Enhanced Bayesian Upper Confidence Bound (EBUCB) framework that can efficiently accommodate bandit problems in the presence of approximate inference. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that for Bernoulli multi-armed bandits, EBUCB can achieve the optimal regret order $O(\log T)$ if the inference error measured by two different $\alpha$-divergences is less than a constant, regardless of how large this constant is. To our best knowledge, our study provides the first theoretical regret bound that is better than $o(T)$ in the setting of constant approximate inference error. Furthermore, in concordance with the negative results in previous studies, we show that only one bounded $\alpha$-divergence is insufficient to guarantee a sub-linear regret.

paragraphs: Bayesian bandit methods use uncertainty estimates to choose among actions, but practical implementations often approximate Bayesian inference. Previous theory showed that Thompson sampling can accumulate linear regret when approximation error is bounded using just one alpha-divergence. Regret measures the accumulated performance shortfall, so linear growth can represent a persistent cost of poor decisions.

The paper proposes Enhanced Bayesian Upper Confidence Bound, or EBUCB, to accommodate approximate inference. For Bernoulli multi-armed bandits, its analysis establishes the optimal logarithmic regret order when error measured by two different alpha-divergences remains below a constant. The constant need not be small, although the statement concerns the growth order rather than identical performance for all error levels.

The authors also show that controlling only one alpha-divergence is insufficient to guarantee sublinear regret. The result therefore separates two forms of approximation control that might otherwise seem similar. It provides a positive guarantee for EBUCB under a specific pair of error conditions, while preserving the negative conclusion for the weaker, single-divergence condition.
summary.tldr: EBUCB achieves logarithmic regret for Bernoulli bandits when approximate-inference error is bounded by two distinct alpha-divergences.

title: Optimal Regret Is Achievable with Bounded Approximate Inference Error: An Enhanced Bayesian Upper Confidence Bound Framework

abstract: In adaptive data analysis, a mechanism gets $n$ i.i.d. samples from an unknown distribution $\cal{D}$, andis required to provide accurate estimations to a sequence of adaptively chosen statistical queries with respect to $\cal{D}$.Hardt and Ullman (FOCS 2014) and Steinke and Ullman (COLT 2015) showed that in general, it is computationally hard to answer more than $\Theta(n^2)$ adaptive queries, assuming the existence of one-way functions. However, these negative results strongly rely on an adversarial model that significantly advantages the adversarial analyst over the mechanism, as the analyst, who chooses the adaptive queries, also chooses the underlying distribution $\cal{D}$. This imbalance raises questions with respect to the applicability of the obtained hardness results -- an analyst who has complete knowledge of the underlying distribution $\cal{D}$ would have little need, if at all, to issue statistical queries to a mechanism which only holds a finite number of samples from $\cal{D}$.We consider more restricted adversaries, called \emph{balanced}, where each such adversary consists of two separated algorithms: The \emph{sampler} who is the entity that chooses the distribution and provides the samples to the mechanism, and the \emph{analyst} who chooses the adaptive queries, but has no prior knowledge of the underlying distribution (and hence has no a priori advantage with respect to the mechanism). We improve the quality of previous lower bounds by revisiting them using an efficient \emph{balanced} adversary, under standard public-key cryptography assumptions. We show that these stronger hardness assumptions are unavoidable in the sense that any computationally bounded \emph{balanced} adversary that has the structure of all known attacks, implies the existence of public-key cryptography.

paragraphs: Adaptive data analysis asks a mechanism to answer statistical questions using samples from an unknown distribution, with later questions depending on earlier answers. Previous computational hardness results relied on an adversarial analyst who also selected the distribution. That analyst therefore had an informational advantage over the mechanism, raising questions about how well the setting represents an analyst seeking unknown information.

This paper studies balanced adversaries by separating two roles. A sampler chooses the distribution and supplies samples, while an analyst selects adaptive queries without prior knowledge of that distribution. Under standard public-key cryptography assumptions, the authors revisit earlier lower bounds using an efficient adversary that respects this separation. Thus, computational difficulty persists in a setting with a more balanced allocation of knowledge.

The paper also examines why stronger cryptographic assumptions appear in this construction. It shows that any computationally bounded balanced adversary with the structure shared by known attacks would imply public-key cryptography. This conclusion concerns that attack structure; it does not establish that every conceivable balanced attack requires it. The contribution clarifies both the hardness result and the assumptions supporting it.
summary.tldr: Adaptive-query hardness persists with a less informed analyst under public-key cryptographic assumptions, whose necessity is established for known attack structures.

title: Adaptive Data Analysis in a Balanced Adversarial Model

abstract: Semi-Supervised Domain Generalization (SSDG) aims to learn a model that is generalizable to an unseen target domain with only a few labels, and most existing SSDG methods assume that unlabeled training and testing samples are all known classes. However, a more realistic scenario is that known classes may be mixed with some unknown classes in unlabeled training and testing data. To deal with such a scenario, we propose the Class-Wise Adaptive Exploration and Exploitation (CWAEE) method. In particular, we explore unlabeled training data by using one-vs-rest classifiers and class-wise adaptive thresholds to detect known and unknown classes, and exploit them by adopting consistency regularization on augmented samples based on Fourier Transformation to improve the unseen domain generalization. The experiments conducted on real-world datasets verify the effectiveness and superiority of our method.

However, a more realistic scenario is that known classes may be mixed with some unknown classes in unlabeled training and testing data. To deal with such a scenario, we propose the Class-Wise Adaptive Exploration and Exploitation (CWAEE) method. In particular, we explore unlabeled training data by using one-vs-rest classifiers and class-wise adaptive thresholds to detect known and unknown classes, and exploit them by adopting consistency regularization on augmented samples based on Fourier Transformation to improve the unseen domain generalization. paragraphs: Semi-supervised domain generalization aims to learn from few labels and still perform well in an unseen domain. Many approaches assume that every unlabeled training example and every test example belongs to a known class. This paper addresses the more difficult situation in which those data also contain classes outside the known set.

The proposed CWAEE method separates the work into exploring and exploiting unlabeled data. For exploration, it uses one-versus-rest classifiers together with thresholds adapted to individual classes to detect known and unknown classes. This makes class identification sensitive to differences among classes instead of imposing one shared decision threshold on all of them.

For exploitation, the method applies consistency regularization to augmented samples produced using Fourier Transformation. This component encourages consistent predictions across those transformations to improve generalization to the unseen domain. Experiments on real-world datasets support the method's effectiveness and superiority in the evaluated setting. Its central contribution is to combine class-aware detection with a generalization objective while explicitly accounting for unknown classes in both unlabeled training data and testing.
summary.tldr: CWAEE combines class-specific detection thresholds with Fourier-based consistency training to generalize across domains when unlabeled data include unknown classes.

title: Semi-Supervised Domain Generalization with Known and Unknown Classes

abstract: Weakly-Supervised Concealed Object Segmentation (WSCOS) aims to segment objects well blended with surrounding environments using sparsely-annotated data for model training. It remains a challenging task since (1) it is hard to distinguish concealed objects from the background due to the intrinsic similarity and (2) the sparsely-annotated training data only provide weak supervision for model learning. In this paper, we propose a new WSCOS method to address these two challenges. To tackle the intrinsic similarity challenge, we design a multi-scale feature grouping module that first groups features at different granularities and then aggregates these grouping results. By grouping similar features together, it encourages segmentation coherence, helping obtain complete segmentation results for both single and multiple-object images. For the weak supervision challenge, we utilize the recently-proposed vision foundation model, ``Segment Anything Model (SAM)'', and use the provided sparse annotations as prompts to generate segmentation masks, which are used to train the model. To alleviate the impact of low-quality segmentation masks, we further propose a series of strategies, including multi-augmentation result ensemble, entropy-based pixel-level weighting, and entropy-based image-level selection. These strategies help provide more reliable supervision to train the segmentation model. We verify the effectiveness of our method on various WSCOS tasks, and experiments demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on these tasks.

paragraphs: Segmenting concealed objects is difficult because their appearance closely resembles the surrounding background. Sparse training annotations add another challenge by providing only limited supervision. This paper addresses both problems with a method that combines multi-scale feature grouping and training masks generated using the Segment Anything Model, or SAM.

The feature-grouping module organizes similar features at several granularities and aggregates the results. This encourages coherent segmentation and helps recover complete objects in images containing one or several objects. For supervision, the method uses the available sparse annotations as prompts to SAM, producing segmentation masks that serve as training labels.

Because those generated masks can be poor, the authors add three reliability measures: combining results across multiple augmentations, weighting individual pixels using entropy, and selecting images using entropy. These steps improve the supervision available to the segmentation model. Experiments across several weakly supervised concealed-object segmentation tasks report state-of-the-art performance, supporting the combined treatment of visual ambiguity and sparse labeling.
summary.tldr: Multi-scale feature grouping and reliability-filtered SAM masks improve concealed-object segmentation from sparse annotations.

title: Weakly-Supervised Concealed Object Segmentation with SAM-based Pseudo Labeling and Multi-scale Feature Grouping

abstract: In the era of extensive intersection between art and Artificial Intelligence (AI), such as image generation and fiction co-creation, AI for music remains relatively nascent, particularly in music understanding. This is evident in the limited work on deep music representations, the scarcity of large-scale datasets, and the absence of a universal and community-driven benchmark. To address this issue, we introduce the Music Audio Representation Benchmark for universaL Evaluation, termed MARBLE. It aims to provide a benchmark for various Music Information Retrieval (MIR) tasks by defining a comprehensive taxonomy with four hierarchy levels, including acoustic, performance, score, and high-level description. We then establish a unified protocol based on 18 tasks on 12 public-available datasets, providing a fair and standard assessment of representations of all open-sourced pre-trained models developed on music recordings as baselines. Besides, MARBLE offers an easy-to-use, extendable, and reproducible suite for the community, with a clear statement on copyright issues on datasets. Results suggest recently proposed large-scale pre-trained musical language models perform the best in most tasks, with room for further improvement. The leaderboard and toolkit repository are published to promote future music AI research.

paragraphs: Music understanding involves several kinds of information, so evaluating a learned audio representation requires more than a single task. MARBLE provides a shared benchmark intended to make those evaluations more systematic. It addresses the lack of a broad, community-oriented assessment framework for representations learned from music recordings.

The benchmark organizes music information retrieval into four levels: acoustics, performance, score, and high-level description. It combines 18 tasks across 12 publicly available datasets under a unified evaluation protocol. Open-source pretrained models developed on music recordings serve as baselines, allowing their representations to be assessed within the same framework.

MARBLE also supplies an extensible, reproducible toolkit, a leaderboard, and explicit information about dataset copyright issues. Results suggest that recently proposed large-scale pretrained musical language models perform best on most tasks, while leaving room for further improvement. The benchmark's contribution is therefore both comparative evidence about existing representations and shared infrastructure for studying capabilities across different levels of music understanding.
summary.tldr: MARBLE standardizes music-representation evaluation across 18 tasks and 12 datasets spanning four levels of music understanding.

title: MARBLE: Music Audio Representation Benchmark for Universal Evaluation

abstract: Existing 3D instance segmentation methods typically assume that all semantic classes to be segmented would be available during training and only seen categories are segmented at inference. We argue that such a closed-world assumption is restrictive and explore for the first time 3D indoor instance segmentation in an open-world setting, where the model is allowed to distinguish a set of known classes as well as identify an unknown object as unknown and then later incrementally learning the semantic category of the unknown when the corresponding category labels are available. To this end, we introduce an open-world 3D indoor instance segmentation method, where an auto-labeling scheme is employed to produce pseudo-labels during training and induce separation to separate known and unknown category labels. We further improve the pseudo-labels quality at inference by adjusting the unknown class probability based on the objectness score distribution. We also introduce carefully curated open-world splits leveraging realistic scenarios based on inherent object distribution, region-based indoor scene exploration and randomness aspect of open-world classes. Extensive experiments reveal the efficacy of the proposed contributions leading to promising open-world 3D instance segmentation performance. Code and splits are available at: https://github.com/aminebdj/3D-OWIS.
originalAbstract: Existing 3D instance segmentation methods typically assume that all semantic classes to be segmented would be available during training and only seen categories are segmented at inference. We argue that such a closed-world assumption is restrictive and explore for the first time 3D indoor instance segmentation in an open-world setting, where the model is allowed to distinguish a set of known classes as well as identify an unknown object as unknown and then later incrementally learning the semantic category of the unknown when the corresponding category labels are available. To this end, we introduce an open-world 3D indoor instance segmentation method, where an auto-labeling scheme is employed to produce pseudo-labels during training and induce separation to separate known and unknown category labels. We further improve the pseudo-labels quality at inference by adjusting the unknown class probability based on the objectness score distribution. We also introduce carefully curated open-world splits leveraging realistic scenarios based on inherent object distribution, region-based indoor scene exploration and randomness aspect of open-world classes. Extensive experiments reveal the efficacy of the proposed contributions leading to promising open-world 3D instance segmentation performance. Code and splits are available at: https://github.com/aminebdj/3D-OWIS.

paragraphs: A system that separates individual objects in a 3D room usually learns a fixed list of categories. This paper studies a broader setting: the system should recognize familiar categories, mark unfamiliar objects as unknown, and later learn their categories when labels become available. This makes recognizing uncertainty part of the segmentation task.

The proposed method creates provisional labels automatically during training. These pseudo-labels help the model separate known categories from unknown ones. At inference, it further adjusts the probability of the unknown class using the distribution of objectness scores, which indicate whether a candidate corresponds to an object. This adjustment aims to improve pseudo-label quality.

The researchers also construct evaluation splits reflecting object distributions, exploration of different indoor regions, and randomly selected unknown classes. Their experiments report promising performance and support the effectiveness of the proposed components. The contribution combines a method with evaluation settings for studying how 3D segmentation can accommodate objects whose category labels arrive after initial training.
summary.tldr: The paper develops 3D indoor object segmentation that identifies unknown objects and can learn their categories when labels become available.

title: 3D Indoor Instance Segmentation in an Open-World

abstract: Distributed training of Deep Learning models has been critical to many recent successes in the field. Current standard methods primarily rely on synchronous centralized algorithms which induce major communication bottlenecks and synchronization locks at scale. Decentralized asynchronous algorithms are emerging as a potential alternative but their practical applicability still lags. In order to mitigate the increase in communication cost that naturally comes with scaling the number of workers, we introduce a principled asynchronous, randomized, gossip-based optimization algorithm which works thanks to a continuous local momentum named $\textbf{A}^2\textbf{CiD}^2$. Our method allows each worker to continuously process mini-batches without stopping, and run a peer-to-peer averaging routine in parallel, reducing idle time. In addition to inducing a significant communication acceleration at no cost other than adding a local momentum variable, minimal adaptation is required to incorporate $\textbf{A}^2\textbf{CiD}^2$ to standard asynchronous approaches. Our theoretical analysis proves accelerated rates compared to previous asynchronous decentralized baselines and we empirically show that using our $\textbf{A}^2\textbf{CiD}^2$ momentum significantly decrease communication costs in poorly connected networks. In particular, we show consistent improvement on the ImageNet dataset using up to 64 asynchronous workers (A100 GPUs) and various communication network topologies.

paragraphs: Distributed training can lose time when workers must synchronize or communicate through a central bottleneck. Decentralized asynchronous training offers an alternative, but communication becomes harder as more workers participate. A²CiD² introduces a randomized gossip-based optimization method designed to accelerate communication while allowing computation to continue.

Each worker processes mini-batches continuously and runs peer-to-peer averaging in parallel. The method adds a continuous local momentum variable that supports faster communication without requiring workers to stop their training work. The authors describe the integration with standard asynchronous approaches as requiring minimal changes, making the momentum mechanism a practical addition to existing decentralized procedures.

The theoretical analysis proves accelerated rates relative to previous asynchronous decentralized baselines. Experiments show reduced communication costs in poorly connected networks and consistent improvements on ImageNet with up to 64 asynchronous A100 GPU workers across several network topologies. The results connect the momentum-based acceleration to practical distributed training, particularly where the communication graph makes information exchange difficult.
summary.tldr: A²CiD² adds continuous local momentum to asynchronous decentralized training, accelerating communication while workers continue processing mini-batches.

title: $\textbf{A}^2\textbf{CiD}^2$: Accelerating Asynchronous Communication in Decentralized Deep Learning

abstract: A common concern when a policymaker draws causal inferences from and makes decisions based on observational data is that the measured covariates are insufficiently rich to account for all sources of confounding, i.e., the standard no confoundedness assumption fails to hold. The recently proposed proximal causal inference framework shows that proxy variables that abound in real-life scenarios can be leveraged to identify causal effects and therefore facilitate decision-making. Building upon this line of work, we propose a novel optimal individualized treatment regime based on so-called outcome and treatment confounding bridges. We then show that the value function of this new optimal treatment regime is superior to that of existing ones in the literature. Theoretical guarantees, including identification, superiority, excess value bound, and consistency of the estimated regime, are established. Furthermore, we demonstrate the proposed optimal regime via numerical experiments and a real data application.

paragraphs: Treatment decisions based on observational data become difficult when measured characteristics do not account for every source of confounding. Proximal causal inference addresses this problem by using proxy variables to help identify causal effects. This paper builds on that framework to develop an individualized treatment regime: a rule for selecting treatment for a person.

The proposed regime uses both outcome and treatment confounding bridges. These are the central components through which the method connects proxy information to treatment decisions. The authors show that the value function of their optimal regime is superior to those of existing regimes considered in the literature, providing a theoretical comparison of the resulting decision rules.

The paper establishes identification, superiority, an excess value bound, and consistency of the estimated regime. Together, these results address whether the target rule can be determined and how its estimated version behaves. Numerical experiments and a real-data application illustrate the method. Its contribution concerns decision-making within the proximal framework when ordinary adjustment for measured covariates is insufficient.
summary.tldr: A proximal causal learning method combines outcome and treatment confounding bridges to derive individualized treatment rules with stronger value guarantees.

title: Optimal Treatment Regimes for Proximal Causal Learning

abstract: Imitation learning from human feedback studies how to train well-performed imitation agents with an annotator's relative comparison of two demonstrations (one demonstration is better/worse than the other), which is usually easier to collect than the perfect expert data required by traditional imitation learning. However, in many real-world applications, it is still expensive or even impossible to provide a clear pairwise comparison between two demonstrations with similar quality. This motivates us to study the problem of imitation learning with vague feedback, where the data annotator can only distinguish the paired demonstrations correctly when their quality differs significantly, i.e., one from the expert and another from the non-expert. By modeling the underlying demonstration pool as a mixture of expert and non-expert data, we show that the expert policy distribution can be recovered when the proportion $\alpha$ of expert data is known. We also propose a mixture proportion estimation method for the unknown $\alpha$ case. Then, we integrate the recovered expert policy distribution with generative adversarial imitation learning to form an end-to-end algorithm. Experiments show that our methods outperform standard and preference-based imitation learning methods on various tasks.

paragraphs: This paper considers imitation learning when people cannot reliably rank demonstrations of similar quality. Its feedback setting assumes that an annotator can correctly distinguish a pair when one demonstration is expert and the other is non-expert. This captures a weaker form of supervision than requiring a clear preference for every pair.

The authors model the demonstration collection as a mixture of expert and non-expert data. Under this formulation, they show that the expert policy distribution can be recovered when the proportion of expert examples, α, is known. When that proportion is unknown, they propose a method to estimate it before using the recovered distribution.

The recovered expert distribution is incorporated into generative adversarial imitation learning to create an end-to-end algorithm. Experiments across several tasks show better performance than standard and preference-based imitation methods. The contribution is a way to extract useful expert behavior from ambiguous comparisons, with the recovery result tied to the mixture formulation and knowledge of the expert proportion.
summary.tldr: A mixture-based approach learns expert behavior from feedback that reliably distinguishes only clearly different demonstration qualities.

title: Imitation Learning from Vague Feedback

abstract: Unrestricted adversarial attacks typically manipulate the semantic content of an image (e.g., color or texture) to create adversarial examples that are both effective and photorealistic, demonstrating their ability to deceive human perception and deep neural networks with stealth and success. However, current works usually sacrifice unrestricted degrees and subjectively select some image content to guarantee the photorealism of unrestricted adversarial examples, which limits its attack performance. To ensure the photorealism of adversarial examples and boost attack performance, we propose a novel unrestricted attack framework called Content-based Unrestricted Adversarial Attack. By leveraging a low-dimensional manifold that represents natural images, we map the images onto the manifold and optimize them along its adversarial direction. Therefore, within this framework, we implement Adversarial Content Attack (ACA) based on Stable Diffusion and can generate high transferable unrestricted adversarial examples with various adversarial contents. Extensive experimentation and visualization demonstrate the efficacy of ACA, particularly in surpassing state-of-the-art attacks by an average of 13.3-50.4\% and 16.8-48.0\% in normally trained models and defense methods, respectively.

paragraphs: Unrestricted adversarial attacks change image content, such as color or texture, to produce realistic images that mislead neural networks. Existing approaches often restrict which content can change to preserve photorealism. The paper argues that these manually chosen restrictions can limit attack performance and explores a broader way to control image changes.

Its framework maps images onto a low-dimensional manifold representing natural images, then optimizes along an adversarial direction within that representation. The purpose is to keep changes tied to natural image structure while allowing varied adversarial content. The authors implement this idea with Stable Diffusion in a method called Adversarial Content Attack, or ACA.

Experiments and visualizations show effective attacks with high transferability. The authors report average improvements over state-of-the-art attacks of 13.3–50.4% on normally trained models and 16.8–48.0% against defense methods. These are reported experimental comparisons. The broader contribution is a content-editing framework that links photorealistic generation with adversarial optimization, allowing attack changes beyond a narrowly selected set of image attributes.
summary.tldr: ACA uses Stable Diffusion to optimize realistic image content into transferable adversarial examples and improves attack performance in the reported evaluations.

title: Content-based Unrestricted Adversarial Attack

abstract: Overparameterized neural networks (NNs) are observed to generalize well even when trained to perfectly fit noisy data. This phenomenon motivated a large body of work on "benign overfitting", where interpolating predictors achieve near-optimal performance. Recently, it was conjectured and empirically observed that the behavior of NNs is often better described as "tempered overfitting", where the performance is non-optimal yet also non-trivial, and degrades as a function of the noise level. However, a theoretical justification of this claim for non-linear NNs has been lacking so far. In this work, we provide several results that aim at bridging these complementing views. We study a simple classification setting with 2-layer ReLU NNs, and prove that under various assumptions, the type of overfitting transitions from tempered in the extreme case of one-dimensional data, to benign in high dimensions. Thus, we show that the input dimension has a crucial role on the overfitting profile in this setting, which we also validate empirically for intermediate dimensions. Overall, our results shed light on the intricate connections between the dimension, sample size, architecture and training algorithm on the one hand, and the type of resulting overfitting on the other hand.

paragraphs: A neural network can perfectly fit noisy training data and still predict well on new examples. Benign overfitting describes cases where such a predictor performs nearly optimally. Tempered overfitting describes useful but suboptimal performance that worsens with increasing noise. This paper investigates how these two behaviors can arise within nonlinear neural networks.

The authors study a simple classification setting using two-layer ReLU networks. Under various assumptions, they prove a transition from tempered overfitting for one-dimensional inputs to benign overfitting in high dimensions. The result gives input dimension a central role in determining what fitting noisy data means for prediction quality in this setting.

Experiments at intermediate dimensions support the importance of this dimensional transition. The work helps connect two seemingly different descriptions of neural-network generalization through a shared theoretical setting. Its conclusions are tied to the studied networks and assumptions, while also highlighting interactions among dimension, sample size, architecture, and training algorithm. Perfect training fit alone therefore does not describe the resulting overfitting behavior.
summary.tldr: For two-layer ReLU classifiers under studied assumptions, increasing input dimension shifts overfitting from useful but suboptimal to nearly optimal.

title: From Tempered to Benign Overfitting in ReLU Neural Networks

abstract: Neural ordinary differential equations (ODEs) are widely recognized as the standard for modeling physical mechanisms, which help to perform approximate inference in unknown physical or biological environments. In partially observable (PO) environments, how to infer unseen information from raw observations puzzled the agents. By using a recurrent policy with a compact context, context-based reinforcement learning provides a flexible way to extract unobservable information from historical transitions. To help the agent extract more dynamics-related information, we present a novel ODE-based recurrent model combines with model-free reinforcement learning (RL) framework to solve partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). We experimentally demonstrate the efficacy of our methods across various PO continuous control and meta-RL tasks. Furthermore, our experiments illustrate that our method is robust against irregular observations, owing to the ability of ODEs to model irregularly-sampled time series.

paragraphs: In a partially observable environment, an agent must choose actions without directly seeing all the information that matters. A recurrent policy can help by maintaining a compact context drawn from past transitions. This paper asks how that context can capture more information about the environment's dynamics, rather than relying only on the current observation.

The proposed approach combines an ordinary differential equation-based recurrent model with model-free reinforcement learning. The recurrent component uses historical information to help infer what is hidden, while the ODE formulation provides a way to represent evolution over time. The aim is to make the policy's internal context more informative about dynamics in partially observable decision problems.

Experiments demonstrate effectiveness across partially observable continuous-control and meta-reinforcement-learning tasks. They also show robustness when observations arrive irregularly, which the authors attribute to the ability of ODEs to handle irregularly sampled time series. This connects the representation choice to a concrete observation challenge: useful temporal context must account for how observations are distributed over time.
summary.tldr: An ODE-based recurrent model improves temporal context for model-free reinforcement learning under partial and irregular observation.

title: ODE-based Recurrent Model-free Reinforcement Learning for POMDPs

abstract: Decision trees are regarded for high interpretability arising from their hierarchical partitioning structure built on simple decision rules. However, in practice, this is not realized because axis-aligned partitioning of realistic data results in deep trees, and because ensemble methods are used to mitigate overfitting. Even then, model complexity and performance remain sensitive to transformation of the input, and extensive expert crafting of features from the raw data is common. We propose the first system to alternate sparse feature learning with differentiable decision tree construction to produce small, interpretable trees with good performance. We benchmark against conventional tree-based models and demonstrate several notions of interpretation of a model and its predictions.

paragraphs: Decision trees seem easy to interpret because predictions follow a hierarchy of simple rules. In practice, realistic inputs can require deep trees when each split uses an individual input coordinate. Ensembles used to address overfitting add further complexity, while both performance and tree size remain sensitive to how the input features are represented.

This paper tackles that representation problem by alternating sparse feature learning with differentiable decision tree construction. The system learns features and builds the tree in a coordinated process, aiming to produce a compact predictor with good performance. Its motivation is closely tied to the extensive manual feature crafting often needed for conventional tree models.

The authors benchmark their system against conventional tree-based approaches and demonstrate several ways to interpret the resulting model and its predictions. The stated outcome is small, interpretable trees with good predictive performance. The contribution places feature learning inside the tree-building process, addressing how the choice of representation affects the practical simplicity of the final decision rules.
summary.tldr: Alternating sparse feature learning with differentiable tree construction produces compact, interpretable decision trees with good performance.

title: Feature Learning for Interpretable, Performant Decision Trees

abstract: Recent years have witnessed a significant increase in the storage density of NAND flash memory, making it a critical component in modern electronic devices. However, with the rise in storage capacity comes an increased likelihood of errors in data storage and retrieval. The growing number of errors poses ongoing challenges for system designers and engineers, in terms of the characterization, modeling, and optimization of NAND-based systems. We present a novel approach for modeling and preventing errors by utilizing the capabilities of generative and unsupervised machine learning methods. As part of our research, we constructed and trained a neural modulator that translates information bits into programming operations on each memory cell in NAND devices. Our modulator, tailored explicitly for flash memory channels, provides a smart writing scheme that reduces programming errors as well as compensates for data degradation over time. Specifically, the modulator is based on an auto-encoder architecture with an additional channel model embedded between the encoder and the decoder. A conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) was used to construct the channel model. Optimized for the end-of-life work-point, the learned memory system outperforms the prior art by up to 56\% in raw bit error rate (RBER) and extends the lifetime of the flash memory block by up to 25\%.
