paragraphs: As NAND flash memory stores more information, errors in writing and reading data become a greater challenge. This paper tackles reliability by learning how information bits should be translated into programming operations for individual memory cells. The goal is to reduce programming errors while also compensating for degradation as the memory ages.

The authors build a neural modulator around an autoencoder, with a model of the flash-memory channel placed between its encoder and decoder. A conditional generative adversarial network learns that channel model. Embedding the channel inside the learning architecture allows the writing scheme to be optimized with the modeled behavior of the memory in the loop. Generative and unsupervised learning thus contribute directly to how data are written.

When optimized for the end-of-life operating point, the learned system improves raw bit error rate over prior art by up to 56% and extends flash-block lifetime by up to 25%. These are reported maximum improvements under that optimization setting. They indicate that adapting the programming scheme to the channel can benefit both data reliability and usable memory lifetime.
summary.tldr: A learned flash-memory writing scheme reports up to 56% improvement in raw bit error rate and 25% longer block lifetime.

title: Neural Modulation for Flash Memory: An Unsupervised Learning Framework for Improved Reliability

abstract: Gaussian processes are the model of choice in Bayesian optimization and active learning. Yet, they are highly dependent on cleverly chosen hyperparameters to reach their full potential, and little effort is devoted to finding good hyperparameters in the literature. We demonstrate the impact of selecting good hyperparameters for GPs and present two acquisition functions that explicitly prioritize hyperparameter learning. Statistical distance-based Active Learning (SAL) considers the average disagreement between samples from the posterior, as measured by a statistical distance. SAL outperforms the state-of-the-art in Bayesian active learning on several test functions. We then introduce Self-Correcting Bayesian Optimization (SCoreBO), which extends SAL to perform Bayesian optimization and active learning simultaneously. SCoreBO learns the model hyperparameters at improved rates compared to vanilla BO, while outperforming the latest Bayesian optimization methods on traditional benchmarks. Moreover, we demonstrate the importance of self-correction on atypical Bayesian optimization tasks.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes are widely used to guide Bayesian optimization and active learning, but their effectiveness depends heavily on suitable hyperparameters. This paper treats learning those settings as an explicit objective when selecting new observations. The aim is to improve the model while using it to learn or optimize.

Statistical distance-based Active Learning, or SAL, chooses observations using the average disagreement among posterior samples, measured through a statistical distance. This explicitly prioritizes hyperparameter learning. Self-Correcting Bayesian Optimization, or SCoreBO, extends that idea so that active learning and objective optimization take place together.

The authors report that SAL outperforms leading active-learning methods on several test functions. SCoreBO learns hyperparameters faster than vanilla Bayesian optimization and outperforms recent optimization methods on traditional benchmarks. Further experiments on atypical optimization tasks demonstrate the importance of self-correction. Together, the findings support choosing observations partly for their ability to improve the model’s own settings, rather than assuming those settings are already adequate for effective search.
summary.tldr: SAL and SCoreBO select observations that explicitly improve Gaussian-process hyperparameters, strengthening active learning and Bayesian optimization in reported experiments.

title: Self-Correcting Bayesian Optimization through Bayesian Active Learning

abstract: We present a generative dialogue system capable of operating in a full-duplex manner, allowing for seamless interaction. It is based on a large language model (LLM) carefully aligned to be aware of a perception module, a motor function module, and the concept of a simple finite state machine (called neural FSM) with two states. The perception and motor function modules operate in tandem, allowing the system to speak and listen to the user simultaneously. The LLM generates textual tokens for inquiry responses and makes autonomous decisions to start responding to, wait for, or interrupt the user by emitting control tokens to the neural FSM. All these tasks of the LLM are carried out as next token prediction on a serialized view of the dialogue in real-time. In automatic quality evaluations simulating real-life interaction, the proposed system reduces the average conversation response latency by more than threefold compared with LLM-based half-duplex dialogue systems while responding within less than 500 milliseconds in more than 50% of evaluated interactions. Running an LLM with only 8 billion parameters, our system exhibits an 8% higher interruption precision rate than the best available commercial LLM for voice-based dialogue.

paragraphs: This paper develops a speech dialogue system that can listen while speaking. Its central problem is deciding when to respond, keep waiting, or interrupt during an ongoing conversation. The system connects a large language model to perception and speech-production modules that operate together, allowing incoming speech to remain relevant while the system is producing an answer.

The language model handles both conversational content and timing decisions through next-token prediction. Alongside ordinary text, it emits control tokens that operate a two-state mechanism called a neural finite state machine. A serialized, real-time representation of the conversation lets the model use the same prediction process to generate answers and coordinate conversational actions.

In automatic evaluations designed to simulate real interactions, the system reduced average response latency by more than threefold relative to LLM-based half-duplex systems. More than half of evaluated interactions received a response within 500 milliseconds. The authors also report 8% higher interruption precision than the best available commercial voice-dialogue LLM, using an eight-billion-parameter model.
summary.tldr: An LLM coordinates simultaneous listening and speaking through control tokens, improving response latency and interruption precision in evaluated speech interactions.

title: A Full-duplex Speech Dialogue Scheme Based On Large Language Model

abstract: PAC-Bayesian analysis is a frequentist framework for incorporating prior knowledge into learning. It was inspired by Bayesian learning, which allows sequential data processing and naturally turns posteriors from one processing step into priors for the next. However, despite two and a half decades of research, the ability to update priors sequentially without losing confidence information along the way remained elusive for PAC-Bayes. While PAC-Bayes allows construction of data-informed priors, the final confidence intervals depend only on the number of points that were not used for the construction of the prior, whereas confidence information in the prior, which is related to the number of points used to construct the prior, is lost. This limits the possibility and benefit of sequential prior updates, because the final bounds depend only on the size of the final batch.We present a novel and, in retrospect, surprisingly simple and powerful PAC-Bayesian procedure that allows sequential prior updates with no information loss. The procedure is based on a novel decomposition of the expected loss of randomized classifiers. The decomposition rewrites the loss of the posterior as an excess loss relative to a downscaled loss of the prior plus the downscaled loss of the prior, which is bounded recursively. As a side result, we also present a generalization of the split-kl and PAC-Bayes-split-kl inequalities to discrete random variables, which we use for bounding the excess losses, and which can be of independent interest. In empirical evaluation the new procedure significantly outperforms state-of-the-art.
originalAbstract: PAC-Bayesian analysis is a frequentist framework for incorporating prior knowledge into learning. It was inspired by Bayesian learning, which allows sequential data processing and naturally turns posteriors from one processing step into priors for the next. However, despite two and a half decades of research, the ability to update priors sequentially without losing confidence information along the way remained elusive for PAC-Bayes. While PAC-Bayes allows construction of data-informed priors, the final confidence intervals depend only on the number of points that were not used for the construction of the prior, whereas confidence information in the prior, which is related to the number of points used to construct the prior, is lost. This limits the possibility and benefit of sequential prior updates, because the final bounds depend only on the size of the final batch.We present a novel and, in retrospect, surprisingly simple and powerful PAC-Bayesian procedure that allows sequential prior updates with no information loss. The procedure is based on a novel decomposition of the expected loss of randomized classifiers. The decomposition rewrites the loss of the posterior as an excess loss relative to a downscaled loss of the prior plus the downscaled loss of the prior, which is bounded recursively. As a side result, we also present a generalization of the split-kl and PAC-Bayes-split-kl inequalities to discrete random variables, which we use for bounding the excess losses, and which can be of independent interest. In empirical evaluation the new procedure significantly outperforms state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: PAC-Bayesian analysis provides frequentist guarantees while incorporating prior knowledge. Updating that prior from earlier data creates a difficulty: conventional final confidence bounds use only the data left after prior construction. Earlier observations can influence the prior, but their contribution to confidence is lost, limiting the usefulness of sequential updates.

Recursive PAC-Bayes preserves that confidence information through a decomposition of the expected loss of randomized classifiers. It expresses posterior loss as an excess relative to a scaled prior loss, plus that scaled prior loss itself. The prior term is then bounded recursively, carrying information from earlier stages into the final guarantee.

The authors also generalize split-kl and PAC-Bayes-split-kl inequalities to discrete random variables and use those results to bound excess losses. Their empirical evaluation reports substantial improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The central advance is a procedure whose sequential updates retain confidence information from earlier data. Here, no information loss refers to that statistical accounting across updates, specifically addressing the dependence on only the final batch that motivated the work.
summary.tldr: Recursive PAC-Bayes updates priors sequentially while preserving earlier data's contribution to confidence guarantees.

title: Recursive PAC-Bayes: A Frequentist Approach to Sequential Prior Updates with No Information Loss

abstract: One-shot Federated Learning (OFL) significantly reduces communication costs in FL by aggregating trained models only once. However, the performance of advanced OFL methods is far behind the normal FL. In this work, we provide a causal view to find that this performance drop of OFL methods comes from the isolation problem, which means that local isolatedly trained models in OFL may easily fit to spurious correlations due to the data heterogeneity. From the causal perspective, we observe that the spurious fitting can be alleviated by augmenting intermediate features from other clients. Built upon our observation, we propose a novel learning approach to endow OFL with superb performance and low communication and storage costs, termed as FuseFL. Specifically, FuseFL decomposes neural networks into several blocks, and progressively trains and fuses each block following a bottom-up manner for feature augmentation, introducing no additional communication costs. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that FuseFL outperforms existing OFL and ensemble FL by a significant margin. We conduct comprehensive experiments to show that FuseFL supports high scalability of clients, heterogeneous model training, and low memory costs. Our work is the first attempt using causality to analyze and alleviate data heterogeneity of OFL.

paragraphs: One-shot federated learning reduces communication by aggregating trained models only once, but its performance can lag behind ordinary federated learning. This paper analyzes that gap through a causal perspective. It identifies isolation during local training as a problem: clients with differing data may learn spurious relationships that do not transfer well.

The authors observe that augmenting intermediate features with features from other clients can alleviate this spurious fitting. FuseFL implements that idea by dividing networks into blocks, then progressively training and fusing those blocks from the bottom upward. Feature augmentation is therefore built into the model’s development, with the method introducing no additional communication costs according to the abstract.

Experiments show substantial improvements over existing one-shot and ensemble federated learning methods. They also demonstrate support for many clients, heterogeneous models, and low memory costs. These findings connect the proposed explanation of the performance gap to a concrete intervention: giving local learning access to richer intermediate representations can reduce the effects of training in isolation.
summary.tldr: FuseFL progressively fuses network blocks to share intermediate features and reduce spurious fitting in one-shot federated learning.

title: FuseFL: One-Shot Federated Learning through the Lens of Causality with Progressive Model Fusion

abstract: Trajectory prediction is a crucial technology to help systems avoid traffic accidents, ensuring safe autonomous driving. Previous methods typically use a fixed-length and sufficiently long trajectory of an agent as observations to predict its future trajectory. However, in real-world scenarios, we often lack the time to gather enough trajectory points before making predictions, e.g., when a car suddenly appears due to an obstruction, the system must make immediate predictions to prevent a collision. This poses a new challenge for trajectory prediction systems, requiring them to be capable of making accurate predictions based on observed trajectories of arbitrary lengths, leading to the failure of existing methods. In this paper, we propose a Length-agnostic Knowledge Distillation framework, named LaKD, which can make accurate trajectory predictions, regardless of the length of observed data. Specifically, considering the fact that long trajectories, containing richer temporal information but potentially additional interference, may perform better or worse than short trajectories, we devise a dynamic length-agnostic knowledge distillation mechanism for exchanging information among trajectories of arbitrary lengths, dynamically determining the transfer direction based on prediction performance. In contrast to traditional knowledge distillation, LaKD employs a unique model that simultaneously serves as both the teacher and the student, potentially causing knowledge collision during the distillation process. Therefore, we design a dynamic soft-masking mechanism, where we first calculate the importance of neuron units and then apply soft-masking to them, so as to safeguard critical units from disruption during the knowledge distillation process. In essence, LaKD is a general and principled framework that can be naturally compatible with existing trajectory prediction models of different architectures. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets, Argoverse 1, nuScenes and Argoverse 2, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: Trajectory prediction systems often assume they can observe a sufficiently long, fixed history before forecasting movement. Real traffic can violate that assumption when an obstructed vehicle suddenly becomes visible. LaKD is designed to support predictions from observation histories of varying lengths, allowing existing prediction models to work with this less uniform information.

Its knowledge-distillation mechanism does not assume that longer histories always provide better guidance. They contain more temporal information but may also introduce interference. Instead, LaKD determines the direction of knowledge transfer from prediction performance, allowing information to pass between different history lengths according to which currently offers better predictions.

A single model acts as both teacher and student, creating the possibility that learning from one history length disrupts useful knowledge associated with another. LaKD addresses this with a dynamic soft mask based on neuron importance, protecting critical units during transfer. Experiments on Argoverse 1, nuScenes, and Argoverse 2 support the framework's effectiveness, and the approach is designed to accommodate different trajectory-prediction architectures.
summary.tldr: LaKD transfers knowledge dynamically between observation lengths and protects important neurons to improve trajectory prediction with variable amounts of history.

title: LaKD: Length-agnostic Knowledge Distillation for Trajectory Prediction with Any Length Observations

abstract: Visual Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods often require extensive amounts of data. As opposed to model-free RL, model-based RL (MBRL) offers a potential solution with efficient data utilization through planning. Additionally, RL lacks generalization capabilities for real-world tasks. Prior work has shown that incorporating pre-trained visual representations (PVRs) enhances sample efficiency and generalization. While PVRs have been extensively studied in the context of model-free RL, their potential in MBRL remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we benchmark a set of PVRs on challenging control tasks in a model-based RL setting. We investigate the data efficiency, generalization capabilities, and the impact of different properties of PVRs on the performance of model-based agents. Our results, perhaps surprisingly, reveal that for MBRL current PVRs are not more sample efficient than learning representations from scratch, and that they do not generalize better to out-of-distribution (OOD) settings. To explain this, we analyze the quality of the trained dynamics model. Furthermore, we show that data diversity and network architecture are the most important contributors to OOD generalization performance.

paragraphs: This paper tests whether pretrained visual representations improve model-based reinforcement learning. Such representations have helped sample efficiency and generalization in prior reinforcement-learning work, especially in model-free settings. Model-based agents use learned dynamics for planning, so the authors investigate whether those benefits carry over to this different use of visual information.

The study benchmarks a set of pretrained representations on challenging control tasks. It examines how much data agents need, how well they generalize outside the training distribution, and which representation properties influence performance. The authors also analyze the quality of the learned dynamics model to investigate the observed results.

In the evaluated model-based setting, current pretrained representations are no more sample-efficient than representations learned from scratch and do not provide better out-of-distribution generalization. The study identifies data diversity and network architecture as the most important contributors to generalization performance. These findings question the assumption that visual pretraining benefits transfer automatically to model-based agents and redirect attention toward the data and architecture used to learn their predictive models.
summary.tldr: The evaluated pretrained visual representations do not improve model-based RL sample efficiency or generalization over learning representations from scratch.

title: The Surprising Ineffectiveness of Pre-Trained Visual Representations for Model-Based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Pearson's $r$, the most widely-used correlation coefficient, is traditionally regarded as exclusively capturing linear dependence, leading to its discouragement in contexts involving nonlinear relationships. However, recent research challenges this notion, suggesting that Pearson's $r$ should not be ruled out a priori for measuring nonlinear monotone relationships. Pearson's $r$ is essentially a scaled covariance, rooted in the renowned Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality. Our findings reveal that different scaling bounds yield coefficients with different capture ranges, and interestingly, tighter bounds actually expand these ranges. We derive a tighter inequality than Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality, leverage it to refine Pearson's $r$, and propose a new correlation coefficient, i.e., rearrangement correlation. This coefficient is able to capture arbitrary monotone relationships, both linear and nonlinear ones. It reverts to Pearson's $r$ in linear scenarios. Simulation experiments and real-life investigations show that the rearrangement correlation is more accurate in measuring nonlinear monotone dependence than the three classical correlation coefficients, and other recently proposed dependence measures.

paragraphs: The paper revisits how correlation measures relationships that consistently increase or decrease, even when those relationships are curved. Pearson’s correlation is commonly treated as a measure of linear dependence. The authors investigate whether changing its mathematical normalization can extend what it captures while retaining its connection to covariance.

Their starting point is that Pearson’s correlation scales covariance using a bound supplied by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. They show that the choice of scaling bound affects the range of relationships a coefficient can capture, with tighter bounds expanding that range. They derive a tighter inequality and use it to construct a measure called rearrangement correlation.

The resulting coefficient captures arbitrary monotone relationships, including nonlinear ones, and reduces to Pearson’s correlation in linear scenarios. Simulations and real-world investigations report more accurate measurement of nonlinear monotone dependence than the classical and newer measures considered. The contribution is a principled adjustment to covariance normalization, with both a mathematical account of its scope and empirical evidence for its usefulness.
summary.tldr: Rearrangement correlation adjusts Pearson’s covariance normalization to capture nonlinear as well as linear monotone relationships.

title: Adjust Pearson's $r$ to Measure Arbitrary Monotone Dependence

abstract: Continual learning aims to sequentially learn new tasks without forgetting previous tasks' knowledge (catastrophic forgetting). One factor that can cause forgetting is the interference between the gradients on losses from different tasks. When the gradients on the current task's loss are in opposing directions to those on previous tasks' losses, updating the model for the current task may cause performance degradation on previous tasks. In this paper, we first identify causes of the above interference, and hypothesize that correlations between data representations are a key factor of interference. We then propose a method for promoting appropriate correlations between arbitrary tasks' data representations (i.e., global alignment) in individual task learning. Specifically, we learn the data representation as a task-specific composition of pre-trained token representations shared across all tasks. Then the correlations between different tasks' data representations are grounded by correlations between pre-trained token representations. We explore different ways to learn such compositions. Without experience replay, our model achieves SOTA performance in continual learning tasks. It also achieves advanced class-incremental performance through task-incremental training.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model to acquire new tasks without losing what it learned earlier. One source of forgetting is conflict between updates: a change that reduces the current task's loss can point against changes that would help previous tasks. This paper investigates that interference and hypothesizes that correlations between data representations play an important role.

The proposed global alignment method aims to establish suitable relationships between representations across tasks. It constructs each task's data representations as task-specific combinations of pretrained token representations shared by all tasks. This gives otherwise separate tasks a common foundation: their representation correlations are grounded in the relationships already present among the shared tokens. The authors explore different ways to learn these combinations.

The method achieves reported state-of-the-art continual-learning performance without replaying past experiences. It also produces strong class-incremental performance through task-incremental training. These findings support the usefulness of coordinating representation structure across tasks, while the proposed explanation linking correlations to interference remains a hypothesis in the abstract. The central contribution is a way to encourage cross-task alignment during individual task learning.
summary.tldr: Global alignment builds task representations from shared pretrained tokens to reduce forgetting, achieving strong continual-learning results without experience replay.

title: Continual Learning with Global Alignment

abstract: The ability to perform different skills can encourage agents to explore. In this work, we aim to construct a set of diverse skills that uniformly cover the state space. We propose a formalization of this search for diverse skills, building on a previous definition based on the mutual information between states and skills. We consider the distribution of states reached by a policy conditioned on each skill and leverage the successor state representation to maximize the difference between these skill distributions. We call this approach LEADS: Learning Diverse Skills through Successor State Representations. We demonstrate our approach on a set of maze navigation and robotic control tasks which show that our method is capable of constructing a diverse set of skills which exhaustively cover the state space without relying on reward or exploration bonuses. Our findings demonstrate that this new formalization promotes more robust and efficient exploration by combining mutual information maximization and exploration bonuses.

We call this approach LEADS: Learning Diverse Skills through Successor State Representations. We demonstrate our approach on a set of maze navigation and robotic control tasks which show that our method is capable of constructing a diverse set of skills which exhaustively cover the state space without relying on reward or exploration bonuses. paragraphs: An agent with several distinct skills has more ways to explore its environment. LEADS formalizes the goal of learning skills that collectively cover the state space uniformly. It builds on an earlier formulation using mutual information between skills and states, asking how each skill changes the distribution of places the agent reaches.

The method uses successor state representations to describe states reached under a policy conditioned on a particular skill. It then maximizes differences between the resulting distributions. This makes diversity a property of where skills take the agent, linking the skill-learning objective directly to coverage of the environment.

In maze navigation and robotic control experiments, the authors report learning diverse skills that exhaustively cover the tested state spaces without relying on rewards or exploration bonuses. They also describe more robust and efficient exploration through combining mutual information maximization with exploration bonuses. These statements distinguish the demonstrated ability to construct coverage-producing skills without bonuses from the broader exploration benefits discussed for combining objectives.
summary.tldr: LEADS learns diverse skills by separating their future-state distributions, achieving broad exploration in the tested navigation and robotic control tasks.

title: Exploration by Learning Diverse Skills through Successor State Representations

abstract: Graph is a prevalent discrete data structure, whose generation has wide applications such as drug discovery and circuit design. Diffusion generative models, as an emerging research focus, have been applied to graph generation tasks. Overall, according to the space of states and time steps, diffusion generative models can be categorized into discrete-/continuous-state discrete-/continuous-time fashions. In this paper, we formulate the graph diffusion generation in a discrete-state continuous-time setting, which has never been studied in previous graph diffusion models. The rationale of such a formulation is to preserve the discrete nature of graph-structured data and meanwhile provide flexible sampling trade-offs between sample quality and efficiency. Analysis shows that our training objective is closely related to the generation quality and our proposed generation framework enjoys ideal invariant/equivariant properties concerning the permutation of node ordering. Our proposed model shows competitive empirical performance against other state-of-the-art graph generation solutions on various benchmarks while at the same time can flexibly trade off the generation quality and efficiency in the sampling phase.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a graph diffusion model whose states are discrete but whose time variable is continuous. These are separate design choices: the states describe the form of the data, while time describes how the diffusion process evolves. The formulation preserves the discrete character of graphs while allowing flexibility in how generation is sampled.

That flexibility matters because the model can trade generation quality against computational efficiency during sampling. The authors also analyze the training objective and show that it is closely related to generation quality. Their framework has invariance and equivariance properties with respect to node ordering, so its behavior respects the fact that changing a graph's node ordering should be handled consistently.

Across several benchmarks, the model achieves competitive empirical performance against state-of-the-art graph generation approaches. The stated result combines this competitiveness with an adjustable sampling trade-off, rather than claiming the best quality at every computational budget. The contribution is a formulation that brings discrete graph structure, continuous-time sampling flexibility, and appropriate node-ordering behavior into the same generation framework.
summary.tldr: A discrete-state, continuous-time graph diffusion model preserves graph structure while allowing flexible quality-efficiency trade-offs during sampling.

title: Discrete-state Continuous-time Diffusion for Graph Generation

abstract: Incomplete spatio-temporal data in real-world has spawned many research.However, existing methods often utilize iterative message-passing across temporal and spatial dimensions, resulting in substantial information loss and high computational cost.We provide a theoretical analysis revealing that such iterative models are not only susceptible to data sparsity but also to graph sparsity, causing unstable performances on different datasets.To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel method named One-step Propagation and Confidence-based Refinement (OPCR).In the first stage, OPCR leverages inherent spatial and temporal relationships by employing sparse attention mechanism.These modules propagate limited observations directly to the global context through one-step imputation, which are theoretically effected only by data sparsity.Following this, we assign confidence levels to the initial imputations by correlating missing data with valid data.This confidence-based propagation refines the seperate spatial and temporal imputation results through spatio-temporal dependencies.We evaluate the proposed model across various downstream tasks involving highly sparse spatio-temporal data.Empirical results indicate that our model outperforms state-of-the-art imputation methods, demonstrating its superior effectiveness and robustness.

paragraphs: Spatiotemporal data can contain many missing observations across locations and times. Existing imputation methods often pass information repeatedly through spatial and temporal connections. The paper's analysis finds that these iterative models are sensitive both to missing data and to sparse graph connections, helping explain unstable performance across datasets.

The proposed One-step Propagation and Confidence-based Refinement method, OPCR, first uses sparse attention to spread available observations directly into a global context. This produces initial spatial and temporal imputations without repeated propagation. The authors' theoretical analysis attributes the sparsity dependence of these one-step modules to data sparsity alone, addressing the additional sensitivity to graph sparsity identified for iterative methods.

OPCR then estimates confidence by relating missing entries to valid observations. It uses that confidence and spatiotemporal dependencies to refine the separate initial estimates. This second stage gives the method a way to distinguish estimates according to their support in observed data. Experiments across downstream tasks with highly sparse inputs report better effectiveness and robustness than state-of-the-art imputation methods.
summary.tldr: OPCR fills sparse spatiotemporal data through direct propagation followed by confidence-based refinement, improving reported imputation effectiveness and robustness.

title: Learning from Highly Sparse Spatio-temporal Data

abstract: Working memory is a central cognitive ability crucial for intelligent decision-making. Recent experimental and computational work studying working memory has primarily used categorical (i.e., one-hot) inputs, rather than ecologically-relevant, multidimensional naturalistic ones. Moreover, studies have primarily investigated working memory during single or few number of cognitive tasks. As a result, an understanding of how naturalistic object information is maintained in working memory in neural networks is still lacking. To bridge this gap, we developed sensory-cognitive models, comprising of a convolutional neural network (CNN) coupled with a recurrent neural network (RNN), and trained them on nine distinct N-back tasks using naturalistic stimuli. By examining the RNN’s latent space, we found that: 1) Multi-task RNNs represent both task-relevant and irrelevant information simultaneously while performing tasks; 2) While the latent subspaces used to maintain specific object properties in vanilla RNNs are largely shared across tasks, they are highly task-specific in gated RNNs such as GRU and LSTM; 3) Surprisingly, RNNs embed objects in new representational spaces in which individual object features are less orthogonalized relative to the perceptual space; 4) Interestingly, the transformation of WM encodings (i.e., embedding of visual inputs in the RNN latent space) into memory was shared across stimuli, yet the transformations governing the retention of a memory in the face of incoming distractor stimuli were distinct across time. Our findings indicate that goal-driven RNNs employ chronological memory subspaces to track information over short time spans, enabling testable predictions with neural data.

paragraphs: This paper studies how neural networks maintain information about naturalistic objects in working memory. It moves beyond categorical inputs and a small number of tasks by coupling a convolutional network with a recurrent network and training on nine N-back tasks. The analysis examines the recurrent network’s internal representations during task performance.

The trained multitask networks retain both relevant and irrelevant object information. Their organization depends on the recurrent architecture: vanilla RNNs largely share the subspaces for particular object properties across tasks, whereas GRU and LSTM networks use more task-specific subspaces. Object features also become less orthogonal relative to their organization in the perceptual representation.

The authors distinguish the transformation that places an input into memory from those that preserve it through subsequent distractions. The former is shared across stimuli, while retention transformations differ across time. These findings suggest that the trained networks track short-term information through chronologically organized memory subspaces, providing predictions that could be tested against neural data.
summary.tldr: Networks trained on naturalistic working-memory tasks organize object information in architecture-dependent and time-dependent internal subspaces.

title: Geometry of naturalistic object representations in recurrent neural network models of working memory

abstract: Signed Distance Function (SDF)-based volume rendering has demonstrated significant capabilities in surface reconstruction. Although promising, SDF-based methods often fail to capture detailed geometric structures, resulting in visible defects. By comparing SDF-based volume rendering to density-based volume rendering, we identify two main factors within the SDF-based approach that degrade surface quality: SDF-to-density representation and geometric regularization. These factors introduce challenges that hinder the optimization of the SDF field. To address these issues, we introduce NeuRodin, a novel two-stage neural surface reconstruction framework that not only achieves high-fidelity surface reconstruction but also retains the flexible optimization characteristics of density-based methods. NeuRodin incorporates innovative strategies that facilitate transformation of arbitrary topologies and reduce artifacts associated with density bias. Extensive evaluations on the Tanks and Temples and ScanNet++ datasets demonstrate the superiority of NeuRodin, showing strong reconstruction capabilities for both indoor and outdoor environments using solely posed RGB captures. originalAbstract: Signed Distance Function (SDF)-based volume rendering has demonstrated significant capabilities in surface reconstruction. Although promising, SDF-based methods often fail to capture detailed geometric structures, resulting in visible defects. By comparing SDF-based volume rendering to density-based volume rendering, we identify two main factors within the SDF-based approach that degrade surface quality: SDF-to-density representation and geometric regularization. These factors introduce challenges that hinder the optimization of the SDF field. To address these issues, we introduce NeuRodin, a novel two-stage neural surface reconstruction framework that not only achieves high-fidelity surface reconstruction but also retains the flexible optimization characteristics of density-based methods. NeuRodin incorporates innovative strategies that facilitate transformation of arbitrary topologies and reduce artifacts associated with density bias. Extensive evaluations on the Tanks and Temples and ScanNet++ datasets demonstrate the superiority of NeuRodin, showing strong reconstruction capabilities for both indoor and outdoor environments using solely posed RGB captures. Project website:https://open3dvlab.github.io/NeuRodin/

paragraphs: Neural surface reconstruction can represent geometry through a signed distance function and recover it using volume rendering. Although this approach is powerful, it can miss fine geometric structures and produce visible defects. The paper compares it with density-based rendering to identify where its optimization becomes difficult.

The authors identify two contributing factors: converting the signed distance representation into density and applying geometric regularization. NeuRodin addresses these issues through a two-stage framework intended to combine high-fidelity surfaces with the optimization flexibility of density-based methods. Its strategies support changes in arbitrary topology and reduce artifacts associated with density bias.

The method is evaluated on Tanks and Temples and ScanNet++, using only RGB images with known camera poses. The reported results show superior reconstruction and strong performance in both indoor and outdoor environments. The contribution is therefore both diagnostic and methodological: it identifies sources of surface degradation and introduces a reconstruction framework designed to improve the resulting geometry.
summary.tldr: NeuRodin uses a two-stage reconstruction framework to improve geometric detail and reduce artifacts from posed RGB images.

title: NeuRodin: A Two-stage Framework for High-Fidelity Neural Surface Reconstruction

abstract: Continuous normalizing flows (CNFs) learn the probability path between a reference distribution and a target distribution by modeling the vector field generating said path using neural networks. Recently, Lipman et al. (2022) introduced a simple and inexpensive method for training CNFs in generative modeling, termed flow matching (FM). In this paper, we repurpose this method for probabilistic inference by incorporating Markovian sampling methods in evaluating the FM objective, and using the learned CNF to improve Monte Carlo sampling. Specifically, we propose an adaptive Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm, which combines a local Markov transition kernel with a non-local, flow-informed transition kernel, defined using a CNF. This CNF is adapted on-the-fly using samples from the Markov chain, which are used to specify the probability path for the FM objective. Our method also includes an adaptive tempering mechanism that allows the discovery of multiple modes in the target distribution. Under mild assumptions, we establish convergence of our method to a local optimum of the FM objective. We then benchmark our approach on several synthetic and real-world examples, achieving similar performance to other state-of-the-art methods but often at a significantly lower computational cost.

This paper adapts flow matching, a method for training these flows, to probabilistic inference. Its central idea is to connect learning the flow with the ongoing process of sampling from the target.

The proposed adaptive MCMC algorithm combines local transitions with nonlocal transitions informed by the learned flow. Samples from the Markov chain continuously update the flow and define the probability path used in its training objective. An adaptive tempering mechanism also helps the sampler discover multiple modes, or separated regions of high probability, in the target distribution.

The results support jointly adapting a transport model and a sampling process.
summary.tldr: Markovian Flow Matching trains a flow from ongoing MCMC samples and uses it to propose efficient nonlocal sampling moves.

title: Markovian Flow Matching: Accelerating MCMC with Continuous Normalizing Flows

abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) inference on Central Processing Units (CPU) is challenging due to the vast quantities of Multiply-Add (MAD) matrix operations in the attention computations. This paper highlights a rare gem in modern CPUs, Single-Instruction-Multiple-Data (SIMD) registers, which allows for ultra-low-latency lookups in a batch. We leverage this unique capability to propose NoMAD-Attention, an efficient attention algorithm that replaces MAD operations with in-register lookups. Through hardware-aware algorithmic designs, NoMAD-Attention achieves the computation of attention scores using repeated fast accesses to SIMD registers. NoMAD-Attention works with pre-trained attention-based LLMs without model finetuning. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that NoMAD-Attention maintains the quality of the original LLMs well and speeds up the 4-bit quantized LLaMA-7B-based model by up to $2 \times$ at 16k context length.

paragraphs: Running language models on CPUs is challenging partly because attention requires many multiply-add operations. NoMAD-Attention changes how attention scores are computed to exploit a specific CPU capability: SIMD registers can perform batches of lookups with very low latency.

The algorithm replaces multiply-add work in its attention computation with repeated lookups inside these registers. Its design therefore connects the attention algorithm directly to the hardware operations that CPUs can execute quickly. It can be applied to pretrained attention-based language models without fine-tuning, allowing the computational change to be used with an existing model.

The empirical evaluation reports that model quality is well maintained. For a 4-bit quantized model based on LLaMA-7B at a context length of 16k, the reported speedup reaches up to two times. This is a result for the evaluated configuration, rather than a uniform speedup claim for every model or context length. The paper's central contribution is a hardware-aware route to faster CPU attention through register-based lookup operations.
summary.tldr: NoMAD-Attention replaces attention multiply-add operations with fast CPU register lookups, speeding inference without model fine-tuning.

title: NoMAD-Attention: Efficient LLM Inference on CPUs Through Multiply-add-free Attention

abstract: Ensuring that the outputs of neural networks satisfy specific constraints is crucial for applying neural networks to real-life decision-making problems. In this paper, we consider making a batch of neural network outputs satisfy bounded and general linear constraints. We first reformulate the neural network output projection problem as an entropy-regularized linear programming problem. We show that such a problem can be equivalently transformed into an unconstrained convex optimization problem with Lipschitz continuous gradient according to the duality theorem. Then, based on an accelerated gradient descent algorithm with numerical performance enhancement, we present our architecture, GLinSAT, to solve the problem. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first general linear satisfiability layer in which all the operations are differentiable and matrix-factorization-free. Despite the fact that we can explicitly perform backpropagation based on automatic differentiation mechanism, we also provide an alternative approach in GLinSAT to calculate the derivatives based on implicit differentiation of the optimality condition. Experimental results on constrained traveling salesman problems, partial graph matching with outliers, predictive portfolio allocation and power system unit commitment demonstrate the advantages of GLinSAT over existing satisfiability layers. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/HunterTracer/GLinSAT.

paragraphs: Neural-network outputs used for decision making may need to obey bounds and linear constraints. GLinSAT is a layer designed to enforce these requirements on a batch of outputs. The paper treats the adjustment of network predictions as an optimization problem that can remain connected to network training.

The authors formulate output projection as entropy-regularized linear programming. Using duality, they transform it into an equivalent unconstrained convex problem with a Lipschitz-continuous gradient. They solve that formulation using accelerated gradient descent with numerical enhancements. All operations are differentiable and avoid matrix factorization; the authors describe this combination as a first for general linear satisfiability layers.

Training can propagate derivatives through automatic differentiation or through an alternative based on implicitly differentiating the optimality condition. Experiments cover constrained traveling salesman problems, graph matching with outliers, portfolio allocation, and power system unit commitment. The reported advantages over existing layers support this optimization-based design as a way to integrate linear feasibility requirements into neural-network systems.
summary.tldr: GLinSAT enforces bounds and general linear constraints through a differentiable optimization layer that avoids matrix factorization.

title: GLinSAT: The General Linear Satisfiability Neural Network Layer By Accelerated Gradient Descent

abstract: High-dimensional linear bandits with low-dimensional structure have received considerable attention in recent studies due to their practical significance. The most common structure in the literature is sparsity. However, it may not be available in practice. Symmetry, where the reward is invariant under certain groups of transformations on the set of arms, is another important inductive bias in the high-dimensional case that covers many standard structures, including sparsity. In this work, we study high-dimensional symmetric linear bandits where the symmetry is hidden from the learner, and the correct symmetry needs to be learned in an online setting. We examine the structure of a collection of hidden symmetry and provide a method based on model selection within the collection of low-dimensional subspaces. Our algorithm achieves a regret bound of $ O(d_0^{2/3} T^{2/3} \log(d))$, where $d$ is the ambient dimension which is potentially very large, and $d_0$ is the dimension of the true low-dimensional subspace such that $d_0 \ll d$. With an extra assumption on well-separated models, we can further improve the regret to $ O(d_0 \sqrt{T\log(d)} )$.

paragraphs: A high-dimensional decision problem may have a simpler underlying structure that makes learning easier. This paper studies symmetry in linear bandits: transformations of available actions that leave rewards unchanged. Unlike a setting where that symmetry is supplied in advance, the learner must discover the relevant structure while selecting actions and observing outcomes.

The authors examine a collection of possible hidden symmetries and develop a method that selects among corresponding low-dimensional subspaces. The true subspace has dimension d0, much smaller than the ambient dimension d. This turns learning hidden symmetry into a model-selection problem, allowing the algorithm to exploit structure that is not directly visible at the start.

The algorithm's regret is bounded by an order of d0 to the two-thirds power times T to the two-thirds power times log(d). With an additional assumption that candidate models are well separated, the bound improves to order d0 times the square root of T log(d). That stronger result is conditional: separation enables the improved guarantee. Both bounds show how hidden low-dimensional structure can reduce dependence on the large ambient dimension.
summary.tldr: Model selection over low-dimensional subspaces enables linear-bandit learning with hidden symmetry, with stronger regret guarantees when models are well separated.

title: Symmetric Linear Bandits with Hidden Symmetry

abstract: As the usage of large language models (LLMs) grows, it becomes increasingly important to serve them quickly and efficiently. While speculative decoding has recently emerged as a promising direction for accelerating LLM serving, existing methods are limited in their ability to scale to larger speculation budgets and adapt to different hyperparameters. This paper introduces Sequoia, a scalable and robust algorithm for speculative decoding. To improve scalability, Sequoia introduces a dynamic programming algorithm to find an optimal tree structure for the speculated tokens. To achieve robust speculative decoding, Sequoia uses a novel sampling and verification method that outperforms prior work across different decoding temperatures. Sequoia improves the decoding speed of Llama2-7B, Llama2-13B, and Vicuna-33B on an A100 GPU by up to $4.04\times$, $3.73\times$, and $2.27 \times$. To serve Llama3-70B-Instruct on a single L40 GPU through offloading, Sequoia reduces the per-token decoding latency to 0.60 s/token, $9.5\times$ faster than DeepSpeed-Zero-Inference.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model generation by proposing tokens for subsequent verification. Existing approaches can struggle to benefit from larger speculation budgets or remain effective across decoding settings. Sequoia addresses both issues, focusing on how proposed tokens are organized and how they are sampled and checked.

For scalability, Sequoia uses dynamic programming to find an optimal tree structure for speculative tokens. For robustness, it introduces a sampling and verification method that outperforms earlier work across different decoding temperatures. These are results for the stated configurations, illustrating improvements both in conventional serving and in the reported offloading setup.
summary.tldr: Sequoia optimizes speculative token trees and verification, delivering substantial decoding speedups across the reported model and hardware configurations.

title: Sequoia: Scalable and Robust Speculative Decoding

abstract: This paper presents an auditing procedure for the Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD) algorithm in the black-box threat model that is substantially tighter than prior work.The main intuition is to craft worst-case initial model parameters, as DP-SGD's privacy analysis is agnostic to the choice of the initial model parameters.For models trained on MNIST and CIFAR-10 at theoretical $\varepsilon=10.0$, our auditing procedure yields empirical estimates of $\varepsilon_{emp} = 7.21$ and $6.95$, respectively, on a 1,000-record sample and $\varepsilon_{emp} = 6.48$ and $4.96$ on the full datasets.By contrast, previous audits were only (relatively) tight in stronger white-box models, where the adversary can access the model's inner parameters and insert arbitrary gradients.Overall, our auditing procedure can offer valuable insight into how the privacy analysis of DP-SGD could be improved and detect bugs and DP violations in real-world implementations.The source code needed to reproduce our experiments is available from https://github.com/spalabucr/bb-audit-dpsgd.

paragraphs: This paper develops a stronger empirical audit for Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent, or DP-SGD, under a black-box threat model. The goal is to probe privacy behavior without the stronger access assumed by earlier relatively tight audits, which could inspect internal parameters and insert arbitrary gradients.

The central idea is to craft worst-case initial model parameters. DP-SGD’s theoretical privacy analysis does not depend on the particular initialization, making this a useful place to construct a demanding audit. The procedure produces empirical privacy estimates substantially closer to the theoretical level than prior black-box work.

For models with theoretical epsilon 10.0, the audit estimates epsilon at 7.21 on MNIST and 6.95 on CIFAR-10 using 1,000-record samples. On the full datasets, the corresponding estimates are 6.48 and 4.96. These figures describe the audit’s empirical findings rather than replacing the theoretical analysis. The authors present the procedure as a way to inform improvements to privacy analysis and detect implementation bugs or differential-privacy violations.
summary.tldr: Carefully chosen model initializations enable substantially tighter black-box privacy audits of DP-SGD.

title: Nearly Tight Black-Box Auditing of Differentially Private Machine Learning

abstract: Diffusion models, a specific type of generative model, have achieved unprecedented performance in recent years and consistently produce high-quality synthetic samples. A critical prerequisite for their notable success lies in the presence of a substantial number of training samples, which can be impractical in real-world applications due to high collection costs or associated risks. Consequently, various finetuning and regularization approaches have been proposed to transfer knowledge from existing pre-trained models to specific target domains with limited data. This paper introduces the Transfer Guided Diffusion Process (TGDP), a novel approach distinct from conventional finetuning and regularization methods. We prove that the optimal diffusion model for the target domain integrates pre-trained diffusion models on the source domain with additional guidance from a domain classifier. We further extend TGDP to a conditional version for modeling the joint distribution of data and its corresponding labels, together with two additional regularization terms to enhance the model performance. We validate the effectiveness of TGDP on both simulated and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can produce high-quality samples, but training them successfully typically requires substantial data. When a target domain has few examples, transferring knowledge from an existing model becomes valuable. This paper proposes the Transfer Guided Diffusion Process, or TGDP, as a different approach from conventional fine-tuning and regularization-based transfer.

The authors prove a relationship in which the optimal target-domain diffusion model combines pretrained source-domain diffusion models with guidance from a domain classifier. That result provides the basis for the proposed transfer process. The classifier supplies domain-related guidance, while the pretrained models contribute knowledge already learned from source data.

The paper also develops a conditional version that models data together with its labels and adds two regularization terms to improve performance. Experiments on simulated and real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of TGDP. The contribution connects a theoretical characterization of the target model with a practical transfer method, offering a way to use source-domain generative knowledge when target-domain training data is limited.
summary.tldr: TGDP transfers diffusion models through domain-classifier guidance, supported by a theoretical characterization of the optimal target-domain model.

title: Transfer Learning for Diffusion Models

abstract: Data assimilation is a vital component in modern global medium-range weather forecasting systems to obtain the best estimation of the atmospheric state by combining the short-term forecast and observations. Recently, AI-based data assimilation approaches have attracted increasing attention for their significant advantages over traditional techniques in terms of computational consumption. However, existing AI-based data assimilation methods can only handle observations with a specific resolution, lacking the compatibility and generalization ability to assimilate observations with other resolutions. Considering that complex real-world observations often have different resolutions, we propose the Fourier Neural Processes (FNP) for arbitrary-resolution data assimilation in this paper. Leveraging the efficiency of the designed modules and flexible structure of neural processes, FNP achieves state-of-the-art results in assimilating observations with varying resolutions, and also exhibits increasing advantages over the counterparts as the resolution and the amount of observations increase. Moreover, our FNP trained on a fixed resolution can directly handle the assimilation of observations with out-of-distribution resolutions and the observational information reconstruction task without additional fine-tuning, demonstrating its excellent generalization ability across data resolutions as well as across tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/OpenEarthLab/FNP.

paragraphs: Weather forecasting uses data assimilation to combine short-term forecasts with observations and estimate the atmosphere’s current state. Existing AI approaches can reduce computational demands, but the paper identifies a restriction: they handle observations at a particular resolution. Real observations vary in resolution, making that restriction an obstacle to their use.

Fourier Neural Processes, or FNP, are designed to assimilate observations at arbitrary resolutions. The approach combines efficient modules with the flexible structure of neural processes. Experiments report state-of-the-art assimilation results across varying resolutions, with its advantages over comparison methods increasing as observation resolution and the amount of available observational data increase.

The same model performs observational-information reconstruction without additional fine-tuning. These findings demonstrate transfer across both resolutions and tasks in the reported evaluation, making resolution flexibility a central part of the contribution alongside assimilation performance.
summary.tldr: FNP combines forecasts and observations across varying resolutions, including unseen resolutions, without additional fine-tuning.

title: FNP: Fourier Neural Processes for Arbitrary-Resolution Data Assimilation

abstract: In this paper, we examine the robustness of Nash equilibria in continuous games, under both strategic and dynamic uncertainty. Starting with the former, we introduce the notion of a robust equilibrium as those equilibria that remain invariant to small—but otherwise arbitrary—perturbations to the game’s payoff structure, and we provide a crisp geometric characterization thereof. Subsequently, we turn to the question of dynamic robustness, and we examine which equilibria may arise as stable limit points of the dynamics of “follow the regularized leader” (FTRL) in the presence of randomness and uncertainty. Despite their very distinct origins, we establish a structural correspondence between these two notions of robustness: strategic robustness implies dynamic robustness, and, conversely, the requirement of strategic robustness cannot be relaxed if dynamic robustness is to be maintained. Finally, we examine the rate of convergence to robust equilibria as a function of the underlying regularizer, and we show that entropically regularized learning converges at a geometric rate in games with affinely constrained action spaces.

Subsequently, we turn to the question of dynamic robustness, and we examine which equilibria may arise as stable limit points of the dynamics of “follow the regularized leader” (FTRL) in the presence of randomness and uncertainty. Despite their very distinct origins, we establish a structural correspondence between these two notions of robustness: strategic robustness implies dynamic robustness, and, conversely, the requirement of strategic robustness cannot be relaxed if dynamic robustness is to be maintained. Finally, we examine the rate of convergence to robust equilibria as a function of the underlying regularizer, and we show that entropically regularized learning converges at a geometric rate in games with affinely constrained action spaces.

paragraphs: This paper connects two meanings of robustness for Nash equilibria in continuous games. Strategic robustness asks whether an equilibrium remains unchanged when the payoff structure receives small, otherwise arbitrary perturbations. Dynamic robustness asks whether learning under randomness and uncertainty can stably approach that equilibrium.

The authors define strategically robust equilibria and give a geometric characterization of them. They then study stable limit points of follow-the-regularized-leader dynamics. Although the two robustness notions originate from different questions, the analysis establishes a structural correspondence: strategic robustness implies dynamic robustness, and its requirement cannot be weakened while preserving the stated dynamic robustness.

The paper also examines convergence speed and its dependence on the regularizer used by the learning dynamics. With entropic regularization, it proves geometric convergence to robust equilibria in games with affinely constrained action spaces. This rate result has a specific setting, while the broader contribution links stability of game solutions under payoff changes with stability of learning trajectories under uncertainty. The connection helps explain which equilibria are resilient in both senses.
summary.tldr: The paper connects payoff-robust equilibria with stable learning dynamics and proves geometric convergence for entropic learning under affine action constraints.

title: Robust Equilibria in Continuous Games: From Strategic to Dynamic Robustness

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) on graph-structured data typically faces non-IID challenges, particularly in scenarios where each client holds a distinct subgraph sampled from a global graph. In this paper, we introduce **Fed**erated learning with **Aux**iliary projections (FedAux), a personalized subgraph FL framework that learns to align, compare, and aggregate heterogeneously distributed local models without sharing raw data or node embeddings. In FedAux, each client jointly trains (i) a local GNN and (ii) a learnable auxiliary projection vector (APV) that differentiably projects node embeddings onto a 1D space. A soft-sorting operation followed by a lightweight 1D convolution refines these embeddings in the ordered space, enabling the APV to effectively capture client-specific information. After local training, these APVs serve as compact signatures that the server uses to compute inter‑client similarities and perform similarity‑weighted parameter mixing, yielding personalized models while preserving cross‑client knowledge transfer. Moreover, we provide rigorous theoretical analysis to establish the convergence and rationality of our design. Empirical evaluations across diverse graph benchmarks demonstrate that FedAux substantially outperforms existing baselines in both accuracy and personalization performance. The code is available at [https://github.com/JhuoW/FedAux](https://github.com/JhuoW/FedAux).

paragraphs: FedAux addresses federated learning when different clients hold different subgraphs of a larger graph. Their local data distributions can differ substantially, creating a need to share useful knowledge while retaining client-specific behavior. The framework learns how to compare and combine local models without exchanging raw data or node embeddings.

Each client trains a graph neural network together with an auxiliary projection vector that maps node embeddings into one dimension. Soft sorting and a lightweight one-dimensional convolution refine this ordered representation, helping the projection capture information specific to the client. After training, the projection vectors act as compact signatures that the server uses to estimate similarities between clients.

Those similarities determine how model parameters are mixed, producing personalized models while retaining cross-client knowledge transfer. The authors provide theoretical analysis of convergence and the rationale for the design. Across diverse graph benchmarks, FedAux substantially outperforms the evaluated baselines in accuracy and personalization. The main contribution is a learned client-comparison mechanism that guides selective sharing under heterogeneous graph data.
summary.tldr: FedAux learns compact client signatures to guide personalized model sharing across heterogeneous subgraphs without sharing raw data or node embeddings.

title: Personalized Subgraph Federated Learning with Differentiable Auxiliary Projections

abstract: Retrieval systems rely on representations learned by increasingly powerful models. However, due to the high training cost and inconsistencies in learned representations, there is significant interest in facilitating communication between representations and ensuring compatibility across independently trained neural networks. In the literature, two primary approaches are commonly used to adapt different learned representations: affine transformations, which adapt well to specific distributions but can significantly alter the original representation, and orthogonal transformations, which preserve the original structure with strict geometric constraints but limit adaptability. A key challenge is adapting the latent spaces of updated models to align with those of previous models on downstream distributions while preserving the newly learned representation spaces. In this paper, we impose a relaxed orthogonality constraint, namely $\lambda$-Orthogonality regularization, while learning an affine transformation, to obtain distribution-specific adaptation while retaining the original learned representations. Extensive experiments across various architectures and datasets validate our approach, demonstrating that it preserves the model's zero-shot performance and ensures compatibility across model updates. Code available at: \href{https://github.com/miccunifi/lambda_orthogonality.git}{https://github.com/miccunifi/lambda\_orthogonality}.

paragraphs: Retrieval systems need representations from different models to remain compatible, especially when a newer model replaces an older one. Independently trained networks can organize their representation spaces differently. Aligning those spaces therefore involves preserving what the new model has learned while adapting it to representations already used by the system.

The paper addresses a tension between two transformation families. Affine transformations can adapt to a particular data distribution but may substantially alter the original representation. Orthogonal transformations preserve its geometry more strictly, which restricts their flexibility. The proposed lambda-Orthogonality regularization relaxes the orthogonality requirement while an affine transformation is learned, combining adaptation with a constraint on geometric distortion.

Experiments across architectures and datasets report compatibility across model updates while preserving zero-shot performance. This matters because successful alignment should retain the newer model's capabilities as well as allow its representations to communicate with older ones. The results support relaxed geometric regularization as a way to manage that balance in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Relaxing orthogonality during representation alignment helps maintain compatibility across model updates while preserving zero-shot performance.

title: $\boldsymbol{\lambda}$-Orthogonality Regularization for Compatible Representation Learning

abstract: Industrial anomaly segmentation relies heavily on pixel-level annotations, yet real-world anomalies are often scarce, diverse, and costly to label. Segmentation-oriented industrial anomaly synthesis (SIAS) has emerged as a promising alternative; however, existing methods struggle to balance sampling efficiency and generation quality. Moreover, most approaches treat all spatial regions uniformly, overlooking the distinct statistical differences between anomaly and background areas. This uniform treatment hinders the synthesis of controllable, structure-specific anomalies tailored for segmentation tasks. In this paper, we propose FAST, a foreground-aware diffusion framework featuring two novel modules: the Anomaly-Informed Accelerated Sampling (AIAS) and the Foreground-Aware Reconstruction Module (FARM). AIAS is a training-free sampling algorithm specifically designed for segmentation-oriented industrial anomaly synthesis, which accelerates the reverse process through coarse-to-fine aggregation and enables the synthesis of state-of-the-art segmentation-oriented anomalies in as few as 10 steps. Meanwhile, FARM adaptively adjusts the anomaly-aware noise within the masked foreground regions at each sampling step, preserving localized anomaly signals throughout the denoising trajectory. Extensive experiments on multiple industrial benchmarks demonstrate that FAST consistently outperforms existing anomaly synthesis methods in downstream segmentation tasks. We release the code in https://github.com/Chhro123/fast-foreground-aware-anomaly-synthesis.

paragraphs: Industrial anomaly segmentation needs examples with pixel-level labels, but real defects can be scarce, varied, and expensive to annotate. Synthesizing anomalies offers another source of training data. The authors identify two obstacles: balancing generation quality with sampling speed, and treating anomalous regions and background uniformly despite their different statistical properties.

FAST combines two modules to address these obstacles. Anomaly-Informed Accelerated Sampling is a training-free sampling procedure that uses coarse-to-fine aggregation to accelerate diffusion’s reverse process. It can generate high-quality anomalies for segmentation in as few as ten steps. The Foreground-Aware Reconstruction Module adjusts anomaly-related noise inside masked foreground regions at every sampling step.

The foreground adjustment preserves localized anomaly information as denoising proceeds, supporting control over where and how a defect appears. Evaluations across multiple industrial benchmarks find that FAST consistently improves downstream segmentation over existing anomaly synthesis methods. The reported benefit therefore concerns the usefulness of generated examples for learning segmentation, alongside the reduction in sampling steps needed to produce them.
summary.tldr: FAST combines accelerated diffusion sampling with foreground-specific noise control to generate anomalies that improve industrial segmentation.

title: FAST: Foreground‑aware Diffusion with Accelerated Sampling Trajectory for Segmentation‑oriented Anomaly Synthesis

abstract: In this paper, we present RigAnyFace (RAF), a scalable neural auto-rigging framework for facial meshes of diverse topologies, including those with multiple disconnected components. RAF deforms a static neutral facial mesh into industry-standard FACS poses to form an expressive blendshape rig. Deformations are predicted by a triangulation-agnostic surface learning network augmented with our tailored architecture design to condition on FACS parameters and efficiently process disconnected components. For training, we curated a dataset of facial meshes, with a subset meticulously rigged by professional artists to serve as accurate 3D ground truth for deformation supervision. Due to the high cost of manual rigging, this subset is limited in size, constraining the generalization ability of models trained exclusively on it. To address this, we design a 2D supervision strategy for unlabeled neutral meshes without rigs. This strategy increases data diversity and allows for scaled training, thereby enhancing the generalization ability of models trained on this augmented data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RAF is able to rig meshes of diverse topologies on not only our artist-crafted assets but also in-the-wild samples, outperforming previous works in accuracy and generalizability. Moreover, our method advances beyond prior work by supporting multiple disconnected components, such as eyeballs, for more detailed expression animation.

paragraphs: A facial animation rig needs controlled deformations that turn a neutral mesh into expressions. It handles varied mesh topologies, including faces with disconnected parts such as separate eyeballs.

Its surface-learning network is designed to work independently of a particular triangulation, condition predictions on facial-action parameters, and process disconnected components efficiently. Training uses a professionally rigged subset of a curated mesh dataset for accurate 3D supervision. Because manual rigging is costly, that labeled subset alone limits the diversity available for learning.

The authors add a 2D supervision strategy that can use neutral meshes without existing rigs. This expands the training data and improves generalization. Experiments on artist-created assets and in-the-wild samples report better accuracy and generalizability than previous methods. The contribution combines broader mesh compatibility with a way to learn from unlabeled assets, while supporting more detailed animation through disconnected components.
summary.tldr: RigAnyFace uses unlabeled meshes and 2D supervision to scale facial auto-rigging across diverse topologies and disconnected components.

title: RigAnyFace: Scaling Neural Facial Mesh Auto-Rigging with Unlabeled Data

abstract: Achieving fine-grained spatio-temporal understanding in videos remains a major challenge for current Video Large Multimodal Models (Video LMMs). Addressing this challenge requires mastering two core capabilities: video referring understanding, which captures the semantics of video regions, and video grounding, which segments object regions based on natural language descriptions. However, most existing approaches tackle these tasks in isolation, limiting progress toward unified, referentially grounded video interaction. We identify a key bottleneck in the lack of high-quality, unified video instruction data and a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating referentially grounded video chat. To address these challenges, we contribute in three core aspects: dataset, model, and benchmark. First, we introduce SAMA-239K, a large-scale dataset comprising 15K videos specifically curated to enable joint learning of video referring understanding, grounding, and multi-turn video chat. Second, we propose the SAMA model, which incorporates a versatile spatio-temporal context aggregator and a Segment Anything Model to jointly enhance fine-grained video comprehension and precise grounding capabilities. Finally, we establish SAMA-Bench, a meticulously designed benchmark consisting of 5,067 questions from 522 videos, to comprehensively evaluate the integrated capabilities of Video LMMs in multi-turn, spatio-temporal referring understanding and grounded dialogue. Extensive experiments and benchmarking results show that SAMA not only achieves strong performance on SAMA-Bench but also sets a new state-of-the-art on general grounding benchmarks, while maintaining highly competitive performance on standard visual understanding benchmarks.

These abilities are often studied separately, leaving a gap in unified systems for grounded, multi-turn video interaction.

The model combines a spatio-temporal context aggregator with a Segment Anything Model to connect detailed video comprehension with precise region segmentation.
