Together, these findings support training and evaluating language-based video understanding alongside explicit region grounding, so that dialogue can stay connected to the visual content it refers to.
summary.tldr: SAMA combines a dataset, model, and benchmark for video conversations that understand references and segment the corresponding regions across time.

title: SAMA: Towards Multi-Turn Referential Grounded Video Chat with Large Language Models

abstract: Process Reward Models (PRMs) have shown promise in enhancing the mathematical reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) through Test-Time Scaling (TTS). However, their integration into multimodal reasoning remains largely unexplored. In this work, we take the first step toward unlocking the potential of PRMs in multimodal mathematical reasoning. We identify three key challenges: (i) the scarcity of high-quality reasoning data constrains the capabilities of foundation Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), which imposes further limitations on the upper bounds of TTS and reinforcement learning (RL); (ii) a lack of automated methods for process labeling within multimodal contexts persists; (iii) the employment of process rewards in unimodal RL faces issues like reward hacking, which may extend to multimodal scenarios. To address these issues, we introduce URSA, a three-stage Unfolding multimodal pRocess-Supervision Aided training framework. We first construct MMathCoT-1M, a high-quality large-scale multimodal Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning dataset, to build a stronger math reasoning foundation MLLM, URSA-8B. Subsequently, we go through an automatic process to synthesize process supervision data, which emphasizes both logical correctness and perceptual consistency. We introduce DualMath-1.1M to facilitate the training of URSA-8B-RM. Finally, we propose Process-Supervised Group-Relative-Policy-Optimization (PS-GRPO), pioneering a multimodal PRM-aided online RL method that outperforms vanilla GRPO. With PS-GRPO application, URSA-8B-PS-GRPO outperforms Gemma3-12B and GPT-4o by 8.4% and 2.7% on average across 6 benchmarks.

paragraphs: URSA investigates process reward models for mathematical reasoning that combines visual and textual information. Such models evaluate reasoning steps, making the quality of intermediate work a training signal. The paper identifies three obstacles: limited high-quality reasoning data, insufficient automated process labeling, and the possibility that reward hacking seen in unimodal settings could also arise here.

summary.tldr: URSA combines multimodal reasoning data, automated step supervision, and process-reward-guided reinforcement learning to improve mathematical reasoning across six benchmarks.

title: Unlocking Multimodal Mathematical Reasoning via Process Reward Model

abstract: We study the finite-horizon Restless Multi-Armed Bandit (RMAB) problem with $N$ homogeneous arms. Prior work has shown that when an RMAB satisfies a non-degeneracy condition, Linear-Programming-based (LP-based) policies derived from the fluid approximation, which captures the mean dynamics of the system, achieve an exponentially small optimality gap. However, it is common for RMABs to be degenerate, in which case LP-based policies can result in a $\Theta(1/\sqrt{N})$ optimality gap per arm. In this paper, we propose a novel Stochastic-Programming-based (SP-based) policy that, under a uniqueness assumption, achieves an $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/N)$ optimality gap for degenerate RMABs. Our approach is based on the construction of a Gaussian stochastic system that captures not only the mean but also the variance of the RMAB dynamics, resulting in a more accurate approximation than the fluid approximation. We then solve a stochastic program for this system to obtain our policy. This is the first result to establish an $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/N)$ optimality gap for degenerate RMABs.

paragraphs: The paper studies finite-horizon restless bandits with N homogeneous arms. A common planning approach replaces random system behavior with its average evolution and solves a linear program. Under a non-degeneracy condition, policies from this fluid approximation can be extremely close to optimal. In degenerate problems, however, their per-arm optimality gap can instead scale as one over the square root of N.

The authors construct a Gaussian approximation that represents both the mean evolution and its variance. This gives the planner information about fluctuations that the fluid approximation omits. They then solve a stochastic program for this approximate system to obtain a policy.

Under a uniqueness assumption, the proposed policy achieves an optimality gap of order one over N, up to logarithmic factors, for degenerate problems. The abstract identifies this as the first such result. The contribution is therefore a conditional theoretical improvement: explicitly accounting for variability can sharpen policy guarantees in a setting where planning around the mean can be insufficient.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian approximation enables a stochastic-programming policy with a near-1/N optimality gap for degenerate restless bandits under a uniqueness assumption.

title: Achieving $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/N)$ Optimality Gap in Restless Bandits through Gaussian Approximation

abstract: The process of editing an image can be naturally modeled as evaluating a counterfactual query: “What would an image look like if a particular feature had changed?” While recent advances in text-guided image editing leverage powerful pre-trained models to produce visually appealing images, they often lack counterfactual consistency -- ignoring how features are causally related and how changing one may affect others. In contrast, existing causal-based editing approaches offer solid theoretical foundations and perform well in specific settings, but remain limited in scalability and often rely on labeled data. In this work, we aim to bridge the gap between causal editing and large-scale text-to-image generation through two main contributions. First, we introduce Backdoor Disentangled Causal Latent Space (BD-CLS), a new class of latent spaces that allows for the encoding of causal inductive biases. One desirable property of this latent space is that, even under weak supervision, it can be shown to exhibit counterfactual consistency. Second, and building on this result, we develop BD-CLS-Edit, an algorithm capable of learning a BD-CLS from a (non-causal) pre-trained Stable Diffusion model. This enables counterfactual image editing without retraining. Our method ensures that edits respect the causal relationships among features, even when some features are unlabeled or unprompted and the original latent space is oblivious to the environment’s underlying cause-and-effect relationships.

paragraphs: An image edit can ask what a scene would look like if one feature changed. Answering that question consistently requires accounting for causal relationships: changing one feature may require changes to others. The paper addresses a gap between visually effective text-guided editing and causal editing methods that have stronger foundations but face scalability and labeling constraints.

The authors introduce Backdoor Disentangled Causal Latent Space, or BD-CLS, a representation designed to encode assumptions about causal structure. They show that this class of representations can exhibit counterfactual consistency under weak supervision. The representation therefore gives the editing procedure a way to account for connected changes rather than treating every feature as independent.

Building on that result, BD-CLS-Edit learns the proposed representation from a pretrained Stable Diffusion model, enabling editing without retraining that model. The method is designed to respect causal relationships even when some affected features are unlabeled or absent from the prompt. Its contribution connects causal structure with a generative model whose original representation does not encode the environment’s causal relationships.
summary.tldr: BD-CLS-Edit adds a causally structured representation to pretrained Stable Diffusion to support consistent counterfactual edits under weak supervision.

title: Counterfactual Image Editing with Disentangled Causal Latent Space

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in video understanding. However, hallucination, where the model generates plausible yet incorrect outputs, persists as a significant and under-addressed challenge in the video domain. Among existing solutions, activation engineering has proven successful in mitigating hallucinations in LLMs and ImageLLMs, yet its applicability to VideoLLMs remains largely unexplored. In this work, we are the first to systematically investigate the effectiveness and underlying mechanisms of activation engineering for mitigating hallucinations in VideoLLMs. We initially conduct an investigation of the key factors affecting the performance of activation engineering and find that a model’s sensitivity to hallucination depends on $\textbf{temporal variation}$ rather than task type. Moreover, selecting appropriate internal modules and dataset for activation engineering is critical for reducing hallucination. Guided by these findings, we propose a temporal-aware activation engineering framework for VideoLLMs, which adaptively identifies and manipulates hallucination-sensitive modules based on the temporal variation characteristic, substantially mitigating hallucinations without additional LLM fine-tuning. Experiments across multiple models and benchmarks demonstrate that our method markedly reduces hallucination in VideoLLMs, thereby validating the robustness of our findings.

paragraphs: Video language models can produce convincing statements that do not match the video. This paper studies activation engineering as a way to reduce those hallucinations by manipulating internal model activity. Although that approach has been useful for text and image models, the authors investigate its effectiveness and mechanisms specifically in video models.

Their analysis identifies temporal variation as the relevant factor governing hallucination sensitivity, rather than task type. They also find that the choice of internal modules and the dataset used for activation engineering materially affects the outcome. These observations motivate a framework that adaptively identifies hallucination-sensitive modules using the video's temporal variation characteristics.

The framework intervenes in those modules without additional language-model fine-tuning. Experiments across multiple models and benchmarks show substantial reductions in hallucination, supporting the robustness of the findings across the tested settings. The practical contribution is a way to make activation interventions responsive to how video content varies over time, guided by an investigation of where those interventions are most effective.
summary.tldr: A temporally aware activation framework reduces video-model hallucinations by adaptively modifying sensitive internal modules without additional fine-tuning.

title: Mitigating Hallucination in VideoLLMs via Temporal-Aware Activation Engineering

abstract: Positive and Unlabeled (PU) learning is a special case of binary classification with weak supervision, where only positive labeled and unlabeled data are available. Previous studies suggest several specific risk estimators of PU learning such as non-negative PU (nnPU), which are unbiased and consistent with the expected risk of supervised binary classification. In nnPU, the negative-class empirical risk is estimated by positive labeled and unlabeled data with a non-negativity constraint. However, its negative-class empirical risk estimator approaches 0, so the negative class is over-played, resulting in imbalanced error rates between positive and negative classes. To solve this problem, we suppose that the expected risks of the positive-class and negative-class should be close. Accordingly, we constrain that the negative-class empirical risk estimator is lower bounded by the positive-class empirical risk, instead of 0; and also incorporate an explicit equality constraint between them. we suggest a risk estimator of PU learning that balances positive and negative classification error rates, named $\mathrm{D{\small C-PU} }$, and suggest an efficient training method for $\mathrm{D{\small C-PU} }$ based on the augmented Lagrange multiplier framework. We theoretically analyze the estimation error of $\mathrm{D{\small C-PU} }$ and empirically validate that $\mathrm{D{\small C-PU} }$ achieves higher accuracy and converges more stable than other risk estimators of PU learning. Additionally, $\mathrm{D{\small C-PU} }$ also performs competitive accuracy performance with practical PU learning methods.

This requires estimating the negative-class contribution to training risk indirectly. The paper identifies a problem with non-negative PU learning: its negative-risk estimate can approach zero, producing an imbalance between errors on positive and negative examples.

The proposed estimator, DC-PU, starts from the assumption that the two classes' expected risks should be close. It replaces the zero lower bound on estimated negative risk with the estimated positive risk, and adds an explicit equality constraint between them. These constraints make class balance part of the training objective rather than relying only on preventing a negative risk estimate.

The authors develop an efficient training procedure using an augmented Lagrange multiplier framework and analyze the estimator's error theoretically. Empirical comparisons show higher accuracy and more stable convergence than other PU risk estimators, alongside competitive accuracy against practical PU learning methods. The approach's motivation rests on its stated risk-balancing assumption, which directly shapes how the classifier is trained.
summary.tldr: DC-PU constrains positive and negative risk estimates to improve error balance, accuracy, and training stability in positive-unlabeled learning.

title: Balancing Positive and Negative Classification Error Rates in Positive-Unlabeled Learning

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across various tasks, but fine-tuning them for domain-specific applications often requires substantial domain-specific data that may be distributed across multiple organizations. Federated Learning (FL) offers a privacy-preserving solution, but faces challenges with computational constraints when applied to LLMs. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has emerged as a parameter-efficient fine-tuning approach, though a single LoRA module often struggles with heterogeneous data across diverse domains. This paper addresses two critical challenges in federated LoRA fine-tuning: 1. determining the optimal number and allocation of LoRA experts across heterogeneous clients, and 2. enabling clients to selectively utilize these experts based on their specific data characteristics. We propose FedLEASE (Federated adaptive LoRA Expert Allocation and SElection), a novel framework that adaptively clusters clients based on representation similarity to allocate and train domain-specific LoRA experts. It also introduces an adaptive top-$M$ Mixture-of-Experts mechanism that allows each client to select the optimal number of utilized experts. Our extensive experiments on diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate that FedLEASE significantly outperforms existing federated fine-tuning approaches in heterogeneous client settings while maintaining communication efficiency.

Federated learning supports collaboration across those clients, while LoRA makes adaptation less computationally demanding. The findings support adapting the organization and use of lightweight experts to differences among participating clients.

title: Adaptive LoRA Experts Allocation and Selection for Federated Fine-Tuning

abstract: Non-log-concave sampling from an unnormalized density is fundamental in machine learning and statistics. As datasets grow larger, computational efficiency becomes increasingly important, particularly in reducing adaptive complexity, namely the number of sequential rounds required for sampling algorithms. In this work, we initiate the study of the adaptive complexity of non-log-concave sampling within the framework of relative Fisher information introduced by Balasubramanian et al. in 2022. To obtain a relative fisher information of at most $\varepsilon^2$ from the target distribution, we propose a novel algorithm that reduces the adaptive complexity from $\mathcal{O}(d^2/\varepsilon^4)$ to $\mathcal{O}(d/\varepsilon^2)$ by leveraging parallelism. Furthermore, we show our algorithm is optimal for a specific regime of large $\varepsilon$. Our algorithm builds on a diagonally parallelized Picard iteration, while the lower bound is based on a reduction from the problem of finding stationary points.

paragraphs: Sampling from an unnormalized distribution can require many computational steps that depend on earlier results. This paper studies how many sequential rounds are needed when the target distribution is not log-concave. It measures sampling accuracy through relative Fisher information and focuses on adaptive complexity, the part of computation that cannot simply be performed simultaneously.

For a target relative Fisher information of at most epsilon squared, the proposed algorithm reduces the sequential-round bound from O(d²/epsilon⁴) to O(d/epsilon²), where d is dimension. It achieves this through parallelism using a diagonally parallelized Picard iteration. The result concerns the number of dependent rounds, so its stated improvement specifically describes how the computation can be organized across parallel work.

The authors also establish a matching optimality result in a particular regime of large epsilon. Their lower bound comes from reducing the problem of finding stationary points to this sampling setting. This provides both an improved algorithm and a boundary on further improvements within that regime, while leaving the optimality claim explicitly tied to the stated accuracy range.
summary.tldr: A parallel sampling algorithm reduces sequential-round complexity for controlling relative Fisher information and is optimal in a specified large-epsilon regime.

title: The Adaptive Complexity of Minimizing Relative Fisher Information

abstract: Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) achieves strong generalization in vision-language tasks by aligning images and texts in a shared embedding space. However, recent findings show that CLIP-like models still underutilize fine-grained semantic signals in text, and this issue becomes even more pronounced when dealing with long and detailed captions. This stems from CLIP’s training objective, which optimizes only global image-text similarity and overlooks token-level supervision—limiting its ability to achieve fine-grained visual-text alignment. To address this, we propose SuperCLIP, a simple yet effective framework that augments contrastive learning with classification-based supervision. By adding only a lightweight linear layer to the vision encoder, SuperCLIP leverages token-level cues to enhance visual-textual alignment — with just a 0.077\% increase in total FLOPs, and no need for additional annotated data. Experiments show that SuperCLIP consistently improves zero-shot classification, image-text retrieval, and purely visual tasks. These gains hold regardless of whether the model is trained on original web data or rich re-captioned data, demonstrating SuperCLIP’s ability to recover textual supervision in both cases. Furthermore, SuperCLIP alleviates CLIP’s small-batch performance drop through classification-based supervision that avoids reliance on large batch sizes. Code and models will be made open source.

The findings suggest that using existing caption information more directly can improve alignment without a substantial architectural expansion.
summary.tldr: SuperCLIP adds lightweight token-informed classification supervision to improve image-text alignment and downstream performance with minimal added computation.

title: SuperCLIP: CLIP with Simple Classification Supervision

abstract: In this paper, we study the evolution of tokens through the depth of encoder-only transformer models at inference time by modeling them as a system of particles interacting in a mean-field way and studying the corresponding dynamics. More specifically, we consider this problem in the moderate interaction regime, where the number $N$ of tokens is large and the inverse temperature parameter $\beta$ of the model scales together with $N$. In this regime, the dynamics of the system displays a multiscale behavior: a fast phase, where the token empirical measure collapses on a low-dimensional space, an intermediate phase, where the measure further collapses into clusters, and a slow one, where such clusters sequentially merge into a single one. We provide a rigorous characterization of the limiting dynamics in each of these phases and prove convergence in the above mentioned limit, exemplifying our results with some simulations.

paragraphs: This paper studies how token representations change as they pass through the depth of an encoder-only transformer during inference. It treats tokens as interacting particles and analyzes their collective evolution. The object being tracked is the empirical measure of the tokens: a mathematical description of how their representations are distributed, rather than a separate account of every token.

The analysis concerns a specific limit called the moderate interaction regime. The number of tokens becomes large while the model’s inverse temperature parameter grows along with it. Under this scaling, the dynamics unfold at three different rates. First, representations rapidly concentrate in a lower-dimensional space. Next, they form clusters. Finally, those clusters merge sequentially on a slower timescale until one remains.

The authors rigorously characterize the limiting dynamics of each phase and prove convergence in the stated regime, with simulations illustrating the results. The contribution is a mathematical explanation of distinct stages of collective token evolution. Its conclusions concern the modeled inference dynamics and scaling assumptions, rather than an unrestricted claim about every transformer.
summary.tldr: A mathematical analysis identifies three timescales of token concentration and merging in mean-field transformers under a specified large-token scaling regime.

title: A multiscale analysis of mean-field transformers in the moderate interaction regime

abstract: Large language models are trained with tokenizers that map text to a fixed vocabulary, yet the resulting token distribution is highly imbalanced: a few words dominate the stream while most occur rarely. Recent practice favours ever-larger vocabularies, but it is unclear whether the benefit comes from better word segmentation or from amplifying this frequency skew. To this end, we perform a controlled study that scales the vocabulary of a constant-size Transformer from 24K to 196K symbols while holding data, compute and optimisation unchanged. Above 24K every common word is already a single token, so further growth only increases imbalance. Word-level loss decomposition shows that larger vocabularies reduce cross-entropy almost exclusively by lowering uncertainty on the ~$2,500$ most frequent words, even though loss on the rare tail rises. Same frequent words cover roughly $80\%$ of tokens in downstream benchmarks, this training advantage transfers intact. We further show that enlarging model parameters with a fixed tokenizer yields the same frequent-word benefit, revealing a shared mechanism behind vocabulary and model scaling. Our results recast “bigger vocabularies help” as “sharper frequency imbalance helps,” offering a simple, principled knob for tokenizer–model co-design and clarifying the loss dynamics that govern language-model scaling in pre-training.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why larger token vocabularies can improve language-model training. The authors distinguish two possible explanations: better splitting of words into tokens, and a stronger imbalance between frequent and rare tokens. They run a controlled study that increases vocabulary size from 24,000 to 196,000 symbols while keeping Transformer size, data, compute, and optimization unchanged.

In their setting, common words already occupy single tokens at the smallest vocabulary size. Further vocabulary growth therefore increases frequency imbalance without improving segmentation for those words. Those frequent words account for roughly 80% of tokens in the downstream benchmarks, allowing their training advantage to carry over. Increasing model parameters while keeping the tokenizer fixed produces a similar frequent-word benefit. The findings identify frequency imbalance as a shared mechanism in the studied vocabulary and model scaling settings, with implications for designing tokenizers and models together.
summary.tldr: A controlled study finds that larger vocabularies improve loss mainly on frequent words, even as rare-word loss rises.

title: Exploiting Vocabulary Frequency Imbalance in Language Model Pre-training

abstract: Finetuning large pretrained neural networks is known to be resource-intensive, both in terms of memory and computational cost. To mitigate this, a common approach is to restrict training to a subset of the model parameters. By analyzing the relationship between gradients and weights during finetuning, we observe a notable pattern: large gradients are often associated with small-magnitude weights. This correlation is more pronounced in fine-tuning settings than in training from scratch. Motivated by this observation, we propose \textsc{NanoAdam}, which dynamically updates only the small-magnitude weights during fine-tuning and offers several practical advantages: first, the criterion is \emph{gradient-free}—the parameter subset can be determined without gradient computation; second, it preserves large-magnitude weights, which are likely to encode critical features learned during pre-training, thereby reducing the risk of catastrophic forgetting; thirdly, it permits the use of larger learning rates and consistently leads to better generalization performance in experiments. We demonstrate this for both NLP and vision tasks.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning large pretrained networks consumes substantial memory and computation, motivating methods that update only some parameters. This paper examines how parameter values relate to their gradients. The authors observe that large gradients often occur at small-magnitude weights, and that this relationship is stronger during fine-tuning than during training from scratch.

Based on that observation, they introduce NanoAdam, which dynamically restricts updates to small-magnitude weights. Selecting this subset does not require computing gradients: the selection criterion uses weight magnitudes. The gradient-free claim therefore concerns choosing parameters, rather than claiming that the entire fine-tuning process operates without gradients.

Leaving large-magnitude weights unchanged is intended to preserve features learned during pretraining, since those weights are likely to encode important information. The authors argue that this reduces the risk of catastrophic forgetting. They also report that the method permits larger learning rates and consistently improves generalization in experiments spanning language and vision tasks. The contribution is a simple parameter-selection principle grounded in an observed relationship between weight size and fine-tuning gradients.
summary.tldr: NanoAdam dynamically fine-tunes small-magnitude weights, using a gradient-free selection rule motivated by their association with large gradients.

title: Pay Attention to Small Weights

abstract: Multimodal large language models have unlocked new possibilities for various multimodal tasks. However, their potential in image manipulation detection remains unexplored. When directly applied to the IMD task, M-LLMs often produce reasoning texts that suffer from hallucinations and overthinking. To address this, we propose ForgerySleuth, which leverages M-LLMs to perform comprehensive clue fusion and generate segmentation outputs indicating specific regions that are tampered with. Moreover, we construct the ForgeryAnalysis dataset through the Chain-of-Clues prompt, which includes analysis and reasoning text to upgrade the image manipulation detection task. A data engine is also introduced to build a larger-scale dataset for the pre-training phase. Our extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of ForgeryAnalysis and show that ForgerySleuth significantly outperforms existing methods in generalization, robustness, and explainability.

The paper identifies a problem with using these models directly: their explanations can contain hallucinations and excessive reasoning. Its approach combines analysis of manipulation clues with an explicit spatial output, so the system can indicate which parts of an image it judges to have been tampered with.

The contribution brings together training data, clue-based analysis, and region-level detection. Its stated findings suggest that this combination can make multimodal models more effective at both locating image edits and explaining the evidence behind their assessments.
summary.tldr: ForgerySleuth combines manipulation-clue reasoning with region segmentation and dedicated training data to improve image forgery detection.

title: ForgerySleuth: Empowering Multimodal Large Language Models for Image Manipulation Detection

abstract: This paper proposes Virtual Fitting Room (VFR), a novel video generative model that produces arbitrarily long virtual try-on videos. Our VFR models long video generation tasks as an auto-regressive, segment-by-segment generation process, eliminating the need for resource-intensive generation and lengthy video data, while providing the flexibility to generate videos of arbitrary length. The key challenges of this task are twofold: ensuring local smoothness between adjacent segments and maintaining global temporal consistency across different segments. To address these challenges, we propose our VFR framework, which ensures smoothness through a prefix video condition and enforces consistency with the anchor video — a 360°-view video that comprehensively captures the human's whole-body appearance. Our VFR generates minute-scale virtual try-on videos with both local smoothness and global temporal consistency under various motions, making it a pioneering work in long virtual try-on video generation. Project Page: https://immortalco.github.io/VirtualFittingRoom/.

paragraphs: Virtual Fitting Room generates virtual try-on videos from a single image using a process that can extend to arbitrary lengths. It generates successive segments autoregressively, making long videos through repeated segment generation. This formulation avoids the resource-intensive generation and lengthy video data requirements identified by the authors.

Segmented generation creates two distinct consistency problems. Neighboring segments must join smoothly, and the person's appearance must remain coherent across the entire sequence. VFR uses a prefix video condition to guide local continuity. It also conditions on an anchor video showing a 360-degree view of the person's whole-body appearance, providing a shared reference across segments.

The authors report minute-scale try-on videos with smooth local transitions and global temporal consistency under varied motions. The arbitrary-length capability comes from the repeatable generation structure, while the stated demonstration concerns minute-scale outputs. The contribution connects scalable segment generation with explicit conditioning for both nearby transitions and appearance consistency over longer stretches of video.
summary.tldr: VFR generates long virtual try-on videos segment by segment, using prefix and anchor videos to maintain continuity and appearance.

title: Virtual Fitting Room: Generating Arbitrarily Long Videos of Virtual Try-On from a Single Image

abstract: Adam is the de facto optimization algorithm for several deep learning applications, but an understanding of its implicit bias and how it differs from other algorithms, particularly standard first-order methods such as (stochastic) gradient descent (GD), remains limited. In practice, neural networks (NNs) trained with SGD are known to exhibit simplicity bias --- a tendency to find simple solutions. In contrast, we show that Adam is more resistant to such simplicity bias. First, we investigate the differences in the implicit biases of Adam and GD when training two-layer ReLU NNs on a binary classification task with Gaussian data. We find that GD exhibits a simplicity bias, resulting in a linear decision boundary with a suboptimal margin, whereas Adam leads to much richer and more diverse features, producing a nonlinear boundary that is closer to the Bayes' optimal predictor. This richer decision boundary also allows Adam to achieve higher test accuracy both in-distribution and under certain distribution shifts. We theoretically prove these results by analyzing the population gradients. Next, to corroborate our theoretical findings, we present extensive empirical results showing that this property of Adam leads to superior generalization across various datasets with spurious correlations where NNs trained with SGD are known to show simplicity bias and do not generalize well under certain distributional shifts.

paragraphs: This paper examines how the choice of optimizer influences the kinds of solutions a neural network learns. Gradient-based training can favor simple patterns even when richer patterns would generalize better. The authors investigate this simplicity bias and find that Adam is more resistant to it than gradient descent in their theoretical setting.

They analyze two-layer ReLU networks performing binary classification on Gaussian data. Gradient descent learns a linear decision boundary with a suboptimal margin, whereas Adam develops richer, more diverse features and a nonlinear boundary closer to the Bayes-optimal predictor. The authors then present experiments on datasets with spurious correlations, where SGD-trained networks are known to rely on simple patterns that can fail under shifts. The empirical results support improved generalization from Adam's richer representations in those settings. The paper connects optimizer behavior to feature learning and robustness, with its conclusions tied to the analyzed task and evaluated forms of distribution shift.
summary.tldr: Theory and experiments show Adam resisting simplicity bias and learning richer features that improve generalization in the studied settings.

title: The Rich and the Simple: On the Implicit Bias of Adam and SGD

abstract: The research on robust principal component analysis (RPCA) has been attracting much attention recently. The original RPCA model assumes sparse noise, and use the L_1-norm to characterize the error term. In practice, however, the noise is much more complex and it is not appropriate to simply use a certain L_p-norm for noise modeling. We propose a generative RPCA model under the Bayesian framework by modeling data noise as a mixture of Gaussians (MoG). The MoG is a universal approximator to continuous distributions and thus our model is able to fit a wide range of noises such as Laplacian, Gaussian, sparse noises and any combinations of them. A variational Bayes algorithm is presented to infer the posterior of the proposed model. All involved parameters can be recursively updated in closed form. The advantage of our method is demonstrated by extensive experiments on synthetic data, face modeling and background subtraction.

paragraphs: Robust principal component analysis seeks useful underlying structure in data affected by noise. The original formulation assumes sparse noise and measures its error with an L1 norm. This paper argues that practical noise can have a more complicated distribution, making a single fixed norm an inadequate model for some datasets.

The authors propose a Bayesian generative formulation that represents noise with a mixture of Gaussians. Because such mixtures can approximate continuous distributions, the model can accommodate a broad range of noise forms, including Gaussian, Laplacian, sparse noise, and combinations of these. The method therefore makes the noise distribution a flexible part of the model.

Inference uses a variational Bayes algorithm, with recursive closed-form updates for all involved parameters. Experiments on synthetic data, face modeling, and background subtraction demonstrate the approach’s advantages. These findings support the practical value of adapting the noise representation in the tested settings. The central contribution combines that flexibility with an explicit inference procedure, rather than leaving a richer noise model without a computational method.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian RPCA model uses a Gaussian mixture to accommodate varied noise distributions and supports closed-form variational updates.

title: Robust Principal Component Analysis with Complex Noise

abstract: We consider the problem of controlling a Markov decision process (MDP) with a large state space, so as to minimize average cost. Since it is intractable to compete with the optimal policy for large scale problems, we pursue the more modest goal of competing with a low-dimensional family of policies. We use the dual linear programming formulation of the MDP average cost problem, in which the variable is a stationary distribution over state-action pairs, and we consider a neighborhood of a low-dimensional subset of the set of stationary distributions (defined in terms of state-action features) as the comparison class. We propose two techniques, one based on stochastic convex optimization, and one based on constraint sampling. In both cases, we give bounds that show that the performance of our algorithms approaches the best achievable by any policy in the comparison class. Most importantly, these results depend on the size of the comparison class, but not on the size of the state space. Preliminary experiments show the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms in a queuing application.

Since it is intractable to compete with the optimal policy for large scale problems, we pursue the more modest goal of competing with a low-dimensional family of policies. We use the dual linear programming formulation of the MDP average cost problem, in which the variable is a stationary distribution over state-action pairs, and we consider a neighborhood of a low-dimensional subset of the set of stationary distributions (defined in terms of state-action features) as the comparison class. We propose two techniques, one based on stochastic convex optimization, and one based on constraint sampling. In both cases, we give bounds that show that the performance of our algorithms approaches the best achievable by any policy in the comparison class. Most importantly, these results depend on the size of the comparison class, but not on the size of the state space. Preliminary experiments show the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms in a queuing application.

paragraphs: The paper considers control of Markov decision processes with large state spaces and an average-cost objective. Competing with the unrestricted optimal policy is treated as intractable at this scale. The authors instead aim to approach the best performance available within a low-dimensional comparison family of policies.

They use a dual linear programming formulation whose variable describes a stationary distribution over state-action pairs. State-action features define a low-dimensional subset of these distributions, and a neighborhood of that subset supplies the comparison class. This shifts the representation of the control problem toward a restricted family that can be handled computationally.

Two solution techniques are proposed: stochastic convex optimization and constraint sampling. For both, performance bounds approach the best achievable within the comparison class. Crucially, the stated results depend on the size of that class rather than the number of states. Preliminary experiments in a queuing application support the algorithms' effectiveness. The guarantee is therefore meaningful relative to the chosen family, without claiming competition with every possible policy.
summary.tldr: Two linear-programming-based methods approach the best policy in a restricted comparison class with bounds independent of state-space size.

title: Linear Programming for Large-Scale Markov Decision Problems

abstract: The emergence of compact GPS systems and the establishment of open data initiatives has resulted in widespread availability of spatial data for many urban centres. These data can be leveraged to develop data-driven intelligent resource allocation systems for urban issues such as policing, sanitation, and transportation. We employ techniques from Bayesian non-parametric statistics to develop a process which captures a common characteristic of urban spatial datasets. Specifically, our new spatial process framework models events which occur repeatedly at discrete spatial points, the number and locations of which are unknown a priori. We develop a representation of our spatial process which facilitates posterior simulation, resulting in an interpretable and computationally tractable model. The framework’s superiority over both empirical grid-based models and Dirichlet process mixture models is demonstrated by fitting, interpreting, and comparing models of graffiti prevalence for both downtown Vancouver and Manhattan.

A model of these data should be able to represent repeated activity at discrete points even when neither the number nor the locations of those points are known beforehand. This paper develops a Bayesian nonparametric spatial process specifically around that characteristic.

The framework allows the unknown collection of event locations to be part of what is inferred from the observations. The authors also develop a representation that makes posterior simulation practical. That computational contribution matters because a model must support workable inference as well as describe the intended spatial structure. The resulting model is presented as both interpretable and computationally tractable.

Through fitting, interpreting, and comparing models, the authors demonstrate superiority over empirical grid-based models and Dirichlet process mixture models in those studies. The work connects a specific recurring-location pattern to a statistical model that could inform data-driven urban resource allocation, while its reported comparisons concern the graffiti applications.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian nonparametric spatial process models repeated events at unknown discrete locations and improves on comparison models in two urban graffiti studies.

title: Atomic Spatial Processes

abstract: We consider the problem of quickly localizing multiple targets by asking questions of the form “How many targets are within this set" while obtaining noisy answers. This setting is a generalization to multiple targets of the game of 20 questions in which only a single target is queried. We assume that the targets are points on the real line, or in a two dimensional plane for the experiments, drawn independently from a known distribution. We evaluate the performance of a policy using the expected entropy of the posterior distribution after a fixed number of questions with noisy answers. We derive a lower bound for the value of this problem and study a specific policy, named the dyadic policy. We show that this policy achieves a value which is no more than twice this lower bound when answers are noise-free, and show a more general constant factor approximation guarantee for the noisy setting. We present an empirical evaluation of this policy on simulated data for the problem of detecting multiple instances of the same object in an image. Finally, we present experiments on localizing multiple faces simultaneously on real images.

The modeled targets are drawn independently from a known distribution, with the theoretical setting using points on a line and experiments also considering a plane.

A questioning policy is evaluated by the expected uncertainty remaining in the posterior distribution after a fixed number of questions. The authors express this uncertainty through entropy and derive a lower bound for the problem's value. This supplies a theoretical benchmark for judging how well a practical questioning strategy performs.

Experiments examine repeated-object detection in simulated image data and simultaneous face localization in real images, connecting the questioning formulation to locating multiple visual targets.
summary.tldr: A dyadic questioning policy locates multiple targets from noisy counts, with approximation guarantees under a known independent target distribution.

title: Bayesian Multiple Target Localization

abstract: We consider linear dynamical systems, particularly coupled linear oscillators, where the parameters represent meaningful values in a domain theory and thus learning what affects them contributes to explanation. Rather than allow perturbations of latent states, we assume that temporal variation beyond noise is explained by parameter drift, and variation across coupled systems is a function of moderating variables. This change of focus reduces opportunities for efficient inference, and we propose sampling procedures to learn and fit the models. We test our approach on a real dataset of physiological measures of heterosexual couples engaged in a conversation about a potentially emotional topic, with body mass index (BMI) being considered as a moderator. We evaluate several models on their ability to predict future conversation dynamics (the last 20% of the data for each test couple), with shared parameters being learned using held out data. As proof of concept, we validate the hypothesis that BMI affects the conversation dynamic in the experimentally chosen topic.

Learning how those parameters vary can therefore contribute to explanation as well as prediction. The model attributes temporal variation beyond noise to parameter drift and differences across coupled systems to moderating variables.

That modeling choice shifts attention from perturbations of hidden states to changes in the parameters governing the dynamics. It also reduces opportunities for efficient inference, so the authors develop sampling procedures to learn and fit the models. The approach explicitly makes parameter variation part of the phenomenon to be explained.

summary.tldr: Sampling-based dynamical models explain temporal change through parameter drift and between-system differences through moderators.

title: Moderated and Drifting Linear Dynamical Systems

abstract: There are various parametric models for analyzing pairwise comparison data, including the Bradley-Terry-Luce (BTL) and Thurstone models, but their reliance on strong parametric assumptions is limiting. In this work, we study a flexible model for pairwise comparisons, under which the probabilities of outcomes are required only to satisfy a natural form of stochastic transitivity. This class includes parametric models including the BTL and Thurstone models as special cases, but is considerably more general. We provide various examples of models in this broader stochastically transitive class for which classical parametric models provide poor fits. Despite this greater flexibility, we show that the matrix of probabilities can be estimated at the same rate as in standard parametric models. On the other hand, unlike in the BTL and Thurstone models, computing the minimax-optimal estimator in the stochastically transitive model is non-trivial, and we explore various computationally tractable alternatives. We show that a simple singular value thresholding algorithm is statistically consistent but does not achieve the minimax rate. We then propose and study algorithms that achieve the minimax rate over interesting sub-classes of the full stochastically transitive class. We complement our theoretical results with thorough numerical simulations.

paragraphs: Pairwise comparison models estimate the probability that one item wins against another. Classical models such as Bradley–Terry–Luce and Thurstone impose strong parametric structure. This paper studies a broader class requiring a natural form of stochastic transitivity. The class contains those familiar models while also admitting comparison patterns that they fit poorly.

The authors show that this greater flexibility does not force a worse statistical estimation rate for the matrix of comparison probabilities. The best achievable rate matches that of standard parametric models. However, obtaining that statistical performance computationally is more difficult: constructing a minimax-optimal estimator for the broader class is nontrivial.

The paper therefore investigates tractable alternatives. A simple singular value thresholding method is statistically consistent, but it does not reach the minimax rate. Other proposed algorithms achieve that rate on particular subclasses of stochastically transitive models. Numerical simulations complement the theory. The results distinguish the accuracy that is statistically possible from the accuracy attained by particular computational procedures.
summary.tldr: Stochastic transitivity permits flexible pairwise comparison models with strong statistical rates, while making optimal computation more challenging.

title: Stochastically Transitive Models for Pairwise Comparisons: Statistical and Computational Issues

abstract: We propose a new selection rule for the coordinate selection in coordinate descent methods for huge-scale optimization. The efficiency of this novel scheme is provably better than the efficiency of uniformly random selection, and can reach the efficiency of steepest coordinate descent (SCD), enabling an acceleration of a factor of up to $n$, the number of coordinates. In many practical applications, our scheme can be implemented at no extra cost and computational efficiency very close to the faster uniform selection. Numerical experiments with Lasso and Ridge regression show promising improvements, in line with our theoretical guarantees.

In many practical applications, our scheme can be implemented at no extra cost and computational efficiency very close to the faster uniform selection. Numerical experiments with Lasso and Ridge regression show promising improvements, in line with our theoretical guarantees.

paragraphs: Coordinate descent tackles optimization by updating selected coordinates of the parameter vector. The selection decision matters especially when there are many coordinates: a cheap choice may make limited progress, while a more effective choice can require additional work. This paper proposes a new rule for making that decision in very large optimization problems.

The authors prove that their selection scheme has better efficiency than choosing coordinates uniformly at random. Its efficiency can reach that of steepest coordinate descent, with a potential acceleration of up to n, where n is the number of coordinates. This is an upper extent of the possible gain, rather than a speedup promised for every problem.

A practical attraction is that, in many applications, the scheme can be implemented without extra cost and with computational efficiency close to uniform selection. Experiments on Lasso and Ridge regression show promising improvements consistent with the theory. Together, the results suggest that better coordinate choices can improve optimization progress while preserving the inexpensive updates that make coordinate descent useful.
summary.tldr: A new coordinate-selection rule provably improves on uniform sampling and can approach steepest coordinate descent efficiency at little practical overhead.

title: Approximate Steepest Coordinate Descent

abstract: Previously, the exploding gradient problem has been explained to be central in deep learning and model-based reinforcement learning, because it causes numerical issues and instability in optimization. Our experiments in model-based reinforcement learning imply that the problem is not just a numerical issue, but it may be caused by a fundamental chaos-like nature of long chains of nonlinear computations. Not only do the magnitudes of the gradients become large, the direction of the gradients becomes essentially random. We show that reparameterization gradients suffer from the problem, while likelihood ratio gradients are robust. Using our insights, we develop a model-based policy search framework, Probabilistic Inference for Particle-Based Policy Search (PIPPS), which is easily extensible, and allows for almost arbitrary models and policies, while simultaneously matching the performance of previous data-efficient learning algorithms. Finally, we invent the total propagation algorithm, which efficiently computes a union over all pathwise derivative depths during a single backwards pass, automatically giving greater weight to estimators with lower variance, sometimes improving over reparameterization gradients by $10^6$ times.

paragraphs: This paper examines why gradients can become unreliable in model-based reinforcement learning. The authors’ experiments suggest that long chains of nonlinear computations may behave in a chaos-like way. Gradients can grow large while their directions become essentially random, making the problem more fundamental than numerical magnitude alone.

The study finds that reparameterization gradients suffer from this behavior, whereas likelihood ratio gradients are robust to it. These observations motivate PIPPS, a framework for model-based policy search that supports almost arbitrary models and policies. The authors report that this flexibility is compatible with performance matching earlier data-efficient learning algorithms.

They also introduce total propagation, which combines estimators across different pathwise derivative depths in a single backward pass. It automatically assigns greater weight to estimators with lower variance. The authors report improvements over reparameterization gradients of up to a factor of one million in some cases. This is a conditional result, with the contribution centered on adapting the gradient estimate to its reliability.
summary.tldr: PIPPS addresses unreliable gradients in nonlinear model-based policy search by combining gradient estimators according to their variance.

title: PIPPS: Flexible Model-Based Policy Search Robust to the Curse of Chaos

abstract: Many artificial intelligence tasks appear in dual forms like English$\leftrightarrow$French translation and speech$\leftrightarrow$text transformation. Existing dual learning schemes, which are proposed to solve a pair of such dual tasks, explore how to leverage such dualities from data level. In this work, we propose a new learning framework, model-level dual learning, which takes duality of tasks into consideration while designing the architectures for the primal/dual models, and ties the model parameters that playing similar roles in the two tasks. We study both symmetric and asymmetric model-level dual learning. Our algorithms achieve significant improvements on neural machine translation and sentiment analysis.

paragraphs: Some artificial intelligence tasks naturally come in pairs that reverse the direction of a transformation, such as translation between two languages or conversion between speech and text. Dual learning uses the relationship between such tasks to help solve them. This paper asks how that relationship can shape the models themselves, extending an approach previously explored at the data level.

The proposed framework incorporates task duality into the architectures of the two models. Parameters that play similar roles in the paired tasks are tied together. This makes their correspondence an explicit part of model design: the relationship between tasks determines which parts of their models share parameters.

The authors investigate both symmetric and asymmetric forms of model-level dual learning. Their algorithms achieve significant improvements in neural machine translation and sentiment analysis. These findings support using the relationship between paired tasks as a guide to architecture and parameter sharing, adding a model-design route for exploiting duality alongside the existing use of data-level relationships.
summary.tldr: Model-level dual learning uses paired tasks to guide architecture design and parameter sharing, improving translation and sentiment analysis.

title: Model-Level Dual Learning

abstract: Despite its empirical success and recent theoretical progress, there generally lacks a quantitative analysis of the effect of batch normalization (BN) on the convergence and stability of gradient descent. In this paper, we provide such an analysis on the simple problem of ordinary least squares (OLS), where the precise dynamical properties of gradient descent (GD) is completely known, thus allowing us to isolate and compare the additional effects of BN. More precisely, we show that unlike GD, gradient descent with BN (BNGD) converges for arbitrary learning rates for the weights, and the convergence remains linear under mild conditions. Moreover, we quantify two different sources of acceleration of BNGD over GD – one due to over-parameterization which improves the effective condition number and another due having a large range of learning rates giving rise to fast descent. These phenomena set BNGD apart from GD and could account for much of its robustness properties. These findings are confirmed quantitatively by numerical experiments, which further show that many of the uncovered properties of BNGD in OLS are also observed qualitatively in more complex supervised learning problems.

paragraphs: Batch normalization often helps neural network training, but measuring exactly how it changes optimization is difficult. This paper studies ordinary least squares, where the behavior of standard gradient descent is already understood precisely. That controlled setting lets the authors isolate the extra effects of batch normalization on convergence speed and stability.

For this problem, the analysis shows that gradient descent with batch normalization converges for arbitrary learning rates for the weights. Under mild conditions, convergence also remains linear, meaning the error shrinks at a geometric rate. The paper identifies two sources of acceleration: additional parameterization improves the effective condition number, and a broad range of learning rates produces fast descent.

Together, these results offer a quantitative explanation for why batch normalization could make optimization more robust to learning-rate choices. Numerical experiments confirm the least-squares predictions quantitatively. Experiments on more complex supervised learning problems also display many of the same properties qualitatively, extending the observations beyond the simple setting without turning the least-squares analysis into a general theorem about neural networks.
summary.tldr: An analysis of least squares identifies how batch normalization can accelerate gradient descent and broaden its tolerance for weight learning rates.

title: A Quantitative Analysis of the Effect of Batch Normalization on Gradient Descent

abstract: Recently it has been shown that the step sizes of a family of variance reduced gradient methods called the JacSketch methods depend on the expected smoothness constant. In particular, if this expected smoothness constant could be calculated a priori, then one could safely set much larger step sizes which would result in a much faster convergence rate. We fill in this gap, and provide simple closed form expressions for the expected smoothness constant and careful numerical experiments verifying these bounds. Using these bounds, and since the SAGA algorithm is part of this JacSketch family, we suggest a new standard practice for setting the step and mini-batch sizes for SAGA that are competitive with a numerical grid search. Furthermore, we can now show that the total complexity of the SAGA algorithm decreases linearly in the mini-batch size up to a pre-defined value: the optimal mini-batch size. This is a rare result in the stochastic variance reduced literature, only previously shown for the Katyusha algorithm. Finally we conjecture that this is the case for many other stochastic variance reduced methods and that our bounds and analysis of the expected smoothness constant is key to extending these results.

paragraphs: The step sizes available to JacSketch variance-reduced gradient methods depend on an expected smoothness constant. Knowing this quantity in advance can justify larger steps and faster convergence. This paper provides simple closed-form expressions and bounds for that quantity, then examines them through numerical experiments.

Because SAGA belongs to the JacSketch family, the authors use the bounds to recommend choices of both step size and mini-batch size. Their proposed practice is competitive with numerical grid search. The contribution turns an analytical quantity into practical parameter guidance, reducing the need to determine useful settings solely by trying many alternatives.

The analysis also shows that SAGA's total complexity decreases linearly as mini-batch size increases up to a specified optimal value. The improvement is explicitly limited to that range; it does not imply that ever-larger batches keep helping. The authors conjecture that similar behavior holds for many other stochastic variance-reduced methods, with their expected-smoothness analysis offering a possible route to proving it.
summary.tldr: Expected-smoothness bounds guide SAGA tuning and establish linear complexity improvements up to an optimal mini-batch size.

title: Optimal Mini-Batch and Step Sizes for SAGA

abstract: We develop an extension of the knockoff inference procedure, introduced by Barber & Candes (2015). This new method, called Aggregation of Multiple Knockoffs (AKO), addresses the instability inherent to the random nature of knockoff-based inference. Specifically, AKO improves both the stability and power compared with the original knockoff algorithm while still maintaining guarantees for false discovery rate control. We provide a new inference procedure, prove its core properties, and demonstrate its benefits in a set of experiments on synthetic and real datasets.

We provide a new inference procedure, prove its core properties, and demonstrate its benefits in a set of experiments on synthetic and real datasets.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a reliability problem in knockoff inference: randomness in the procedure can make its findings unstable. A method may control false discoveries while still producing results that vary across random runs. The authors treat that variability as a problem worth addressing alongside the ability to detect meaningful findings.

Their extension, Aggregation of Multiple Knockoffs, combines multiple knockoffs into a new inference procedure. The aim is to make results more stable while also increasing statistical power, meaning the ability to identify genuine discoveries. Crucially, the method retains guarantees for controlling the false discovery rate, so improved detection is accompanied by a formal safeguard against false findings.

The authors prove the procedure’s core properties and examine its behavior on both synthetic and real datasets. They report improvements in stability and power relative to the original knockoff algorithm. The contribution therefore brings together three desirable properties: more reproducible selections, stronger detection, and continued control over false discoveries.
summary.tldr: Aggregating multiple knockoffs improves inference stability and power while retaining false discovery rate guarantees.

title: Aggregation of Multiple Knockoffs

abstract: In multi-label learning, each instance can be associated with multiple and non-exclusive labels. Previous studies assume that all the labels in the learning process are fixed and static; however, they ignore the fact that the labels will emerge continuously in changing environments. In order to fill in these research gaps, we propose a novel deep neural network (DNN) based framework, Deep Streaming Label Learning (DSLL), to classify instances with newly emerged labels effectively. DSLL can explore and incorporate the knowledge from past labels and historical models to understand and develop emerging new labels. DSLL consists of three components: 1) a streaming label mapping to extract deep relationships between new labels and past labels with a novel label-correlation aware loss; 2) a streaming feature distillation propagating feature-level knowledge from the historical model to a new model; 3) a senior student network to model new labels with the help of knowledge learned from the past. Theoretically, we prove that DSLL admits tight generalization error bounds for new labels in the DNN framework. Experimentally, extensive empirical results show that the proposed method performs significantly better than the existing state-of-the-art multi-label learning methods to handle the continually emerging new labels.

paragraphs: In multi-label learning, a single example can belong to several categories at once. Many approaches assume the available labels stay fixed, but changing environments can introduce new labels over time. Deep Streaming Label Learning, or DSLL, addresses this setting by using knowledge from earlier labels and models to help learn newly emerging categories.

DSLL combines three components. A streaming label mapping learns relationships between old and new labels using a loss that accounts for label correlations. A feature distillation component transfers knowledge from a historical model into a new model at the representation level. A senior student network then learns the new labels with support from the accumulated knowledge.

The paper proves tight bounds on generalization error for new labels within its deep neural network framework. Its experiments also report significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art multi-label methods for continually emerging labels. The contribution is a coordinated approach to transferring both label relationships and learned features, supported by theoretical analysis and empirical comparisons in the changing-label setting.
summary.tldr: DSLL transfers knowledge from past labels and models to classify examples under continually emerging labels.

title: Deep Streaming Label Learning

abstract: How can we explain the predictions of a machine learning model? When the data is structured as a multivariate time series, this question induces additional difficulties such as the necessity for the explanation to embody the time dependency and the large number of inputs. To address these challenges, we propose dynamic masks (Dynamask). This method produces instance-wise importance scores for each feature at each time step by fitting a perturbation mask to the input sequence. In order to incorporate the time dependency of the data, Dynamask studies the effects of dynamic perturbation operators. In order to tackle the large number of inputs, we propose a scheme to make the feature selection parsimonious (to select no more feature than necessary) and legible (a notion that we detail by making a parallel with information theory). With synthetic and real-world data, we demonstrate that the dynamic underpinning of Dynamask, together with its parsimony, offer a neat improvement in the identification of feature importance over time. The modularity of Dynamask makes it ideal as a plug-in to increase the transparency of a wide range of machine learning models in areas such as medicine and finance, where time series are abundant.

In order to incorporate the time dependency of the data, Dynamask studies the effects of dynamic perturbation operators. With synthetic and real-world data, we demonstrate that the dynamic underpinning of Dynamask, together with its parsimony, offer a neat improvement in the identification of feature importance over time. The modularity of Dynamask makes it ideal as a plug-in to increase the transparency of a wide range of machine learning models in areas such as medicine and finance, where time series are abundant.

Temporal dependencies complicate this task, and a long sequence can contain many candidate inputs. Dynamask addresses these challenges by fitting a perturbation mask to an individual sequence and assigning importance scores to each feature at each time step.

The method studies how predictions respond to dynamic perturbations that incorporate the temporal character of the data. It also encourages parsimonious feature selection, seeking to select no more inputs than necessary. A further objective is legibility, which the authors discuss through a connection with information theory. These elements make compactness and temporal structure part of the explanation process.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world data report improved identification of feature importance over time from combining dynamic perturbations with parsimony. The method is modular, allowing it to serve as an explanation component for a range of prediction models. Its contribution is an instance-specific account of importance organized across both features and time.
summary.tldr: Dynamask explains individual time-series predictions using temporally informed perturbations and compact feature-at-time importance masks.

title: Explaining Time Series Predictions with Dynamic Masks

abstract: We consider a robust linear regression model $y=X\beta^* + \eta$, where an adversary oblivious to the design $X\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ may choose $\eta$ to corrupt all but an $\alpha$ fraction of the observations $y$ in an arbitrary way. Prior to our work, even for Gaussian $X$, no estimator for $\beta^*$ was known to be consistent in this model except for quadratic sample size $n \gtrsim (d/\alpha)^2$ or for logarithmic inlier fraction $\alpha\ge 1/\log n$. We show that consistent estimation is possible with nearly linear sample size and inverse-polynomial inlier fraction. Concretely, we show that the Huber loss estimator is consistent for every sample size $n= \omega(d/\alpha^2)$ and achieves an error rate of $O(d/\alpha^2n)^{1/2}$ (both bounds are optimal up to constant factors). Our results extend to designs far beyond the Gaussian case and only require the column span of $X$ to not contain approximately sparse vectors (similar to the kind of assumption commonly made about the kernel space for compressed sensing). We provide two technically similar proofs. One proof is phrased in terms of strong convexity, extending work of [Tsakonas et al. ’14], and particularly short. The other proof highlights a connection between the Huber loss estimator and high-dimensional median computations. In the special case of Gaussian designs, this connection leads us to a strikingly simple algorithm based on computing coordinate-wise medians that achieves nearly optimal guarantees in linear time, and that can exploit sparsity of $\beta^*$. The model studied here also captures heavy-tailed noise distributions that may not even have a first moment.

title: Consistent regression when oblivious outliers overwhelm

abstract: Deep extreme multi-label learning (XML) requires training deep architectures that can tag a data point with its most relevant subset of labels from an extremely large label set. XML applications such as ad and product recommendation involve labels rarely seen during training but which nevertheless hold the key to recommendations that delight users. Effective utilization of label metadata and high quality predictions for rare labels at the scale of millions of labels are thus key challenges in contemporary XML research. To address these, this paper develops the SiameseXML framework based on a novel probabilistic model that naturally motivates a modular approach melding Siamese architectures with high-capacity extreme classifiers, and a training pipeline that effortlessly scales to tasks with 100 million labels. SiameseXML offers predictions 2–13% more accurate than leading XML methods on public benchmark datasets, as well as in live A/B tests on the Bing search engine, it offers significant gains in click-through-rates, coverage, revenue and other online metrics over state-of-the-art techniques currently in production. Code for SiameseXML is available at https://github.com/Extreme-classification/siamesexml

summary.tldr: SiameseXML combines Siamese models and extreme classifiers at 100-million-label scale, with reported benchmark and live recommendation gains.

title: SiameseXML: Siamese Networks meet Extreme Classifiers with 100M Labels

abstract: Variational data assimilation optimizes for an initial state of a dynamical system such that its evolution fits observational data. The physical model can subsequently be evolved into the future to make predictions. This principle is a cornerstone of large scale forecasting applications such as numerical weather prediction. As such, it is implemented in current operational systems of weather forecasting agencies across the globe. However, finding a good initial state poses a difficult optimization problem in part due to the non-invertible relationship between physical states and their corresponding observations. We learn a mapping from observational data to physical states and show how it can be used to improve optimizability. We employ this mapping in two ways: to better initialize the non-convex optimization problem, and to reformulate the objective function in better behaved physics space instead of observation space. Our experimental results for the Lorenz96 model and a two-dimensional turbulent fluid flow demonstrate that this procedure significantly improves forecast quality for chaotic systems.

paragraphs: Variational data assimilation estimates a dynamical system’s initial state by finding one whose subsequent evolution matches observations. That state can then be evolved forward to make forecasts. A major optimization difficulty comes from the relationship between physical states and observations: it is not invertible, making it hard to work backward from measurements to a suitable starting state.

The paper learns a mapping from observations to physical states and uses it in two ways. First, it supplies a better initialization for the nonconvex optimization problem. Second, it reformulates the objective in physical-state space, which the authors describe as better behaved than observation space. The learned mapping therefore changes both where optimization begins and how agreement is assessed.

Experiments with the Lorenz96 model and a two-dimensional turbulent fluid flow show significant improvements in forecast quality for chaotic systems. These findings support using a learned observation-to-state mapping within variational assimilation. The physical model still supplies the evolving forecast, while the learned component improves the process of finding its initial condition.
summary.tldr: A learned observation-to-state mapping improves initialization and reformulates variational assimilation, yielding better forecasts in two chaotic-system experiments.

title: Variational Data Assimilation with a Learned Inverse Observation Operator

abstract: This paper develops a methodology for regret minimization with stochastic first-order oracle feedback in online, constrained, non-smooth, non-convex problems. In this setting, the minimization of external regret is beyond reach for first-order methods, and there are no gradient-based algorithmic frameworks capable of providing a solution. On that account, we propose a conceptual approach that leverages non-convex optimality measures, leading to a suitable generalization of the learner’s local regret. We focus on a local regret measure defined via a proximal-gradient mapping, that also encompasses the original notion proposed by Hazan et al. (2017). To achieve no local regret in this setting, we develop a proximal-gradient method based on stochastic first-order feedback, and a simpler method for when access to a perfect first-order oracle is possible. Both methods are order-optimal (in the min-max sense), and we also establish a bound on the number of proximal-gradient queries these methods require. As an important application of our results, we also obtain a link between online and offline non-convex stochastic optimization manifested as a new proximal-gradient scheme with complexity guarantees matching those obtained via variance reduction techniques.

paragraphs: Online learning becomes particularly difficult when objectives are nonconvex and nonsmooth, decisions are constrained, and gradient information is noisy. In the setting studied here, first-order methods cannot achieve the usual external-regret objective. The paper instead develops a local-regret criterion based on nonconvex optimality measures.

Its criterion uses a proximal-gradient mapping, allowing local regret to account for the constraints and nonsmooth structure of the problem. It also includes an earlier local-regret definition as a special case. The authors develop a method using stochastic first-order feedback and a simpler alternative for exact first-order feedback, both designed to achieve no local regret.
