The analysis also connects online learning with offline stochastic nonconvex optimization. This yields a new proximal-gradient scheme with complexity guarantees matching those obtained through variance-reduction techniques. The guarantees concern the proposed local criterion rather than a claim of globally minimizing arbitrary nonconvex objectives.
summary.tldr: A proximal-gradient definition of local regret enables order-optimal learning guarantees for constrained, nonsmooth, nonconvex problems with stochastic feedback.

title: Regret Minimization in Stochastic Non-Convex Learning via a Proximal-Gradient Approach

abstract: Much of the theory for classical sparse recovery is based on conditions on the dictionary that are both necessary and sufficient (e.g., nullspace property) or only sufficient (e.g., incoherence and restricted isometry). In contrast, much of the theory for subspace-preserving recovery, the theoretical underpinnings for sparse subspace classification and clustering methods, is based on conditions on the subspaces and the data that are only sufficient (e.g., subspace incoherence and data inner-radius). This paper derives a necessary and sufficient condition for subspace-preserving recovery that is inspired by the classical nullspace property.Based on this novel condition, called here the subspace nullspace property, we derive equivalent characterizations that either admit a clear geometric interpretation that relates data distribution and subspace separation to the recovery success, or can be verified using a finite set of extreme points of a properly defined set. We further exploit these characterizations to derive new sufficient conditions, based on inner-radius and outer-radius measures and dual bounds, that generalize existing conditions and preserve the geometric interpretations. These results fill an important gap in the subspace-preserving recovery literature.

paragraphs: Subspace-preserving recovery asks whether a data point can be represented using points from its own underlying subspace. This question supports methods for grouping or classifying data drawn from several subspaces. Existing theory largely offered sufficient conditions: satisfying them guaranteed success, but failing them did not establish failure.

The paper introduces a subspace nullspace property that is both necessary and sufficient for recovery. Inspired by a corresponding idea in sparse recovery, it gives an exact characterization rather than only a collection of safe cases. The authors develop equivalent formulations that explain recovery geometrically through the distribution of data and the separation between subspaces.

Another formulation can be checked using finitely many extreme points of a suitable set. The authors also derive new sufficient conditions involving inner and outer radii and dual bounds. These extend existing conditions while retaining geometric meaning. Together, the results connect an exact mathematical criterion to more interpretable ways of understanding when recovery succeeds.
summary.tldr: A new necessary and sufficient condition characterizes subspace-preserving recovery and yields geometric interpretations and broader sufficient guarantees.

title: A Nullspace Property for Subspace-Preserving Recovery

abstract: For machine learning systems to be reliable, we must understand their performance in unseen, out- of-distribution environments. In this paper, we empirically show that out-of-distribution performance is strongly correlated with in-distribution performance for a wide range of models and distribution shifts. Specifically, we demonstrate strong correlations between in-distribution and out-of- distribution performance on variants of CIFAR- 10 & ImageNet, a synthetic pose estimation task derived from YCB objects, FMoW-WILDS satellite imagery classification, and wildlife classification in iWildCam-WILDS. The correlation holds across model architectures, hyperparameters, training set size, and training duration, and is more precise than what is expected from existing domain adaptation theory. To complete the picture, we also investigate cases where the correlation is weaker, for instance some synthetic distribution shifts from CIFAR-10-C and the tissue classification dataset Camelyon17-WILDS. Finally, we provide a candidate theory based on a Gaussian data model that shows how changes in the data covariance arising from distribution shift can affect the observed correlations.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how closely performance on familiar data tracks performance after the data distribution changes. Across a broad collection of experiments, models that perform better on data from their training distribution also tend to perform better on shifted data. The central finding is a strong empirical correlation across models and settings.

The study covers image classification variants, synthetic pose estimation, satellite imagery, and wildlife classification. The relationship persists while changing architectures, hyperparameters, training set sizes, and training duration. Its precision exceeds what existing domain adaptation theory would lead the authors to expect, making it a pattern that calls for a more specific explanation.

The authors also examine weaker correlations, including some synthetic image corruptions and tissue classification. These cases establish that the pattern is not universal. A proposed explanation uses a Gaussian data model to connect changes in covariance—the way data features vary together—to changes in the correlation. This supplies a candidate account of both the strong pattern and its variation across shifts.
summary.tldr: Across many tested distribution shifts, accuracy on familiar data strongly predicts accuracy on shifted data, with informative exceptions.

title: Accuracy on the Line: on the Strong Correlation Between Out-of-Distribution and In-Distribution Generalization

abstract: Direct Feedback Alignment (DFA) is emerging as an efficient and biologically plausible alternative to backpropagation for training deep neural networks. Despite relying on random feedback weights for the backward pass, DFA successfully trains state-of-the-art models such as Transformers. On the other hand, it notoriously fails to train convolutional networks. An understanding of the inner workings of DFA to explain these diverging results remains elusive. Here, we propose a theory of feedback alignment algorithms. We first show that learning in shallow networks proceeds in two steps: an alignment phase, where the model adapts its weights to align the approximate gradient with the true gradient of the loss function, is followed by a memorisation phase, where the model focuses on fitting the data. This two-step process has a degeneracy breaking effect: out of all the low-loss solutions in the landscape, a net-work trained with DFA naturally converges to the solution which maximises gradient alignment. We also identify a key quantity underlying alignment in deep linear networks: the conditioning of the alignment matrices. The latter enables a detailed understanding of the impact of data structure on alignment, and suggests a simple explanation for the well-known failure of DFA to train convolutional neural networks. Numerical experiments on MNIST and CIFAR10 clearly demonstrate degeneracy breaking in deep non-linear networks and show that the align-then-memorize process occurs sequentially from the bottom layers of the network to the top.

This paper develops a theory aimed at explaining how this alternative learning process works and why those differences arise.

The findings connect the feedback mechanism to both learning order and the solutions training favors.
summary.tldr: A theory of feedback alignment describes how networks first align learning signals and then fit data, helping explain architecture-dependent training behavior.

title: Align, then memorise: the dynamics of learning with feedback alignment

abstract: Despite the accomplishments of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) in modeling data distributions, training them remains a challenging task. A contributing factor to this difficulty is the non-intuitive nature of the GAN loss curves, which necessitates a subjective evaluation of the generated output to infer training progress. Recently, motivated by game theory, Duality Gap has been proposed as a domain agnostic measure to monitor GAN training. However, it is restricted to the setting when the GAN converges to a Nash equilibrium. But GANs need not always converge to a Nash equilibrium to model the data distribution. In this work, we extend the notion of duality gap to proximal duality gap that is applicable to the general context of training GANs where Nash equilibria may not exist. We show theoretically that the proximal duality gap can monitor the convergence of GANs to a broader spectrum of equilibria that subsumes Nash equilibria. We also theoretically establish the relationship between the proximal duality gap and the divergence between the real and generated data distributions for different GAN formulations. Our results provide new insights into the nature of GAN convergence. Finally, we validate experimentally the usefulness of proximal duality gap for monitoring and influencing GAN training.

Duality gap offers a game-theoretic monitoring measure, but its use is restricted to convergence toward a Nash equilibrium. The paper points out that modeling the data distribution does not always require convergence to that kind of equilibrium.

The authors introduce proximal duality gap to cover a more general training setting, including cases where Nash equilibria may not exist. They theoretically show that it can monitor convergence to a broader family of equilibria containing Nash equilibria. This expands the kinds of training outcomes the measure is designed to characterize.

summary.tldr: Proximal duality gap broadens GAN convergence monitoring beyond Nash equilibria and connects it theoretically to distributional mismatch.

title: On Characterizing GAN Convergence Through Proximal Duality Gap

abstract: Most current classifiers are vulnerable to adversarial examples, small input perturbations that change the classification output. Many existing attack algorithms cover various settings, from white-box to black-box classifiers, but usually assume that the answers are deterministic and often fail when they are not. We therefore propose a new adversarial decision-based attack specifically designed for classifiers with probabilistic outputs. It is based on the HopSkipJump attack by Chen et al. (2019), a strong and query efficient decision-based attack originally designed for deterministic classifiers. Our P(robabilisticH)opSkipJump attack adapts its amount of queries to maintain HopSkipJump’s original output quality across various noise levels, while converging to its query efficiency as the noise level decreases. We test our attack on various noise models, including state-of-the-art off-the-shelf randomized defenses, and show that they offer almost no extra robustness to decision-based attacks. Code is available at https://github.com/cjsg/PopSkipJump.

paragraphs: Adversarial examples make small input changes that alter a classifier’s decision. Many attacks assume that querying the same input gives a deterministic answer, so randomized outputs can disrupt their operation. This paper introduces PopSkipJump, a decision-based attack designed to handle classifiers whose responses are probabilistic.

The method builds on HopSkipJump, an attack developed for deterministic classifiers. PopSkipJump adjusts how many queries it uses to preserve the original attack’s output quality across different noise levels. As noise decreases, its query efficiency approaches that of HopSkipJump. The adaptation therefore connects the amount of information gathered from the classifier to the uncertainty in its responses.

The authors evaluate several noise models, including existing randomized defenses, and find that the tested defenses provide almost no additional robustness against decision-based attacks. The result distinguishes disrupting a deterministic attack from resisting an attack adapted to randomness. In the examined settings, probabilistic responses call for an adjusted query strategy but do little to prevent adversarial examples from being found.
summary.tldr: PopSkipJump adapts decision-based attacks to randomized classifier outputs and finds little added robustness from the tested randomized defenses.

title: PopSkipJump: Decision-Based Attack for Probabilistic Classifiers

abstract: Deep neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Due to their black-box nature, it is rather challenging to interpret and properly repair these incorrect behaviors. This paper focuses on interpreting and repairing the incorrect behaviors of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs). We propose a lightweight model-based approach (RNNRepair) to help understand and repair incorrect behaviors of an RNN. Specifically, we build an influence model to characterize the stateful and statistical behaviors of an RNN over all the training data and to perform the influence analysis for the errors. Compared with the existing techniques on influence function, our method can efficiently estimate the influence of existing or newly added training samples for a given prediction at both sample level and segmentation level. Our empirical evaluation shows that the proposed influence model is able to extract accurate and understandable features. Based on the influence model, our proposed technique could effectively infer the influential instances from not only an entire testing sequence but also a segment within that sequence. Moreover, with the sample-level and segment-level influence relations, RNNRepair could further remediate two types of incorrect predictions at the sample level and segment level.

Based on the influence model, our proposed technique could effectively infer the influential instances from not only an entire testing sequence but also a segment within that sequence. paragraphs: Understanding and correcting a recurrent neural network’s mistakes is difficult because its predictions depend on internal state as well as the sequence it processes. RNNRepair addresses this problem with a lightweight model-based analysis. It constructs an influence model describing the network’s stateful and statistical behavior across the training data.

The model estimates how training examples affect a particular prediction, considering both complete samples and segments within sequences. It can analyze existing training examples as well as newly added ones. This finer-grained view connects an incorrect prediction to potentially influential training material without treating every sequence as an indivisible unit.

The empirical evaluation finds that the influence model extracts accurate, understandable features and can identify influential instances for entire test sequences or particular segments. The authors then use these influence relations to remediate two types of incorrect predictions at the sample and segment levels. The contribution connects interpretation with repair: the same analysis that helps explain a mistake also supplies relationships used to address it in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: RNNRepair models training-data influence at sequence and segment levels to help explain and repair recurrent-network prediction errors.

title: RNNRepair: Automatic RNN Repair via Model-based Analysis

abstract: We consider a best arm identification (BAI) problem for stochastic bandits with adversarial corruptions in the fixed-budget setting of T steps. We design a novel randomized algorithm, Probabilistic Sequential Shrinking(u) (PSS(u)), which is agnostic to the amount of corruptions. When the amount of corruptions per step (CPS) is below a threshold, PSS(u) identifies the best arm or item with probability tending to 1 as T{\rightarrow}$\infty$. Otherwise, the optimality gap of the identified item degrades gracefully with the CPS.We argue that such a bifurcation is necessary. In PSS(u), the parameter u serves to balance between the optimality gap and success probability. The injection of randomization is shown to be essential to mitigate the impact of corruptions. To demonstrate this, we design two attack strategies that are applicable to any algorithm. We apply one of them to a deterministic analogue of PSS(u) known as Successive Halving (SH) by Karnin et al. (2013). The attack strategy results in a high failure probability for SH, but PSS(u) remains robust. In the absence of corruptions, PSS(2)’s performance guarantee matches SH’s. We show that when the CPS is sufficiently large, no algorithm can achieve a BAI probability tending to 1 as T{\rightarrow}$\infty$. Numerical experiments corroborate our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to identify the best option from noisy observations when an adversary can corrupt some of the evidence. The learner has a fixed sampling budget and does not know the corruption amount. The proposed randomized algorithm, Probabilistic Sequential Shrinking, uses a parameter to balance identification success against how far the selected option may be from optimal.

When corruption per step stays below a threshold, the probability of finding the best option approaches one as the budget grows. Above that threshold, the quality gap degrades gracefully with corruption. The authors also prove that sufficiently large corruption prevents any algorithm from achieving identification probability approaching one, establishing a genuine boundary on what more sampling can accomplish.

Without corruption, its parameter-two setting matches Successive Halving's guarantee. Numerical experiments support the theory, including the distinction between reliable exact identification and controlled degradation.
summary.tldr: Randomized sequential shrinking identifies the best option under limited corruption and degrades gracefully when corruption is larger.

title: Probabilistic Sequential Shrinking: A Best Arm Identification Algorithm for Stochastic Bandits with Corruptions

abstract: We view disentanglement learning as discovering an underlying structure that equivariantly reflects the factorized variations shown in data. Traditionally, such a structure is fixed to be a vector space with data variations represented by translations along individual latent dimensions. We argue this simple structure is suboptimal since it requires the model to learn to discard the properties (e.g. different scales of changes, different levels of abstractness) of data variations, which is an extra work than equivariance learning. Instead, we propose to encode the data variations with groups, a structure not only can equivariantly represent variations, but can also be adaptively optimized to preserve the properties of data variations. Considering it is hard to conduct training on group structures, we focus on Lie groups and adopt a parameterization using Lie algebra. Based on the parameterization, some disentanglement learning constraints are naturally derived. A simple model named Commutative Lie Group VAE is introduced to realize the group-based disentanglement learning. Experiments show that our model can effectively learn disentangled representations without supervision, and can achieve state-of-the-art performance without extra constraints.

paragraphs: Disentanglement learning seeks representations in which separate factors of variation have distinct, structured effects. Conventional approaches often represent those changes as movement along individual coordinates in a vector space. This paper argues that this choice can create extra work: the model must discard properties of the variations, such as differences in scale or level of abstraction, to fit that structure.

The authors instead represent variations using groups, mathematical structures that describe how transformations combine. Their goal is to learn a structure that reflects changes in the data while preserving more of their properties. To make training manageable, they focus on Lie groups and parameterize them through Lie algebra, from which they derive constraints for disentanglement learning.

They implement this approach in a Commutative Lie Group VAE. Experiments show that the model can learn disentangled representations without supervision and achieve leading performance without extra constraints. The results support changing the structure of the latent representation itself as a way to improve how a model captures separate sources of variation.
summary.tldr: A group-based VAE learns disentangled representations using a latent structure designed to preserve properties of data variations.

title: Commutative Lie Group VAE for Disentanglement Learning

abstract: For traffic routing platforms, the choice of which route to recommend to a user depends on the congestion on these routes – indeed, an individual’s utility depends on the number of people using the recommended route at that instance. Motivated by this, we introduce the problem of Congested Bandits where each arm’s reward is allowed to depend on the number of times it was played in the past $\Delta$ timesteps. This dependence on past history of actions leads to a dynamical system where an algorithm’s present choices also affect its future pay-offs, and requires an algorithm to plan for this. We study the congestion aware formulation in the multi-armed bandit (MAB) setup and in the contextual bandit setup with linear rewards. For the multi-armed setup, we propose a UCB style algorithm and show that its policy regret scales as $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{K \Delta T})$. For the linear contextual bandit setup, our algorithm, based on an iterative least squares planner, achieves policy regret $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{dT} + \Delta)$. From an experimental standpoint, we corroborate the no-regret properties of our algorithms via a simulation study.

paragraphs: A route recommendation changes the congestion that later travelers encounter. To represent this interaction, the paper introduces congested bandits, where an action’s reward can depend on how often that action was selected during the previous Δ steps. Learning therefore involves a dynamic system: current choices change both immediate rewards and future opportunities.

The authors study this formulation for ordinary multi-armed bandits and for contextual bandits with linear rewards. In the first setting, they propose an algorithm based on upper confidence bounds. In the second, they use a planner based on iterative least squares. Both address the need to plan around the effects of recent action history.

For K arms over T steps, the multi-armed algorithm has policy regret scaling as the square root of KΔT, up to suppressed logarithmic factors. In the linear contextual setting with dimension d, the bound scales as the square root of dT plus Δ, again suppressing logarithmic factors. Simulations support the algorithms’ no-regret behavior. These results quantify how learning can accommodate congestion effects within the proposed finite-history model.
summary.tldr: Congested bandits model how recent choices affect future rewards and provide planning algorithms with policy-regret guarantees.

title: Congested Bandits: Optimal Routing via Short-term Resets

abstract: We present energy-based generative flow networks (EB-GFN), a novel probabilistic modeling algorithm for high-dimensional discrete data. Building upon the theory of generative flow networks (GFlowNets), we model the generation process by a stochastic data construction policy and thus amortize expensive MCMC exploration into a fixed number of actions sampled from a GFlowNet. We show how GFlowNets can approximately perform large-block Gibbs sampling to mix between modes. We propose a framework to jointly train a GFlowNet with an energy function, so that the GFlowNet learns to sample from the energy distribution, while the energy learns with an approximate MLE objective with negative samples from the GFlowNet. We demonstrate EB-GFN’s effectiveness on various probabilistic modeling tasks. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/zdhNarsil/EB_GFN.

Building upon the theory of generative flow networks (GFlowNets), we model the generation process by a stochastic data construction policy and thus amortize expensive MCMC exploration into a fixed number of actions sampled from a GFlowNet. We show how GFlowNets can approximately perform large-block Gibbs sampling to mix between modes. We propose a framework to jointly train a GFlowNet with an energy function, so that the GFlowNet learns to sample from the energy distribution, while the energy learns with an approximate MLE objective with negative samples from the GFlowNet. paragraphs: Modeling high-dimensional discrete data requires both assigning probabilities to configurations and finding representative samples. This paper introduces energy-based generative flow networks, or EB-GFN, to connect those tasks. A stochastic construction policy generates data through a fixed number of actions, allowing learned generation to absorb work otherwise spent on expensive Markov chain exploration.

The framework jointly trains an energy function and a GFlowNet. The GFlowNet learns to sample from the distribution defined by the energy function, while the energy function learns through an approximate maximum-likelihood objective using negative samples supplied by the GFlowNet. Each component therefore provides part of the training process needed by the other.

The authors also show how GFlowNets can approximately implement large-block Gibbs sampling to move between different modes of a distribution. This links sequential construction with exploration across distinct likely configurations. Experiments demonstrate effectiveness on multiple probabilistic modeling tasks. The contribution is a joint modeling and sampling framework whose stated sampling and likelihood procedures retain their approximate character.
summary.tldr: EB-GFN jointly trains an energy model and a generative construction policy to support sampling and learning for discrete data.

title: Generative Flow Networks for Discrete Probabilistic Modeling

abstract: Polynomial filters, a kind of Graph Neural Networks, typically use a predetermined polynomial basis and learn the coefficients from the training data. It has been observed that the effectiveness of the model is highly dependent on the property of the polynomial basis. Consequently, two natural and fundamental questions arise: Can we learn a suitable polynomial basis from the training data? Can we determine the optimal polynomial basis for a given graph and node features? In this paper, we propose two spectral GNN models that provide positive answers to the questions posed above. First, inspired by Favard’s Theorem, we propose the FavardGNN model, which learns a polynomial basis from the space of all possible orthonormal bases. Second, we examine the supposedly unsolvable definition of optimal polynomial basis from Wang et al. (2022) and propose a simple model, OptBasisGNN, which computes the optimal basis for a given graph structure and graph signal. Extensive experiments are conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed models. Our code is available at https://github.com/yuziGuo/FarOptBasis.

paragraphs: Polynomial graph neural networks typically choose a polynomial basis in advance and learn how to combine its elements. Yet model effectiveness can depend strongly on that initial basis. This paper asks whether the basis itself can be learned from data and whether an optimal basis can be computed for a particular graph and its node features.

The authors introduce two spectral graph neural networks. FavardGNN, inspired by Favard's theorem, learns a polynomial basis within the space of possible orthonormal bases. This lets training adjust the building blocks of the filter instead of restricting learning to their coefficients. OptBasisGNN takes a complementary approach by computing a basis from the graph structure and graph signal.

For OptBasisGNN, optimality refers to the particular definition of an optimal polynomial basis examined in the paper. The authors show that this previously considered difficult construction admits a simple model. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of both proposed approaches. The overall contribution is to make basis selection an explicit, adaptable part of polynomial graph learning.
summary.tldr: FavardGNN learns polynomial bases, while OptBasisGNN computes an optimal basis under the studied definition for a given graph and signal.

title: Graph Neural Networks with Learnable and Optimal Polynomial Bases

abstract: Recently, Language Models (LMs) instruction-tuned on multiple tasks, also known as multitask-prompted fine-tuning (MT), have shown capabilities to generalize to unseen tasks. Previous work has shown that scaling the number of finetuning datasets and instructions is the key component in making stronger MT LMs. In this work, we report surprising findings that show an expert LM trained on just a single task can outperform an MT LM trained with 300+ different tasks on 11 different unseen datasets and on 13 datasets of the BIG-bench benchmark by an average of 3.20% and 1.29%, respectively. This finding casts doubt on the previously held belief that simply scaling the number of tasks makes stronger MT LMs. Leveraging this finding, we further show that this distributed approach of training multiple expert LMs instead of a single MT LM for zero-shot inference possesses many benefits including (1) avoiding negative task transfer that often occurs during instruction tuning, (2) being able to continually learn new tasks without having to re-train on previous tasks to avoid catastrophic forgetting, and (3) showing compositional capabilities when merging individual experts together.

paragraphs: Instruction tuning on many tasks is a common route to language models that handle unseen tasks. This paper examines whether increasing the number of training tasks necessarily produces stronger generalization. It reports a striking counterexample: a language model trained as an expert on one task can outperform a multitask model trained on more than 300 tasks.

The reported average advantages are 3.20% across 11 unseen datasets and 1.29% across 13 BIG-bench datasets. These comparisons challenge the idea that task count alone is a reliable guide to generalization quality. They motivate a distributed approach in which multiple expert models are trained for zero-shot inference, with expertise developed separately across tasks.

The authors report several benefits of that approach: avoiding harmful transfer between tasks during instruction tuning, learning new tasks without retraining on previous ones to prevent catastrophic forgetting, and combining individual experts to obtain compositional capabilities. Together, these findings present expert training as a useful alternative to placing all task learning inside one multitask model, rather than establishing universal superiority for single-task training.
summary.tldr: Single-task experts outperform a broadly instruction-tuned model in reported unseen-task evaluations and offer benefits for continual learning and expert composition.

title: Exploring the Benefits of Training Expert Language Models over Instruction Tuning

abstract: Parameter inference, i.e. inferring the posterior distribution of the parameters of a statistical model given some data, is a central problem to many scientific disciplines. Posterior inference with generative models is an alternative to methods such as Markov Chain Monte Carlo, both for likelihood-based and simulation-based inference. However, assessing the accuracy of posteriors encoded in generative models is not straightforward. In this paper, we introduce "Tests of Accuracy with Random Points" (TARP) coverage testing as a method to estimate coverage probabilities of generative posterior estimators. Our method differs from previously-existing coverage-based methods, which require posterior evaluations. We prove that our approach is necessary and sufficient to show that a posterior estimator is accurate. We demonstrate the method on a variety of synthetic examples, and show that TARP can be used to test the results of posterior inference analyses in high-dimensional spaces. We also show that our method can detect inaccurate inferences in cases where existing methods fail.

paragraphs: Posterior inference estimates a distribution over model parameters after observing data. Generative models offer a way to represent such distributions, but assessing whether their inferred posteriors are accurate is difficult. This paper introduces Tests of Accuracy with Random Points, or TARP, to examine generative posterior estimators through coverage testing.

TARP estimates coverage probabilities using a sampling-based approach. This distinguishes it from earlier coverage methods that require evaluating the posterior itself. The authors prove a necessary-and-sufficient characterization of posterior accuracy for their approach, giving the test a theoretical connection to whether the estimated distribution is correct.

Demonstrations on synthetic examples show that TARP can assess posterior inference in high-dimensional spaces. The authors also report cases where it detects inaccurate inference that existing methods miss. These findings make the method relevant to both likelihood-based and simulation-based inference. Its contribution combines a theoretical accuracy criterion with evidence that sampling-based testing can reveal errors in practical posterior estimates.
summary.tldr: TARP uses sampling-based coverage tests to assess generative posterior accuracy, with a necessary-and-sufficient theoretical criterion and demonstrations in high dimensions.

title: Sampling-Based Accuracy Testing of Posterior Estimators for General Inference

abstract: The spatiotemporal resolution of Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) plays important roles in the mathematical description of the world’s physical phenomena. In general, scientists and engineers solve PDEs numerically by the use of computationally demanding solvers. Recently, deep learning algorithms have emerged as a viable alternative for obtaining fast solutions for PDEs. Models are usually trained on synthetic data generated by solvers, stored on disk and read back for training. This paper advocates that relying on a traditional static dataset to train these models does not allow the full benefit of the solver to be used as a data generator. It proposes an open source online training framework for deep surrogate models. The framework implements several levels of parallelism focused on simultaneously generating numerical simulations and training deep neural networks. This approach suppresses the I/O and storage bottleneck associated with disk-loaded datasets, and opens the way to training on significantly larger datasets. Experiments compare the offline and online training of four surrogate models, including state-of-the-art architectures. Results indicate that exposing deep surrogate models to more dataset diversity, up to hundreds of GB, can increase model generalization capabilities. Fully connected neural networks, Fourier Neural Operator (FNO), and Message Passing PDE Solver prediction accuracy is improved by 68%, 16% and 7%, respectively.

paragraphs: Deep surrogate models learn to approximate solutions of partial differential equations using examples generated by numerical solvers. A conventional workflow stores those examples on disk before training. This paper argues that a fixed dataset and its associated storage and input/output costs prevent full use of the solver as an ongoing source of training data.

The authors propose an open-source online training framework that runs numerical simulation and neural-network training concurrently. Several levels of parallelism support this arrangement. summary.tldr: An online framework generates PDE simulations alongside training, reducing storage bottlenecks and improving reported surrogate accuracy through greater data diversity.

title: Training Deep Surrogate Models with Large Scale Online Learning

abstract: We propose Beam Tree Recursive Cell (BT-Cell) - a backpropagation-friendly framework to extend Recursive Neural Networks (RvNNs) with beam search for latent structure induction. We further extend this framework by proposing a relaxation of the hard top-$k$ operators in beam search for better propagation of gradient signals. We evaluate our proposed models in different out-of-distribution splits in both synthetic and realistic data. Our experiments show that BT-Cell achieves near-perfect performance on several challenging structure-sensitive synthetic tasks like ListOps and logical inference while maintaining comparable performance in realistic data against other RvNN-based models. Additionally, we identify a previously unknown failure case for neural models in generalization to unseen number of arguments in ListOps. The code is available at: https://github.com/JRC1995/BeamTreeRecursiveCells.

We evaluate our proposed models in different out-of-distribution splits in both synthetic and realistic data. Our experiments show that BT-Cell achieves near-perfect performance on several challenging structure-sensitive synthetic tasks like ListOps and logical inference while maintaining comparable performance in realistic data against other RvNN-based models. paragraphs: Some prediction tasks depend strongly on how parts of an input combine into a larger structure. Recursive neural networks address this by composing representations recursively, but learning the underlying structure introduces choices about which compositions to pursue. Beam Tree Recursive Cell, or BT-Cell, adds beam search to this process so that the model can consider multiple candidate latent structures.

The framework is designed to work with backpropagation. The authors also introduce a relaxation of the hard top-k selections used in beam search, aiming to let gradient signals propagate more effectively through those decisions. This connects a search procedure for choosing structures with the continuous optimization used to train neural networks.

Across out-of-distribution evaluations, BT-Cell achieves nearly perfect results on several demanding synthetic tasks, including ListOps and logical inference, while matching the performance of other recursive models on realistic data. The study also uncovers a failure when neural models face unseen numbers of arguments in ListOps. That finding distinguishes success on some structural tests from reliable generalization across all structural changes.
summary.tldr: BT-Cell makes beam search compatible with training recursive networks, achieving strong structural-task results while exposing a specific generalization failure.

title: Beam Tree Recursive Cells

abstract: We propose the attention-inspired numerical solver (AttNS), a concise method that helps the generalization and robustness issues faced by the AI-Hybrid numerical solver in solving differential equations due to limited data. AttNS is inspired by the effectiveness of attention modules in Residual Neural Networks (ResNet) in enhancing model generalization and robustness for conventional deep learning tasks. Drawing from the dynamical system perspective of ResNet, We seamlessly incorporate attention mechanisms into the design of numerical methods tailored for the characteristics of solving differential equations. Our results on benchmarks, ranging from high-dimensional problems to chaotic systems, showcase AttNS consistently enhancing various numerical solvers without any intricate model crafting. Finally, we analyze AttNS experimentally and theoretically, demonstrating its ability to achieve strong generalization and robustness while ensuring the convergence of the solver. This includes requiring less data compared to other advanced methods to achieve comparable generalization errors and better prevention of numerical explosion issues when solving differential equations.

paragraphs: AttNS addresses a problem in numerical methods that combine conventional solvers with learned components: limited training data can weaken their generalization and robustness when solving differential equations. The paper proposes a compact, attention-inspired modification intended to improve existing solvers without requiring elaborate model design.

The method draws inspiration from attention modules used in residual neural networks. By interpreting those networks through a dynamical-systems perspective, the authors adapt attention mechanisms to the structure of numerical equation solving. This connection matters because it gives a route for incorporating a successful learning mechanism into numerical methods while still considering the solver’s mathematical behavior.

Benchmarks covering high-dimensional problems and chaotic systems show improvements across multiple numerical solvers. The paper combines experiments and theory to support strong generalization and robustness together with solver convergence. In the reported comparisons, AttNS needs less data to reach comparable generalization errors and better prevents numerical explosions. These findings position it as a way to make learned numerical solving more dependable when training examples are scarce.
summary.tldr: AttNS incorporates attention-inspired mechanisms into numerical solvers to improve generalization and stability with limited training data.

title: AttNS: Attention-Inspired Numerical Solving For Limited Data Scenarios

abstract: Language models deployed in the wild make errors. However, simply updating the model with the corrected error instances causes catastrophic forgetting—the updated model makes errors on instances learned during the instruction tuning or upstream training phase. Randomly replaying upstream data yields unsatisfactory performance and often comes with high variance and poor controllability. To this end, we try to forecast upstream examples that will be forgotten due to a model update for improved controllability of the replay process and interpretability. We train forecasting models given a collection of online learned examples and corresponding forgotten upstream pre-training examples. We propose a partially interpretable forecasting model based on the observation that changes in pre-softmax logit scores of pretraining examples resemble that of online learned examples, which performs decently on BART but fails on T5 models. We further show a black-box classifier based on inner products of example representations achieves better forecasting performance over a series of setups. Finally, we show that we reduce forgetting of upstream pretraining examples by replaying examples that are forecasted to be forgotten, demonstrating the practical utility of forecasting example forgetting.
originalAbstract: Language models deployed in the wild make errors. However, simply updating the model with the corrected error instances causes catastrophic forgetting—the updated model makes errors on instances learned during the instruction tuning or upstream training phase. Randomly replaying upstream data yields unsatisfactory performance and often comes with high variance and poor controllability. To this end, we try to forecast upstream examples that will be forgotten due to a model update for improved controllability of the replay process and interpretability. We train forecasting models given a collection of online learned examples and corresponding forgotten upstream pre-training examples. We propose a partially interpretable forecasting model based on the observation that changes in pre-softmax logit scores of pretraining examples resemble that of online learned examples, which performs decently on BART but fails on T5 models. We further show a black-box classifier based on inner products of example representations achieves better forecasting performance over a series of setups. Finally, we show that we reduce forgetting of upstream pretraining examples by replaying examples that are forecasted to be forgotten, demonstrating the practical utility of forecasting example forgetting.

paragraphs: Correcting a deployed language model’s errors can make it fail on examples learned earlier. Replaying randomly selected earlier examples can help, but the authors describe its performance as unsatisfactory, variable, and difficult to control. They investigate predicting which specific examples an update will cause the model to forget.

Forecasting models are trained on collections of newly learned examples paired with earlier examples subsequently forgotten. One partially interpretable approach uses similarities in changes to pre-softmax scores. It performs reasonably on BART but fails on T5, showing that this forecasting mechanism does not transfer successfully across the studied model families.

A black-box classifier based on inner products between example representations forecasts forgetting more effectively across several setups. The authors then replay examples predicted to be at risk and show reduced forgetting of upstream pretraining examples. This connects forecasting to a practical intervention: choosing replay data according to anticipated damage from an update. The findings support targeted replay while preserving the distinction between the more interpretable method and the better-performing black-box approach.
summary.tldr: Forecasting which earlier examples a language-model update will break enables targeted replay that reduces forgetting in the reported experiments.

title: What Will My Model Forget? Forecasting Forgotten Examples in Language Model Refinement

abstract: Off-policy evaluation, and the complementary problem of policy learning, use historical data collected under a logging policy to estimate and/or optimize the value of a target policy. Methods for these tasks typically assume overlap between the target and logging policy, enabling solutions based on importance weighting and/or imputation. Absent such an overlap assumption, existing work either relies on a well-specified model or optimizes needlessly conservative bounds. In this work, we develop methods for no-overlap policy evaluation without a well-specified model, relying instead on non-parametric assumptions on the expected outcome, with a particular focus on Lipschitz smoothness. Under such assumptions we are able to provide sharp bounds on the off-policy value, along with optimal estimators of those bounds. For Lipschitz smoothness, we construct a pair of linear programs that upper and lower bound the contribution of the no-overlap region to the off-policy value. We show that these programs have a concise closed form solution, and that their solutions converge under the Lipschitz assumption to the sharp partial identification bounds at a minimax optimal rate, up to log factors. We demonstrate the effectiveness our methods on two semi-synthetic examples, and obtain informative and valid bounds that are tighter than those possible without smoothness assumptions.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a target policy would perform using data collected by another policy. Standard approaches typically require overlap: the historical policy must provide coverage relevant to the target policy. Without that coverage, some contributions to the target policy’s value cannot be directly established from the observations.

This paper replaces a fully specified outcome model with nonparametric assumptions, especially Lipschitz smoothness, which limits how quickly expected outcomes can change. Under these assumptions, the authors derive sharp upper and lower bounds on policy value. Sharpness means the bounds capture the remaining uncertainty permitted by the assumptions, avoiding unnecessary conservatism.

For Lipschitz smoothness, two linear programs bound the contribution from the region without overlap. The authors derive concise closed-form solutions and prove convergence to the sharp bounds at a minimax-optimal rate up to logarithmic factors. Two semi-synthetic examples yield informative, valid bounds tighter than those available without smoothness. The result offers principled partial identification when the data cannot support a single fully identified policy-value estimate.
summary.tldr: Smoothness assumptions enable sharp, efficiently estimated bounds on policy value even where historical data lack overlap.

title: Off-policy Evaluation Beyond Overlap: Sharp Partial Identification Under Smoothness

abstract: The strong performance of neural networks typically hinges on the availability of extensive labeled data, yet acquiring ground-truth labels is often challenging. Instead, noisy supervisions from multiple sources, e.g., by multiple well-designed rules, are more convenient to collect. In this paper, we focus on the realistic problem of learning from multiple noisy label sources, and argue that prior studies have overlooked the crucial self-cognition ability of neural networks, i.e., the inherent capability of autonomously distinguishing noise during training. We theoretically analyze this ability of neural networks when meeting multiple noisy label sources, which reveals that neural networks possess the capability to recognize both instance-wise noise within each single noisy label source and annotator-wise quality among multiple noisy label sources. Inspired by the theoretical analyses, we introduce an approach named Self-cognitive Denoising for Multiple noisy label sources (SDM), which exploits the self-cognition ability of neural networks to denoise during training. Furthermore, we build a selective distillation module following the theoretical insights to optimize computational efficiency. The experiments on various datasets demonstrate the superiority of our method.

paragraphs: Reliable labels can be expensive to obtain, while several imperfect sources may be readily available. This paper studies learning from multiple noisy label sources, such as rule-based supervision. It focuses on what the authors call self-cognition: a neural network's ability to distinguish noise during its own training.

The theoretical analysis identifies two levels of this ability. A network can recognize noise attached to individual examples within one source and distinguish the quality of different sources. These are complementary judgments, since identifying an unreliable label and recognizing an unreliable source operate at different levels of the supervision.

The authors turn these insights into Self-cognitive Denoising for Multiple noisy label sources, or SDM. The method uses the network's noise-recognition ability to denoise during training, and a selective distillation module improves computational efficiency. Experiments on several datasets demonstrate advantages over the evaluated alternatives. The contribution connects a theoretical account of noise recognition with a training method that uses both example-level and source-level information when learning from imperfect supervision.
summary.tldr: SDM uses neural networks' ability to recognize noisy examples and unreliable label sources to denoise training, with selective distillation improving efficiency.

title: Self-cognitive Denoising in the Presence of Multiple Noisy Label Sources

abstract: Despite attaining high empirical generalization, the sharpness of models trained with sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) do not always correlate with generalization error. Instead of viewing SAM as minimizing sharpness to improve generalization, our paper considers a new perspective based on SAM’s training dynamics. We propose that perturbations in SAM perform perturbed forgetting, where they discard undesirable model biases to exhibit learning signals that generalize better. We relate our notion of forgetting to the information bottleneck principle, use it to explain observations like the better generalization of smaller perturbation batches, and show that perturbed forgetting can exhibit a stronger correlation with generalization than flatness. While standard SAM targets model biases exposed by the steepest ascent directions, we propose a new perturbation that targets biases exposed through the model’s outputs. Our output bias forgetting perturbations outperform standard SAM, GSAM, and ASAM on ImageNet, robustness benchmarks, and transfer to CIFAR-10,100, while sometimes converging to sharper regions. Our results suggest that the benefits of SAM can be explained by alternative mechanistic principles that do not require flatness of the loss surface.

paragraphs: Sharpness-aware minimization, or SAM, often improves generalization, yet the sharpness of its final models does not always track their generalization error. This paper proposes a different explanation based on the training process. Its central idea is perturbed forgetting: perturbations discard undesirable model biases and reveal learning signals that transfer better beyond the training data.

The authors connect this account to the information bottleneck principle and use it to explain observations such as the benefits of smaller perturbation batches. They show that their forgetting measure can correlate more strongly with generalization than flatness does. They also introduce perturbations targeting biases visible through model outputs, extending beyond the steepest-ascent directions used by standard SAM.

These output bias forgetting perturbations outperform SAM, GSAM, and ASAM on ImageNet, robustness benchmarks, and transfer to CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. Some resulting solutions occupy sharper regions. The findings support an alternative mechanistic explanation of SAM's benefits in which improved generalization need not depend on reaching a flatter loss surface.
summary.tldr: The paper explains SAM through forgetting undesirable biases and introduces output-based perturbations that improve tested results, sometimes at sharper solutions.

title: Forget Sharpness: Perturbed Forgetting of Model Biases Within SAM Dynamics

abstract: Post-training quantization of Large Language Models (LLMs) is challenging. In this work, we introduce Low-rank Quantization Error Reduction (LQER), which combines quantization and low-rank approximation to recover the model capability. LQER leverages an activation-induced scale matrix to drive the singular value distribution of quantization error towards a desirable distribution, which enables nearly-lossless W4A8 quantization on various LLMs and downstream tasks without the need for knowledge distillation, grid search, or gradient-based iterative optimization. Unlike existing methods, the computation pattern of LQER eliminates the need for specialized Scatter and Gather processes to collect high-precision weights from irregular memory locations. Our W4A8 LLMs achieve near-lossless performance on six popular downstream tasks, while using $1.36 \times$ fewer hardware resources than the leading state-of-the-art method. We will open-source our framework at https://github.com/ChengZhang-98/lqer

paragraphs: Quantizing a trained language model reduces numerical precision but introduces errors that can damage its capabilities. LQER combines quantization with a low-rank approximation of the resulting error. The goal is to recover capability while keeping the benefits of reduced precision, using an error structure that can be represented compactly.

The method uses a scale matrix derived from activations to reshape the singular-value distribution of quantization error. This makes the error more suitable for low-rank approximation. It supports W4A8 quantization, using four-bit weights and eight-bit activations, without knowledge distillation, grid search, or gradient-based iterative optimization. Its computation also avoids specialized Scatter and Gather operations for collecting high-precision weights from irregular memory locations.

Across the reported language models and six downstream tasks, LQER achieves nearly lossless performance. The authors report using 1.36 times fewer hardware resources than the leading comparison method. The findings connect numerical error reconstruction with hardware-friendly computation, showing that compression quality and implementation structure can be addressed together.
summary.tldr: LQER reshapes and approximates quantization error to achieve nearly lossless four-bit-weight language models with reduced hardware requirements.

title: LQER: Low-Rank Quantization Error Reconstruction for LLMs

abstract: Most works studying representation learning focus only on classification and neglect regression. Yet, the learning objectives and, therefore, the representation topologies of the two tasks are fundamentally different: classification targets class separation, leading to disconnected representations, whereas regression requires ordinality with respect to the target, leading to continuous representations. We thus wonder how the effectiveness of a regression representation is influenced by its topology, with evaluation based on the Information Bottleneck (IB) principle. The IB principle is an important framework that provides principles for learning effective representations. We establish two connections between it and the topology of regression representations. The first connection reveals that a lower intrinsic dimension of the feature space implies a reduced complexity of the representation $Z$. This complexity can be quantified as the conditional entropy of $Z$ on the target $Y$, and serves as an upper bound on the generalization error. The second connection suggests a feature space that is topologically similar to the target space will better align with the IB principle. Based on these two connections, we introduce PH-Reg, a regularizer specific to regression that matches the intrinsic dimension and topology of the feature space with the target space. Experiments on synthetic and real-world regression tasks demonstrate the benefits of PH-Reg. Code: https://github.com/needylove/PH-Reg.

paragraphs: Representation learning often emphasizes separating classes, but regression asks a different question: how should features reflect an ordered, continuous target? This paper studies the topology of regression representations, meaning the structural relationships within their feature spaces. It uses the Information Bottleneck principle to connect those relationships with the quality of learned representations.

The authors establish two connections. First, lower intrinsic feature dimension implies reduced representation complexity, measured by the conditional entropy of features given the target. That complexity provides an upper bound on generalization error. Second, their analysis suggests that a feature space with topology resembling the target space better fits the Information Bottleneck principle.

These connections motivate PH-Reg, a regression-specific regularizer that encourages the feature space to match the target space in both intrinsic dimension and topology. Experiments on synthetic and real-world regression tasks demonstrate benefits. The approach makes representation structure part of the training objective, with theoretical motivation tied to complexity and target alignment rather than class separation.
summary.tldr: PH-Reg improves regression representations by encouraging their dimension and topology to match the target space.

title: Deep Regression Representation Learning with Topology

abstract: Considering generating samples with high rewards, we focus on optimizing deep neural networks parameterized stochastic differential equations (SDEs), the advanced generative models with high expressiveness, with policy gradient, the leading algorithm in reinforcement learning. Nevertheless, when applying policy gradients to SDEs, since the policy gradient is estimated on a finite set of trajectories, it can be ill-defined, and the policy behavior in data-scarce regions may be uncontrolled. This challenge compromises the stability of policy gradients and negatively impacts sample complexity. To address these issues, we propose constraining the SDE to be consistent with its associated perturbation process. Since the perturbation process covers the entire space and is easy to sample, we can mitigate the aforementioned problems. Our framework offers a general approach allowing for a versatile selection of policy gradient methods to effectively and efficiently train SDEs. We evaluate our algorithm on the task of structure-based drug design and optimize the binding affinity of generated ligand molecules. Our method achieves the best Vina score (-9.07) on the CrossDocked2020 dataset.

paragraphs: Neural stochastic differential equations can serve as expressive generative models, and policy gradients offer a way to optimize them for high-reward samples. However, estimating those gradients from finitely many trajectories can make the update ill-defined and leave behavior uncontrolled in regions with little data. This undermines training stability and sample efficiency.

The proposed solution constrains the learned SDE to remain consistent with its associated perturbation process. That process covers the whole space and is easy to sample, giving the method a way to address regions poorly represented by the available trajectories. The framework supports a range of policy-gradient algorithms, so the consistency constraint provides a general training principle.

The authors evaluate the approach in structure-based drug design, optimizing generated ligand molecules for binding affinity. They report the best Vina score of −9.07 on CrossDocked2020. This result supplies an application-level demonstration of the framework: consistency with the perturbation process supports reward-directed SDE training and produces a strong reported score for the molecule-generation task.
summary.tldr: Constraining generative SDEs to match their perturbation processes stabilizes policy-gradient training and improves reported drug-design results.

title: Stabilizing Policy Gradients for Stochastic Differential Equations via Consistency with Perturbation Process

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have the potential to tackle sequential decision-making problems due to their generalist capabilities. Instead of optimizing “myopic” surrogate objectives such as human preferences within a single turn, in such problems, we wish to directly optimize long-term objectives, such as user satisfaction over an entire dialogue with an LLM or delayed success metrics in web navigation. Multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) provides an appealing approach to directly optimize long-term objectives, but how can we design effective and efficient multi-turn RL algorithms for LLMs? In this work, we propose an algorithmic framework to multi-turn RL for LLMs that preserves the flexibility of token-by-token RL used in single-turn RL problems, while still accommodating long horizons and delayed rewards more effectively. Our framework, the Actor-Critic Framework with a Hierarchical Structure (ArCHer), combines a high-level off-policy RL algorithm that trains a value function with a low-level RL algorithm that trains a token-by-token policy. While ArCHer can be instantiated with multiple RL algorithms, a particularly convenient instantiation is to use temporal difference (TD) learning at the high level and on-policy token-level policy gradient at the low level. Empirically, we show that ArCHer significantly improves efficiency and performance of multi-turn LLM tasks, attaining sample efficiency boosts of about 100x over prior on-policy methods and converging to a much better performance than other off-policy methods.

paragraphs: A language-model agent can produce a good individual response yet still fail at an objective that unfolds over many turns. ArCHer addresses this gap by training for longer-term outcomes, such as satisfaction across a dialogue or success after a sequence of navigation actions. The challenge is to handle delayed rewards while retaining control over individual generated tokens.

In the reported multi-turn experiments, ArCHer improves both efficiency and performance. It achieves approximately 100-fold gains in sample efficiency over prior on-policy methods and converges to better performance than the compared off-policy methods. These findings support the hierarchy as a practical way to train language agents around delayed objectives.
summary.tldr: ArCHer combines high-level value learning with token-level reinforcement learning to improve language agents on multi-turn tasks with delayed rewards.

title: ArCHer: Training Language Model Agents via Hierarchical Multi-Turn RL

abstract: The rapid rise of Generative AI (GenAI) tools has sparked debate over their role in complementing or replacing human workers across job contexts. We present a mathematical framework that models jobs, workers, and worker-job fit, introducing a novel decomposition of skills into decision-level and action-level subskills to reflect the complementary strengths of humans and GenAI. We analyze how changes in subskill abilities affect job success, identifying conditions for sharp transitions in success probability. We also establish sufficient conditions under which combining workers with complementary subskills significantly outperforms relying on a single worker. This explains phenomena such as productivity compression, where GenAI assistance yields larger gains for lower-skilled workers. We demonstrate the framework’s practicality using data from O*NET and Big-Bench Lite, aligning real-world data with our model via subskill-division methods. Our results highlight when and how GenAI complements human skills, rather than replacing them.

paragraphs: This paper develops a mathematical way to study when generative AI can improve human work. It represents jobs, workers, and the match between them, then divides skills into decision-level and action-level components. That division lets the model describe complementary abilities more precisely than a single overall measure of worker skill.

The analysis examines how changes in these component abilities affect the probability of completing a job successfully. It identifies conditions under which improvements produce sharp changes in success probability. It also establishes sufficient conditions for combining workers with complementary abilities to substantially outperform a single worker; those conditions describe when the advantage follows, rather than claiming that collaboration always helps.

The framework explains productivity compression: assistance can give larger gains to workers who initially have lower skill levels. The authors connect the model to O*NET and Big-Bench Lite data using methods that divide skills into subskills. This demonstrates a practical route for studying which combinations of human and AI abilities support better job performance.
summary.tldr: A mathematical model identifies conditions under which complementary human and AI subskills improve job success.

title: A Mathematical Framework for AI-Human Integration in Work

abstract: Measuring the similarity between data points plays a vital role in lots of popular representation learning tasks such as metric learning and contrastive learning. Most existing approaches utilize point-level distances to learn the point-to-point similarity between pairwise instances. However, since the finite number of training data points cannot fully cover the whole sample space consisting of an infinite number of points, the generalizability of the learned distance is usually limited by the sample size. In this paper, we thus extend the conventional form of data point to the new form of data ball with a predictable volume, so that we can naturally generalize the existing point-level distance to a new volume-aware distance (VAD) which measures the field-to-field geometric similarity. The learned VAD not only takes into account the relationship between observed instances but also uncovers the similarity among those unsampled neighbors surrounding the training data. This practice significantly enriches the coverage of sample space and thus improves the model generalizability. Theoretically, we prove that VAD tightens the error bound of traditional similarity learning and preserves crucial topological properties. Experiments on multi-domain data demonstrate the superiority of VAD over existing approaches in both supervised and unsupervised tasks.

paragraphs: Similarity learning usually measures relationships between individual observed data points. This paper argues that finite training samples leave much of the surrounding sample space uncovered, limiting how well a learned distance generalizes. It proposes representing each example as a data ball with a predictable volume, extending the comparison beyond the observed point itself.

Volume-aware distance measures geometric similarity between these regions. This allows learning to account for relationships among observed examples and their unsampled neighbors. The central idea is to give each training example a surrounding region of influence, so that similarity learning covers more of the sample space without relying only on point-to-point comparisons.

The authors prove that their formulation tightens the error bound of traditional similarity learning and preserves important topological properties. Experiments across multiple data domains report improvements over existing approaches in both supervised and unsupervised tasks. The theoretical and empirical results support region-based similarity as a way to improve generalization, linking the geometry around training examples to performance beyond the exact instances observed during learning.
summary.tldr: Volume-aware distance compares regions around data points, improving sample-space coverage and yielding stronger theoretical bounds and empirical similarity-learning results.

title: Volume-Aware Distance for Robust Similarity Learning

abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models (LLMs), which leverage dynamic routing and sparse activation to enhance efficiency and scalability, have achieved higher performance while reducing computational costs. However, these models face significant memory overheads, limiting their practical deployment and broader adoption. Post-training quantization (PTQ), a widely used method for compressing LLMs, encounters severe accuracy degradation and diminished generalization performance when applied to MoE models. This paper investigates the impact of MoE’s sparse and dynamic characteristics on quantization and identifies two primary challenges: (1) Inter-expert imbalance, referring to the uneven distribution of samples across experts, which leads to insufficient and biased calibration for less frequently utilized experts; (2) Intra-expert imbalance, arising from MoE’s unique aggregation mechanism, which leads to varying degrees of correlation between different samples and their assigned experts. To address these challenges, we propose MoEQuant, a novel quantization framework tailored for MoE LLMs. MoEQuant includes two novel techniques: 1) Expert-Balanced Self-Sampling (EBSS) is an efficient sampling method that efficiently constructs a calibration set with balanced expert distributions by leveraging the cumulative probabilities of tokens and expert balance metrics as guiding factors. 2) Affinity-Guided Quantization (AGQ), which incorporates affinities between experts and samples into the quantization process, thereby accurately assessing the impact of individual samples on different experts within the MoE layer. Experiments demonstrate that MoEQuant achieves substantial performance gains (more than 10 points accuracy gain in the HumanEval for DeepSeekMoE-16B under 4-bit quantization) and boosts efficiency.

Post-training quantization (PTQ), a widely used method for compressing LLMs, encounters severe accuracy degradation and diminished generalization performance when applied to MoE models. This paper investigates the impact of MoE’s sparse and dynamic characteristics on quantization and identifies two primary challenges: (1) Inter-expert imbalance, referring to the uneven distribution of samples across experts, which leads to insufficient and biased calibration for less frequently utilized experts; (2) Intra-expert imbalance, arising from MoE’s unique aggregation mechanism, which leads to varying degrees of correlation between different samples and their assigned experts. To address these challenges, we propose MoEQuant, a novel quantization framework tailored for MoE LLMs. MoEQuant includes two novel techniques: 1) Expert-Balanced Self-Sampling (EBSS) is an efficient sampling method that efficiently constructs a calibration set with balanced expert distributions by leveraging the cumulative probabilities of tokens and expert balance metrics as guiding factors. 2) Affinity-Guided Quantization (AGQ), which incorporates affinities between experts and samples into the quantization process, thereby accurately assessing the impact of individual samples on different experts within the MoE layer. Experiments demonstrate that MoEQuant achieves substantial performance gains (more than 10 points accuracy gain in the HumanEval for DeepSeekMoE-16B under 4-bit quantization) and boosts efficiency.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts language models save computation by activating selected experts, but storing all those experts still requires substantial memory. Post-training quantization can compress models, yet applying it to MoE models can sharply reduce accuracy and generalization. This paper traces part of the difficulty to how sparse, dynamic routing distributes calibration information.

MoEQuant addresses two forms of imbalance. Across experts, infrequently used components receive too few or biased calibration samples. Within an expert, assigned samples differ in their relationship to that expert. Expert-Balanced Self-Sampling builds a more balanced calibration set using cumulative token probabilities and expert-balance measures. Affinity-Guided Quantization then accounts for expert-sample relationships when evaluating each sample’s influence.

Together, these techniques make calibration sensitive to both expert coverage and the importance of individual samples. Experiments report substantial gains, including more than ten accuracy points on HumanEval for DeepSeekMoE-16B under four-bit quantization, as well as improved efficiency. The findings support tailoring compression to MoE routing and aggregation rather than treating all calibration samples as equally informative.
summary.tldr: MoEQuant improves MoE quantization by balancing expert calibration coverage and accounting for the affinity between samples and experts.

title: MoEQuant: Enhancing Quantization for Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models via Expert-Balanced Sampling and Affinity Guidance

abstract: Prediction-powered inference (PPI) enables valid statistical inference by combining experimental data with machine learning predictions. When a sufficient number of high-quality predictions is available, PPI results in more accurate estimates and tighter confidence intervals than traditional methods. In this paper, we propose to inform the PPI framework with prior knowledge on the quality of the predictions. The resulting method, which we call frequentist, assisted by Bayes, PPI (FAB-PPI), improves over PPI when the observed prediction quality is likely under the prior, while maintaining its frequentist guarantees. Furthermore, when using heavy-tailed priors, FAB-PPI adaptively reverts to standard PPI in low prior probability regions. We demonstrate the benefits of FAB-PPI in real and synthetic examples.

paragraphs: Prediction-powered inference combines experimental data with machine learning predictions to support valid statistical conclusions. When enough high-quality predictions are available, it can improve estimation accuracy and tighten confidence intervals. FAB-PPI extends this framework by incorporating prior knowledge about how good those predictions are expected to be.

The method uses Bayesian information to assist a procedure that retains frequentist guarantees. Its improvement over standard PPI is conditional: it occurs when the observed prediction quality is plausible under the prior. The prior therefore supplies useful information when its expectations agree with the observed evidence, without replacing the method’s frequentist validity guarantees.

The paper also describes a protective adaptation obtained with heavy-tailed priors. In regions assigned low prior probability, FAB-PPI moves back toward standard PPI. This behavior matters when actual prediction quality differs from prior expectations, because the method can reduce its reliance on that prior. Real and synthetic examples demonstrate benefits, supporting a way to use prior knowledge while retaining the underlying statistical guarantees.
summary.tldr: FAB-PPI uses prior knowledge about prediction quality to improve inference when that knowledge fits the data while retaining frequentist guarantees.

title: FAB-PPI: Frequentist, Assisted by Bayes, Prediction-Powered Inference

abstract: We derive a controlled generation objective within the framework of Variational Flow Matching (VFM), which casts flow matching as a variational inference problem. We demonstrate that controlled generation can be implemented two ways: (1) by way of end-to-end training of conditional generative models, or (2) as a Bayesian inference problem, enabling post hoc control of unconditional models without retraining. Furthermore, we establish the conditions required for equivariant generation and provide an equivariant formulation of VFM tailored for molecular generation, ensuring invariance to rotations, translations, and permutations. We evaluate our approach on both uncontrolled and controlled molecular generation, achieving state-of-the-art performance on uncontrolled generation and outperforming state-of-the-art models in controlled generation, both with end-to-end training and in the Bayesian inference setting. This work strengthens the connection between flow-based generative modeling and Bayesian inference, offering a scalable and principled framework for constraint-driven and symmetry-aware generation.
