paragraphs: Controlled generation asks a model to produce samples that satisfy specified requirements. This paper derives an objective for doing so within Variational Flow Matching, which interprets flow matching as a variational inference problem. That perspective gives the authors a common framework for connecting generative modeling with Bayesian reasoning about desired outputs.

The framework supports two routes to control. A conditional generator can be trained end to end, or an existing unconditional generator can be controlled afterward through Bayesian inference without retraining. The paper also establishes conditions for equivariant generation and develops a molecular formulation that respects rotations, translations, and permutations. This addresses the need for molecular generation to handle equivalent spatial descriptions consistently.

In molecular experiments, the approach achieves state-of-the-art results for uncontrolled generation. For controlled generation, it outperforms state-of-the-art models through both end-to-end training and the Bayesian inference route. The stated findings support a shared treatment of control and symmetry, while demonstrating that control can also be applied to unconditional models after training.
summary.tldr: An equivariant Variational Flow Matching framework controls molecular generation through either conditional training or Bayesian inference without retraining.

title: Controlled Generation with Equivariant Variational Flow Matching

abstract: Language model (LLM) post-training can refine behaviors and unlock new skills, but the open science supporting these post-training techniques is still in its infancy. One limiting factor has been the difficulty of conducting large-scale comparative analyses of synthetic data generating models and LLM judges. To close this gap, we introduce WildChat-50M, the largest public chat dataset to date. We extend the existing WildChat dataset to include responses not only from GPT, but from over 50 different open-weight models, ranging in size from 0.5B to 104B parameters. We conduct an extensive comparative analysis and demonstrate the potential of this dataset by creating Re-Wild, our own public SFT mix, which outperforms the recent Tulu-3 SFT mixture from Allen AI with only 40% as many samples.

paragraphs: Post-training can refine language-model behavior and develop capabilities, but studying the role of synthetic data requires broad comparisons among data-generating models and model-based judges. The paper introduces WildChat-50M to make such large-scale comparisons more accessible. It expands the existing WildChat resource with responses from a much wider collection of models.

The dataset includes GPT responses alongside responses from more than 50 open-weight models, ranging from 0.5 billion to 104 billion parameters. This breadth supports comparative analysis across different sources of synthetic conversational data. The authors describe the dataset as the largest public chat dataset at the time of their work and conduct an extensive analysis using it.

They demonstrate its practical value by constructing Re-Wild, a public mixture for supervised finetuning. In the reported comparison, Re-Wild outperforms the Tulu-3 supervised-finetuning mixture while using only 40% as many samples. This result shows that the resource can support useful training-data curation, alongside its role in enabling research on synthetic responses and their evaluation.
summary.tldr: WildChat-50M broadens synthetic chat-data research and supports a finetuning mixture that outperforms Tulu-3's mixture with 40% as many samples.

title: WildChat-50M: A Deep Dive Into the Role of Synthetic Data in Post-Training

abstract: Large language models(LLMs) have garnered significant attention and demonstrated impressive capabilities in a wide range of applications. However, due to their enormous computational costs, the deployment and application of LLMs are often severely limited. To address this issue, structured pruning is an effective solution to compress the parameters of LLMs. Determining the importance of each sub-module in LLMs and minimizing performance loss are critical issues that need to be carefully addressed in structured pruning. In this paper, we propose an effective and fast structured pruning method named SlimLLM for large language models. For channel and attention head pruning, we evaluate the importance based on the entire channel or head, rather than merely aggregating the importance of individual elements within a sub-module. This approach enables a more holistic consideration of the interdependence among elements within the sub-module. In addition, we design a simple linear regression strategy for the output matrix to quickly recover performance. We also propose layer-based importance ratio to determine the pruning ratio for each layer. Based on the LLaMA benchmark results, our SlimLLM outperforms other methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Structured pruning reduces a language model by removing components such as channels or attention heads. The challenge is deciding which components matter and limiting the performance lost when they disappear. SlimLLM addresses both decisions with a fast pruning method designed around the structure of the model's submodules.

For channels and attention heads, SlimLLM evaluates importance at the level of the entire component. This accounts for interdependence among its elements instead of relying only on an aggregation of individual element scores. The method also uses layer-based importance ratios to decide how much to prune from each layer, making the allocation depend on layer importance.

After pruning, a simple linear regression strategy adjusts the output matrix to recover performance quickly. The authors report that SlimLLM outperforms other methods and achieves state-of-the-art results on LLaMA benchmarks. The approach combines component-level assessment, layer-specific pruning allocation, and output recovery, showing how several targeted choices can work together to preserve quality while reducing model parameters.
summary.tldr: SlimLLM combines whole-component importance scoring, layer-specific pruning, and linear-regression recovery to improve structured pruning on LLaMA benchmarks.

title: SlimLLM: Accurate Structured Pruning for Large Language Models

abstract: Gesture recognition based on surface electromyography (sEMG) has been gaining importance in many 3D Interactive Scenes. However, sEMG is easily influenced by various forms of noise in real-world environments, leading to challenges in providing long-term stable interactions through sEMG. Existing methods often struggle to enhance model noise resilience through various predefined data augmentation techniques. In this work, we revisit the problem from a short-term enhancement perspective to improve precision and robustness against various common noisy scenarios with learnable denoise using sEMG intrinsic pattern information and sliding-window attention. We propose a Short Term Enhancement Module(STEM), which can be easily integrated with various models. STEM offers several benefits: 1) Noise-resistant, enhanced robustness against noise without manual data augmentation; 2) Adaptability, adaptable to various models; and 3) Inference efficiency, achieving short-term enhancement through minimal weight-sharing in an efficient attention mechanism. In particular, we incorporate STEM into a transformer, creating the Short-Term Enhanced Transformer (STET). Compared with best-competing approaches, the impact of noise on STET is reduced by more than 20%. We report promising results on classification and regression tasks and demonstrate that STEM generalizes across different gesture recognition tasks. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/short_term_semg.

Existing approaches often try to improve resilience through predefined data augmentation. This paper instead learns to enhance short segments of the signal using information already present in its intrinsic patterns.

The proposed Short Term Enhancement Module, or STEM, combines learnable denoising with sliding-window attention. It is designed to integrate into different models and improve noise robustness without manual data augmentation. An efficient attention mechanism using minimal weight-sharing supports the intended inference efficiency, making short-term signal enhancement a reusable component.

Compared with the strongest competing approaches, they report that noise has more than 20% less impact on STET; this describes a reduction in noise impact, not a stated absolute accuracy increase. Results on classification and regression tasks are promising, and experiments show STEM transferring across different gesture-recognition tasks. The findings support learned short-term enhancement as a practical strategy for noisy muscle-signal analysis.
summary.tldr: STEM learns short-term enhancement of muscle signals, improving gesture-recognition robustness to noise across models and tasks.

title: Revisiting Noise Resilience Strategies in Gesture Recognition: Short-Term Enhancement in sEMG Analysis

abstract: The notion of duality – that a given physical system can have two different mathematical descriptions – is a key idea in modern theoretical physics. Establishing a duality in lattice statistical mechanics models requires the construction of a dual Hamiltonian and a map from the original to the dual observables. By using neural networks to parameterize these maps and introducing a loss function that penalises the difference between correlation functions in original and dual models, we formulate the process of duality discovery as an optimization problem. We numerically solve this problem and show that our framework can rediscover the celebrated Kramers-Wannier duality for the 2d Ising model, numerically reconstructing the known mapping of temperatures. We further investigate the 2d Ising model deformed by a plaquette coupling and find families of “approximate duals”. We discuss future directions and prospects for discovering new dualities within this framework.

paragraphs: A duality gives two mathematical descriptions of the same physical system. Finding one requires more than matching a few outputs: researchers must construct a corresponding Hamiltonian and a mapping between observables in the two descriptions. This paper turns that search into an optimization problem that neural networks can help solve.

The networks parameterize the relevant mappings, while a loss measures differences between correlation functions in the original and proposed dual models. Training therefore seeks descriptions whose correlations agree. This connects a theoretical physics problem to a concrete learning objective, making candidate dual descriptions accessible through numerical optimization.

The framework numerically rediscovers Kramers–Wannier duality for the two-dimensional Ising model, including its known temperature mapping. For an Ising model modified by a plaquette coupling, it finds families of approximate duals. The distinction matters: reproducing a known duality demonstrates the approach on an established case, while the modified model provides approximate correspondences. Discovering new dualities remains a prospective direction.
summary.tldr: Neural networks turn duality discovery into an optimization problem, recovering a known Ising-model duality and finding approximate duals for a modified model.

title: A Machine Learning Approach to Duality in Statistical Physics

abstract: As large language models (LLMs) play an increasingly important role in code generation, enhancing both correctness and efficiency has become crucial. Current methods primarily focus on correctness, often overlooking efficiency. To address this gap, we introduce SWIFTCODE to improve both aspects by fine-tuning LLMs on a high-quality dataset comprising correct and efficient code samples. Our methodology involves leveraging multiple LLMs to generate diverse candidate code solutions for various tasks across different programming languages. We then evaluate these solutions by directly measuring their execution time and memory usage through local execution. The code solution with the lowest execution time and memory consumption is selected as the final output for each task. Experimental results demonstrate significant improvements when fine-tuning with SWIFTCODE. For instance, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct’s pass@1 score increases from 44.8% to 57.7%, while the average execution time for correct tasks decreases by 48.4%. SWIFTCODE offers a scalable and effective solution for advancing AI-driven code generation, benefiting both software development and computational problem-solving.

paragraphs: A generated program can produce the right answer while taking unnecessarily long to run or consuming excessive memory. This paper addresses the tendency of code-generation training to emphasize correctness without giving comparable attention to execution efficiency. Its proposed approach, SWIFTCODE, builds a fine-tuning dataset containing code selected for both qualities.

Multiple language models generate diverse candidate solutions for programming tasks across different languages. The candidates are executed locally so that their running time and memory use can be measured directly. The method selects solutions with the lowest execution time and memory consumption for the dataset, grounding the efficiency signal in observed program behavior.

For Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, pass@1 rises from 44.8% to 57.7%, while average execution time on correct tasks falls by 48.4%. These results suggest that selecting efficient training examples can improve the programs a model produces, making execution quality part of learning rather than evaluating only whether the output is correct.
summary.tldr: SWIFTCODE fine-tunes code models on correct solutions selected through execution measurements, improving both correctness and runtime in reported experiments.

title: EffiCoder: Enhancing Code Generation in Large Language Models through Efficiency-Aware Fine-tuning

abstract: Watermarking for large language models (LLMs) offers a promising approach to identifying AI-generated text. Existing approaches, however, either compromise the distribution of original generated text by LLMs or are limited to embedding zero-bit information that only allows for watermark detection but ignores identification. We present StealthInk, a stealthy multi-bit watermarking scheme that preserves the original text distribution while enabling the embedding of provenance data, such as userID, TimeStamp, and modelID, within LLM-generated text. This enhances fast traceability without requiring access to the language model’s API or prompts. We derive a lower bound on the number of tokens necessary for watermark detection at a fixed equal error rate, which provides insights on how to enhance the capacity. Comprehensive empirical evaluations across diverse tasks highlight the stealthiness, detectability, and resilience of StealthInk, establishing it as an effective solution for LLM watermarking applications.

paragraphs: A watermark can help identify machine-generated text, but a simple detection signal does not say where the text came from. StealthInk embeds multiple bits of provenance information, such as a user identifier, timestamp, or model identifier. It is designed to do so while preserving the language model’s original distribution over generated text.

That combination addresses two shortcomings identified in earlier approaches: changing the text distribution or supporting only a yes-or-no watermark signal. By carrying provenance data, StealthInk supports tracing text without access to the model’s API or the prompts used to generate it. The additional information extends watermarking from recognizing a signal to identifying associated provenance.

The authors also derive a lower bound on the number of tokens needed for detection at a fixed equal error rate, connecting detection requirements with watermark capacity. Empirical evaluations across diverse tasks report stealthiness, detectability, and resilience. Together, the theoretical bound and experimental results support a watermarking approach that combines distribution preservation, detection, and recoverable provenance information.
summary.tldr: StealthInk embeds multi-bit provenance in generated text while preserving its original distribution and enabling tracing without model API or prompt access.

title: StealthInk: A Multi-bit and Stealthy Watermark for Large Language Models

abstract: Feature attribution methods aim to improve the transparency of deep neural networks by identifying the input features that influence a model’s decision. Pixel-based heatmaps have become the standard for attributing features to high-dimensional inputs, such as images, audio representations, and volumes. While intuitive and convenient, these pixel-based attributions fail to capture the underlying structure of the data. Moreover, the choice of domain for computing attributions has often been overlooked. This work demonstrates that the wavelet domain allows for informative and meaningful attributions. It handles any input dimension and offers a unified approach to feature attribution. Our method, the Wavelet Attribution Method (WAM), leverages the spatial and scale-localized properties of wavelet coefficients to provide explanations that capture both the where and what of a model’s decision-making process. We show that WAM quantitatively matches or outperforms existing gradient-based methods across multiple modalities, including audio, images, and volumes. Additionally, we discuss how WAM bridges attribution with broader aspects of model robustness and transparency. Project page: https://gabrielkasmi.github.io/wam/

paragraphs: Feature attribution seeks to identify which parts of an input influence a neural network’s decision. Pixel-level heatmaps offer a convenient visualization, but individual pixels do not adequately capture the underlying structure of images, audio representations, or volumes. This paper examines how changing the representation in which attribution is computed can produce more informative explanations.

The proposed Wavelet Attribution Method operates on wavelet coefficients, which localize information in both space and scale. These properties let explanations describe where influential information occurs and what scale of structure it involves. The approach supports inputs of any dimension, providing a common attribution framework across different types of data.

In quantitative evaluations across audio, images, and volumes, the method matches or exceeds existing gradient-based attribution methods. The authors also discuss connections between attribution, robustness, and transparency. The contribution is to make the attribution domain an explicit design choice: explaining a decision through spatially localized structures at multiple scales can reveal information that a pixel-based view fails to capture.
summary.tldr: Wavelet-based attribution explains influential input structures by location and scale, matching or outperforming compared gradient-based methods across several modalities.

title: One Wave To Explain Them All: A Unifying Perspective On Feature Attribution

abstract: This paper studies phase transitions for the existence of unregularized M-estimators under proportional asymptotics where the sample size $n$ and feature dimension $p$ grow proportionally with $n/p \to \delta \in (1, \infty)$. We study the existence of M-estimators in single-index models where the response $y_i$ depends on covariates $x_i \sim N(0, I_p)$ through an unknown index ${w} \in \mathbb{R}^p$ and an unknown link function. An explicit expression is derived for the critical threshold $\delta_\infty$ that determines the phase transition for the existence of the M-estimator, generalizing the results of Candés & Sur (2020) for binary logistic regression to other single-index models. Furthermore, we investigate the existence of a solution to the nonlinear system of equations governing the asymptotic behavior of the M-estimator when it exists. The existence of solution to this system for $\delta > \delta_\infty$ remains largely unproven outside the global null in binary logistic regression. We address this gap with a proof that the system admits a solution if and only if $\delta > \delta_\infty$, providing a comprehensive theoretical foundation for proportional asymptotic results that require as a prerequisite the existence of a solution to the system.

paragraphs: Before analyzing an estimator’s accuracy, it matters whether the estimator exists. This paper studies that question for unregularized M-estimators in high-dimensional single-index models. It considers a regime where sample size and feature dimension grow together, with their ratio approaching a finite value greater than one.

The covariates are standard Gaussian, and the response depends on them through an unknown index vector and an unknown link function. Within this setting, the authors derive an explicit critical threshold for the existence phase transition. The result extends earlier work on binary logistic regression to other single-index models.

The paper also resolves an existence question for the nonlinear equations used to describe the estimator’s asymptotic behavior. It proves that this system has a solution exactly when the limiting sample-to-dimension ratio exceeds the critical threshold. This supplies a prerequisite for asymptotic analyses that depend on those equations. The contribution therefore links existence of the statistical estimator with existence of the mathematical description used to study it under the stated proportional-growth and Gaussian assumptions.
summary.tldr: The paper derives an existence threshold for high-dimensional unregularized M-estimators and proves the associated asymptotic equations are solvable exactly above that threshold.

title: Phase transitions for the existence of unregularized M-estimators in single index models

abstract: Recent years have seen significant progress in Text-To-Audio (TTA) synthesis, enabling users to enrich their creative workflows with synthetic audio generated from natural language prompts. Despite this progress, the effects of data, model architecture, training objective functions, and sampling strategies on target benchmarks are not well understood. With the purpose of providing a holistic understanding of the design space of TTA models, we set up a large-scale empirical experiment focused on diffusion and flow matching models. Our contributions include: 1) AF-Synthetic, a large dataset of high quality synthetic captions obtained from an audio understanding model; 2) a systematic comparison of different architectural, training, and inference design choices for TTA models; 3) an analysis of sampling methods and their Pareto curves with respect to generation quality and inference speed. We leverage the knowledge obtained from this extensive analysis to propose our best model dubbed Elucidated Text-To-Audio (ETTA). When evaluated on AudioCaps and MusicCaps, ETTA provides improvements over the baselines trained on publicly available data, while being competitive with models trained on proprietary data. Finally, we show ETTA’s improved ability to generate creative audio following complex and imaginative captions – a task that is more challenging than current benchmarks.

paragraphs: Text-to-audio systems generate sound from written descriptions, but their performance depends on many interacting design choices. This paper conducts a large empirical study of diffusion and flow-matching models to understand how training data, architecture, objectives, and sampling affect the resulting audio.

The study introduces AF-Synthetic, a dataset of high-quality synthetic captions produced by an audio-understanding model. It systematically compares choices made during model construction, training, and inference. Its sampling analysis examines quality-speed tradeoffs through Pareto curves, making the relationship between generation quality and inference cost an explicit part of the design study.

The authors combine lessons from these comparisons into ETTA. On AudioCaps and MusicCaps, it improves over baselines trained with publicly available data and remains competitive with models trained on proprietary data. They also demonstrate improved generation for complex, imaginative captions, which they identify as more challenging than current benchmarks. The contribution includes both a resulting model and empirical evidence for understanding the design decisions behind stronger text-to-audio generation.
summary.tldr: A systematic study of text-to-audio design choices yields ETTA, with improved benchmark results and handling of imaginative prompts.

title: ETTA: Elucidating the Design Space of Text-to-Audio Models

abstract: Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) rely heavily on architectural choices for good generalization. Developing theoretically grounded approaches for architecture design remains an active area of research. Via theoretical analysis of the infinite-width limit, we establish a methodology that characterizes INR’s generalization by means of kernel alignment. We first formulate the optimal kernel that minimizes pointwise expected squared error, then demonstrate that the Neural Tangent Kernel of the composed function (INR with input encoding) can approximate any positive semidefinite dot-product kernels through input feature mapping adjustments. Building upon these insights, we propose a Kernel Alignment Regularizer (KAR) that naturally integrates with existing INR systems to enhance kernel alignment. We further develop Plug-in Encoding for Aligned Kernels (PEAK) to refine INR models with KAR using learnable input encoding. This work contributes to the ongoing research efforts in bridging theory and practice for principled INR architecture design. Code is available at https://github.com/lizhemin15/KAR.

paragraphs: Implicit neural representations depend strongly on architectural choices for their ability to generalize. This paper develops a theoretical basis for choosing input encodings by studying the infinite-width limit. It describes generalization through kernel alignment, connecting the model’s induced relationships between inputs to a kernel designed around prediction error.

The authors first formulate an optimal kernel that minimizes pointwise expected squared error. They then show that adjusting the input feature mapping allows the neural tangent kernel of the encoded network to approximate any positive semidefinite dot-product kernel. This result identifies input encoding as a mathematically motivated means of changing the kernel associated with the full representation system.

The practical proposals are a Kernel Alignment Regularizer, or KAR, and Plug-in Encoding for Aligned Kernels, or PEAK. KAR integrates an alignment objective into existing systems, while PEAK uses learnable input encodings to refine models through that objective. Together, they translate the infinite-width analysis into tools for more principled architecture design.
summary.tldr: Infinite-width kernel analysis motivates a regularizer and learnable input encodings for principled implicit neural representation design.

title: Learning Input Encodings for Kernel-Optimal Implicit Neural Representations

abstract: Although Multi-Vector Retrieval (MVR) has achieved the state of the art on many information retrieval (IR) tasks, its performance highly depends on how to decompose queries into smaller pieces, say phrases or tokens. However, optimizing query decomposition for MVR performance is not end-to-end differentiable. Even worse, jointly solving this problem and training the downstream retrieval-based systems, say RAG systems could be highly inefficient. To overcome these challenges, we propose Performance-Oriented Query Decomposer (POQD), a novel query decomposition framework for MVR. POQD leverages one LLM for query decomposition and searches the optimal prompt with an LLM-based optimizer. We further propose an end-to-end training algorithm to alternatively optimize the prompt for query decomposition and the downstream models. This algorithm can achieve superior MVR performance at a reasonable training cost as our theoretical analysis suggests. POQD can be integrated seamlessly into arbitrary retrieval-based systems such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. Extensive empirical studies on representative RAG-based QA tasks show that POQD outperforms existing query decomposition strategies in both retrieval performance and end-to-end QA accuracy. POQD is available at https://github.com/PKU-SDS-lab/POQD-ICML25.

paragraphs: Multi-vector retrieval depends heavily on how a query is divided into smaller pieces, such as phrases or tokens. Choosing that decomposition to improve retrieval is not end-to-end differentiable, making direct optimization difficult. Training decomposition jointly with a downstream retrieval-based system can also be inefficient.

POQD uses a language model to perform decomposition and an LLM-based optimizer to search for a suitable prompt. It then alternates between optimizing the decomposition prompt and training the downstream models. This gives the decomposition procedure a route to improve according to system performance, while coordinating its changes with the components that use the retrieved information.

The theoretical analysis suggests that this alternating algorithm can achieve strong retrieval performance at a reasonable training cost. POQD is designed for integration into retrieval-based systems, including retrieval-augmented generation. In representative question-answering experiments using such systems, it outperforms existing decomposition strategies in both retrieval quality and final answer accuracy. These results connect better query decomposition with benefits at both the search stage and the completed task.
summary.tldr: POQD alternates LLM-driven query-prompt optimization with downstream training to improve multi-vector retrieval and question answering.

title: POQD: Performance-Oriented Query Decomposer for Multi-vector retrieval

abstract: The canonical setup of learning a reward model (RM) from human preferences with binary feedback discards potentially useful samples (such as "tied" between the two responses) and loses fine-grained information (such as "slightly better’"). This paper proposes a framework for learning RMs under ordinal feedback, generalizing the binary feedback to arbitrary granularity. We first identify a marginal unbiasedness condition, which generalizes the existing assumption of the binary feedback. The condition is validated via the sociological concept called "wisdom of the crowd". Under this condition, we develop a natural probability model and prove the benefits of fine-grained feedback in terms of reducing the Rademacher complexity, which may be of independent interest to another problem: the bias-variance trade-off in knowledge distillation. The framework also sheds light on designing guidelines for human annotators. Our numerical experiments validate that: (1) fine-grained feedback leads to better RM learning for both in- and out-of-distribution settings; (2) incorporating a certain proportion of tied samples boosts RM learning.

paragraphs: Binary preference labels record which response is better but can discard ties and distinctions such as a slight preference. This paper develops reward modeling with ordinal feedback, allowing judgments at arbitrary levels of granularity. The aim is to retain information that a simple winner-loser decision would otherwise remove.

The theoretical framework rests on a marginal unbiasedness condition that generalizes an assumption used for binary feedback. The authors validate this condition through the sociological idea of crowd wisdom. Under that condition, they construct a probability model and prove that finer feedback reduces Rademacher complexity, a measure relevant to controlling a model's ability to fit varying labels.

Numerical experiments find better reward-model learning with finer feedback both within and outside the training distribution. They also find benefits from including a certain proportion of tied samples. These results support collecting richer judgments rather than automatically excluding ambiguous comparisons. The framework additionally informs annotator guidelines and offers a possible connection to the bias-variance trade-off in knowledge distillation, while its theoretical benefits remain tied to the stated condition.
summary.tldr: Ordinal feedback preserves preference strength and ties, improving reward learning with theoretical benefits under a marginal unbiasedness condition.

title: Reward Modeling with Ordinal Feedback: Wisdom of the Crowd

abstract: TabPFN has emerged as a promising in-context learning model for tabular data, capable of directly predicting the labels of test samples given labeled training examples. It has demonstrated competitive performance, particularly on small-scale classification tasks. However, despite its effectiveness, TabPFN still requires further refinement in several areas, including handling high-dimensional features, aligning with downstream datasets, and scaling to larger datasets. In this paper, we revisit existing variants of TabPFN and observe that most approaches focus either on reducing bias or variance, often neglecting the need to address the other side, while also increasing inference overhead. To fill this gap, we propose Beta (Bagging and Encoder-based Fine-tuning for TabPFN Adaptation), a novel and effective method designed to minimize both bias and variance. To reduce bias, we introduce a lightweight encoder to better align downstream tasks with the pre-trained TabPFN. By increasing the number of encoders in a lightweight manner, Beta mitigates variance, thereby further improving the model’s performance. Additionally, bootstrapped sampling is employed to further reduce the impact of data perturbations on the model, all while maintaining computational efficiency during inference. Our approach enhances TabPFN’s ability to handle high-dimensional data and scale to larger datasets. Experimental results on over 200 benchmark classification datasets demonstrate that Beta either outperforms or matches state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: TabPFN predicts labels for tabular examples by using labeled training examples as context. Its strengths on small classification problems do not fully resolve challenges involving many features, larger datasets, or mismatch with a downstream task. This paper argues that adaptations often address either bias or variance while neglecting the other and increasing inference costs.

Beta combines encoder-based adaptation with bagging to address both. A lightweight encoder aligns downstream data more closely with the pretrained TabPFN, targeting bias. Increasing the number of lightweight encoders targets variance, while bootstrapped sampling further reduces sensitivity to data perturbations. These components are designed to improve adaptation while keeping inference computationally efficient.

On more than 200 benchmark classification datasets, Beta reportedly matches or exceeds state-of-the-art methods. The authors also report improved handling of high-dimensional inputs and scaling to larger datasets. The contribution is the coordinated treatment of task alignment and prediction variability, showing how several lightweight adaptation mechanisms can broaden the usefulness of an existing in-context tabular model.
summary.tldr: Beta combines lightweight encoders and bootstrapped sampling to improve TabPFN’s adaptation, stability, and scalability across tabular classification tasks.

title: TabPFN Unleashed: A Scalable and Effective Solution to Tabular Classification Problems

abstract: Mixture of Experts (MoE) architectures have significantly increased computational efficiency in both research and real-world applications of large-scale machine learning models. However, their scalability and efficiency under memory constraints remain relatively underexplored. In this work, we present joint scaling laws for dense and MoE models, incorporating key factors such as the number of active parameters, dataset size, and the number of experts. Our findings provide a principled framework for selecting the optimal MoE configuration under fixed memory and compute budgets. Surprisingly, we show that MoE models can be more memory-efficient than dense models, contradicting conventional wisdom. Extensive empirical validation confirms the theoretical predictions of our scaling laws. These results offer actionable insights for designing and deploying MoE models in practical large-scale training scenarios.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts models are known for computational efficiency, but their behavior under memory constraints is less well understood. This paper asks how to choose between dense and expert-based models when both memory and computation are limited. The question matters because a configuration that looks efficient on computation alone may not be the best use of a fixed overall resource budget.

The authors develop joint scaling laws that account for active parameter count, training dataset size, and the number of experts. Bringing these factors into one framework allows the configuration decision to consider their combined effects. The resulting laws provide a principled way to select an MoE configuration under specified memory and compute budgets.

A central finding is that MoE models can be more memory-efficient than dense models, challenging the conventional expectation described in the paper. Extensive empirical evaluations support the scaling laws' predictions. The practical implication is conditional but useful: memory constraints need not rule out expert architectures, and model selection can be guided by the joint resource relationships.
summary.tldr: Joint scaling laws show how to configure mixture-of-experts models under fixed budgets and identify cases where they can be more memory-efficient than dense models.

title: Joint MoE Scaling Laws: Mixture of Experts Can Be Memory Efficient

abstract: Backpropagation is the foundational algorithm for training neural networks and a key driver of deep learning’s success. However, its biological plausibility has been challenged due to three primary limitations: weight symmetry, reliance on global error signals, and the dual-phase nature of training, as highlighted by the existing literature. Although various alternative learning approaches have been proposed to address these issues, most either fail to satisfy all three criteria simultaneously or yield suboptimal results. Inspired by the dynamics and plasticity of pyramidal neurons, we propose Dendritic Localized Learning (DLL), a novel learning algorithm designed to overcome these challenges. Extensive empirical experiments demonstrate that DLL satisfies all three criteria of biological plausibility while achieving state-of-the-art performance among algorithms that meet these requirements. Furthermore, DLL exhibits strong generalization across a range of architectures, including MLPs, CNNs, and RNNs. These results, benchmarked against existing biologically plausible learning algorithms, offer valuable empirical insights for future research. We hope this study can inspire the development of new biologically plausible algorithms for training multilayer networks and advancing progress in both neuroscience and machine learning. Our code is available at https://github.com/Lvchangze/Dendritic-Localized-Learning.

paragraphs: Backpropagation trains neural networks effectively, but the paper highlights three obstacles to treating it as biologically plausible: weight symmetry, dependence on global error signals, and a training process with two phases. Existing alternatives often either leave some of these obstacles unresolved or sacrifice performance. The authors seek a learning algorithm that addresses all three together.

Dendritic Localized Learning draws inspiration from the dynamics and plasticity of pyramidal neurons. Its design aims to train multilayer networks while satisfying the paper’s three biological plausibility criteria. The important comparison is therefore with learning algorithms that meet the same requirements, since high task performance alone would not establish that the biological constraints had been addressed.

The reported experiments find that DLL meets all three criteria and achieves state-of-the-art performance among qualifying algorithms. The method also generalizes across multilayer perceptrons, convolutional networks, and recurrent networks. These findings provide empirical support for its usefulness across architectures and for pursuing biologically motivated training mechanisms without abandoning competitive performance within that constrained class.
summary.tldr: Dendritic Localized Learning meets three stated biological plausibility criteria and leads the evaluated algorithms satisfying those criteria.

title: Dendritic Localized Learning: Toward Biologically Plausible Algorithm

abstract: Multi-Label Online Continual Learning (MOCL) requires models to learn continuously from endless multi-label data streams, facing complex challenges including persistent catastrophic forgetting, potential missing labels, and uncontrollable imbalanced class distributions. While existing MOCL methods attempt to address these challenges through various techniques, they all overlook label-specific region identifying and feature learning - a fundamental solution rooted in multi-label learning but challenging to achieve in the online setting with incremental and partial supervision. To this end, we first leverage the inherent structural information of input data to evaluate and verify the innate localization capability of different pre-trained models. Then, we propose CUTER (CUT-out-and-Experience-Replay), a simple yet versatile strategy that provides fine-grained supervision signals by further identifying, strengthening and cutting out label-specific regions for efficient experience replay. It not only enables models to simultaneously address catastrophic forgetting, missing labels, and class imbalance challenges, but also serves as an orthogonal solution that seamlessly integrates with existing approaches. Extensive experiments on multiple multi-label image benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method. The code is available at https://github.com/wxr99/Cut-Replay

paragraphs: Learning continuously from images with multiple labels creates overlapping difficulties: earlier knowledge can be forgotten, some labels may be missing, and class frequencies can be uneven. This paper focuses on the image regions associated with individual labels. Such regions offer more specific learning signals, but identifying them is difficult when supervision arrives incrementally and is incomplete.

The authors first use structural information in the input to assess how well different pretrained models can already localize relevant regions. Their CUTER strategy then identifies and strengthens label-specific regions, cuts them out, and uses them for experience replay. Replaying these targeted pieces gives the learner finer-grained supervision than relying only on the original multi-label image context.

The proposed strategy is designed to address forgetting, missing labels, and class imbalance together. It is also presented as complementary to existing approaches, allowing region-focused replay to be integrated with other techniques. Experiments on multiple multi-label image benchmarks report superior performance. The findings support label-specific localization and replay as a useful shared mechanism for several difficulties that arise in continual learning.
summary.tldr: CUTER replays label-specific image regions to help continual learners handle forgetting, missing labels, and class imbalance together.

title: Cut out and Replay: A Simple yet Versatile Strategy for Multi-Label Online Continual Learning

abstract: The rapid advancement of large language model (LLM) agents has raised new concerns regarding their safety and security. In this paper, we propose GuardAgent, the first guardrail agent to protect target agents by dynamically checking whether their actions satisfy given safety guard requests. Specifically, GuardAgent first analyzes the safety guard requests to generate a task plan, and then maps this plan into guardrail code for execution. By performing the code execution, GuardAgent can deterministically follow the safety guard request and safeguard target agents. In both steps, an LLM is utilized as the reasoning component, supplemented by in-context demonstrations retrieved from a memory module storing experiences from previous tasks. In addition, we propose two novel benchmarks: EICU-AC benchmark to assess the access control for healthcare agents and Mind2Web-SC benchmark to evaluate the safety policies for web agents. We show that GuardAgent effectively moderates the violation actions for different types of agents on these two benchmarks with over 98% and 83% guardrail accuracies, respectively. Project page: https://guardagent.github.io/

paragraphs: GuardAgent checks whether another language-model agent’s actions comply with a supplied safety request. Its approach turns the request into an executable checking procedure. This addresses the need to apply safety rules dynamically as agents take actions, with the guardrail itself using language-model reasoning to interpret what should be enforced.

The process has two stages. GuardAgent first produces a task plan from the safety request, then converts that plan into guardrail code. Executing the code provides deterministic enforcement of the implemented checks. Both stages draw on demonstrations retrieved from a memory of previous tasks, giving the reasoning component relevant examples of earlier guardrail work.

The authors introduce two benchmarks: EICU-AC for healthcare-agent access control and Mind2Web-SC for web-agent safety policies. GuardAgent achieves guardrail accuracies above 98% and 83%, respectively, and effectively moderates violating actions in those evaluations. The results support combining reasoning with executable checks, while the measured accuracies distinguish overall guardrail performance from the determinism of code execution.
summary.tldr: GuardAgent translates safety requests into executable guardrail code, achieving strong measured accuracy for healthcare and web agents.

title: GuardAgent: Safeguard LLM Agents via Knowledge-Enabled Reasoning

abstract: Training deep neural networks–and more recently, large models–demands efficient and scalable optimizers. Adaptive gradient algorithms like Adam, AdamW, and their variants have been central to this task. Despite the development of numerous variance reduction algorithms in the past decade aimed at accelerating stochastic optimization in both convex and nonconvex settings, variance reduction has not found widespread success in training deep neural networks or large language models. Consequently, it has remained a less favored approach in modern AI. In this paper, to unleash the power of variance reduction for efficient training of large models, we propose a unified optimization framework, MARS (Make vAriance Reduction Shine), which reconciles preconditioned gradient methods with variance reduction via a scaled stochastic recursive momentum technique. Within our framework, we introduce three instances of MARS that leverage preconditioned gradient updates based on AdamW, Lion, and Shampoo, respectively. We also draw a connection between our algorithms and existing optimizers. Experimental results on training GPT-2 models indicate that MARS consistently outperforms AdamW by a large margin.

paragraphs: Large-model training depends heavily on optimizers that turn noisy gradient estimates into useful parameter updates. Although variance reduction has a substantial history in stochastic optimization, the paper notes that it has not achieved widespread success in deep-network and language-model training. MARS aims to make this family of techniques effective alongside the adaptive methods already used for these workloads.

The framework combines preconditioned gradient methods with variance reduction through scaled stochastic recursive momentum. Preconditioning changes how gradient updates are scaled, while variance reduction addresses their stochastic variability. MARS brings these functions together in one optimization framework, rather than treating the choice of update geometry and the handling of gradient noise as unrelated decisions.

The authors instantiate the framework with updates based on AdamW, Lion, and Shampoo, and establish connections to existing optimizers. In GPT-2 training experiments, MARS consistently outperforms AdamW by a large margin. The reported finding supports the usefulness of this combination for the tested models and gives several concrete optimizer variants through which the framework can be applied.
summary.tldr: MARS combines variance reduction with preconditioned updates and consistently outperforms AdamW by a large margin in reported GPT-2 training experiments.

title: MARS: Unleashing the Power of Variance Reduction for Training Large Models

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently achieved remarkable results in complex multi-step tasks, such as mathematical reasoning and agentic software engineering. However, they often struggle to maintain consistent performance across multiple solution attempts. One effective approach to narrow the gap between average-case and best-case performance is guided test-time search, which explores multiple solution paths to identify the most promising one. Unfortunately, effective search techniques (e.g. MCTS) are often unsuitable for non-serializable RL environments, such as Docker containers, where intermediate environment states cannot be easily saved and restored. We investigate two complementary search strategies applicable to such environments: 1-step lookahead and trajectory selection, both guided by a learned action-value function estimator. On the SWE-bench Verified benchmark, a key testbed for agentic software engineering, we find these methods to double the average success rate of a fine-tuned Qwen-72B model, achieving $40.8$%, the new state-of-the-art for open-weights models. Additionally, we show that these techniques are transferable to more advanced closed models, yielding similar improvements with GPT-4o.

paragraphs: An agent can sometimes solve a task successfully yet perform inconsistently across repeated attempts. Guided search tries to improve average performance by examining alternative solution paths. Similar improvements transfer to GPT-4o. These results suggest that value-guided selection can recover more of an agent's demonstrated capability even when its operating environment restricts conventional search.
summary.tldr: Value-guided lookahead and trajectory selection improve software agents in environments where saving and restoring intermediate states is difficult.

title: Guided Search Strategies in Non-Serializable Environments with Applications to Software Engineering Agents

abstract: Operations Research practitioners debug infeasible models through an iterative process: inspecting Irreducible Infeasible Subsystems (IIS), identifying constraint conflicts, and repairing formulations until feasibility is restored. Existing LLM benchmarks mostly treat OR as one-shot translation from problem descriptions to solver code, omitting this diagnostic loop. We formalize infeasible-model repair as a solver-in-the-loop Markov Decision Process in which each action triggers solver re-execution and IIS recomputation, yielding deterministic, verifiable feedback. We introduce ORLoopBench, a benchmark suite with two components: ORDebug releases 5,362 LP/MILP repair instances, while ORBias evaluates closed-form operational decision rationality across inventory settings. Solver-verified RLVR training enables an 8B model to surpass frontier APIs on LP repair (95.3% vs 92.4% RR@5), improves diagnostic behavior, and transfers to MILP repair. The same evaluation exposes semantic drift in whole-model code regeneration: feasible regenerated MILPs can solve the wrong problem. Process-level evaluation with solver oracles enables targeted training for reliable OR self-correction.

This paper builds a benchmark around that workflow, going beyond a single attempt to translate a problem description into solver code. After every repair action, the solver runs again and identifies an irreducible infeasible subsystem, providing verifiable feedback about conflicting constraints.

ORLoopBench contains two components. ORDebug supplies 5,362 repair instances involving linear and mixed-integer linear programs. ORBias tests operational decision rationality in inventory settings with closed-form answers. The repair process is formalized as a Markov decision process, making iterative solver feedback part of both evaluation and training.

This distinction makes process-level evaluation useful for checking whether self-correction preserves the intended optimization task.
summary.tldr: ORLoopBench evaluates iterative optimization-model repair, showing gains from solver-verified training and exposing feasible repairs that change the problem.

title: ORLoopBench: Solver-in-the-Loop Benchmarks for Self-Correction and Behavioral Rationality in Operations Research

abstract: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) and off-policy learning (OPL) are foundational for decision-making in offline contextual bandits. Recent advances in OPL primarily optimize OPE estimators with improved statistical properties, assuming that better estimators inherently yield superior policies. Although theoretically justified, this estimator-centric approach neglects a critical practical obstacle: challenging optimization landscapes. In this paper, we provide theoretical insights and empirical evidence showing that current OPL methods encounter severe optimization issues, particularly as the action space grows. We show that estimator-aware policy parametrization can mitigate, but not fully resolve, optimization challenges. Building on this, we explore simpler weighted log-likelihood objectives and demonstrate that they enjoy substantially better optimization properties and still recover competitive, often superior, learned policies. Our findings emphasize the necessity of explicitly addressing optimization considerations in the development of OPL algorithms for large action spaces.

paragraphs: Off-policy learning uses previously collected contextual-bandit data to train a decision policy. A common strategy optimizes an estimator of policy performance, with improved statistical estimation expected to produce better decisions. This paper examines a practical obstacle to that strategy: the resulting objective may be difficult to optimize, especially when many actions are available.

The authors provide theoretical insights and empirical evidence that current approaches face severe optimization problems as the action space grows. Choosing a policy parameterization that accounts for the estimator can reduce those difficulties, but does not fully eliminate them. This separates the quality of a performance estimate from the ease of finding a good policy by optimizing it.

The paper then studies simpler weighted log-likelihood objectives. These have substantially better optimization properties and produce competitive, often superior, learned policies in the reported experiments. The finding supports treating trainability as a central design consideration alongside statistical estimation. For large action spaces, an objective’s practical value depends partly on whether optimization can successfully use the information it contains.
summary.tldr: In large action spaces, easier-to-optimize weighted likelihood objectives can learn better policies than optimizing sophisticated evaluation estimators.

title: Off-Policy Learning in Large Action Spaces: Optimization Matters More Than Estimation

abstract: One of the most common machine learning setups is logistic regression. In many classification models, including neural networks, the final prediction is obtained by applying a logistic link function to a linear score. In binary logistic regression, the feedback can be either soft labels, corresponding to the true conditional probability of the data (as in distillation), or sampled hard labels (taking values $\pm 1$). We point out a fundamental problem that arises even in a particularly favorable setting, where the goal is to learn a noise-free soft target of the form $\sigma(\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{w}^{\star})$. In the over-constrained case (i.e. the number of samples $n$ exceeds the input dimension $d$) with examples $(\mathbf{x}_i,\sigma(\mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\mathbf{w}^{\star}))$, it is sufficient to recover $\mathbf{w}^{\star}$ and hence achieve the Bayes risk. However, we prove that when the examples are labeled by hard labels $y_i$ sampled from the same conditional distribution $\sigma(\mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\mathbf{w}^{\star})$ and $\mathbf{w}^{\star}$ is $s$-sparse, then rotation-invariant algorithms are provably suboptimal: they incur an excess risk $\Omega\!\left(\frac{d-1}{n}\right)$, while there are simple non-rotation invariant algorithms with excess risk $O(\frac{s\log d}{n})$. The simplest rotation invariant algorithm is gradient descent on the logistic loss (with early stopping). A simple non-rotation-invariant algorithm for sparse targets that achieves the above upper bounds uses gradient descent on the weights $u_i,v_i$, where now the linear weight $w_i$ is reparameterized as $u_iv_i$.

paragraphs: Binary logistic regression can receive either the true probability of each outcome or a sampled binary label. This paper shows that the distinction changes which algorithms work well, even when the underlying probability function has a simple form. In the studied over-constrained setting, noiseless soft labels suffice to recover the target weights and achieve Bayes risk.

With sampled hard labels and an s-sparse target in d dimensions, rotation-invariant algorithms incur excess risk of at least order (d−1)/n. Such algorithms do not favor a particular coordinate system. By comparison, simple algorithms that are sensitive to coordinates achieve an upper bound of order s log(d)/n, exploiting the target's sparsity.

Gradient descent on logistic loss, including early stopping, is an example of the rotation-invariant class. A successful alternative represents each weight as a product of two trainable parameters and performs gradient descent on those factors. The result isolates how label sampling interacts with algorithmic bias: for sparse targets, coordinate-sensitive parameterization can provide a substantially better statistical rate.
summary.tldr: For sparse logistic targets with sampled hard labels, rotation-invariant algorithms have worse excess-risk rates than simple coordinate-sensitive alternatives.

title: Hard labels sampled from sparse targets mislead rotation invariant algorithms

abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) for high-dimensional constrained problems remains a significant challenge due to the curse of dimensionality. We propose Local Constrained Bayesian Optimization (LCBO), a novel framework tailored for such settings. Unlike trust-region methods that are prone to premature shrinking when confronting tight or complex constraints, LCBO leverages the differentiable landscape of constraint-penalized surrogates to alternate between rapid local descent and uncertainty-driven exploration. Theoretically, we prove that LCBO achieves a convergence rate for the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) residual that depends polynomially on the dimension $d$ for common kernels under mild assumptions, offering a rigorous alternative to global BO where regret bounds typically scale exponentially. Extensive evaluations on high-dimensional benchmarks (up to 100D) demonstrate that LCBO consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Optimizing an expensive function becomes especially difficult when there are many input dimensions and constraints on acceptable solutions. Local Constrained Bayesian Optimization, or LCBO, addresses this setting. It targets a weakness of trust-region approaches, whose search regions can shrink prematurely when constraints are tight or geometrically complex.

LCBO uses differentiable surrogate models that incorporate penalties for constraint violations. It alternates between local descent, which rapidly follows promising directions in the surrogate landscape, and exploration guided by uncertainty. This pairing gives the method a way to pursue local improvement while continuing to investigate uncertain parts of the search space.

For common kernels under mild assumptions, the authors prove a convergence rate for the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker residual with polynomial dependence on dimension. That residual measures progress toward constrained stationarity; the result concerns this criterion rather than global regret. Evaluations on benchmarks with up to 100 dimensions consistently outperform state-of-the-art baselines, supporting the local approach in the tested high-dimensional constrained problems.
summary.tldr: LCBO alternates local descent with uncertainty-driven exploration and provides a dimension-polynomial constrained-stationarity guarantee under stated assumptions.

title: Local Constrained Bayesian Optimization

abstract: Supervised fine-tuning with expert demonstrations often produces models that imitate outputs without internalizing the reasoning processes needed for robust generalization. While critique-based approaches show promise, training models to generate critiques directly, such as Critique Fine-Tuning (CFT), can lead to output-format drift and degradation of general capabilities. We propose $\textbf{C}$ritique-$\textbf{G}$uided $\textbf{D}$istillation (CGD), a training framework that decouples critique consumption from critique generation. During fine-tuning, the student is trained to refine flawed responses conditioned on teacher critiques. CGD treats critiques as a $\textit{training-time-only}$ supervision signal, encouraging internalization of error-aware reasoning: critiques guide learning but are absent at inference. Across five model families, CGD consistently outperforms CFT and standard distillation on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, yielding 7% average improvements and gains of up to +15.0% on AMC23 and +12.2% on MATH-500. On challenging competition problems such as AIME24 and AIME25, CGD achieves substantially higher Pass@1 and stronger performance at low Pass@k, indicating improved reasoning quality per sample. Importantly, CGD preserves general instruction-following capabilities where CFT degrades significantly ($-$21.3% on IFEval). These results position CGD as a practical and compute-efficient intermediate training paradigm for reasoning-centric tasks without introducing architectural inference-time overhead.

Critique-Guided Distillation instead teaches a student to use feedback while refining flawed responses.

During fine-tuning, a teacher supplies critiques and the student learns to revise the associated responses. The critique is a training signal only; inference does not require it. This separates consuming useful feedback from generating that feedback and aims to internalize error-aware reasoning without adding architectural overhead when the trained model answers questions.

Across five model families, the method outperforms critique fine-tuning and standard distillation on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with a reported average improvement of 7%. Competition-problem evaluations also show higher first-attempt success and stronger performance with few samples. The method preserves general instruction-following capabilities in settings where critique fine-tuning degrades them. The results support refinement under teacher feedback as a practical way to improve reasoning quality per generated answer.
summary.tldr: Training students to repair answers using teacher critiques improves evaluated mathematical reasoning without requiring critiques at inference.

title: Critique-Guided Distillation for Robust Reasoning via Refinement

abstract: Unlearning in diffusion models aims to remove undesirable data or concepts while preserving the utility of pretrained models—two fundamentally conflicting objectives. We propose a principled constrained optimization framework that formulates unlearning as minimizing the deviation from a pretrained model, subject to explicit separation constraints from the unlearning distributions. Specifically, we formulate three constrained optimization problems based on reverse and forward KL divergences, and likelihood constraints. The first two generalize existing approaches for concept and data unlearning, while the third offers a novel and natural formulation for unlearning. Despite the nonconvexity of the KL constraints, we establish strong duality for all three problems, enabling us to explicitly characterize their optimal solutions as unlearning targets and develop primal–dual algorithms for each formulation. Experimental results demonstrate that our KL-constrained approach achieves superior retention-unlearning tradeoffs compared to weight-based baselines for concept and data unlearning, and that our likelihood-based approach matches unlearning effectiveness while better preserving retained concepts compared to baselines.

paragraphs: Removing unwanted concepts or data from a diffusion model can also damage capabilities that should remain. This paper formulates that tension as constrained optimization: keep the updated model close to the pretrained model while explicitly requiring separation from the distributions targeted for unlearning. Preservation becomes the objective, and removal is expressed through constraints.

The authors develop three formulations based on reverse KL divergence, forward KL divergence, and likelihood constraints. The first two generalize existing concept- and data-unlearning approaches, while the likelihood formulation offers a new alternative. Despite the nonconvex KL constraints, they establish strong duality for all three problems, characterize optimal target distributions, and derive primal–dual algorithms.

Experiments show that the KL-constrained method achieves better retention–unlearning trade-offs than weight-based baselines for both concepts and data. The likelihood-based method matches baseline unlearning effectiveness while better preserving retained concepts. These findings connect the mathematical formulation to the practical goal of removing targeted content while limiting disruption to the rest of the model’s behavior.
summary.tldr: Constrained optimization gives diffusion-model unlearning explicit removal targets and improves the trade-off between forgetting and retention.

title: Unlearning in Diffusion Models: A Unified Framework with KL Divergence and Likelihood Constraints

abstract: Empirically, option-based hierarchical reinforcement (HRL) learning often produces longer and more diverse options when a deliberation cost is charged at option boundaries. However, when options are executed for many steps under an approximate dynamics model, small model errors compound along the option, degrading the quality of the resulting plan. In this work, we introduce the commitment loss to formalize the tradeoff between deliberation cost and model error as a function of option duration. We characterize how optimal termination probabilities vary with this tradeoff under two model-error mechanisms. First, the model is learned from finite data via maximum-likelihood estimation, producing statistical error that interacts with option duration. Second, we consider an input-driven setting where an exogenous input is only observed at option boundaries and evolves unobserved between them, creating a drift-induced mismatch between planned and realized dynamics. In both cases, we solve for the optimal termination behavior as a function of deliberation cost and the error scale, clarifying the behavior of some popular HRL algorithms that approach the deliberation cost as a heuristic.

paragraphs: In hierarchical reinforcement learning, options let an agent commit to a behavior for multiple steps. Charging a deliberation cost at option boundaries can encourage longer options, but planning with an approximate dynamics model introduces a competing cost: small prediction errors accumulate during execution. This paper formalizes that tension through a quantity called commitment loss.

The analysis considers two sources of mismatch. In the first, a dynamics model estimated from finite data has statistical error that interacts with option duration. In the second, an external input is visible only at option boundaries and continues changing while the option runs. The plan can therefore become misaligned with actual dynamics as the unobserved input drifts.

For both mechanisms, the authors solve for optimal termination behavior as a function of the deliberation cost and the scale of model error. This makes the decision to continue or end an option an explicit tradeoff between costs. The results clarify the behavior of hierarchical learning algorithms that otherwise use deliberation penalties heuristically, connecting option duration to the reliability of the model supporting the plan.
summary.tldr: Commitment loss formalizes how option termination should balance deliberation costs against model errors that accumulate during execution.

title: The Cost of Commitment in Option-Based Hierarchical RL

abstract: Designing dense rewards is crucial for reinforcement learning (RL), yet in robotics it often demands extensive manual effort and lacks scalability. One promising solution is to view task progress as a dense reward signal, as it quantifies the degree to which actions advance the system toward task completion over time. We present TimeRewarder, a simple yet effective reward learning method that derives progress estimation signals from passive videos, including robot demonstrations and human videos, by modeling temporal distances between frame pairs. We then demonstrate how TimeRewarder can supply step-wise proxy rewards to guide reinforcement learning. In our comprehensive experiments on ten challenging Meta-World tasks, we show that TimeRewarder dramatically improves RL for sparse-reward tasks, achieving nearly perfect success in 9/10 tasks with only 200,000 interactions per task with the environment. This approach outperforms previous methods and even the manually designed environment dense reward on both the final success rate and sample efficiency. Moreover, we show that TimeRewarder pretraining can exploit real-world human videos, highlighting its potential as a scalable approach to rich reward signals from diverse video sources.

paragraphs: TimeRewarder learns signals of task progress from passive videos so that reinforcement learning can receive feedback at individual steps. Such dense rewards are useful in robotics but often require substantial manual design. The paper uses the progression visible in robot demonstrations and human videos as a source of supervision for estimating progress.

The method models temporal distances between pairs of frames and converts progress estimates into step-wise proxy rewards. These rewards guide learning on tasks whose original rewards are sparse. Their role is to supply more frequent information about advancement toward completion, using a learned visual measure rather than requiring a manually specified dense reward for each task.

On ten Meta-World tasks, TimeRewarder achieves nearly perfect success on nine with 200,000 environment interactions per task. It outperforms previous methods and the manually designed environment dense reward in final success and sample efficiency. The paper also demonstrates pretraining with real-world human videos. Together, these findings support passive video as a potentially scalable source of reward information, with the strongest quantitative evidence coming from the reported Meta-World experiments.
summary.tldr: TimeRewarder turns temporal relationships in passive videos into dense proxy rewards that improve robotic reinforcement learning.

title: TimeRewarder: Learning Dense Reward from Passive Videos via Frame-wise Temporal Distance

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have recently made strong progress in vision-language reasoning, yet their performance often degrades as generations grow longer. A key factor is that they frequently lose track of earlier visual evidence and intermediate constraints under a monolithic growing context. Inspired by how humans separately recall what they see and what they infer when solving complex tasks, we propose DLMR, a parameter-efficient mechanism that equips MLLMs with Dual Latent Memories: a visual memory that compresses image evidence and a reasoning memory that tracks intermediate conclusions and constraints. A Router then dynamically decides which memory and how much to reuse during inference, preserving visual grounding while maintaining coherent long-horizon reasoning. DLMR is trained in three stages, from latent memory construction to selective router learning, while keeping the base MLLM frozen, yielding substantial gains on both general and reasoning benchmarks with only a small number of additional trainable parameters. Analyses further show interpretable, state-dependent routing with specialized memory roles and reduced decoding tokens over long generations. Code is available at https://github.com/Hunter-Wrynn/DLMR.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can lose track of earlier image evidence and intermediate constraints as their responses grow longer. The paper attributes part of this degradation to keeping everything in one expanding context. DLMR addresses the problem by giving visual evidence and reasoning progress separate latent memories.

The visual memory compresses information from the image, while the reasoning memory records intermediate conclusions and constraints. A router dynamically selects which memory to reuse and how much information to draw from it during inference. This division is intended to preserve grounding in the image while maintaining coherence across a long reasoning process.

Training proceeds in three stages, spanning memory construction and selective router learning, while the base multimodal model remains frozen. The authors report substantial gains on general and reasoning benchmarks using only a small number of additional trainable parameters. Their analyses find state-dependent routing, distinct roles for the two memories, and fewer decoding tokens over long generations. These observations support selective memory reuse as a parameter-efficient way to sustain reasoning across extended outputs.
summary.tldr: DLMR routes between separate visual and reasoning memories to improve extended vision-language reasoning with few additional trainable parameters.

title: Dual-Latent Memory Routing for Vision-Language Reasoning

abstract: Pretraining transformers on long sequences, such as entire code repositories or collections of related documents, is bottlenecked by quadratic attention costs. We present Multipole Semantic Attention (MuSe), which accelerates 64k-context pretraining by 36% while matching baseline loss, requiring no architectural changes. MuSe is a training-time approximation that clusters queries and keys separately in representation space. This yields query-specific summaries that substantially outperform spatial blocking at matched sparsity, while also enabling drop-in compatibility with existing pretrained models—we validate on Llama 3.1-8B and 3.2-1B without retraining. We pretrain language models up to 1B parameters at 64k context on code and scientific documents, confirming that MuSe preserves quality and long-context utilization during training.

We present Multipole Semantic Attention (MuSe), which accelerates 64k-context pretraining by 36% while matching baseline loss, requiring no architectural changes. MuSe is a training-time approximation that clusters queries and keys separately in representation space. This yields query-specific summaries that substantially outperform spatial blocking at matched sparsity, while also enabling drop-in compatibility with existing pretrained models—we validate on Llama 3.1-8B and 3.2-1B without retraining. We pretrain language models up to 1B parameters at 64k context on code and scientific documents, confirming that MuSe preserves quality and long-context utilization during training.

paragraphs: Long-context pretraining is expensive because standard attention costs grow quadratically with sequence length. This becomes a bottleneck when training on material such as entire code repositories or collections of related documents. Multipole Semantic Attention, or MuSe, approximates attention during training to reduce that cost while retaining useful access to long contexts.

MuSe groups queries and keys separately in representation space and constructs summaries tailored to the queries. The grouping is therefore based on learned representations rather than only where tokens sit in the sequence. At matched sparsity, the authors report that these summaries substantially outperform spatial blocking. The method requires no architectural changes.

Pretraining experiments on code and scientific documents use models up to 1B parameters with 64k contexts. MuSe accelerates this training by 36% while matching baseline loss and preserving reported quality and long-context utilization. The authors also validate compatibility with existing Llama 3.1-8B and 3.2-1B models without retraining, supporting its use as a drop-in attention approximation.
summary.tldr: MuSe uses semantic query and key clustering to accelerate reported 64k-context pretraining by 36% while matching baseline loss.

title: Multipole Semantic Attention: A Fast Approximation of Softmax Attention for Pretraining

abstract: In AI for Science, physics-informed losses are increasingly used to train learned compressors for scientific data, but their rate–distortion implications remain poorly understood. At fixed bitrate, these objectives often improve preservation of a target physical observable while degrading standard reconstruction fidelity. We develop a local geometric theory showing that this tradeoff is governed by the interaction of latent-space sensitivities induced by the entropy model, the physical observable, and the distortion metric. At each operating point, these induce preferred directions along which compression noise should be suppressed, yielding an anisotropic error-allocation mechanism. When these directions are misaligned, improving the observable at fixed rate necessarily worsens standard distortion, establishing a fundamental limit on simultaneous preservation. We formalise this through a local tangent-space rate–distortion law and introduce a practical alignment diagnostic based on dominant eigenspace overlap. Experiments across scientific domains test the theory and validate that the alignment diagnostic correlates with observed data- and physics-space trade-offs.
