paragraphs: Compressing scientific data involves deciding which information can tolerate error. A compressor trained to preserve a physical quantity may protect that quantity while making the reconstructed data less accurate by conventional measures. This paper develops a local geometric explanation of why these objectives can conflict even when the storage budget stays fixed.

The analysis examines how the entropy model, physical observable, and reconstruction metric respond to changes in the compressor’s latent representation. Each favors particular directions in which compression noise should be reduced. Their interaction determines how error is distributed across directions. Within this local theory, when the preferred directions are misaligned, improving preservation of the physical observable at a fixed bitrate necessarily worsens standard reconstruction distortion.

The authors formalize this relationship as a local rate–distortion law and propose a practical diagnostic based on overlap between dominant eigenspaces. Experiments across scientific domains show that this alignment measure correlates with observed tradeoffs. The contribution connects competing compression objectives to measurable representation geometry, helping explain when preserving physics and preserving conventional fidelity pull in different directions.
summary.tldr: A local geometric theory explains when preserving physical quantities during compression necessarily trades off against reconstruction fidelity.

title: A Geometric Lens on Physics-Aligned Data Compression

abstract: Emerging Omni-modal Large Language Models (OmniLLMs) enable real-time interaction across video, audio, and text but suffer from prohibitive computational costs due to the quadratic complexity of processing continuous streaming inputs. Existing token compression strategies remain suboptimal as they typically rely on biased modality-centric priors or enforce uniform retention policies, neglecting the heterogeneity across layers and the critical role of cross-modality alignment. To address these challenges, we propose OmniFit, a training-free framework that decouples interaction profiling from inference execution. OmniFit incorporates Layer-Adaptive Heterogeneity Profiling (LAHP) to dynamically allocate computational budgets based on layer-wise redundancy and modality preferences, preserving tokens according to the characteristics of each layer. Furthermore, we introduce Alignment-Rectified Token Selection (ARTS), a lightweight mechanism that efficiently identifies tokens semantically aligned with cross-modal cues. Extensive experiments on 3 model series across 10 benchmarks demonstrate that OmniFit establishes a new Pareto frontier, retaining 98% of model performance with only 20% token usage and achieves up to 2.31$\times$ end-to-end inference speedup and 2.5$\times$ VRAM saving, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Models that handle streaming video, audio, and text can face high computational costs as input grows. Token compression reduces the amount of information processed, but uniform retention rules overlook differences between layers. The paper also argues that compression driven by a single modality can miss the importance of alignment across modalities.

OmniFit is a training-free framework that separates profiling of these interactions from inference execution. They also report up to 2.31× end-to-end inference speedup and 2.5× VRAM savings. These results support the value of allocating compression unevenly and preserving cross-modal connections, producing a stronger measured trade-off between performance and computational resources than the compared methods.
summary.tldr: OmniFit compresses tokens according to layer needs and cross-modal alignment, retaining 98% of reported performance with 20% token usage.

title: OmniFit: Bridging Modalities via Layer-Adaptive Token Compression for Omnimodal Large Language Models

abstract: Text-to-Music diffusion models are increasingly used in real-world applications, yet deployment remains challenging: generations can collapse to limited patterns even with diverse initial noise and prompts, and inference-time diversity control often harms text alignment and fidelity by distorting key prompt cues established in early denoising. To address this, we propose Padding-Annealed Diffusion Sampling, which perturbs only a padding-indexed subspace while keeping non-padding conditioning fixed, enabling controlled exploration with reduced semantic drift. However, in a text-unaware VAE latent space, such exploration is less likely to stay within genre-faithful neighborhoods, limiting genre-consistent diversity. We therefore introduce Text-Aware Latent space that aligns local neighborhoods with text-implied genre structure, promoting genre-consistent diversity. Together, the two techniques form a unified pipeline that, compared to prior methods that perturb the full conditioning, achieves a better text alignment–diversity trade-off: at comparable text alignment, it delivers 15.4% higher diversity with a relatively small fidelity drop, and further improves within-genre diversity by 71.6%. Generated samples are available at https://pads-tal.github.io/PADS-TAL.io

PADS-TAL addresses this trade-off by controlling both where sampling perturbations occur and how the latent space organizes musical variation.

summary.tldr: PADS-TAL increases text-to-music diversity through selective perturbations and genre-aware latent neighborhoods while better preserving text alignment.

title: PADS-TAL: Padding-Annealed Diffusion Sampling in Text-Aware Latent Space for Robust and Diverse Text-to-Music Generation

abstract: Flow matching models have recently emerged as an efficient alternative to diffusion, especially for text-guided image generation and editing, offering faster inference through continuous-time dynamics. However, existing flow-based editors predominantly support global or single-instruction edits and struggle with multi-instance scenarios, where multiple parts of a reference input must be edited independently without semantic interference. We identify this limitation as a consequence of globally conditioned velocity fields and joint attention mechanisms, which entangle concurrent edits. To address this issue, we introduce Instance-Disentangled Attention, a mechanism that partitions joint attention operations, enforcing binding between instance-specific textual instructions and spatial regions during velocity field estimation. We evaluate our approach on both natural image editing and a newly introduced benchmark of text-dense infographics with region-level editing instructions. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach promotes edit disentanglement and locality while preserving global output coherence, enabling single-pass, instance-level editing.

paragraphs: Editing several separate parts of an image at once requires each instruction to affect its intended region without interfering with the others. Existing flow-based editors struggle with this setting. The paper attributes the problem to globally conditioned velocity fields and joint attention, which mix information from concurrent edits during image transformation.

Instance-Disentangled Attention addresses that mixing by partitioning joint attention operations. It binds each instance-specific text instruction to its corresponding spatial region while the model estimates the velocity field that drives editing. The design targets the internal interaction between instructions and image regions, supporting independent local edits within a single editing pass.

The authors evaluate the method on natural images and introduce a benchmark of text-heavy infographics with region-level instructions. Results show improved separation and locality of edits while preserving coherence across the full output. These findings suggest that controlling attention at the instance level can help flow-based editors handle multiple simultaneous requests without losing the overall consistency of the generated image.
summary.tldr: Instance-Disentangled Attention links separate editing instructions to their image regions, improving simultaneous local edits in flow-matching models.

title: Shifting the Breaking Point of Flow Matching for Multi-Instance Editing

abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) have demonstrated strong performance on established benchmarks such as GIFT-Eval, Monash, and TSFM-Bench. However, these benchmarks pool datasets from many domains with uneven representation, which can obscure performance within specific application areas such as healthcare, finance, nature, retail, and transport. The necessity for domain-specific evaluation arises from the inherent structural diversity of time series data: clinical records often feature irregular sampling and informative missingness; financial sequences are characterized by high noise and stochastic trajectories; and environmental data, such as energy and weather, are governed by deterministic physical laws and strong seasonal hierarchies. Motivated by this heterogeneity, we argue that TSFMs require explicit domain-specific benchmarks so practitioners can reliably assess a model’s utility within their own application area. This is because cross-domain differences in data generation, sampling irregularity, and nonstationarity under concept drift fundamentally shape forecasting difficulty and failure modes. As a result, strong performance on aggregated leaderboards may not translate to reliable deployment within a specific domain. To test this, we evaluated seven TSFMs across 72 datasets from six domains (healthcare, finance, energy, nature, transport, and retail) and found substantial cross-domain variability. These findings confirm that global benchmark scores can be misleading and that domain-aware evaluations are essential for trustworthy TSFM selection.

paragraphs: The paper argues that a strong overall time-series benchmark score can hide weaknesses in a particular application area. Existing benchmarks combine datasets from unevenly represented domains, although the structures underlying those datasets differ substantially. Clinical records can have irregular sampling and meaningful missingness, financial sequences can be noisy and stochastic, and environmental signals can reflect physical laws and seasonal hierarchies.

To investigate the consequences, the authors evaluate seven time-series foundation models on 72 datasets across healthcare, finance, energy, nature, transport, and retail. They find substantial performance variation across domains. This supports their concern that aggregate rankings can conceal differences relevant to choosing a model for a specific use.

The authors call for explicit domain-specific benchmarks that reflect differences in data generation, sampling, and changing distributions. Their findings mean that success on a pooled leaderboard may not translate into reliable performance in a practitioner’s domain. Domain-aware evaluation would make the evidence behind model selection more directly relevant to the forecasting difficulties and failure modes of the intended application.
summary.tldr: Evaluating seven models across 72 datasets reveals domain variability that motivates explicit domain-level time-series benchmarks.

abstract: In many application domains there is a large amount of unlabeled data but onlya very limited amount of labeled training data. One general approach that hasbeen explored for utilizing this unlabeled data is to construct a graph on allthe data points based on distance relationships among examples, and then touse the known labels to perform some type of graph partitioning. One naturalpartitioning to use is the minimum cut that agrees with the labeled data (Blumand Chawla, 2001), which can be thought of as giving the most probable labelassignment if one views labels as generated according to a Markov Random Fieldon the graph. Zhu et al. (2003) propose a cut based on a relaxation of thisfield, and Joachims (2003) gives an algorithm based on finding an approximatemin-ratio cut. In this paper, we extend the mincut approach by adding randomness to the graphstructure. The resulting algorithm addresses several shortcomings of thebasic mincut approach, and can be given theoretical justification from both aMarkov random field perspective and from sample complexity considerations. Incases where the graph does not have small cuts for a given classificationproblem, randomization may not help. However, our experiments on severaldatasets show that when the structure of the graph supports small cuts, thiscan result in highly accurate classifiers with good accuracy/coveragetradeoffs. In addition, we are able to achieve good performance with a verysimple graph-construction procedure.

A minimum-cut method assigns labels by partitioning that graph while respecting the known labels. This paper extends that approach by introducing randomness into the graph structure to address shortcomings of the basic minimum-cut method.

The authors provide theoretical justification from two perspectives: a Markov random field interpretation and sample-complexity considerations. The first connects graph partitions with probabilistic label assignments. The second examines learning in relation to the amount of data. These perspectives support the randomized method alongside its empirical evaluation.

The benefit depends on the graph’s structure. The authors explicitly note that randomization may not help when the classification problem lacks small cuts. When suitable small cuts exist, experiments show highly accurate classifiers and favorable tradeoffs between accuracy and coverage. The method also achieves good performance with a simple graph-construction procedure, making the structural condition more central than an elaborate graph-building process.
summary.tldr: Randomizing graph structure improves minimum-cut semi-supervised learning in tested settings where the graph supports suitable small cuts.

title: Semi-supervised learning using randomized mincuts

abstract: Reminder systems support people with impaired prospective memory and/or executive function, by providing them with reminders of their functional daily activities. We integrate temporal constraint reasoning withreinforcement learning (RL) to build an adaptive reminder system and in asimulated environment demonstrate that it can personalize to a user and adaptto both short- and long-term changes. In addition to advancing the applicationdomain, our integrated algorithm contributes to research on temporal constraint reasoning by showing how RL can select an optimal policy from amongst a set of temporally consistent ones, and it contributes to the work on RL by showing how temporal constraint reasoning can be used to dramatically reduce the space of actions from which an RL agent needs to learn.

We integrate temporal constraint reasoning withreinforcement learning (RL) to build an adaptive reminder system and in asimulated environment demonstrate that it can personalize to a user and adaptto both short- and long-term changes. In addition to advancing the applicationdomain, our integrated algorithm contributes to research on temporal constraint reasoning by showing how RL can select an optimal policy from amongst a set of temporally consistent ones, and it contributes to the work on RL by showing how temporal constraint reasoning can be used to dramatically reduce the space of actions from which an RL agent needs to learn.

paragraphs: The paper develops an adaptive reminder system for people who have difficulty remembering intended activities or managing their execution. Its central problem is how to personalize reminders while respecting the timing relationships among daily activities. The proposed system combines temporal constraint reasoning, which handles those timing requirements, with reinforcement learning, which learns a policy for providing assistance.

The two components support each other. Temporal reasoning restricts the available choices to ones that are consistent with the timing constraints. Reinforcement learning can then select an optimal policy from that feasible set. This division substantially reduces the action space that the learning component must explore, while giving the constraint system a way to choose among multiple consistent policies.

In a simulated environment, the integrated system demonstrates personalization and adaptation to both short-term and long-term changes. These findings support the combination as a mechanism for adaptive reminders within the studied setting. The contribution also extends beyond the application: it shows how explicit temporal knowledge and learned decision making can each resolve a difficulty faced by the other.
summary.tldr: A simulated reminder system combines temporal constraints with reinforcement learning to personalize assistance and adapt to changing user needs.

title: Adaptive cognitive orthotics: combining reinforcement learning and constraint-based temporal reasoning

abstract: First-order probabilistic models allow us to model situations in which a random variable in the first-order model may have a large and varying numbers of parent variables in the ground (“unrolled”) model. One approach to compactly describing such models is to independently specify the probability of a random variable conditioned on each individual parent (or small sets of parents) and then combine these conditional distributions via a combining rule (e.g., NoisyOR). This paper presents algorithms for learning with combining rules. Specifically, algorithms based on gradient descent and expectation maximization are derived, implemented, and evaluated on synthetic data and on a real-world task. The results demonstrate that the algorithms are able to learn the parameters of both the individual parent-target distributions and the combining rules.

One approach to compactly describing such models is to independently specify the probability of a random variable conditioned on each individual parent (or small sets of parents) and then combine these conditional distributions via a combining rule (e.g., NoisyOR). This paper presents algorithms for learning with combining rules. Specifically, algorithms based on gradient descent and expectation maximization are derived, implemented, and evaluated on synthetic data and on a real-world task. The results demonstrate that the algorithms are able to learn the parameters of both the individual parent-target distributions and the combining rules.

paragraphs: In a first-order probabilistic model, a variable can have many parent variables once the model is expanded into a concrete network. The number of parents can also vary. This makes it useful to describe influences compactly, without specifying a separate full conditional distribution for every possible collection of parents.

One approach describes the target’s probability conditioned on each individual parent, or on small parent groups, and then combines those distributions using a rule such as NoisyOR. This separates the description of individual influences from the mechanism that combines them. The paper develops algorithms for learning within this representation.

The authors derive and implement learning methods based on gradient descent and expectation maximization. They evaluate the methods using synthetic data and a real-world task. The reported results show that the algorithms can learn parameters for both the parent-to-target distributions and the combining rules. This matters because the overall model depends on both pieces: how each parent influences the target and how those influences are brought together.
summary.tldr: Gradient-based and expectation-maximization algorithms learn both individual influences and the rules that combine them in first-order probabilistic models.

title: Learning first-order probabilistic models with combining rules

abstract: Modeling long-term dependencies in time series has proved very difficult to achieve with traditional machine learning methods. This problem occurs when considering music data. In this paper, we introduce a model for rhythms based on the distributions of distances between subsequences. A specific implementation of the model when considering Hamming distances over a simple rhythm representation is described. The proposed model consistently outperforms a standard Hidden Markov Model in terms of conditional prediction accuracy on two different music databases.
originalAbstract: Modeling long-term dependencies in time series has proved very difficult to achieve with traditional machine learning methods. This problem occurs when considering music data. In this paper, we introduce a model for rhythms based on the distributions of distances between subsequences. A specific implementation of the model when considering Hamming distances over a simple rhythm representation is described. The proposed model consistently outperforms a standard Hidden Markov Model in terms of conditional prediction accuracy on two different music databases.

paragraphs: Rhythm modeling raises a difficult time-series problem: useful relationships can extend across long stretches of a sequence. The paper introduces a model motivated by the difficulty traditional machine learning methods have in representing such long-term dependencies. Its focus is on relationships between subsequences within musical rhythm data.

The model uses distributions of distances between subsequences. This makes the resemblance between stretches of a sequence a central part of the representation. The authors describe a concrete implementation using Hamming distances and a simple representation of rhythms. That implementation turns the general proposal into a specific way to model rhythmic sequences through their patterns of differences.

On two music databases, the proposed model consistently achieves better conditional prediction accuracy than a standard Hidden Markov Model. This supports the usefulness of the distance-based representation for the prediction tasks tested. The result concerns conditional prediction on those databases; its significance is that comparing subsequences provides an effective alternative for rhythm modeling in a setting motivated by long-range dependencies.
summary.tldr: A rhythm model based on distances between subsequences improves conditional prediction over a standard Hidden Markov Model on two music databases.

title: A distance model for rhythms

abstract: The exploration-exploitation dilemma has been an intriguing and unsolved problem within the framework of reinforcement learning. Optimism in the face of uncertainty and model building play central roles in advanced exploration methods. Here, we integrate several concepts and obtain a fast and simple algorithm. We show that the proposed algorithm finds a near-optimal policy in polynomial time, and give experimental evidence that it is robust and efficient compared to its ascendants.
originalAbstract: The exploration-exploitation dilemma has been an intriguing and unsolved problem within the framework of reinforcement learning. Optimism in the face of uncertainty and model building play central roles in advanced exploration methods. Here, we integrate several concepts and obtain a fast and simple algorithm. We show that the proposed algorithm finds a near-optimal policy in polynomial time, and give experimental evidence that it is robust and efficient compared to its ascendants.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning must balance exploring uncertain possibilities with exploiting behavior that already appears useful. The paper focuses on two ideas used in advanced exploration methods: optimism under uncertainty and building a model. Its aim is to integrate several concepts into an algorithm that is both fast and simple.

The theoretical result states that the proposed algorithm finds a near-optimal policy in polynomial time. This connects the exploration strategy to a formal claim about both policy quality and computational growth. Near-optimality allows some gap from the best policy, while polynomial time characterizes the guarantee's computational scale rather than specifying a fixed running time.

The authors also provide experimental evidence that the algorithm is robust and efficient compared with its predecessors. These experiments complement the theory by examining practical behavior relative to the methods from which the approach develops. The contribution is a unified exploration algorithm with a polynomial-time near-optimality result and supporting empirical evidence, rather than a claim to resolve every exploration problem.
summary.tldr: A unified optimism-based exploration algorithm finds a near-optimal policy in polynomial time and shows empirical robustness and efficiency.

title: The many faces of optimism: a unifying approach

abstract: We analyze computational aspects of variational approximate inference techniques for sparse linear models, which have to be understood to allow for large scale applications. Gaussian covariances play a key role,whose approximation is computationally hard. While most previous methods gain scalability by not even representing most posterior dependencies, harmful factorization assumptions can be avoided by employing data-dependent low-rank approximations instead. We provide theoretical and empirical insights into algorithmic and statistical consequences of low-rank covariance approximation errors on decision outcomes in nonlinear sequential Bayesian experimental design.
originalAbstract: We analyze computational aspects of variational approximate inference techniques for sparse linear models, which have to be understood to allow for large scale applications. Gaussian covariances play a key role,whose approximation is computationally hard. While most previous methods gain scalability by not even representing most posterior dependencies, harmful factorization assumptions can be avoided by employing data-dependent low-rank approximations instead. We provide theoretical and empirical insights into algorithmic and statistical consequences of low-rank covariance approximation errors on decision outcomes in nonlinear sequential Bayesian experimental design.

paragraphs: This paper examines the computational work needed to scale variational approximate inference for sparse linear models. Gaussian covariance calculations are central to that work because they represent posterior dependencies, yet approximating them is computationally difficult. The authors focus on how choices made to simplify these calculations affect the usefulness of the resulting inference.

Many earlier approaches obtain scalability by leaving most posterior dependencies unrepresented. The paper considers data-dependent low-rank covariance approximations as a way to avoid harmful factorization assumptions. This changes the approximation strategy: dependencies can remain represented through a more compact covariance description, although that description still introduces approximation error.

The authors study the algorithmic and statistical consequences of those errors using both theory and empirical analysis. Their setting is nonlinear sequential Bayesian experimental design, where inferred uncertainty influences decisions about experiments. This makes the consequences concrete: covariance approximations matter through the decisions they produce. The contribution explains the connection between computational shortcuts, uncertainty representation, and downstream decision outcomes.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes how data-dependent low-rank covariance approximations enable scalable inference and affect decisions in sequential Bayesian experimental design.

title: Gaussian Covariance and Scalable Variational Inference

abstract: Many applications require optimizing an unknown, noisy function that is expensive to evaluate. We formalize this task as a multi-armed bandit problem, where the payoff function is either sampled from a Gaussian process (GP) or has low RKHS norm. We resolve the important open problem of deriving regret bounds for this setting, which imply novel convergence rates for GP optimization. We analyze GP-UCB, an intuitive upper-confidence based algorithm, and bound its cumulative regret in terms of maximal information gain, establishing a novel connection between GP optimization and experimental design. Moreover, by bounding the latter in terms of operator spectra, we obtain explicit sublinear regret bounds for many commonly used covariance functions. In some important cases, our bounds have surprisingly weak dependence on the dimensionality. In our experiments on real sensor data, GP-UCB compares favorably with other heuristical GP optimization approaches.
originalAbstract: Many applications require optimizing an unknown, noisy function that is expensive to evaluate. We formalize this task as a multi-armed bandit problem, where the payoff function is either sampled from a Gaussian process (GP) or has low RKHS norm. We resolve the important open problem of deriving regret bounds for this setting, which imply novel convergence rates for GP optimization. We analyze GP-UCB, an intuitive upper-confidence based algorithm, and bound its cumulative regret in terms of maximal information gain, establishing a novel connection between GP optimization and experimental design. Moreover, by bounding the latter in terms of operator spectra, we obtain explicit sublinear regret bounds for many commonly used covariance functions. In some important cases, our bounds have surprisingly weak dependence on the dimensionality. In our experiments on real sensor data, GP-UCB compares favorably with other heuristical GP optimization approaches.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization of an unknown function whose evaluations are noisy and expensive. It models this as a bandit problem under two alternative descriptions of the payoff function: a sample from a Gaussian process, or a function with low reproducing-kernel Hilbert-space norm. These assumptions provide the structure needed for the analysis.

The authors analyze GP-UCB, which uses upper confidence estimates to guide evaluation choices. They bound cumulative regret, the accumulated cost of choosing points below the optimum, through maximal information gain. This establishes a connection to experimental design: the information obtainable from evaluations helps characterize the difficulty of optimization.

Bounds on information gain through operator spectra yield explicit sublinear regret bounds for many commonly used covariance functions. These results imply convergence rates, and some important cases have only weak dependence on dimension. Experiments using real sensor data also show favorable comparisons with heuristic GP optimization methods. The theoretical guarantees and empirical findings provide distinct support for the algorithm under the settings studied.
summary.tldr: GP-UCB receives regret and convergence guarantees by linking Gaussian process optimization to information gain and experimental design.

title: Gaussian Process Optimization in the Bandit Setting: No Regret and Experimental Design

abstract: We analyze variations of multiplicative updates for learning linear functions online. These can be described as substituting exponentiation in the Exponentiated Gradient (EG) algorithm with quadratic and linear functions. Both kinds of updates substitute exponentiation with simpler operations and reduce dependence on the parameter that specifies the sum of the weights during learning. In particular, the linear multiplicative update places no restrictions on the sum of the weights, and, under a wide range of conditions, achieves worst-case behavior close to the EG algorithm. We perform our analysis for square loss and absolute loss, and for regression and classification. We also describe some experiments showing that the performance of our algorithms are comparable to EG and the $p$-norm algorithm.

Both kinds of updates substitute exponentiation with simpler operations and reduce dependence on the parameter that specifies the sum of the weights during learning. In particular, the linear multiplicative update places no restrictions on the sum of the weights, and, under a wide range of conditions, achieves worst-case behavior close to the EG algorithm. paragraphs: The paper investigates simpler multiplicative updates for learning linear functions online. Starting from the Exponentiated Gradient algorithm, it replaces exponentiation with quadratic or linear functions. The aim is to simplify the operations used in learning while reducing dependence on the parameter that specifies the total sum of the model’s weights.

Both proposed update families reduce that dependence. The linear multiplicative update goes further by placing no restriction on the sum of the weights. Under a wide range of conditions, it achieves worst-case behavior close to Exponentiated Gradient. This is a qualified theoretical comparison: the closeness is established under the conditions considered in the analysis.

The authors analyze square and absolute losses across regression and classification. They also describe experiments in which their algorithms perform comparably to Exponentiated Gradient and the p-norm algorithm. The contribution shows that simpler update operations can retain competitive behavior in the studied settings, combining theoretical analysis with empirical comparisons across alternative online learning rules.
summary.tldr: Quadratic and linear multiplicative updates simplify online linear learning while retaining performance comparable to established methods in the studied settings.

title: Learning Linear Functions with Quadratic and Linear Multiplicative Updates

abstract: We present SampleRank, an alternative to contrastive divergence (CD) for estimating parameters in complex graphical models. SampleRank harnesses a user-provided loss function to distribute stochastic gradients across an MCMC chain. As a result, parameter updates can be computed between arbitrary MCMC states. SampleRank is not only faster than CD, but also achieves better accuracy in practice (up to 23\% error reduction on noun-phrase coreference).
originalAbstract: We present SampleRank, an alternative to contrastive divergence (CD) for estimating parameters in complex graphical models. SampleRank harnesses a user-provided loss function to distribute stochastic gradients across an MCMC chain. As a result, parameter updates can be computed between arbitrary MCMC states. SampleRank is not only faster than CD, but also achieves better accuracy in practice (up to 23\% error reduction on noun-phrase coreference).

paragraphs: SampleRank addresses parameter estimation in complex graphical models. The paper presents it as an alternative to contrastive divergence, with learning organized around states visited by a Markov chain Monte Carlo procedure. The central question is how to obtain useful parameter updates from that sequence of states while fitting the model.

The method uses a loss function supplied by the user to distribute stochastic gradients along the chain. As a result, updates can be computed between arbitrary MCMC states. This gives the loss function a direct role in shaping learning and makes intermediate states useful locations for parameter estimation, rather than treating the chain only as a way to obtain a final sample.

The authors report that SampleRank is faster than contrastive divergence and achieves better accuracy in practice. On noun-phrase coreference, the reported error reduction reaches up to 23%. That figure is a task-specific empirical result. The broader contribution is a way to use loss-guided, local updates throughout sampling when training complex factor-graph models.
summary.tldr: SampleRank uses a user-provided loss to update graphical-model parameters between MCMC states, improving speed and accuracy over contrastive divergence in practice.

title: SampleRank: Training Factor Graphs with Atomic Gradients

abstract: We describe novel subgradient methods for a broad class of matrix optimization problems involving nuclear norm regularization. Unlike existing approaches, our method executes very cheap iterations by combining low-rank stochastic subgradients with efficient incremental SVD updates, made possible by highly optimized and parallelizable dense linear algebra operations on small matrices. Our practical algorithms always maintain a low-rank factorization of iterates that can be conveniently held in memory and efficiently multiplied to generate predictions in matrix completion settings. Empirical comparisons confirm that our approach is highly competitive with several recently proposed state-of-the-art solvers for such problems.
originalAbstract: We describe novel subgradient methods for a broad class of matrix optimization problems involving nuclear norm regularization. Unlike existing approaches, our method executes very cheap iterations by combining low-rank stochastic subgradients with efficient incremental SVD updates, made possible by highly optimized and parallelizable dense linear algebra operations on small matrices. Our practical algorithms always maintain a low-rank factorization of iterates that can be conveniently held in memory and efficiently multiplied to generate predictions in matrix completion settings. Empirical comparisons confirm that our approach is highly competitive with several recently proposed state-of-the-art solvers for such problems.

paragraphs: The paper develops optimization methods for a broad class of matrix problems using nuclear norm regularization. Its focus is making individual optimization steps inexpensive while keeping the evolving matrix representation compact. This is especially relevant to matrix completion, where the learned matrix must also support efficient predictions for entries that have not been observed.

The approach combines low-rank stochastic subgradients with incremental updates to a singular value decomposition. These operations are implemented through optimized dense linear algebra on small matrices and can be parallelized. The combination connects the structure of each update with the structure of the stored solution, allowing the algorithm to maintain a low-rank factorization throughout optimization.

That factorization serves two practical purposes: it can be held conveniently in memory, and its factors can be multiplied efficiently to produce matrix-completion predictions. Empirical comparisons show that the resulting algorithms are highly competitive with several contemporary solvers. The contribution therefore concerns the cost of optimization, storage, and prediction together, rather than treating computational efficiency as only the number of iterations.
summary.tldr: Low-rank stochastic updates and incremental SVD make nuclear-norm matrix optimization inexpensive per iteration and compact in memory.

title: Efficient and Practical Stochastic Subgradient Descent for Nuclear Norm Regularization

abstract: In many multilingual text classification problems, the documents in different languages often share the same set of categories. To reduce the labeling cost of training a classification model for each individual language, it is important to transfer knowledge gained from the labeled data in one language to another language by conducting cross language classification. In this paper we develop a novel subspace co-regularized multi-view learning method for cross language text classification. This method is built on parallel corpora produced by machine translation. It jointly minimizes the training error of each classifier in each language while penalizing the distance between the subspace representations of parallel documents. Our empirical study on a large set of cross language text classification tasks shows the proposed method consistently outperforms the alternative inductive methods, domain adaptation methods, and multi-view learning methods.
originalAbstract: In many multilingual text classification problems, the documents in different languages often share the same set of categories. To reduce the labeling cost of training a classification model for each individual language, it is important to transfer knowledge gained from the labeled data in one language to another language by conducting cross language classification. In this paper we develop a novel subspace co-regularized multi-view learning method for cross language text classification. This method is built on parallel corpora produced by machine translation. It jointly minimizes the training error of each classifier in each language while penalizing the distance between the subspace representations of parallel documents. Our empirical study on a large set of cross language text classification tasks shows the proposed method consistently outperforms the alternative inductive methods, domain adaptation methods, and multi-view learning methods.

paragraphs: Documents in different languages often need to be assigned to the same categories. Training a separate classifier for each language can require substantial labeling effort. This paper aims to transfer information from labeled documents in one language to classification in another, using the relationship between translated versions of documents.

The method builds parallel corpora through machine translation and treats the languages as different views of the classification problem. It jointly minimizes the training errors of the language-specific classifiers. At the same time, it penalizes differences between the subspace representations of corresponding documents. This encourages translated documents to have similar learned representations while retaining a classification objective for each language.

The joint objective connects cross-language agreement with predictive learning, giving the transferred information an explicit role in training. Across a large collection of cross-language classification tasks, the authors report consistent improvements over the inductive, domain adaptation, and multi-view methods they compare against. These findings support the proposed representation-sharing mechanism in the evaluated multilingual setting.
summary.tldr: The method transfers text-classification knowledge across languages by jointly training classifiers and aligning representations of machine-translated document pairs.

title: Cross Language Text Classification via Subspace Co-regularized Multi-view Learning

abstract: In this paper, we formulate the Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) problem on matrix manifolds. This framework provides a natural way for dealing with matrix constraints and tools for building efficient algorithms even in an adaptive setting. Finally, an adaptive CCA algorithm is proposed and applied to a change detection problem in EEG signals.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we formulate the Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) problem on matrix manifolds. This framework provides a natural way for dealing with matrix constraints and tools for building efficient algorithms even in an adaptive setting. Finally, an adaptive CCA algorithm is proposed and applied to a change detection problem in EEG signals.

paragraphs: This paper develops an adaptive approach to canonical correlation analysis, or CCA, by expressing the problem on matrix manifolds. Its focus is the geometry of the matrices involved in the optimization. The matrix constraints are part of the mathematical setting in which the algorithm operates, making their treatment central to the proposed formulation.

A matrix manifold provides a structured space for matrices that satisfy the relevant constraints. The authors use this viewpoint because it offers a natural way to handle those constraints and tools for constructing efficient algorithms. The framework is intended to remain useful in an adaptive setting, so the contribution connects the constrained formulation directly to an updating procedure for CCA.

The paper proposes an adaptive CCA algorithm and applies it to detecting changes in EEG signals. This application gives the formulation a concrete signal-analysis use: CCA is incorporated into a change-detection problem. The stated contribution is the combination of a geometric formulation, an adaptive algorithm, and that application; the abstract does not make a comparative accuracy or speed claim.
summary.tldr: The paper formulates CCA on matrix manifolds and develops an adaptive algorithm applied to change detection in EEG signals.

title: Adaptive Canonical Correlation Analysis Based On Matrix Manifolds
